en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Nidāna Vagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
1. Nidāna Saṃyutta 1.
Buddha Vagga 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda Sutta)
1. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ* (Thus have I heard): This is the first discourse on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) in the Nidāna Vagga. Herein, this is the word-by-word commentary:
"There, at that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus. In this context, "there" (*tatra*) indicates the place and time;
for it refers to "at whatever time he was dwelling, at that time," and "in whatever Jeta’s Grove he was dwelling, in that Jeta’s Grove."
He illuminates. Or rather, he illuminates [the Dhamma] at a place and time appropriate for speaking. For the Blessed One does not speak the Dhamma at an inappropriate place or time;

the passage beginning, "It is not the right time, Bāhiya," is the proof for this. The particle *kho* is a mere filler (*padapūraṇamatta*), a particle used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), or to indicate the beginning of a period of time (*ādikālattha*).
The term *Bhagavā* is an illumination of the World-Honored One (*lokagaru*). The term *bhikkhū* is a word for a person suitable for listening to the discourse.
Furthermore, here the meaning of the word should be understood according to such methods as: "A mendicant is a bhikkhu" and "One who has entered upon the practice of begging is a bhikkhu.
"Addressed" means he spoke to, he said to, he called out to; this is the meaning here.
Elsewhere, however, it also occurs in the sense of making known, as it is said: "I address you, O bhikkhus; I announce to you, O bhikkhus."
Also in the case of addressing. As it is said: "Come, bhikkhu, address Sāriputta in my name.

The term *bhikkhave* is an illustration of the manner of addressing. And that is stated because [the title] is established through the possession of qualities such as the habit of begging (*bhikkhana-sīlatā*).

For one is called a *bhikkhu* not only by virtue of possessing the quality of the habit of begging, but also by virtue of possessing the quality of the nature of begging (*bhikkhana-dhammatā*), and by virtue of possessing the quality of being skillful in begging (*bhikkhane sādhukāritā*).

Those skilled in grammar consider this [the correct form]. And by that speech, established through his possession of qualities such as the habit of begging for alms (*bhikkhana-sīlatā*), he reveals the mode of livelihood practiced by those who are inferior or superior, thereby effecting a restraint against the states of arrogance and dejection.

Furthermore, by the word "O monks" (*bhikkhave*), preceded by a gaze from eyes gentle with the expansion of compassion, he brings them before him; and by that very speech, which indicates his desire to speak, [he addresses them].
It generates a desire to hear, and by that very act of addressing them, it enjoins them to pay careful attention; for the success of the Dispensation depends upon careful attention.
If one asks: "Since other gods and humans were also present, why did he address only the bhikkhus?"—it is because they were the eldest, the most excellent, and because of their constant proximity.
For the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is common to all assemblies; yet among these assemblies, the monks are the eldest because they were the first to arise [in the dispensation];
they are the best because, beginning from the state of homelessness, they follow the Teacher’s conduct and receive the entire Dispensation;
they are proximate because they sit near the Teacher among those present there; and they are always in close attendance because they dwell in the Teacher’s presence.
Furthermore, they were vessels for his teaching of the Dhamma because of their presence in practice according to what was instructed.
Moreover, he addressed them in this way, thinking, "This teaching is intended specifically for certain bhikkhus.
But for what purpose did the Blessed One address the bhikkhus first when teaching the Dhamma, rather than teaching the Dhamma alone?

For the purpose of creating mindfulness: monks may be sitting there thinking of other things, with distracted minds, reflecting on the Dhamma, or attending to their meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). If the Dhamma is taught without addressing them, they are unable to discern:
"What is the source of this teaching? What is its condition? For what specific occasion (aṭṭhuppatti) was it taught?"
Whether they might grasp it wrongly or not grasp it at all—for the sake of arousing mindfulness in them, the Blessed One first addresses them and afterwards teaches the Dhamma.
"Bhadante" is a term of respect, or a response to the Teacher. Furthermore, in this context, "bhikkhave" [is used].
The Blessed One, speaking, addressed the bhikkhus. Addressing him as "Venerable Sir," they replied to the Blessed One.
For thus the Blessed One calls out, "Bhikkhus," and they respond, "Venerable Sir.
He causes them to give the response, "Bhikkhus," and they give the response, "Venerable Sir. "Those bhikkhus" refers to those whom the Blessed One addressed.
*Te bhagavato paccassosuṃ*: they replied to the Blessed One; that is to say, facing him, they listened, accepted, and received the Blessed One’s address.
*Bhagavā etadavoca*: the Blessed One spoke this entire discourse which was now to be spoken.
At this point, that which had been [requested] by the Venerable Ānanda regarding the Buddhas’ [teachings] endowed with both meaning and phrasing...

In order that this sutta—which indicates the profound nature of the knowledge of the teaching—may be easily penetrated, the introduction (nidāna), adorned by the time, place, teacher, and assembly, has been spoken;
the commentary on its meaning is now complete.
Now follows the exegesis of the sutta set forth by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with "dependent origination" (paṭiccasamuppāda).

The opportunity has arrived. Now, since this commentary on the sutta becomes clear when spoken after investigating the occasion for its delivery (*suttanikkhepa*), we shall first investigate that occasion for the delivery. For there are four occasions for the delivery of a sutta:

those arising from one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*), those arising from the inclination of others (*parajjhāsaya*), those prompted by a question (*pucchāvasika*), and those arising from a specific circumstance (*aṭṭhuppattika*). Among these, those suttas which the Blessed One spoke without being requested by others...

He speaks solely according to his own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*), such as: "The bearer of the *Dasabala-sutta*, the bearer of the *Candopama*, *Vīṇopama*, *Sammappadhāna*, *Iddhipāda*, *Indriya*, *Bala*, *Bojjhaṅga*, and *Maggaṅga* suttas"—in these cases, it is their own inclination that constitutes the depositing.
However, those [passages] such as: "Rāhula’s qualities conducive to the ripening of liberation are indeed matured. What if I were to [teach] Rāhula..."
"Having further conquered the taints through destruction"— thus these were spoken according to the inclinations of others,
having regard for their disposition, patience, reflective acceptance, mental resolve, and capacity for awakening; namely, the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta,
the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, the Dhammacakkappavattana, and the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta.
The *Āsīvisopama-sutta*, the *Dhātuvibhaṅga-sutta*, and others like them— these are instances where the motivation is the inclination of others.
However, when the four assemblies, the four castes, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas,

asuras, yakkhas, the Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa and other devas, and Mahābrahmā and others approach the Blessed One [and say], "The factors of enlightenment, the factors of enlightenment!"— [this is another case].
"Venerable sir, they say 'hindrances, hindrances. Venerable sir, regarding these five aggregates of clinging, what indeed is the supreme wealth for a person?"—in such a manner they pose questions.
To those thus questioned, the Blessed One spoke the *Bojjhaṅga-saṃyutta* and others, as well as other *Devatā-saṃyutta* discourses.
The *Mārasaṃyutta*, *Brahmasaṃyutta*, *Sakkapañha*, *Cūḷavedalla*, *Mahāvedalla*, *Sāmaññaphala*, *Āḷavaka*, *Sūciloma*, *Kharaloma* Suttas, and so forth—
these are delivered on account of a specific inquiry. However,
those which were spoken in dependence upon a particular occasion that had arisen, such as the *Dhammadāyāda* and the *Cūḷasīhanāda* Suttas— [these are delivered on account of a specific cause].

[The similes] such as "like the flesh of one's own son," "like a block of wood," "like a mass of fire," "like a lump of foam," and "like the Pāricchattaka tree" are presented according to their specific origin (*aṭṭhuppattika*).
Thus, among these four modes of presentation (*nikkhepa*),
this Discourse on Dependent Origination (*Paṭiccasamuppāda-sutta*) is presented according to the inclination of others (*parajjhāsayo*).

This was set forth by the Blessed One according to the inclinations of various individuals. According to the inclinations of which individuals? Of those who understand through a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*).

For there are four types of individuals: those who understand through a brief indication, those who understand through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*), those who must be led (*neyyo*), and those for whom the words are the limit (*padaparamo*).
Among these, the individual for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs at the very moment it is uttered is called an individual who understands through a brief indication.

One who gains knowledge through condensed instruction (*ugghaṭitaññū*). That person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs when the meaning of what was spoken in brief is analyzed in detail—this person is called one who gains knowledge through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*).
That person for whom [realization occurs] by way of recitation, by inquiry, by attending wisely, by serving, associating with, and honoring spiritual friends, gradually...
There is the realization of the Dhamma; this person is called one who is to be guided (*neyya*).

That person who, even though hearing much, retaining much, and reciting much, does not achieve the realization of the Dhamma in that very lifetime—this person is called one for whom the words are the limit (*padaparama*).
Thus, among these four types of persons, by way of the inclinations of those persons who understand through a condensed statement...
This sutta has been set forth.
At that time, it is said, there were five hundred monks from the countryside, all of whom lived alone, in pairs, in threes, in fours, or in fives;
they were companions in conduct, bearers of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), energetic, devoted to yoga, practitioners of insight, subtle and refined.
Desiring an exposition on emptiness (*suññatā*) and the method of conditions (*paccayākāra*), they approached the Blessed One in the evening;
having paid homage, they sat surrounding him, hoping for a teaching as if encircling him with a red woolen blanket.
It was in accordance with their inclinations that the Blessed One began this discourse. For just as a skilled painter...
Having obtained an unplastered wall, he did not produce the form from the very beginning;
rather, having first performed the preparatory work on the wall by applying a thick coating of clay and so forth, he produced the form on the wall that had been thus prepared.
But having obtained a wall already prepared, without performing the labor of further wall-preparation, he mixed various pigments and [applied] the brush-stroke.
Or just as one, having taken a brush or a cloth, produces a form;

even so, when the Blessed One finds a clansman who is a beginner and has no preconceived bias, he does not at the very outset explain to him the subtle, delicate, and empty characteristic of insight—the station of Arahatship.
Rather, joining him to the accomplishment of virtue, concentration, the doctrine of self-action, and right view, he leads him through the preliminary practice.
He explains it thus. With reference to this, it was said:
"Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first purify yourself in wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states?
It is virtue that is well-purified and view that is straight. For when, bhikkhu, your virtue is well-purified..."
And your view will become straight. Then, bhikkhu, relying on virtue and established in virtue, you should develop the four foundations of mindfulness in three ways. What are the four?
Here, bhikkhu, dwell contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“Dwell contemplating the body in the body externally… or internally and externally in the body… or dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena,
ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
When, monk, relying on virtue and established in virtue, you develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this threefold way, then…”
“Bhikkhu, whether night or day comes for you, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.

Having thus spoken the preliminary discourse on virtue for the clansman who is a beginner, he explains the subtle, delicate, and empty characteristic of insight, which has the state of arahantship as its proximate cause.
But having obtained one who possesses pure virtue, has initiated energy, is devoted to yoga, and is a practitioner of insight, he does not explain the preliminary practice to him;
rather, he explains directly the state of Arahatship—the subtle, delicate, empty characteristic of insight which is its foundation.
These five hundred bhikkhus, having purified the preliminary practice and remaining like well-polished gold, [approached].
They resemble a mass of well-polished jewels; for them, only the supramundane path remains yet to come.
Thus, with the aim of its arrival, the Teacher, considering their underlying aspiration, began this discourse.
In that context, "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) refers to the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). For the mode of conditions consists of things existing together in mutual dependence.
It produces phenomena; therefore it is called "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*.

As for the word *vo*: this particle *vo* is seen in the functions of the direct object (*paccatta*), the instrumental (*upayoga*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the dative (*sampadāna*), the genitive (*sāmivacana*), and as a mere filler (*padapūraṇa*).
In such passages as, “But are you, Anuruddhas, living in concord, in mutual harmony? and so forth, it is seen in the sense of the subject (*paccatte*).

In such passages as, “Go, monks, I dismiss you,” it is in the sense of the object (*upayoge*). In such passages as, “You must not live in my presence,” it is in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
In such passages as, “Monks, I shall teach you the discourse on forest retreats,” it is in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāne*). [And] in such passages as, “Of all of you, Sāriputta...”
In such passages as “subhāsitaṃ,” it is used in the sense of the genitive case. In such passages as “ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhakāyakammantā,” it serves merely to complete the meter.
Here, however, it should be understood as the dative case. “Bhikkhave” is a further address to those who have been brought face-to-face by the response [of assent].
“Desessāmi” (I shall teach) is the formal undertaking of the teaching. “Taṃ suṇātha” (Listen to that) refers to that dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
"Listen to the teaching being spoken by me;
attend to it well. Herein, "sādhukaṃ" and "sādhu" have the same meaning.
Furthermore, this word *sādhu* is seen used in the senses of requesting, accepting, encouraging, excellence, and strengthening. "It would be good for me, venerable sir... [and so forth].
In such passages as "May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma in brief," it is seen in the sense of a request.
In such passages as "‘Very well, venerable sir,’ that bhikkhu, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words," it is seen in the sense of acceptance.
In such passages as "‘Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta! it is seen in the sense of encouragement.
In such passages as, “Excellent is the king who delights in the Dhamma; excellent is the man possessed of wisdom;
excellent is one who does not deceive friends; the non-doing of evil is happiness,” the word *sādhu* means “beautiful.
In such passages as, “Therefore, brahmin, listen well (*sādhukaṃ suṇāhi*),” the word *sādhukaṃ* itself [means] “in a firm manner.”
It is also called *āṇatti*. Here, however, its meaning should be understood as both strengthening (*daḷhīkamme*) and instruction (*āṇatti*);
it is also appropriate in the sense of "excellent" (*sundara*). For, in the sense of strengthening: "Listen to this firm Dhamma, grasping it well";
in the sense of instruction: "Listen according to my command"; and in the sense of excellence: "This is excellent, this is auspicious."
"Listen to the Dhamma"—this is what is being illustrated. "Pay attention" means:
apply your minds; this is the meaning. "Be intent" means: having become undistracted in mind, observe; the intention is that you should fix it in your minds.
Here, "listen now to this" is for the purpose of preventing distraction of the sense-faculty of hearing. "Pay close attention" means: pay heed thoroughly.

By means of applying oneself to firm attention, there is the warding off of distraction of the mind-faculty. Herein, the former [exhortation] is for the purpose of warding off the grasping of a distortion of the phrasing, while the latter is for warding off the grasping of a distortion of the meaning.
By the former, one is enjoined to listen to the Dhamma; by the latter, to the retention and investigation of the teachings already heard.
And by the former, [one is led to think]: "This Dhamma possesses beautiful phrasing; therefore..."
The former [phrase] indicates that "it is to be heard," while the latter indicates that "it is meaningful; therefore, it should be attended to.
Alternatively, by joining the word *sādhukaṃ* with both phrases: "Since this Dhamma is profound in its nature and profound in its teaching, therefore listen well (*sādhukaṃ*).
Since it is profound in its meaning and profound in its penetration, therefore attend to it well (*sādhukaṃ*)."
The construction should be understood as: "Listen to that; I shall speak. Regarding "I shall speak," it means "I shall teach. As for "Listen to that," it is said:
"I will not teach the promised teaching merely in brief, but rather I shall speak of it in detail as well.
For these words express both brevity and detail. As the Elder Vaṅgīsa said:
“He teaches in brief as well, and he speaks in detail;
like the song of the maina bird, he utters inspired eloquence.

When this was said, having become filled with enthusiasm, those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One, “So be it, venerable sir,” and they accepted the Teacher’s words—this is what is meant by “they received them.”

Then the Blessed One said this to them: he spoke the entire sutta beginning with, "And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? Therein, "And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? is a question asked out of a desire to explain. For there are five kinds of questions:

the question for the illumination of what has not been seen, the question for the confirmation of what has been seen, the question for the cutting off of doubt, [the question for clarification, and the question for inquiry.]
There is the inquiry for consent and the inquiry out of a desire to speak; this is their distinction.
What is the inquiry for the illumination of the unseen? It is when a characteristic is by nature unknown—unseen, unweighed, unexamined, uncognized, and unmanifested.
For the sake of knowing it, for seeing it, for weighing it, for examining it, and for the purpose of making it cognized and manifested.
He asks a question. This is a question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen.
What is a question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen? One has naturally known, seen, weighed, judged, clarified, and fully understood a characteristic.
He asks a question in order to correlate it with other wise people.
This is the inquiry for the purpose of correlating what has been seen.
What is the inquiry for the purpose of cutting through doubt? One who by nature is prone to uncertainty, prone to perplexity, and full of hesitation—thinking, "Is it thus?
Is it not thus? How indeed is it?"—asks a question for the purpose of cutting through that doubt.
This is the inquiry for cutting through doubt.
What is the inquiry for seeking consent? The Blessed One asks a question with the consent of the bhikkhus:
“What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?”—“Impermanent, venerable sir.”—“And that which is impermanent, is it suffering?”
“Whether it be pleasure, venerable sir, or pain—whatever is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard that as:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “Certainly not, venerable sir. This is a question for assent.

What is a question out of a desire to speak? The Blessed One asks a question because he desires the monks to speak: “Monks, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four? This is a question out of a desire to speak.

In that regard, Buddhas have no first three kinds of questions. Why? Because for Buddhas, among the three periods of time, there is nothing conditioned or unconditioned that is unseen, unknown, unmeasured, uninvestigated, unclarified, or unmanifested.
Therefore, they have no question of "making known what was not seen. As for that which was [not previously known] by the Blessed One—
That which has been penetrated by his own knowledge requires no verification with another—whether a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā.
Therefore, he has no need for a question regarding the verification of what has been seen.

Furthermore, because he is free from doubt, has crossed over uncertainty, and has destroyed all hesitation regarding all phenomena, he has no need for a question regarding the cutting off of perplexity.
[The first] does not exist; however, the other two questions do exist for the Blessed One. Among those, this should be understood as a question asked out of a desire to explain.
Now, analyzing the mode of conditions (paṭiccasamuppāda) as it was asked in that question, he said: "With ignorance as condition, monks, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth.
And here, just as one who has begun with the thought, "I shall speak of the father," might say, "Tissa’s father, Soṇa’s father,"...

Just as he speaks of even the son first, in the same way the Blessed One began to speak of the conditions by the method beginning with, “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,” and while speaking of the phenomena such as ignorance that serve as the conditions for volitional formations and so forth, he also spoke of those things arisen through conditions.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the *Āhāravagga*, [he said]: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)...”
Having begun with both "dependently arisen phenomena," he explained both.
Now, regarding such passages as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," "ignorance" and "condition" together constitute "ignorance-condition.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood in this manner: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be. This is the summary here; for the detailed explanation:
However, the exposition of dependent origination in its forward order, complete in all its aspects, has been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*;
therefore, it should be understood exactly as it was explained there.

In this exposition of the reverse order, however, "of ignorance indeed" (*avijjāya tveva*) means "of ignorance, precisely. "Through its fading away and cessation" (*asesavirāganirodhā*) means through that which is termed fading away...
Through the path, there is the complete cessation [of suffering]. "The cessation of formations" means the cessation of formations as their non-arising.
Furthermore, to show that when formations have ceased in this way, consciousness and the rest also cease, and thus name-and-form and the other factors are indeed ceased, it says:
"With the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness," and so forth; and thus, of this entire mass of suffering...
"It ceases," he said. Therein, "of the whole" means of the entire [mass], or of the pure, that is, devoid of a being;
"of the mass of suffering" means of the heap of suffering. "It ceases" means there is no further arising.

Thus the Blessed One, having explained the discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*) in direct order by means of twelve terms, and having reversed that very cycle, [proceeded] in reverse order.
By explaining the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*) through twelve terms, he reached the climax of his teaching with the attainment of *arahantship*. At the conclusion of the discourse,
those five hundred individuals who were practitioners of insight (*āraddhavipassaka*) and of the "those who understand through a condensed statement" (*ugghaṭitaññū*) awakened to the Truths—
like lotuses that have reached full maturity upon being touched by the rays of the sun— and became established in the fruit of *arahantship*.
"Thus spoke the Blessed One": the Blessed One spoke this entire sutta by way of both the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*).
"Those bhikkhus were uplifted": those five hundred bhikkhus whose taints were exhausted were joyful in heart. "They rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words":
with a Brahma-voice that was as sweet as the song of the *karavīka* bird, pleasing to the ear, and like a consecration of the Deathless for the hearts of wise men.
The meaning is that they rejoiced in the word of the Blessed One as he spoke it, and they both expressed their appreciation and accepted it. Therefore, this is said:
“The monks, rejoicing with their heads bowed, accepted with the words ‘Excellent! Excellent! the well-spoken and well-uttered speech of the Tathāgata.”
The commentary on the First Discourse on Dependent Origination is finished.
2. Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Discourse:

In the second [discourse] as well, the setting forth of the sutta should be understood according to the same method already stated. However, this is the distinction: the first was for persons who understand through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
This has been shown in brief by way of those who understand through what is condensed; this [present explanation] is by way of detail for those who understand through expansion.
Furthermore, in this sutta, four similes of men gathering creepers should be mentioned, which have already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
For just as a man gathering creepers, having seen the tip of a creeper, seeks its root by following it along, and having seen that, [severs] the creeper—
Having cut it at the root, taken it, and brought it to the work, so the Blessed One, while giving a detailed exposition,
brought forth the teaching starting from old age and death— the summit of dependent origination— down to the section on ignorance which constitutes its root;
then, teaching the cycle of existence and its cessation, he brought it to a conclusion.
In this regard, the determination of the meaning for the detailed teaching on aging, death, and so forth is as follows:
First, in the description of aging and death, the phrase "of those various [beings]" should be understood as a concise collective description of many beings.
For even if one were to speak for an entire day, saying, "the aging of Devadatta, the aging of Somadatta," there would still be no end to the enumeration of beings.
They go. By these two phrases, however, no sentient being remains uncomprised. Therefore it was said:
"This is, in brief, a common designation for many kinds of beings. In the phrase "in this or that," this is a common designation for many classes of beings according to their destinies and births.
Regarding the term "class of beings" (*sattanikāya*), [the following applies] to that which has been designated by way of this common designation:

This is an illustration by way of synonyms. In such passages as "aging is the state of decaying," however, "aging" (*jarā*) is a description by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "The state of decaying" (*jīraṇatā*) is a description by way of mode (*ākāra*).
The three terms beginning with "brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*) are descriptions by way of function (*kicca*) occurring after the lapse of time;

the latter two are descriptions by way of natural state (*pakati*). For, by this term "aging," it is illuminated by way of its intrinsic nature; therefore, this is its description by way of intrinsic nature. By the term "the state of decaying,"...
By way of its mode, this is its description of mode. "Brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*) is stated by virtue of its function of causing the teeth and nails to become broken when time has passed.
"Grayness" (*pālicca*) is stated by virtue of its function of causing the hair of the head and body to turn gray.

"Wrinkled skin" (*valittacatā*) is illustrated by virtue of its function of causing the flesh to wither and the skin to form wrinkles. Therefore, these three—brokenness and so forth—are [the modes] of that [aging] when time has passed.
These are descriptions of functions. By means of these, the aging that has become manifest through the observation of these various changes is demonstrated.

For just as the path traversed by water, wind, or fire is made evident by the breaking, the crushing, or the burning of grass, trees, and so forth, yet that traversed path is not those very waters and so on themselves; even so, [aging is revealed by its effects].
The path traversed by aging—manifesting as the breaking off of teeth and so forth—is evident; it is perceived even with the eyes open.
Yet, aging is not merely the breaking off of teeth and such. For aging is not something cognizable by the eye-consciousness.
However, by these terms—"the dwindling of the life-span" and "the maturation of the faculties"—it becomes clearly manifest precisely upon the passing of time.

It is explained as the natural process known as the exhaustion of the life-span and the maturation of the faculties, such as the eye. Therefore, these latter two should be understood as descriptions of the nature [of phenomena].
In that regard, because the life-span diminishes for one who has reached old age, aging is described by way of a metaphorical designation of the result as "the destroyer of the life-span.
And because during childhood the faculties are very clear and perceive even subtle objects...
The faculties, such as the eye and so forth, which are capable of grasping their respective objects with ease, become ripened, agitated, and dull when one has reached old age;
they become incapable of grasping even a coarse object of their own. Therefore, "the ripening of the faculties" is spoken of by way of a metaphorical designation for the result itself.
Furthermore, all this aging thus described is twofold: manifest and concealed.
Therein, because the state of being broken and so forth is seen in the teeth and other such things, aging among material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) is called "manifest aging.
However, because no such transformation is seen in non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*), aging among them is called "concealed aging. Now, as for this state of being broken and so forth...
That which is seen—because such things as teeth and so forth are easily discernible—is indeed their color;

having seen that with the eye and reflected upon it with the mind-door, one knows aging, thinking, "These teeth have been struck by old age," just as one knows the presence of water below by looking at the heads of oxen tied up in a watering place.
Furthermore, it is twofold: "without interval" (avīci) and "with interval" (savīci).
In that regard, because specific variations in color and so forth are difficult to discern—
just as with gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, the sun, and the like among living beings such as humans, or among non-living things such as flowers, fruits, and sprouts—
it is called "uninterrupted aging" (*avīcijara*), meaning continuous aging. However, in other cases among those previously mentioned, [such variations occur] from time to time.
Because the distinctions of complexion and so forth are easily discernible, aging should be understood as "aging with intervals" (*savīcijarā*).

From this point on, the phrases "of this or that" and so forth are to be understood according to the method already stated. Regarding the terms "falling away" (*cuti*) and "perishing" (*cavanatā*) and so on:

"falling away" is spoken of in the sense of the act of falling away; it is a general term for the aggregates (khandhas) taken as one, four, or five. "Perishing" (*cavanatā*) is spoken of by way of an abstract noun (*bhāvavacana*).
The demonstration of characteristics (*lakkhaṇanidassana*). "Dissolution" (*bhedo*) is the indication of the arising of the breakup of the aggregates at death (*cutikkhandhānaṃ*).
"Disappearance" (*antaradhānaṃ*) is the indication of the absence of any state whatsoever for the dissolved aggregates at death, just as in the case of a broken jar.
"Death" (*maccu maraṇaṃ*) refers to death known as *maccu*; by this, he excludes other forms of death such as "annihilation-death" (*samucchedamaraṇa*). "Time" (*kālo*)...
“Antaka” is a name for death; its activity is “the act of passing away. Thus, by means of worldly convention (*lokasammuti*), he illustrates death.
Now, in order to illustrate it according to the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), he says: “The breaking up of the aggregates,” and so forth.
For in the ultimate sense, only the aggregates break up; no so-called “being” dies. However, while the aggregates are breaking up, the being dies; when they have broken up, [the being has died].

The conventional expression "he thinks" occurs here. Furthermore, it should be understood that the dissolution of the aggregates occurs by way of the four- or five-aggregate planes, while the laying down of the physical body occurs by way of the one-aggregate plane;
and the dissolution of the aggregates occurs by way of the four-aggregate plane, while the laying down of the physical body occurs by way of the remaining two.
Why? Because in both of those states of existence, there is the presence of the physical body, which is reckoned as the material aggregate.

Alternatively, because in the realms of the Four Great Kings and so forth the aggregates merely disintegrate and nothing is deposited, death is described as the "disintegration of the aggregates" with reference to those states;
whereas among humans and others, it is the "deposition of the carcass.
In this context, death should be understood as "the deposition of the carcass" in the sense that it is the cause for the deposition of the carcass. Thus.
"This aging and this death"—this is what is called "aging-and-death" (jarāmaraṇa), monks, when these two are taken together as one.

In the explanation of birth (*jāti*), among such terms as "birth" (*jāti*) and "arising" (*sañjāti*), it is "birth" in the sense of being born; that [term] is appropriate in terms of the incomplete sense bases (*aparipuṇṇāyatana*).

In the sense of being born (*sañjāyana*), it is "birth" (*sañjāti*); this is appropriate in the case of those with fully developed sense bases (*paripuṇṇāyatana*). In the sense of descending (*okkamana*), it is "descent" (*okkanti*); this is appropriate in the case of egg-born and womb-born beings (*aṇḍaja-jalābuja*).
For they take rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as if they were descending into or entering the shell of the egg and the membrane of the womb.
In the sense of being produced (*abhinibbattana*), it is "production" (*abhinibbatti*); this is appropriate in the case of moisture-born and spontaneously born beings (*saṃsedaja-opapātika*).
They arise having become manifest. This, first of all, is the teaching in terms of conventional usage (*vohāra*).
Now follows the teaching in terms of ultimate reality (*paramattha*). For it is only the aggregates (*khandha*) that appear in the ultimate sense, not a "being" (*satta*).

And therein, "of the aggregates": in a one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*), there is one; in a four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*), there are four; in a five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*)...

The inclusion of all five [aggregates] should be understood. "Manifestation" (*pātubhāvo*) means arising. Regarding "of the sense bases" (*āyatanānaṃ*), here the inclusion should be understood by way of the sense bases arising in their respective locations. "Acquisition" (*paṭilābho*) is simply manifestation within the continuity (*santati*).
For it is precisely when they are manifesting that they are said to be "acquired. This, monks, is called birth.
With this phrase, he provides a conclusion to birth as taught both in terms of conventional usage (*vohāra*) and in terms of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).

In the exposition of existence (*bhava*), "existence of sense-sphere" (*kāmabhava*) refers to both the existence of karma (*kammabhava*) and the existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*). Therein, what is called the existence of karma is precisely the karma that leads to the existence of sense-sphere rebirth;
for it is the cause of the existence of rebirth therein. Thus [it is said]: "The arising of Buddhas is blissful; the accumulation of evil is suffering," and so forth.

It is called "existence" (bhava) by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit. What is called "existence as rebirth" (upapattibhava) is the pentad of appropriated aggregates produced by that karma.
For it is called "existence" because it comes to be there; thus, in every respect, both this karma and the rebirth itself are here termed "sense-sphere existence" (kāmabhava).
This same method applies to the fine-material and immaterial existences.

In the exposition of clinging (*upādāna*), regarding the terms "clinging to sense-pleasures" (*kāmupādāna*) and so forth: it is called *kāmupādāna* because by means of this one clings to objective sense-pleasures (*vatthukāma*), or because it itself clings to them;
or, it is *kāmupādāna* because it is both sense-pleasure and clinging. "Clinging" (*upādāna*) is said to mean firm grasping.
For here the prefix *upa-* has the sense of "firmness," as in words such as *upāyāsa* (agitation) and *upakaṭṭha* (near). This [term] refers to lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure.

This is a synonym. This is the summary here. In detail, however, this should be understood according to the method stated thus: "In that regard, what is clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*)? It is the lustful desire for sensual pleasures.
Likewise, it is "clinging to views" (*diṭṭhupādāna*) because it is both a view and a clinging; or alternatively, it is so called because one clings to a view, or they cling to it.
Or, "view" here refers to the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*). For one clings to a prior view by means of a subsequent view, and they cling to that view as well.
As it is said: "The self and the world are eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false," and so forth.

This is a designation for all types of speculative views, with the exception of the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) and the clinging to the doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*). This is the meaning here.
This is in brief; however, in detail, this should be understood according to the method stated [in the Paṭisambhidāmagga]: "In that regard, what is clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*)?

'There is no giving'... and so forth. Likewise, it is called clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) because one clings by means of this, or because it itself clings, or because it is both the rules and observances and the clinging.
For practices such as the cow-vow (*gosīla*) and the ox-vow (*govata*) are themselves forms of clinging due to the dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*) that "purity comes through this."

This is the summary here; however, for the detailed explanation, this should be understood according to the method stated [in the Sutta]: "In that regard, what is clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*)? It is the view: 'Outside of this [teaching], purification comes through the moral conduct and observances of recluses and brahmins.
Now, they speak by means of it, thus it is "discourse" (*vāda*); they cling by means of it, thus it is "clinging" (*upādāna*). What do they speak of, or what do they cling to?
*Attavādupādānaṃ*: clinging to the doctrine of self (*attavāda*). Or, it is called clinging to the doctrine of self because by means of it they cling to the mere doctrine of self as "self.
This is a designation for the twenty-based view of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
This is the summary here; however, in detail, it is as follows: "In this regard, what is clinging to the doctrine of self? Here, an uninstructed worldling..."
This should be understood according to the method already stated: "one who does not see the Noble Ones.

In the description of craving (*taṇhā*), the passage from "craving for forms" (*rūpataṇhā*) up to "craving for mental phenomena" (*dhammataṇhā*) refers to the craving that occurs within the cognitive process (*javanavīthi*) of the eye-door and so forth;
it is named after its object—which resembles its parent—just as one might be called "the merchant’s son" or "the brahmin’s son" based on their father.
This is the name. And herein, craving that has visible form as its object is "craving for form" (*rūpataṇhā*).

When it occurs relishing form by way of sensual lust, it is "craving for sense-pleasures" (*kāmataṇhā*); when it occurs relishing form by way of lust accompanied by the eternalist view, thinking "form is permanent, stable, and eternal," it is "craving for existence" (*bhavataṇhā*); [and when it occurs] by way of lust accompanied by the annihilationist view...
“Form is cut off, destroyed, and does not exist after death”—craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*) proceeds by finding gratification in this way.
Thus craving for form (*rūpataṇhā*) is threefold. And just as with craving for form, so it is with craving for sound and the rest;
thus there are eighteen modes of craving’s movement (*taṇhāvicarita*). These eighteen occur with respect to internal form and so forth, and with respect to external form and so forth.
"Eighteen" means thirty-six. Thus, there are thirty-six past, thirty-six future, and thirty-six present;
in this way, there are one hundred and eight modes of craving-conduct (*taṇhāvicarita*).
Based on the internal [basis], there are eighteen such as "I am," "I am thus," and so forth, which depend on internal form and the rest; based on the external...
“Depending on this, ‘I am’ occurs; depending on this, ‘I am such’ occurs”—thus there are thirty-six [cravings] based on external forms and so forth, including these eighteen.
Thus, there are thirty-six past, thirty-six future, and thirty-six present;
in this way, there are one hundred and eight modes of craving. When further condensed, among forms and so forth...
Regarding objects, there are only six groups of craving, which are the three types beginning with sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*). Thus:
"By way of exposition, craving should be understood by the wise through its exposition; by way of detail, through its detail;
and again, through its synthesis."
In the Exposition of Feeling (*Vedanāniddesa*), "bodies of feeling" (*vedanākāyā*) means aggregates of feeling. Regarding "feeling born of eye-contact... pe...

feeling born of mind-contact," because this is presented in the *Vibhaṅga* as: "There is feeling born of eye-contact that is wholesome, there is unwholesome, and there is indeterminate," it refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate feelings occurring in the eye-door and so forth. [Thus] Sāriputta...

In such passages as “Mantāṇiputta,” there is a name based on the mother, just like a name derived from the mother; likewise, there is a name based on the object, which is similar to the mother. As for the meaning of the words here:
feeling born because of eye-contact is “feeling born of eye-contact. This same method applies everywhere. This, then, is the comprehensive explanation here.
However, by way of result (vipāka), there are two [types] at the eye-door.
Feeling should be understood by way of association with these: eye-consciousnesses, the two mind-elements, and the three mind-consciousness-elements.
This same method applies to the ear-door and the others. In the mind-door, it is associated only with the mind-consciousness-element.
In the description of contact (*phassa*), "eye-contact" means contact in the eye; this method applies everywhere. Eye-contact... [and so on].
"Body-contact": by this much, the ten contacts consisting of the fivefold resultant [consciousness]—both wholesome and unwholesome—are stated.
"Mind-contact": by this term, the remaining twenty-two types of worldly resultant contact associated with the mind are included.

Regarding what should be said concerning the "eye-base" and so forth in the *Saḷāyatana-niddesa*, that has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in both the "Aggregates" exposition and the "Bases" exposition.
In the exposition of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), "name" has the characteristic of bending toward an object; "form" has the characteristic of being affected.

In its analysis, however, it should be understood that "feeling" refers to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*); "perception" refers to the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*); and "volition," "contact," and "attention" refer to the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhāra-khandha*).
While it is true that there are other phenomena included within the aggregate of mental formations, these three [factors] are present even in those states that are most feeble.
They exist within states of consciousness; therefore, it is by way of these very [states] that the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is shown here.
Regarding the phrase "the four great elements" (cattāro mahābhūtā): here, "four" is a delimitation by number. "Great elements" is a designation for earth, water, fire, and air.
Now, as for the reason why they are called "great elements," and whatever other method of analysis there is in this regard:
All of this has been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha-niddesa*).

Regarding the phrase "derived from the four great elements" (*catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya*), here the genitive case for "of the four" (*catunnaṃ*) is used in the sense of the accusative; thus, it means "the four great elements.
"Derived from" (*upādāya*) means having taken up or having grasped; some also say it means "relying upon" (*nissāya*). And here, the word "present" (*vattamānaṃ*)...

This is the remainder of the recitation. Alternatively, this genitive case (*sāmivacana*) has the sense of a collection; the meaning here should be understood as "matter existing derived from the collection of the four great elements.
Thus, in every respect, those which are the four great elements beginning with earth, and that which exists derived from the four great elements, distinguished as the eye-base and so forth—
In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka itself, twenty-three kinds of material form are mentioned; all of that should be understood as "matter.
In the exposition of consciousness: "eye-consciousness" means consciousness in the eye, or consciousness born from the eye;
thus also for ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness. The other, however, is simply mind as consciousness.
"Mental consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*) is a designation for resultant consciousness belonging to the three planes, excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness.

In the exposition of formations (*saṅkhāra*), a formation is characterized by the act of forming. In its analysis, "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) refers to a formation that proceeds from the body;
specifically, it refers to the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness that proceed by way of impulsion through the door of the body.
"Twelve from the unwholesome" is a designation for twenty bodily volitions (*kāyasañcetanā*).

"Verbal formation" (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) means a formation that proceeds from speech; it is a designation for exactly twenty verbal volitions (*vacīsañcetanā*) that proceed by way of vocal differentiation at the door of speech.
"Mental formation" (*cittasaṅkhāra*) means a formation that proceeds from the mind; [it refers to those] without having produced any stirring at the doors of body or speech.
This is a designation for the twenty-nine mental volitions that arise when one sits in seclusion and reflects, according to the worldly wholesome and unwholesome states.
In the exposition of ignorance (*avijjā*), "ignorance regarding suffering" means ignorance regarding the truth of suffering; this is a designation for delusion (*moha*).

The same method applies to the phrases "ignorance regarding the origin of suffering," and so forth. Therein, ignorance regarding suffering should be understood by way of four reasons, beginning with its being included within [the aggregates].

By way of its basis (*vatthu*), its object (*ārammaṇa*), and its concealment (*paṭicchādana*). For it is included within the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) because it is comprised within suffering;
and the truth of suffering is its basis by way of being its support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), and its object by way of being its object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
It conceals this truth of suffering by preventing the penetration of its characteristic as it truly is.
And here, it is by way of the non-arising of knowledge.
Ignorance regarding the origin of suffering should be understood through three reasons: by way of its basis, by way of its object, and by way of concealment.
Ignorance regarding cessation and the path should be understood through only one reason: by way of concealment. For, regarding cessation and the path...
Ignorance is indeed a concealer, because it prevents the penetration of the characteristics of things as they truly are and because it does not allow for the arising of knowledge regarding them.
However, that [ignorance] is not included within those two truths, because it is not comprised within them;
nor are those two truths its basis, because they do not arise simultaneously with it; nor are they its object, because knowledge does not arise directed toward them. For the latter...
The two truths are difficult to see because of their profundity; in them, the ignorance that has become blind does not arise.
However, the former [truth] is profound because its specific characteristic, which is to be described, is difficult to see; therein, ignorance arises by way of grasping at distortions (*vipallāsa*).
Furthermore, by the mere term "in suffering," ignorance is illustrated through its inclusion, its basis, its object, and its function.

“Regarding ‘the origin of suffering’ (*dukkhasamudaye*): by this much, it is indicated by way of its basis (*vatthu*), its object (*ārammaṇa*), and its function (*kicca*). Regarding ‘the cessation of suffering and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’ (*dukkhanirodhe dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya*):

by this much, it is indicated by way of its function. However, it should be understood that by the term ‘ignorance’ (*aññāṇa*), it is indicated by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) without distinction.
‘Thus indeed, monks’ (*iti kho, bhikkhave*): thus indeed, monks. ‘Cessation occurs’ (*nirodho hoti*): non-arising occurs. Furthermore, in this context...”
Nibbāna is taught by all those terms for cessation. For it is by coming to Nibbāna that those various phenomena cease;

therefore, it is called their "cessation. Thus, in this sutta, while teaching the cycle of existence and its reversal through twelve terms, the Blessed One concluded the teaching precisely at the pinnacle of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, in the manner already described...
Five hundred bhikkhus were established in arahantship.
The second sutta, the Vibhaṅga Sutta, is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Paṭipadā Sutta.

3. Regarding "wrong practice" (*micchāpaṭipadā*) in the third [verse]: this, first of all, is a practice that does not lead to liberation (*aniyyānika*). But surely there are also meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and imperturbable formations (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) conditioned by ignorance (*avijjā*);
how then can these be wrong practice? Because they belong to the head of the round of existence (*vaṭṭasīsa*).

For whatever is set in motion having aspired toward the round of existence—comprised of the three realms of becoming—even down to the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhiññā*) or the eight [liberations], [is wrong practice].

All meditative attainments (samāpattiyo) belong to the side of the round of existence (vaṭṭapakkhiya); because they are the head of the round (vaṭṭasīsa), they are indeed wrong practice (micchāpaṭipadā).

However, whatever is undertaken with the turning away from the round (vivaṭṭa) and aiming for Nibbāna—even if it be as little as a gift of a spoonful of gruel or a handful of leaves—all that belongs to the side of the turning away (vivaṭṭapakkhiya) and is dependent on the turning away; because it is on the side of the turning away...

It is indeed the right practice (*sammāpaṭipadā*). For whether it be a small wholesome act such as giving a mere handful of leaves, or a great wholesome act such as giving a vast amount of food at the proper time—if it is established wrongly by being dependent on the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) through aspiring for the success of that round, it is able to bring about only the round, not the turning away from it (*vivaṭṭa*).
[One should instead think: "May this gift of mine lead to the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*)."

Furthermore, for one who aspires to the turning away (vivaṭṭa) in this way, even the right application directed toward turning away is capable of bestowing not only Arahantship, but also the knowledge of Pacceka-bodhi and omniscience;
it does not reach its conclusion without attaining Arahantship.
Thus, it should be understood that the wrong practice has been taught by way of the forward order (anuloma), and the right practice by way of the reverse order (paṭiloma).
But surely, here the way (*paṭipadā*) was asked about, Nibbāna was analyzed, and in the handing over as well, it was the way itself that was handed over.
And "the way" is not the name for Nibbāna; rather, this is the name for the four paths together with insight (*vipassanā*).
Therefore, the word-commentary does not coincide with the question and the handing over. [Reply: It is not the case that it does not coincide. Why? Because of the fruit and the way.

Because it has been shown. For here, the path is shown by means of its fruit. "With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations"—this is Nibbāna, known as cessation, which is the fruit of that path. "This, monks, is called the right path"—this is the meaning here.
And in this sense, regarding the phrase "remainderless fading away and cessation," *virāga*...
This is a synonym for cessation itself; "the remainderless fading away" and "the remainderless cessation"—this is the intended meaning here.
Or rather, this word-commentary is stated to show that path, designated as "fading away," by which there is remainderless cessation.
For it being thus, the practice together with its power is analyzed. Thus, even in this sutta, it is precisely the cycle of existence and its reversal [that is shown].
Thus it was said. The third [section].
4. Commentary on the Vipassī Sutta.
Regarding the fourth [sutta], "Vipassī": it is said that for that Bodhisatta, just as for ordinary worldly men, whatever...
Because the kamma-born clarity of the eye produced by limited kamma in those who pass through [the intermediate state] is weak, their eyes blink;

they did not blink in this way. However, because the kamma-born clarity of the eye produced by powerful kamma is strong, he saw with unblinking, non-blinking eyes, just like the gods of the Thirty-three. Therefore it was said: "Without blinking..."
“Monks, because the prince saw clearly (*pekkhati*), the designation ‘Vipassī, Vipassī’ arose for the prince Vipassī.
This is the intended meaning here: he sees with clarity, free from the darkness produced by blinking at intervals, or he sees with open eyes;
thus he is “Vipassī. And in this regard, although for those in their final existence...
Because the sensory clarity (*pasāda*) produced by the powerful karma of all Bodhisattvas is so strong, their eyes do not blink;
that Bodhisattva received his name for this very reason.
Furthermore, he is called *Vipassī* because he sees after having discerned (*viceyya viceyya*); the meaning is that he sees after having investigated (*vicinitvā vicinitvā*). One day...
It is said that while the king was seated in the hall of justice instructing on legal matters, they brought the Great Being, fully adorned and prepared, and placed him upon his lap.
Even as the king held him on his lap and fondled him, the ministers deprived him of his sovereignty.
The Bodhisatta let out a cry of distress. The king asked, "What is this? Investigate!"
Investigating further and seeing no other way, [the king thought], "This must have been done because the legal case was wrongly decided.

Thus, having restored the rightful owner to his rightful status, he wondered, "Does the prince act thus only after knowing [the facts]? Investigating further, they once again deprived the rightful owner of his rights.
Then the Bodhisatta uttered the same sound as before. Thereupon the king thought, "The Great Man knows!"
From that time forth, he became diligent. Therefore it was said:

"Because the prince, having repeatedly discerned, applied himself to the goal according to the method, monks, the designation ‘Vipassī, Vipassī’ arose for him all the more. "Bhagavā" means one endowed with good fortune (*bhāgya*).
"Arahant" means because the enemies such as passion (*rāga*) have been slain, or because the wheel of saṃsāra has been destroyed.

Because he has destroyed the *āravas* (enemies) or because he is worthy (*arahati*) of the requisites, he is called "Arahant"—thus [the word refers] to one who has acquired this name by virtue of his qualities.

"Of the Perfectly Enlightened One" (*sammāsambuddhassa*) means: having awakened (*buddha*) to the four truths by means of the right method (*sammā naya*), that is, by way of cause, through his own personal human effort.
"Even before the enlightenment" (*pubbeva sambodhā*): "enlightenment" (*sambodha*) is said to be the knowledge in the four paths; even prior to that.

Regarding the phrase "of the Bodhisatta himself": here, *bodhi* means knowledge (*ñāṇa*). A being who possesses *bodhi* is a *bodhisatta*; the meaning is that he is one who possesses knowledge, possesses wisdom, and is wise.
Indeed, from the moment he made his formal aspiration (*abhinīhāra*) at the feet of previous Buddhas, that being was already wise and not a blind fool;
thus he is called a *bodhisatta*. Or, just as a lotus that has emerged from the water and stands there, having reached full maturity—
Because he will certainly awaken through contact with the rays of the sun, he is called a "lotus that awakens" (*bujjhanaka-paduma*);

likewise, because he has received a prophecy in the presence of the Buddhas, he will certainly awaken after fulfilling the perfections (*pāramīs*) without obstacle, and thus he is a "being who awakens" (*bujjhanaka-satta*), namely, a Bodhisatta.
Furthermore, desiring that *bodhi*—which is defined as the knowledge of the four paths—[he sets out].

"One who moves about" (*pavattati*) and "one who is attached" (*āsatta*) to enlightenment (*bodhi*) is thus a "Bodhisatta. This refers specifically to one who is a Bodhisatta by virtue of a name derived from his qualities.
"Suffering" (*kiccha*) means pain (*dukkha*). "Has fallen into" (*āpanna*) means has reached it.
This is what is meant: "Alas! This world of beings has fallen into suffering. "Passes away and reappears" refers to the continuous process of death and rebirth.
It has been said. "Escape" (nissaraṇa) means Nibbāna; for because it has escaped from the suffering of aging and death, it is called its escape.
"When indeed? means at what time?
"Through wise attention" (yoniso manasikāra) means through skillful attention, through fundamental attention. "There was the realization through wisdom" (ahu paññāya abhisamayo).
Through wisdom, there was the realization, the convergence, the conjunction of the cause of aging and death;

the meaning is that he saw this: "With birth as condition, aging and death come to be. Alternatively, "through wise attention and wisdom" means that through both wise attention and wisdom, there was the realization: "When there is birth, there is aging and death."
The meaning is that there was thus a penetration of the cause of aging and death. This same method applies everywhere.
"Iti hi" means "thus indeed. By stating "the origin, the origin," he indicates the origin of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and the rest by way of a summary across eleven points.
"In things unheard of before" refers to: "With ignorance as condition, there is the origin of volitional formations."
Thus, regarding these previously unheard-of phenomena—or rather, the four noble truths—terms such as "eye" (*cakkhu*) and so forth are merely synonyms for knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
For here, knowledge itself is called the "eye" in the sense of seeing; "knowledge" in the sense of knowing; "wisdom" (*paññā*) in the sense of understanding;
"true insight" (*vijjā*) in the sense of penetration; and "light" (*āloka*) in the sense of illumination. And this [knowledge] consists of the four...

It should be understood that among the truths, both the mundane and the supramundane are indicated. The meaning in the section on Cessation (nirodha) should also be understood by this same method. Fourth.
5–10. Commentary on the Sīkhī-sutta and others.
5–10. Regarding the phrases beginning with “Sikhissa, bhikkhave,” in the fifth [section] and so forth, the meaning should not be understood by connecting them as “Sikhissa pi, bhikkhave.
Why? Because they were not taught while seated on a single seat. For these were taught in various places;
however, the meaning is identical in all instances. Indeed, for all Bodhisattvas, when they are seated upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), [the same occurs].
No other ascetic or brahmin, nor god, Māra, or Brahmā, declares:

"In the past, Bodhisattas became Buddhas after having comprehended the mode of conditions. Rather, just as at the time of the first aeon, when it rains, the rainwater flows on and on along the very path taken by the previous water, so too did those various former Buddhas.
Following the very same path, each subsequent one follows the one before.

For all Bodhisattvas, having emerged from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), descend into knowledge regarding the conditional relations (paccayākāra) and, after contemplating them in direct and reverse order, become Buddhas;
thus, the "Buddha-insight" is described in succession within the seven suttas.
The First Chapter on the Buddhas.
2. The Chapter on Nutriment. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Nutriment.
11. In the first [sutta] of the *Āhāravagga*, "nutriments" (*āhāra*) means conditions (*paccaya*). For conditions bring their own fruit; therefore, they are called "nutriments.
Regarding the phrases "of beings who have come to be" (*bhūtānaṃ sattānaṃ*) and so forth: "come to be" (*bhūta*) means born or produced.

"Seeking existence" (*sambhavesino*) refers to those who seek and search for existence—that is, birth and production. In that regard, among the four modes of birth (*yoni*), there are the egg-born and the womb-born.
As long as beings have not broken out of the egg-shell or the womb-membrane, they are called "seeking birth" (*sambhavesin*);
having broken out of the egg-shell or the womb-membrane and emerged outside, they are called "born" (*bhūta*).

Moisture-born and spontaneously born beings are called "seeking birth" during the first moment of consciousness, and from the second moment of consciousness onwards, they are called "born. Or, [they are designated] according to the posture in which they are born.
As long as they have not reached another [existence], they are called "seeking rebirth" (*sambhavesino*); beyond that, they are called "beings" (*bhūtā*).

Alternatively, "beings" means those who are born and produced; this is a designation for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), who are merely born and produced and will not come to exist again.
They are "seeking rebirth" because they seek further existence, owing to their failure to abandon the fetter of existence (*bhavasaṃyojana*).
This is a designation for both trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) who are still seeking future rebirth.
Thus, in every respect, all sentient beings are encompassed by these two terms. Furthermore, the word "and" (*vā*) here has a conjunctive sense;
therefore, the meaning should be understood as "of those who have come to be (*bhūta*) and of those seeking rebirth (*sambhavesī*)."
"For stability" (*ṭhitiyā*) means for the purpose of stability. "For support" (*anuggahāya*) means for the purpose of support.

This is merely a difference in phrasing; the meaning of both words is one and the same. Alternatively, "for stability" means for the non-interruption of the phenomena that have arisen in each respective being by way of their continuous succession.
"For support" means for the arising of those [phenomena] not yet arisen. And both of these—
“Either for the maintenance and support of beings that have come to be, or for the maintenance and support of those seeking rebirth”—thus they are to be understood in both senses.
“Edible food” (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) means food that is to be swallowed after being made into morsels; it has as its basis boiled rice, cooked barley, and so forth.
This is a designation for *ojā*. It is "gross" by virtue of its grossness as a physical basis (*vatthu*), and "subtle" by virtue of its subtlety.
However, because it is included within subtle matter by its own nature, edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) is indeed subtle.
Furthermore, its grossness and subtlety as a physical basis should be understood in relation to each successive [basis], such as that of crocodiles. For...
Compared to the food of peacocks, the food of crocodiles is subtle; it is said that crocodiles swallow stones, and these dissolve when they reach their stomachs.
Peacocks eat living creatures such as snakes and scorpions. Compared to the food of peacocks, the food of hyenas is subtle;
it is said that they eat horns and bones discarded three years ago, and these—
Moreover, even when merely moistened by their saliva, these [plants] become as soft as roots and tubers.
Compared to the food of hyenas, the food of elephants is subtle; for they eat the branches and such of various trees.
Compared to the food of elephants, the food of the gavaya, the gokaṇṇa deer, and others is subtle; it is said that they eat the sapless leaves and so forth of various trees.
Compared to their food, the food of cattle is more refined. They eat grass that is both green and dry.
Compared to their food, the food of hares is more refined. Compared to the food of hares, the food of birds is more refined.
Compared to the food of birds, the food of those living in the borderlands is more refined. Compared to the food of those living in the borderlands, the food of village headmen is more refined.

The food of kings, royal ministers, and great officials is more refined than the food of village headmen. The food of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) is more refined than the food of those [officials].

The food of the deities of the earth (bhummā devā) is more refined than the food of the wheel-turning monarch. The food of the deities of the Four Great Kings is more refined than the food of the deities of the earth.
In this manner, the foods up to those of the Paranimmitavasavatti deities should be detailed in full.
But for them, their nutriment is concluded as being only subtle.
In this regard, when the physical basis is gross, the nutritive essence (*ojā*) is slight and weak; when it is subtle, it is powerful.
For instance, even after drinking a bowlful of rice-gruel, one becomes hungry again in a mere moment and desires to eat something or other.
However, having drunk even a mere *pasata* measure of ghee, one becomes unwilling to eat for the rest of the day.

In that case, the bodily heat known as *kammaja-tejo* dispels the danger but is not able to sustain [the body]; the nutritive essence (*ojā*), however, sustains it but is not able to dispel the danger.
But when these two are combined, they both dispel the danger and sustain [the body].
"Contact as the second": contact, which is sixfold—namely, eye-contact and so forth—should be understood as the second nutriment among these four nutriments.
This is merely a method of teaching; therefore, one need not inquire here as to why it is called "the second" or "the third" for such reasons.
"Mental volition" refers simply to volition itself. "Consciousness" refers to the mind (*citta*). Thus...

In this place, the Blessed One, having grouped them into a single heap by way of the appropriated (*upādiṇṇaka*) and the non-appropriated (*anupādiṇṇaka*), demonstrated the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*).
For edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) is both appropriated and non-appropriated; likewise for contact (*phassa*) and the others.
Therein, the appropriated edible food is to be understood by way of frogs and so forth that have been swallowed by snakes and the like. For frogs and the like...

Even when swallowed by snakes and other creatures and remaining inside their bellies, these [nutriments] continue to live for some time. As long as they remain on the side of *upādiṇṇaka* (appropriated), they do not perform the function of nutriment.
However, once they break down and remain on the side of *anupādiṇṇaka* (unappropriated), they do perform it.
Even then, they are still called "nutriment that is appropriated. This, however, is not acceptable to the teachers; thus it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself.

Having rejected that [view], this was said: "Even for these beings, whether they are eating or not eating, consuming or not consuming, there exists what is called 'nutriment born of kamma' (kammaja-ojā) co-nascent with the rebirth-linking consciousness itself; it sustains them for as long as seven days.
This alone should be understood as the 'appropriated edible nutriment' (upādiṇṇaka-kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) by way of the resultant [consciousness] of the three planes."

However, contact and the other [nutriments] should be understood as *upādiṇṇaka* (appropriated) when they function as wholesome, unwholesome, or functional states belonging to the three planes; they are *anupādiṇṇaka* (unappropriated) otherwise.
But those pertaining to the supramundane are spoken of by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*).
Here it is asked: "If the meaning of 'condition' (*paccaya*) is the meaning of 'nutriment' (*āhāra*), then why, when other conditions for beings also exist, [is this alone so designated]?"
“Are these alone the four that have been spoken of? It is replied: Because they are the specific conditions for the internal continuity.
For beings who subsist on physical food, edible food is the specific condition for the material body;

contact is the specific condition for feeling within the mental body; mental volition is the specific condition for consciousness; and consciousness is the specific condition for name-and-form. As it has been said: “Just as, bhikkhus, ...”
“This body is sustained by nutriment; it persists dependent on nutriment, and without nutriment it does not persist.

Likewise, feeling has contact as its condition; consciousness has volitional formations as its condition; and name-and-form has consciousness as its condition. But what is the nutriment here, and what does it nourish?

Edible food nourishes the eight material qualities that have nutritive essence as the eighth; contact-nutriment nourishes the three kinds of feeling; mental volition-nutriment nourishes the three realms of existence; and consciousness-nutriment nourishes the name-and-form of rebirth-linking.
How so? First, edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), merely by being placed in the mouth, arouses eight material phenomena;

furthermore, when it is chewed by the teeth and swallowed, each morsel likewise arouses eight material phenomena. Thus, edible food brings forth the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence (ojā).
As for the nutriment of contact (phassāhāra), a contact to be experienced as pleasant, at the very moment it arises, produces pleasure.
Feeling brings about feeling: that which is to be experienced as painful brings about pain, and that which is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant brings about neither-pain-nor-pleasure;
thus, in every way, the nutriment of contact brings about the three kinds of feeling.

The nutriment of mental volition brings about sensual existence by means of karma leading to sensual existence, and it brings about form and formless existence by means of [karma] leading to those states.
That is existence (*bhava*). Thus, in every respect, the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*) brings about the three types of existence.

As for the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*), however, it is said that it "brings about" those three aggregates associated with it at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), as well as the thirty material phenomena that arise by way of the three time-periods (past, present, and future), through the method of conditions such as co-nascence (*sahajāta*). Thus is the nutriment of consciousness.

"Mind-consciousness-choice brings about rebirth-linking mind-and-matter. Herein, by the statement "mind-consciousness-choice brings about the three existences," only wholesome and unwholesome volitions associated with the taints (*āsava*) are meant.
By the statement "consciousness brings about rebirth-linking mind-and-matter," only the rebirth-linking consciousness itself is meant.
However, in a general sense, these too should be understood as "nutriments" (*āhāra*) because they bring about the states associated with them and originated from them.
Among these four nutriments, edible food fulfills its function as nutriment by supporting [the body]; contact does so by merely touching;
mental volition by merely exerting itself; and consciousness by merely cognizing. How so?
Edible food indeed exists for the maintenance of beings by supporting them through the sustenance of the body. For even this body, though produced by kamma, [persists] through edible food.
Supported, it remains for ten years, even for a hundred years, until the limit of its lifespan. How so?
Just as a child, though born of a mother, remains for a long time while being nourished by a nurse who feeds him milk and other sustenance;
and just as a house supported by a prop remains [standing]. And this has also been said:
“Just as, Great King, a house that is collapsing is supported by another beam so that it does not fall, even so, Great King, this body subsists on nutriment; it stands dependent upon nutriment.
Thus, edible food fulfills its function of supporting.
And while performing this function, edible food becomes a condition for two continuities of matter: for that produced by nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna*)...

And [it is a condition] for that which is appropriated (*upādiṇṇaka*). It acts as a condition by being a preserver of those things born of karma (*kammaja*), and by being a producer of those things originated by nutriment (*āhārasamutthāna*).

Contact (*phassa*), however, serves for the maintenance of beings by causing the occurrence of pleasant and other feelings, precisely while it touches the object that has become the basis for pleasure and so forth.
Mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) serves [for maintenance] by producing the root of existence (*bhava*), through the exertion of wholesome and unwholesome kamma.
It exists for the maintenance of beings. Consciousness exists for the maintenance of beings precisely by cognizing through the process of name-and-form.
Thus, while these [nutriments] fulfill their function as nutriment by way of support and so forth, four dangers should be seen.
Namely: in the case of physical food, attachment itself is the danger; in the case of contact, the approach itself [is the danger]; in the case of mental volition...
It is merely the accumulation [of kamma], and it is merely the descent of consciousness that are the fears. For what reason?

Because beings, having formed an attachment to physical food and being preoccupied with cold and other such conditions, undergo no small amount of suffering while performing tasks such as counting money for the sake of obtaining food.
And some, even after going forth in this Dispensation, engage in improper livelihoods such as the practice of medicine.
Those who seek food are censurable both in this very life and in the future;
as stated in the *Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta* in the manner beginning with, "Even his outer robe is burning and aflame," they become "ghosts of ascetics" (*samaṇapeta*).
For this reason, it should be understood that attachment to physical nutriment is indeed fear.
Even while approaching contact, those who delight in contact offend against the wives, children, and property guarded and protected by others.
The owners of that property seize them along with their belongings, cut them into pieces, and throw them onto heaps of refuse, or hand them over to the king.
Then the king causes various forms of torture to be inflicted upon them. And with the breakup of the body...
A miserable rebirth is to be expected for them. Thus, all fear—both pertaining to the present life and to future lives—is rooted in the gratification of contact (*phassassāda*).
For this reason, it should be understood that the very approach toward the nutriment of contact is itself fear.

Furthermore, when one accumulates wholesome and unwholesome kamma, all fear within the three realms of existence is rooted in that [accumulation]. For this reason, it should be understood that the very accumulation within the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*) is itself fear.
And wherever rebirth-linking consciousness descends, it arises having taken up the name-and-form of rebirth-linking at that very place.
When that has arisen, all fears have already arisen as well, because they are rooted in it.
