For this reason, it should be understood that in the nutriment of consciousness, the "descent" itself is fear.
In the passage beginning with "What is the cause" (*kiṃnidāna*), all terms such as "cause" (*nidāna*) and the rest are synonyms for "reason.
For a reason is called a "cause" (*nidāna*) because it brings forth (*nideti*) the fruit, as if saying, "Come, take this!
It is called "origination" (*samudaya*), "birth" (*jāti*), and "source" (*pabhava*) because from it the fruit emerges, arises, and comes into being. This, then, is the meaning of the words here.
"What is their source? means "having what as their source" (*kiṃnidānā*). "What is their origin? means "having what as their origin" (*kiṃsamudayā*).
"What is their birth? means "having what as their birth" (*kiṃjātikā*). "What is their provenance? means "having what as their provenance" (*kiṃpabhavā*).

Since craving is, in the sense already stated, their source, their origin, their birth, and their provenance, he therefore said, "Having craving as their source," and so forth. In this way, the meaning is to be understood for all the terms.

And here, it should be understood that the source of these four nutriments is craving, by way of the preceding cravings for the nutriments comprised within the individual existence (attabhāva), beginning with rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). How so? First, at the moment of rebirth-linking, for beings with complete sense bases, it is by way of the continuity of the sentient being;
for the rest, it is by way of a continuity progressively diminished from that.

The nutritive essence (*ojā*) produced within the arisen material form exists; this is the nutriment of physical food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), which has craving as its source and is grasped (*upādiṇṇaka*).

Furthermore, contact (*phassa*) and volition (*cetanā*) associated with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*), as well as the mind itself as consciousness (*viññāṇa*), these have craving as their source and are the nutriments of contact, mental volition, and consciousness that are grasped.
Thus, first, those things having craving as their source are the rebirth-linking factors.

These are the nutriments. And just as they are at the moment of rebirth-linking, so too should they be understood as produced from that point onward during the first moment of the life-continuum consciousness and so forth.

Furthermore, since the Blessed One knows not only the cause of the nutriments themselves, but also the cause of craving—which is the cause of the nutriments—and indeed the cause of feeling and the rest which are the causes of craving, therefore [it was said]: "And this craving, monks..."
Having shown the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of the method beginning with "What is its source" (*kiṃnidāna*), he showed the cessation of the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*).

And on this occasion, the Blessed One, having given a teaching directed toward the past, shows the cycle of existence by means of the past. How so? For this personal existence (*attabhāva*) is grasped by way of nutriment (*āhāra*).
"Craving" (*taṇhā*) refers to the karma that produces this personal existence; [and likewise] feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness.

In order to show the personal existence (*attabhāva*) in which the karma was accumulated, [the following] were stated: ignorance and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are the karma that produces that personal existence.

Thus, by showing—in brief—both the personal existence in two places and the karma that produces it in two places, [the Teacher] has given a teaching directed toward the past, demonstrating both the phenomenon of karma and the phenomenon of the result of karma (*kammavipāka*).
The round [of existence] has been shown by means of the past.
In this regard, this teaching should not be regarded as incomplete because the future has not been shown; rather, it should be regarded as complete in terms of its underlying method (*naya*).
For just as a man with sight, seeing a crocodile lying on the surface of the water, [perceives] its far side...
Looking at it, one might see its neck; looking from that side, its back; at the end, the base of its tail;
and looking down at its belly, one would not see the tip of the tail submerged in the water nor its four limbs.
Yet, one does not conclude on this basis alone that "the crocodile is incomplete"; rather, by way of inference, one concludes that it is indeed complete.
This should be understood as follows:
the round of existence in the three realms (*tebhūmaka-vatta*) is like the crocodile lying on the surface of the water; the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) is like the man with eyes standing on the bank;
and the time when that man sees the crocodile on the surface of the water is like the time when the meditator [sees it] by way of nutriment (*āhāra*).
The time when this present existence is seen is like the time when the neck [of a snake] is seen from afar; it is the time when the craving that produces this existence is seen.
The time when that existence is seen through its feelings and so forth is like the time when the back [of the snake] is seen—that is, the existence in which the kamma known as craving was performed.
The time when that existence is seen is like the time when the base of the tail is seen.
This is the time for seeing the ignorance and formations of the Janakas.

However, it is like when one looking down into the belly does not see the tip of the snout or the four limbs of the hands and feet, yet instead of taking it to be "an incomplete crocodile," one takes it by way of inference to be "complete";
likewise, wherever the circle of conditions (*paccayavaṭṭa*) has not been explicitly mentioned in the text, there the teaching—
One should understand that this is not a case of grasping [the cycle] as incomplete, but rather as complete by way of its underlying principle (*naya*).

In this context, one junction (*sandhi*) is shown between nutriment (*āhāra*) and craving (*taṇhā*), another between craving and feeling (*vedanā*), and another between consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and formations (*saṅkhāra*);
thus, the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is shown as having exactly three junctions and four groups (*catusaṅkhepa*). First.
2. Commentary on the Moḷiyaphagguna Sutta. 12.
Regarding the second [verse], "or for the sake of favoring those seeking rebirth," the Blessed One brought his teaching to a conclusion at this very point. Why?
Because a proponent of wrong views was seated there. For in that assembly, there was a monk named Moḷiyaphagguna.

The holder of wrong views was sitting there. Then the Teacher thought, “If he rises and asks me a question, I shall answer it,” and so, in order to grant him the opportunity to ask, he brought his teaching to a conclusion. Regarding the name Moḷiyaphagguna:
*moḷī* means a crest-lock; as it has been said: [the passage continues].
Having cut off his topknot, which was scented with the finest perfumes,
the Bull of the Sakyas cast it into the air;
Vāsava [received it] with his most excellent jeweled casket.
“...with his thousand eyes, he received [it] upon his head.
In his time as a householder, she was great; therefore, the designation “Moḷiyaphagguna” arose for him. Even after he had gone forth, they knew him by that very name.
“He said this” (*etadavoca*)—this phrase connects the sequence of the teaching: “Who indeed... [etc.]
“Venerable sir, who consumes this nutriment of consciousness?”—thus he spoke. The meaning of this is: “Venerable sir, who indeed is that one who eats or consumes this nutriment of consciousness?
But why does he ask about this nutriment alone, without asking about the other three nutriments? It is because of his adherence to the view that “I know.”
For he sees them taking morsel food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) after having formed it into large balls; therefore, his conviction is: "By this I know [that they subsist on nutriment].
Furthermore, seeing partridges, quails, peacocks, chickens, and so forth, sustaining themselves through contact with their mothers, his conviction is:
"These subsist by the nutriment of contact (phassāhāra). As for turtles, however, having emerged from the great ocean during their own breeding season...
Having laid their eggs among the sand on the shore of the ocean and covered them with sand, they enter the great ocean itself.
Those eggs do not rot because of the mother’s mindfulness; they subsist through the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*).
Such is his tenet. Although this is the Elder’s tenet, he does not ask this question based on that tenet.
For one who holds to a wrong view is like a madman.

Just as a madman, having taken a basket, enters the middle of the street and puts into that basket whatever he seizes—whether cow dung, stones, excrement, or pieces of food, whether pleasing or unpleasing—so too does one who holds to a wrong view ask what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. Why? [He asks: "Why..."
He should not be rebuked for asking this; rather, he should be prevented from grasping at whatever points he asks about.

For this very reason, the Blessed One did not say to him, "Why do you ask thus? but instead spoke the words beginning with "This question is not appropriate" in order to release him from his grasping.
"In that case, 'it is not fitting' means it is improper. 'I do not say that anyone eats' means I do not say that any being or person eats.
'And if I were to say that someone eats' means if I were to say that someone eats, then in that case this question would be fitting—namely, 'But why, venerable sir...'"
"Consciousness as nutriment," venerable sir—this means: "Of what phenomenon is this consciousness-nutriment the condition?
"In this case, it is fit to explain"—when this question has been thus asked, this explanation is appropriate:

"Consciousness as nutriment is a condition for the production of renewed existence in the future. And here, "consciousness as nutriment" refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).
"Future production of renewed existence" refers to the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that arises simultaneously with that very consciousness.
"When that has come to be, there are the six sense bases" means that when that name-and-form—designated as the production of renewed existence—has arisen, the six sense bases come to be.
"With the six sense bases as condition, contact": here too, the Blessed One concluded his teaching by providing further scope for the question.
For one who holds to a speculative view (*diṭṭhigatika*) is unable to formulate a new question;

rather, having grasped exactly what has already been explained, he asks. Therefore, the Blessed One granted him the opportunity. Furthermore, the meaning in all instances should be understood according to the method already stated.
Why does he not ask, "Venerable sir, does one exist? For to one who holds a speculative view, a being...
He held the view that what is called "become" is simply "produced"; therefore, he did not ask about this [teaching], as it contradicts his own view.

Furthermore, because it has been stated in many places that "from this condition, this arises; from this condition, this," he had come to accept this designation, and for that reason also he did not ask.
The Teacher thought: "Even though he asks much, there is no satisfaction for him; this is merely a vain inquiry."
From the words “he asks,” the Teacher taught by making the instruction into a single continuous whole.
From the words “But as for Channa,” he spoke thus, taking up only that portion of the teaching which had already been introduced and unfolding the instruction further.

In this sutta, however, there is one link between consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), another between feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*taṇhā*), and another between existence (*bhava*) and birth (*jāti*). This is the second [section].
3. Commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta 13.
In the third [sutta], "whether recluses or brahmins," this refers to outside recluses and brahmins who are incapable of penetrating the truths.

In the phrases beginning with "not fully understanding aging-and-death," they do not understand aging-and-death by way of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), nor do they understand the origin of aging-and-death...

They do not know that birth together with craving is the origin of aging and death, according to the truth of the origin; they do not know the cessation of aging and death, according to the truth of cessation;
and they do not know the way leading thereto, according to the truth of the path. They do not know birth, according to the truth of suffering;
and they do not know the origin of birth—that existence together with craving is the origin of birth—according to the truth of the origin.
Thus, having connected the arising with craving, the meaning should be understood according to the Four Noble Truths in all instances.
Regarding the phrase "the goal of recluseship or the goal of brahminhood," here the Noble Path is both recluseship and brahminhood.
Furthermore, in both cases, "goal" (attha) should be understood as the Noble Fruit (ariyaphala). Thus, in this sutta, the Blessed One [taught] in eleven points.
"He spoke the Four Truths. This is the third [section]. 4.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins:
In the fourth [discourse], after having elaborated with the phrase "What are these things? Which things?", he spoke the teaching.
It was said, "These phenomena are not understood by those individuals capable of penetrating [the truth] according to their own inclinations," and so forth.
The remainder is exactly as before. The fourth [sutta].
5. Commentary on the Kaccānagotta Sutta.
15. In the fifth [section], regarding "right view" (*sammādiṭṭhi*) and "one of right view" (*sammādiṭṭhī*):

whatever the wise among gods and humans call "correct seeing" in various contexts, he asks about all of that by condensing it into two terms. "Dependent on a dyad" (*dvayanissito*) means dependent on two parts.
By the word "for the most part" (*yebhuyyena*), he indicates the general populace with the exception of noble persons (*ariyapuggala*). "That there is" (*atthīti*)...

"Permanence" (*sassata*) [is the view that things exist eternally]. "Non-existence" (*natthita*) is annihilationism (*uccheda*). "The origin of the world" (*lokasamudaya*): the so-called "world" is the world of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*);
it is their arising. "Seeing with right wisdom" (*sammappaññāya passato*): "right wisdom" refers to the path-wisdom accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*);

the meaning is "for one who sees by means of that. "That which is non-existent in the world" (*yā loke natthitā*): while the phenomena arising in the world of formations are indeed appearing, [to say] "that which is non-existent" [is the view of nihilism].

The meaning is that the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*) would arise, but it does not. "The cessation of the world" (*lokanirodha*) refers to the dissolution of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*).

"That which exists in the world": when the phenomena in the world of formations are breaking up and yet still appear, the eternalist view (*sassata-diṭṭhi*) might arise, thinking "this exists," but the meaning is that this does not occur.

Furthermore, "the origin of the world" refers to the mode of conditions in forward order (*anuloma-paccayākāra*). "The cessation of the world" refers to the mode of conditions in reverse order (*paṭiloma-paccayākāra*).

For one who sees the world's dependence [on conditions], because they see that with the non-interruption of the conditions there is no interruption of what has arisen from those conditions, the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*)—the notion that "it does not exist"—does not arise. Even for one who sees the cessation of conditions, through the cessation of the conditions...
For one who sees the cessation of what has arisen through conditions, whatever eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) might arise as "it exists" does not occur; this is also the meaning here.
"Bound by clinging, grasping, and adherence" means bound by clingings (*upaya*), by graspings (*upādāna*), and by adherences (*abhinivesa*).

In that context, there are two types of clinging: the clinging of craving (*taṇhūpaya*) and the clinging of views (*diṭṭhūpaya*). The same method applies to the graspings and so forth. [These refer to] craving and views.
Indeed, because they approach and resort to the phenomena of the three planes through such modes as "I" and "mine," they are called *upāyā* (approachers).
Furthermore, because they cling to and adhere to those phenomena, they are called *upādāna* (clinging) and *abhinivesa* (adherence).
And by these, this world is bound; therefore, it is said: "bound by approach, clinging, and adherence."
And this noble disciple [abandons] that craving and that grasping. "The mental fixation" means that which has become the foundation for the mind.
"Adherence and underlying tendency" means that which has become both adherence and an underlying tendency. For unwholesome consciousness is established upon craving and views;
these two both adhere to it and underlie it. Therefore, both of these are [the mental fixation] of the mind.

He says that there is resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), as well as adherence (*abhinivesa*) and underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). "Does not approach" means he does not go toward it. "Does not cling" means he does not grasp it.
"Does not resolve" means he does not resolve upon it—how so? Thinking, "This is my self.
"Only suffering" means only the mere five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandha*). "Does not doubt" means: "Only suffering arises; suffering ceases; there is no other being here."
He does not entertain doubt, thinking "it exists. He does not waver means he does not give rise to perplexity.
"Not dependent on another" means not by means of another's influence; having not relied on the conviction of another, he possesses here the very knowledge of personal realization.
To this extent, Kaccāna, right view exists—thus, because the perception of a self has been abandoned.
By this much, it is called "right seeing"; thus he speaks of the mixed right view (*missakasammādiṭṭhi*). "This is one extreme" means this is one crooked end, a base end, the first eternalism.
"This is the second" means this is the second, the nihilistic view characterized by the thought "nothing exists at all," which is a crooked end, a base end;
the meaning is that it is the second annihilationism (*uccheda*). The rest here is as follows.
"Quite clear," thus [ends] the fifth. 6.
Commentary on the Dhammakathika Sutta. 16.

In the sixth, "for the sake of disenchantment" means for the purpose of becoming disenchanted; "for the sake of dispassion" means for the purpose of fading away from passion; "for the sake of cessation" means...
"For the sake of cessation. Regarding the phrase "he is practicing," it should be understood that he is practicing from the stage of virtue (sīla) up to the path of Arahatship.

"Practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma" means he is practicing the way of practice that is the secondary Dhamma (anudhamma) to the supramundane Dhamma of Nibbāna. "Secondary Dhamma" means having a nature that is conformable [to it]. "Through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation..."
"By means of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation. "Liberated through non-clinging" means liberated without clinging to any phenomenon (dhamma) by means of the four kinds of clinging.
"Attained to Nibbāna in this very life" means attained to Nibbāna in this very existence (diṭṭhe va dhamme).
"Worthy of being spoken of" means he is fit to be so addressed; the sense is that he is suitable and appropriate. Thus, herein, by one [phrase]...

By way of method, the questions of the Dhamma-preacher were stated; having distinguished him by two [criteria], the stages of the trainee (*sekha*) and the one beyond training (*asekha*) were demonstrated.
This is the sixth [chapter]. 7.

Commentary on the Kassapa the Naked Ascetic Sutta (Acelakassapasutta). In the seventh [sutta]: "The naked ascetic Kassapa" means he was naked (*acela*)—that is, without clothes—by virtue of his outward mark (*liṅga*), and Kassapa by name. "From afar" means from a great distance.
He saw him approaching from afar, surrounded by the community of monks. "Something" means some particular reason.
"An opportunity" means a moment or time for answering questions. "Within a house" (*antaraghara*):
regarding the rule "I shall not sit cross-legged within a house," here "within a house" refers to the interior of a dwelling. "With downcast eyes within a house" (*okkhittacakkhu antaraghare*).
"In 'I shall go,' here the interior of the village begins from the threshold pillar (*indakhīla*). Here too, this very [definition] is intended. As for 'when you wish,' it means whatever you desire.
But why did the Blessed One refuse up to three times when he wished to speak? It was for the sake of generating reverence.
For those who hold wrong views do not show reverence when things are told quickly; they think, 'Even to approach the ascetic Gotama and to question him..."
They did not even believe the words, "It is easy; he will answer as soon as he is asked.
But when [the Buddha] had refused two or three times, they showed respect, thinking, "It is difficult even to approach the ascetic Gotama and to ask him a question.
When it was explained after being requested for the third time, they listened and believed. Thus the Blessed One thought, "This one will listen..."
Having had him entreated up to three times with the words, "He will believe," he spoke. Furthermore, just as a physician cooking oil or molasses,
waiting for the proper time for the cooking of the soft and hard stages, pours it out without letting that time pass, so too the Blessed One,
waiting for the ripening of the wisdom of beings, [spoke] thinking, "In this much time, his wisdom will reach maturity."
Knowing that [the Buddha] would go, he made his request up to three times.
“Do not say so, Kassapa,” [the Buddha replied]. “Kassapa, do not speak thus. It is not permissible to say that suffering is self-made;

for it is demonstrated that there is no such thing as a ‘self’ who is the maker of suffering. The same principle applies to the other views as well. As for the view that things arise by chance (*adhiccasamuppanna*):
“Arising without cause, by chance. When asked thus, why did he speak in this way? It is said that this thought occurred to him:
“When asked whether suffering is self-made and so forth, he says, ‘Let it not be so. When asked whether it does not exist, he says, ‘It exists.
When asked whether Master Gotama neither knows nor sees suffering, he says, ‘I do indeed know it.’”
"He speaks. Have I perhaps missed something in what I asked?"—thus he spoke, clarifying his own question from the very beginning.
And when he says, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One explain it to me," he uses the term "Blessed One" (bhagavā) rather than "Sir" (bhava) because of the reverence he has conceived for the Teacher.
The passage beginning with “He who acts,” etc., is stated for the purpose of refuting the view that “suffering is self-made.
Here, the word *sato* is a genitive used in the sense of a locative; therefore, the meaning should be understood as follows:
“Kassapa, when one first holds the view that ‘he who acts is he who experiences,’ only then does the subsequent view arise that ‘suffering is self-made.’”
And here, "suffering" refers to the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). Thus they speak;

this [word] is connected with the preceding word "beginning" (*ādi*) and the immediately following word "eternalism" (*sassata*). Furthermore, "it illuminates" or "it grasps" is the elliptical phrase (*pāṭhaseso*) to be supplied here.
For this is what is meant: speaking thus, from the very beginning he illuminates eternalism; he grasps eternalism.

Why? Because for him, that view is "other," and for one who grasps the agent and the experiencer as being one and the same, this leads to the acceptance of eternalism (*sassata*); such is the meaning.
The statement beginning with "another acts" and so forth, however, was spoken for the purpose of refuting the tenet that "suffering is created by another. "From the beginning... [etc.]
Furthermore, the word "mindful" (*sato*) should also be supplied here. This is the meaning:
Kassapa, if it were first thought that "one person acts and another experiences [the result]," then subsequently, with the arising of the annihilationist view—"The doer is annihilated right here;
another experiences what was done by him"—there would be feeling associated with that [view].
"When one is struck and pierced, the conviction arises: 'Suffering is caused by another. Thus they say;

this should be construed according to the method already stated. Here is the construction: By speaking thus, from the very beginning he illuminates annihilationism (*uccheda*) and adopts annihilationism.
Why? For his view is "this" (*etaṃ*); the meaning is that it approaches this annihilationism.
"These two" refers to the two extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism. "Not approaching these two extremes, Kassapa, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma;

having abandoned them and not adhering to them, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way"—the meaning is that he teaches while standing upon the Middle Way. If one asks, "What is that Dhamma? it is this:
"Conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise. Here, indeed, the fruit is shown from the cause, and its cessation through the cessation of the cause;
no agent or experiencer whatsoever is pointed out. By this much, the remaining questions are refuted.
By the phrase "without approaching either extreme," the third question is rejected. "Conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise."
By this, it should be understood that both the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannatā*) and ignorance are rejected.
"May I obtain [it]"—this he said while aspiring to the state of a monk in the presence of the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One [considered] that the probation for former members of other sects (*tīrthika-parivāsa*) had been prescribed in the *Khandhaka* on the subject of origins; [namely,] that one who was formerly a member of another sect [must undergo it] at the stage of a novice (*sāmaṇera*).
Having formally undertaken [the procedure] in this manner—beginning with: "Venerable sir, I, named so-and-so, formerly belonging to another sect, desire full ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya.

Therefore, venerable sir, I request a four-month probation from the Saṅgha"—and then remaining [in that state], it is with reference to him that the Blessed One said: "Kassapa, whoever was formerly belonging to another sect," and so forth.
In this context, the word "pabbajjā" (going forth) is used for the sake of euphony. For one indeed receives the going forth without having completed the probationary period.
However, one who seeks full ordination (*upasampadā*) must complete the probationary period while fulfilling the eight observances, such as not entering villages at inappropriate times.
"With a settled mind" means with a mind satisfied by the fulfillment of the eight observances. This is the summary here; however, the detailed account is as follows:

The probation for those belonging to other sects (titthiyaparivāsa) is to be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the Chapter on Going-forth (Pabbajjakkhandhaka) in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
Furthermore, the reading here is "mayā" (by me), whereas elsewhere it is "metthā" (for me). "The diversity of persons is known."
“The diversity of individuals is known to me; ‘this person is worthy of probation, this one is not worthy of probation’—this is clear to me,” he said, showing that it was evident to him.

Then Kassapa thought: “Oh, how wonderful is the Buddha’s teaching, wherein they test and grind things in this way, taking only what is appropriate and discarding what is inappropriate! Thereupon, [he understood] even more thoroughly.
“Venerable Sir,” he said, beginning with the words, “if [you grant] me the going-forth, I have conceived the courage for it.
Then the Blessed One, knowing his intense longing, thought, “Kassapa does not deserve the probationary period,” and addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Go, bhikkhu, bathe Kassapa, give him the going-forth, and bring him back. Having done so, that bhikkhu gave him the going-forth and brought him into the presence of the Blessed One.
He arrived. The Blessed One, having sat down with the assembly, granted him full ordination (*upasampadā*). Therefore it is said:

"The naked ascetic Kassapa received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination. The remainder, beginning with "Not long after his full ordination," has already been stated in the *Brāhmaṇa-saṃyutta*.
This is the seventh [chapter].
8. Commentary on the Timbaruka Sutta 18.
In the eighth [verse], the passage beginning with “That feeling... is stated for the purpose of refuting the tenet that “pleasure and pain are self-made.

Here too, the genitive case in the word *satō* (of a being) is used in the sense of a locative (*bhumm-atthe*). Regarding this, the clarification of the meaning is as follows: “That feeling, he... [and so forth].
“‘One feels,’ Timbaruka—when this is the case from the very beginning, there is the conviction that ‘pleasure and pain are self-made.
For if this were so, feeling itself would have been made by feeling.
And speaking thus, one admits the prior existence of this feeling and demonstrates eternalism; one grasps at eternalism. Why? Because for him, that...”
“*Dassanaṃ etaṃ pareti*” means that this [view] approaches eternalism;
for it was with reference to the former meaning that this was said by the Blessed One. Therefore, having connected it with that [former context], its meaning is explained in the Commentary.
“*Evampāhaṃ na vadāmīti*” means: I do not say even this: “That feeling is the one who feels. Nor do I say: “Pleasure and pain are self-made.”
The meaning is: "I do not speak even thus.
The passage beginning with "another is the feeling" and so forth is stated for the purpose of refuting the view that "pleasure and pain are created by another.
Here too, this is the application of the meaning: "If, Timbaruka, it were as you say from the very beginning—that 'one is the feeling, another is the one who feels'—"
The experience of the agent in the subsequent or prior phase is cut off.
Yet, because another experiences what was done by that [agent], for one who is pierced by the feeling associated with such arisen annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi), there arises this adherence:
"Happiness and suffering are created by another. Speaking thus, the agent is cut off, and rebirth-linking occurs through another.
"Grasped" indicates annihilationism; one grasps at annihilationism. Why? Because that view of his "leans toward this" means it approaches this annihilationism.
Here too, these words have been brought from the Aṭṭhakathā and applied accordingly.
In this sutta, the pleasure and pain of feeling are discussed; moreover, those are exclusively the pleasure and pain of karmic result (vipāka).
"It is allowable," it is said. The eighth [section]. 9.
Commentary on the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta. 19.
In the ninth [verse], "of one hindered by ignorance" means of one obstructed by ignorance (*avijjā*). "Thus this body has come to be" means thus...
This body has arisen precisely because it is obstructed by ignorance and associated with craving.
"This very body" refers to one's own conscious body; "and externally, name-and-form" refers to the conscious bodies of others.
This meaning should be illustrated by means of the five aggregates and the six sense bases, both for oneself and for another.
"This pair" means this very pair. Regarding "contact dependent on a pair": elsewhere, visual contact and so forth are said to be dependent on pairs such as the eye and visible forms;
here, however, it refers to the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*).
This, indeed, is called the "great pair. "The six sense bases alone" means the six bases of contact, the causes of contact, by which—
*Touched* (*phuṭṭho*) means touched by the contact (*phassa*) arisen through those bases (*āyatana*) acting as causes.

Regarding the phrase *by one or another* (*aññatarena*), here "one or another" (*aññataratā*) should be understood in the sense of being complete. *Therein* (*tatra*) refers to that [context] of the production of the body and so forth for both fools and the wise.
*What is the underlying intention?* (*ko adhippāyo*) means what is the additional application (*adhikapayoga*).
"Bhagavaṃmūlakā" means those whose root is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*). This is what is meant:
"Venerable sir, these teachings of ours were originally established by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa;
after he had attained final Nibbāna, for the duration of one *buddhantara*, there was no other ascetic or brahmin capable of establishing these teachings again. But by the Blessed One..."
"These states have not been produced by us. For it is by relying on the Blessed One that we understand and penetrate these states.
Thus, "Venerable Sir, our states are rooted in the Blessed One. "The Blessed One is their guide" means that the Blessed One is the leader, the trainer, and the instructor of the states;
he shows them by taking up each one individually according to its true nature.

The Dhammas are called "having the Blessed One as their guide. They are "having the Blessed One as their refuge" in the sense that all phenomena belonging to the four planes, when coming within the range of the knowledge of omniscience, are said to "return" to the Blessed One; thus they have the Blessed One as their refuge.
To "return" means to converge. Furthermore, through the power of his personal realization, contact (phassa) comes to the Blessed One while he is seated at the Great Seat of Enlightenment.

“Blessed One, what is my name? “In the sense of touching, you are called ‘contact’ (phassa). Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness each come forward and ask, ‘Blessed One, what is my name? In the sense of cognizing, you are called ‘consciousness’ (viññāṇa).
Thus the Blessed One, grasping the individual names of the phenomena belonging to the four planes according to their true nature, [taught them].

"He takes refuge in the Dhamma" means that the Blessed One is his refuge. "May it occur to the Blessed One himself" means that the meaning of this speech should be manifest to the Blessed One alone; the sense is: "Please explain and give it to us yourself.
Regarding the phrase "that very ignorance," although both that ignorance and craving impel karma toward rebirth—

Having been drawn out, they have ceased; yet, just as even today one might say "that same food" because it is similar to the medicine drunk yesterday, so too here it is said "that same ignorance and that same craving" because of their similarity.
"The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the holy life of the Path. "For the destruction of suffering" means:
"For the sake of the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra. "One who enters upon a body" means one who goes to another rebirth-linking existence.
"Namely, the dwelling in the holy life (*brahmacariyavāsa*)" shows that this dwelling in the holy life of the Path is the distinction between the fool and the wise man.
Thus, in this sutta, every ordinary person (*puthujjana*), whether accompanied by rebirth-linking or not, is called a "fool. The one without rebirth-linking...
One whose taints are exhausted is called "wise. However, those who have attained the stages of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning cannot be described as either "wise" or "foolish";
rather, while they may lean toward one side or the other, they belong to the faction of the wise.
Ninth. 10. Commentary on the Paccaya Sutta.
20. "Bhikkhus, today I shall teach you dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) and dependently arisen phenomena (paṭiccasamuppanne dhamme)," said the Teacher;
thus, in this sutta, he undertook both, intending to teach the conditions (paccayā) and the phenomena produced by those conditions (paccayanibbattā sabhāvadhammā).
"Whether Tathāgatas arise... means even upon the arising of Tathāgatas—that is, whether Buddhas have appeared or have not yet appeared.
With birth as condition, there is aging-and-death; birth itself is the condition for aging-and-death. "That element remains" means that the nature of the condition remains;
there is never a time when birth is not a condition for aging-and-death.

By these two terms—“the stability of phenomena” (dhammaṭṭhitatā) and “the fixed order of phenomena” (dhammaniyāmatā)—he speaks precisely of the condition. For it is by means of the condition that the phenomena arising from the condition remain; therefore...
The condition itself is called "the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*). The condition determines phenomena; therefore, it is called "the regularity of phenomena" (*dhammaniyāmatā*).
Regarding "conditionality by this" (*idappaccayatā*): the conditions for these [factors] such as aging-and-death are "conditions by this" (*idappaccayā*);

the state of being those very conditions is "conditionality by this" (*idappaccayatā*). "That" refers to that condition. "He fully awakens to" means he fully awakens to it with knowledge. "He penetrates" means...
One realizes through knowledge. "Explains" means he speaks. "Teaches" means he shows. "Makes known" means he causes to be understood.
"Establishes" means he places it before the door of knowledge. "Uncovers" means having uncovered, he shows.
"Analyzes" means he shows by way of division. "Clarifies" means he makes it manifest. And he says, "Behold!"—that is, he says, "Behold!"
"How so? 'With birth as condition, monks, there is aging-and-death,' and so forth.
'Thus indeed, monks' means: in this way indeed, monks. 'Therein' means: among those [formulas] such as 'with birth as condition, aging-and-death.
'Suchness' and the following terms are synonyms for the mode of conditionality itself. By those various conditions, it is exactly neither deficient nor excessive."
It is called "suchness" (*tathatā*) because each respective phenomenon arises from its conditions;

it is called "non-falsity" (*avitathatā*) because there is no non-arising of the phenomena produced from those conditions for even a moment once the causal factors have come together; it is called "not-otherwise-ness" (*anaññathatā*) because one phenomenon does not arise from the conditions for another phenomenon;
or it is called "specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*) in the sense of being the condition for aging, death, and so forth, or the collection of conditions.

Herein, this is the etymological analysis (*vacanattha*): "conditions for these" are *idappaccayā*; the state of being such conditions is *idappaccayatā*, or else it is the collection of such conditions that is *idappaccayatā*.
As for the definition (*lakkhaṇa*) here, it should be understood from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).

"Impermanent" (*anicca*): in the sense of non-existence after having come to be, it is impermanent. And herein, "impermanent" does not mean that aging-and-death itself is impermanent; [rather, it refers to the fact that] having become, it does not remain.
However, because the aggregates (khandhas), which have the nature of impermanence, are subject to aging and death, they are called "impermanent.
The same method applies to the terms "conditioned" (saṅkhata) and so forth. In this context, "conditioned" means made by coming together through conditions;

"dependently arisen" (paṭiccasamuppanna) means arisen in dependence upon conditions; "subject to destruction" (khayadhamma) means having the nature of destruction; and "subject to vanishing" (vayadhamma) means having the nature of passing away.
"Subject to fading away" (*virāgadhamma*) means having the nature of fading away. "Subject to cessation" (*nirodhadhamma*) means having the nature of ceasing.

Impermanence regarding birth should also be understood in the same manner as previously stated. Alternatively, because the causal conditions for birth are seen at the very moment they exercise their functional power, the terms "impermanent" and so forth are indeed appropriate here by way of this single method.
Existence (*bhava*) and the other factors likewise have the very nature of being impermanent and so forth.
"With right wisdom" means with the path-wisdom accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*). "The prior end" means the former, the past;

this is the meaning. In such phrases as "Was I indeed? and so forth, one doubts the existence or non-existence of oneself in the past, based on the mode of eternalism (*sassata*) and the mode of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppatti*), [respectively] thinking, "Was I indeed, or was I not? It should not be said, "What is the reason? [for this doubt].
Like a madman, the foolish worldling proceeds in whatever manner [he pleases]. Relying on his birth, gender, and rebirth, he wonders, "What indeed was I?
Was I a kshatriya, or one of the brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, or humans?
And relying on his physical form and appearance, he wonders, "How indeed was I? Was I tall..."
He doubts whether it was one of those [beings] characterized by small stature, pure color, black color, measured size, or immeasurable size. Some, however, say:
"He doubts from the perspective of a cause, thinking, 'By what cause did this come to be? based on [theories such as] creation by a Supreme Lord (issaranimmāna) and so forth.

He doubts regarding the sequence of existence, thinking, "Having been what, did I become what? based on birth and so forth: "Having been a khattiya, did I become a brahmin... pe... having been a deva..."
"A human being" means he doubts his own continuity. In all these cases, however, "addhāna" is a designation for time.

"The future limit" (aparanta) refers to the end that has not yet come. "Shall I exist, or shall I not exist?"—relying on the mode of eternalism and the mode of annihilationism, he doubts whether he will exist or not exist in the future. The rest here is exactly as previously explained.
"Or the present time" means either now, or taking the entire present duration beginning from rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and ending with death (cuti).
"He will be full of doubt internally" means he will have perplexity regarding his own aggregates. "Do I exist?"—he doubts his own existence. But is this reasonable?
What need for deliberation here as to whether it is appropriate or inappropriate? Furthermore, they cite this example:
It is said that the son of Cūḷamātā was shaven, while the son of Mahāmātā was not. When they shaved that boy, he arose and thought, "Am I indeed the son of Cūḷamātā?
In this way, there arises the doubt, "Am I indeed [this]? or "Am I not indeed [this]?"

He doubts his own non-existence. In this regard, there is this story: it is said that one man, while catching fish, struck his own thigh—which had become cold from staying long in the water—thinking it was a fish.
Another man, guarding a field near a cemetery, lay down curled up in fear; having woken up, he thought his two knees were two *yakkhas*.
"Having struck [him], he thus doubts: 'Am I not indeed so?
He doubts his own status as a khattiya while being a khattiya, wondering, 'What indeed am I? The same method applies to the others as well.
However, there is no such thing as one who, while being a deva, does not know his own deva-status; yet even he might wonder, 'Am I possessed of form (rūpī) or am I formless (arūpī)?'"
He doubts in the manner beginning with "Is it so? and so forth. If one asks why the kṣatriyas and others do not know [this], it is because their arising in various families is not evident to them.

Furthermore, householders such as the *potthalika* and others perceive those who have gone forth as householders, while those who have gone forth perceive householders in the manner of thinking, "Is my action subject to transgression? and so forth. And humans likewise perceive kings as [mere] men.
They perceive a deity within themselves. "How indeed am I?"—this is exactly as stated in the previous method.

However, here one should understand that, having grasped the notion that there exists something called a "life-principle" (jīva) inside, and based on its shape and form, one wonders, "Am I long, short, square, hexagonal, octagonal, sixteen-sided, or some other such kind?
Thus, one who is doubting, "How indeed am I? is to be understood as being in doubt. [This refers to] the shape of the body.
However, there is no one who does not know the present. He doubts in this way, wondering about the place from which this selfhood has come and where it will go:
"From where has it come? Where will it go? Here, the "noble disciple" refers to the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*);
however, the other three [stages of attainment] are certainly not excluded. The tenth [chapter].
The Second Chapter on Nutriment.
3. The Chapter on the Ten Powers. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Powers.
21. The first [sutta] of the Dasabala-vagga is a summary of the second.
2. Commentary on the Second Dasabala Sutta: 22.
The second was spoken by the Blessed One according to his own inclination. In that context, "endowed with the ten powers" means:
He is endowed with ten powers. Now, this power is twofold: physical power and the power of knowledge.
Of these, the physical power of the Tathāgata is to be understood according to the lineage of elephants. For it has been said by the ancients:
“The Kāḷāvaka, the Gaṅgeyya, the Paṇḍara, and the Tambapiṅgala;”
“Gandha, Maṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta—these are the ten [kinds of] elephant breeds.
Among these, “Kāḷāvaka” should be understood as the ordinary elephant breed.
The physical strength of ten men is equal to that of one Kāḷāvaka elephant; the strength of ten Kāḷāvakas is...
That [value] of one Gaṅgeyya elephant is equal to that of ten Gaṅgeyyas;
that of ten Paṇḍaras is equal to that of one Paṇḍara; that of ten Tambas is equal to that of one Tamba;
that of ten Piṅgalas is equal to that of one Gandhahatthin; that of ten Gandhahatthis is equal to that of...
That which is the merit of ten *maṅgala* elephants is equal to that of one *Hemavata* elephant.
That which is the merit of ten *Hemavata* elephants is equal to that of one *Uposatha* elephant. That which is the merit of ten *Uposatha* elephants is equal to that of one *Chaddanta* elephant.
That which is the merit of ten *Chaddanta* elephants is equal to that of one *Tathāgata*. This very same [merit] is also called the "Nārāyaṇa-compound strength."
It is said. By the standard of counting ordinary elephants, this is the strength of a thousand koṭis of elephants;
by the standard of counting men, it is the strength of ten thousand koṭis of men. This, first of all, is the bodily power of the Tathāgata.
However, in the phrase "endowed with the ten powers," this [bodily power] is not included. For this is external, inferior, and belongs to animals.

This [power] exists even for lions and other such beings; for by depending on this, there is no full understanding of suffering, no abandoning of its origin, no development of the path, or no realization of the fruit.

However, there is another tenfold power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*) consisting of ten aspects, in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of providing support in ten locations. It is with reference to this that it is said, "endowed with the ten powers."
But what is that *taṇti*? It is the knowledge of things as they truly are, such as the possible and the impossible. That is to say:

first, the knowledge of the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible; second, the knowledge of the results of past, future, and present karmic actions as they truly are, according to their basis and their cause; and third, the knowledge of the path leading everywhere.
One is the knowledge of the world with its many and diverse elements; one is the knowledge of the various inclinations of other beings and other persons;

one is the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of those very same beings; one is the knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence regarding the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments;
one is the knowledge of past lives; and [one is] the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
One is the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*). In the Abhidhamma, however, it is said:
"Herein, the Tathāgata understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible.
That the Tathāgata understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible—this too is a quality of the Tathāgata... [and so forth].
"It is the Tathāgata’s power, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.

Thus they have been presented in detail according to this method. Furthermore, the commentary on their meaning has been stated in all its aspects both in the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* and in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*. That [commentary] should be understood according to the method explained therein.

"And by the four grounds of self-confidence" (*vesārajjehi*): here, *vesārajja* is the opposite of timidity (*sārajja*). This is the name for the knowledge consisting of joy that arises in one who reflects upon the state of self-confidence regarding these four points.

What are the four? "Regarding you who claim to be a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddha*), there are these things that have not been fully realized by you," and so forth—these are the bases for challenge.
Herein, this is the canonical text: “‘Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā’ ti ādīsu codanāvatthūsu. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –” [The text continues with the specific challenges.]
“Bhikkhus, there are these four grounds of self-confidence of a Tathāgata... Which four?

‘While claiming to be perfectly enlightened, these things have not been fully realized by me’—in regard to this, let no ascetic or brahmin, or god, or Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, challenge me with reason; this is the first ground of self-confidence.”

“Monks, I do not perceive such a ground. Not perceiving such a ground, monks, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-confidence: ‘While you claim to be one whose taints are destroyed, these taints are not yet destroyed in you’—in this regard, indeed, I see no basis for anyone to rightfully accuse me... Or:
‘Those things which were spoken of by you as obstructive, the practice of them is not sufficient to constitute an obstruction.’”

"In that regard, alas, [if] anyone were to say of me: 'For whatever purpose the Dhamma has been taught by you, it does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering'—in that regard, indeed, I abide having attained fearlessness, whether it be a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa...
"The bull-like position" (āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ) means the preeminent position, the supreme position; or alternatively, the bulls are the former Buddhas, and this is their position.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, *usabha* is a bull that is the leader of a hundred cows; *vasabha* is one that is the leader of a thousand cows;
or alternatively, *usabha* is one that is the leader of a hundred bulls; *vasabha* is one that is the leader of a thousand bulls;

while *nisabha* is the best of all cattle, capable of enduring all hardships, white, beautiful, a bearer of great burdens, and unshakable even by the sound of a hundred thunderclaps—it is this *nisabha* that is intended here as *usabha*.
This, too, is a figurative expression for that [Buddha]. "Āsabhaṃ" means "belonging to a bull (usabha).
"Ṭhānaṃ" refers to standing firm by pressing down upon the earth with all four feet. But this [standing] is like that of a bull; thus it is called "āsabhaṃ.

For just as a bull known as a *nisabha* (the pre-eminent bull), endowed with the strength of a bull, stands in an immovable position by pressing down upon the earth with his four feet, so too does he.
In the same way, the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four grounds of self-confidence,
having pressed down upon the earth of the eight assemblies, stands in an immovable state, unshakable by any adversary or enemy in the world including the devas.
Standing thus, he claims, approaches, and does not disavow that pre-eminent position (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*).
He attributes it to himself. Therefore it is said: “He claims the place of the bull.
Regarding “in assemblies”: “Sāriputta, there are these eight assemblies. Which eight?

The assembly of khattiyas, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā.”
In these eight assemblies, he "roars the lion’s roar" means he roars the best roar, the fearless roar;
or he roars a roar similar to that of a lion. This meaning should be illustrated by the *Sīhanāda-sutta*.

Or, just as a lion is called a "lion" (*sīha*) because of his endurance (*sahana*) and his slaying (*hana*), so too the Tathāgata is called a "lion" because of his endurance of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) and [his slaying] of the doctrines of others.
Because he kills, he is called a lion. The "lion's roar" is the roar of the lion spoken of in this way.
In that regard, just as a lion, endowed with lion-strength, fearless in every respect and free from horripilation, roars his lion’s roar;
even so the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata, is fearless in the eight assemblies and free from horripilation.
By means of the method beginning with “‘Such is form’,” he roars the lion’s roar, endowed with the manifold elegance of teaching. Therefore it is said:
“He roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies.
Regarding the phrase “he turns the Brahma-wheel”: here, *brahma* means supreme or most excellent; this refers to the pure wheel of Dhamma.
This is a designation. Furthermore, that Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*) is twofold: the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*).

Among these, the knowledge of penetration is developed through wisdom (*paññā*) and brings about the noble fruit for oneself; the knowledge of teaching is developed through compassion (*karuṇā*) and brings about the noble fruit for disciples.
Therein, the knowledge of penetration is twofold: that which is arising and that which has arisen.
For that [wisdom] which arises from the time of the Great Renunciation until the attainment of the path of Arahatship is said to have arisen at the moment of the fruition (phala-khaṇa).
Or, that which arises from the Tuṣita heaven until the attainment of the path of Arahatship on the Great Bodhi Seat is said to have arisen at the moment of the fruition.
Or, that which arises from the time of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until the attainment of the path of Arahatship is said to have arisen at the moment of the fruition.

It is called "arisen. The knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) is also twofold: that which is occurring while it is proceeding, and that which has occurred at the moment of the fruit (*phalakkhaṇa*). For as long as it proceeds until the stream-entry path of Aññā Koṇḍañña, it is called "proceeding";
at the moment of the fruit, it is called "occurred. Among these, the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) is supramundane (*lokuttara*), while the knowledge of teaching is mundane (*lokiya*).
Yet both of these are the unique, direct knowledge of the Buddhas alone, not shared by others.
Now, in order to show what the one endowed with this knowledge roars as a lion’s roar, he says:
"Thus, form," and so forth. Therein, "thus, form" means that this is form, this much is form; there is no form beyond this.

Beginning with its essential nature of being subject to change (*ruppana-sabhāva*) and its classification into the primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya*), this is the complete discernment of all form by way of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), function (*rasa*), manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
"...is said. Thus, by the phrase "the arising of form," the arising of form as thus comprehended is stated.
In that context, "iti" means "thus" or "in this way" the arising occurs. Its detailed explanation is: "With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of form;

with the arising of craving, the arising of karma, and the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form"—even one who sees the characteristic of production in this way [sees] the aggregate of form.
It should be understood thus: "He sees its arising. Regarding its passing away as well, the detailed explanation is: "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form... [and so on]...
even one who sees the characteristic of change sees the cessation of the aggregate of form.
Thus, regarding "this is feeling" and so forth: "This is feeling; this is the extent of feeling; beyond this there is no further feeling. This is perception... and so on.
"These are formations; this is consciousness; consciousness is only this much;

beyond this there is no further consciousness"—thus, beginning with the specific categories of feeling, perception, contact, and eye-consciousness, which have the natures of experiencing, perceiving, forming, and cognizing, as well as the forms of pleasure and so forth, the complete discernment of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness has been stated by way of their characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes. Thus, [the passage] beginning with "the origin of feeling" and so forth...
However, the arising of feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, when thus grasped, has been stated.

There too, "thus" (iti) means that such is the arising. Their detailed exposition should also be understood in the same manner as that stated for form: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling," and so forth.
This, however, is the distinction: in the case of the three aggregates, instead of saying "with the arising of nutriment," [it is said "with the arising of contact"].
“From the arising of contact” should be said [for the aggregate of feeling]; for the aggregate of consciousness, “from the arising of name-and-form.
The passage on their cessation should also be applied according to those same principles. This is the summary here.
For a detailed analysis of their arising and passing away, complete in all its aspects, it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"When this exists, that comes to be"—this is another lion's roar. Its meaning is:
when this condition, beginning with ignorance, exists, this result, beginning with volitional formations, comes to be. "With the arising of this, that arises":
with the arising of this condition, beginning with ignorance, this result, beginning with volitional formations, arises. "When this does not exist, that does not come to be."
When this condition, beginning with ignorance, is absent, this result, beginning with volitional formations, does not come to be.
"With the cessation of this, this ceases" means that with the cessation of this condition, beginning with ignorance, this result, beginning with volitional formations, ceases.
Now, in order to show in detail how that [result] both comes to be and ceases, it says: "That is to say..."
He said, "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth.
"Thus well-expounded" means it has been properly explained and taught by way of the analysis of the five aggregates and other such methods.

"Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma consisting of the five aggregates and the mode of conditions (paṭiccasamuppāda). "Shallow" means not crooked or obscure. "Revealed" means set forth after being opened up.
"Proclaimed" means illuminated or made manifest. "One whose rags are cut away": *pilotikā* refers to worn-out cloth that has been cut, torn, and sewn together with knots here and there;

one who does not possess such [rags], but instead wears a new garment (*sāṭaka*) eight or nine cubits in length that has never been washed—that person is called "one whose rags are cut away. This Dhamma is also like that; for herein, there is no...
There is a state of being cut, torn, sewn, or knotted by way of deceit and so forth. Furthermore, even a small garment is called "pilotika";
one who has no such thing, but possesses a large cloth eight or nine cubits long, is also said to have "cut pilotika," meaning his pilotika has been removed.
This Dhamma is like that. For just as one who, having taken a four-cubit garment, makes a formal acquisition [of it]...

A man searching here and there becomes weary; likewise, those who have gone forth in non-Buddhist systems become weary as they repeatedly construct and expand upon their own limited doctrine, thinking, "When this exists, that will come to be.
But just as one who searches with hands eight or nine cubits long puts on his garment according to his desire and does not grow weary, [so it is for the Buddha’s teaching].
There is no need for further patching or enlargement there; likewise, in this Dhamma, once it has been established, there is no need for further analysis.
Thinking, "This Dhamma has been well-analyzed and well-expounded by me alone through various reasons," he said, "one whose rags are torn away" (*chinnapilotiko*).
Furthermore, "rags" (*pilotika*) is also a term for refuse; and in this teaching, the refuse of ascetics is meant.
It does not obtain a footing. Therefore it was said:
"Expel the kāraṇḍava weed; cast out the rubbish;
then winnow away the chaff—the non-recluses who pride themselves on being recluses."
“Having expelled those of evil desires, those of evil conduct and resort,
dwell in purity with the pure, being mindful. Then,
being harmonious and vigilant, you will make an end to suffering.”
Thus, because the refuse of the ascetic life has been cut away, this Dhamma is called "one whose shreds are cut.
"It is indeed sufficient" means it is indeed appropriate. "By one gone forth through faith" means by one who has gone forth out of faith.
"A son of good family": there are two kinds of sons of good family—the son of good family by conduct and the son of good family by birth. Among these, he who has gone forth from whichever family...
One who fulfills the five aggregates of the Dhamma, beginning with virtue (*sīla*), is called a "noble son by conduct" (*ācārakulaputta*).
However, one who has gone forth from a family endowed with high birth, like those noble sons renowned for their fame and so forth, is called a "noble son by birth" (*jātikulaputta*).

Among these, it is the noble son by conduct who is intended here. Yet, if a noble son by birth is also possessed of good conduct, he is indeed the most excellent. [The phrase] "by such a noble son" refers to this.
"To arouse energy" means to exert energy endowed with four factors. Now, showing its four factors, he said:
"Willingly, even skin... and so forth. For here, skin is one factor, sinew is one, bone is one, and flesh and blood are one.
Furthermore, by one who resolves upon this energy endowed with four factors, in nine instances...
One should apply oneself before the meal, after the meal, during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch;
while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
"Monks, it is painful for one who dwells indolent" means that in this teaching, the person who is indolent experiences suffering.
He dwells. But in the external system, it is the one who is indolent who dwells in ease.
"Mingled" means mixed together. "One's own goal" (*sadattha*) means either a beautiful goal or one's own goal; by either sense, only Arahantship is intended.
"He lets fall" means he causes to fall away; he does not attain it. For the six doors of an indolent person remain unguarded.
There are three kinds of impure actions, and the morality of the eightfold livelihood is unpurified;
he has a corrupted livelihood and is one who frequents families. Being like dust fallen into the eye of his fellow celibates, he dwells in suffering;
he is a mere "cushion-crusher" and a "dung-filler," and he is unable to grasp the Teacher’s intention—this is difficult to find.
If one violates even for a moment, then even the alms-food of the entire kingdom, when eaten by him, does not yield great fruit.
But as for the one who has aroused energy, monks—that person who has aroused energy dwells happily right here in this teaching.
However, in an external system, he who has aroused energy dwells in suffering. "Secluded" means secluded.
Having become detached, he fulfills his own goal; that is, he attains arahantship.

For one who has aroused energy, the six doors are well-guarded, the three types of action are purified, and the eightfold morality of livelihood becomes radiant—becoming as pleasing as cool collyrium in the eye of a fellow celibate practitioner or like sandalwood applied to a wound.
He dwells in happiness and is able to grasp the Teacher’s intention.
For when Gotamī had thus paid homage, saying, “Live long, O Great Hero;

remain for an eon, O Great Sage,” the Teacher rejected it, saying, “Gotamī, the Tathāgatas are not to be honored in this way. Then, being requested by her, he explained the proper manner of homage and spoke as follows:
“Behold the disciples who are resolute in energy, dedicated, and always firm in their exertion,
living in harmony— this is the homage paid to the Buddhas.
Thus, one who has aroused energy is able to grasp the Teacher’s intention and does not squander this rare opportunity.
For him, indeed, the arising of a Buddha, the teaching of the Dhamma, and the excellent practice of the Saṅgha become fruitful and productive;
even the alms-food he has eaten becomes of great fruit.
"By the inferior for the superior" means: by inferior faith, by inferior energy, by inferior mindfulness, by inferior concentration, and by inferior...

The attainment of Arahantship, which is reckoned as the foremost, does not occur through wisdom alone. Rather, it is "by the foremost" (aggena) that the attainment of the foremost Arahantship occurs—namely, by means of the foremost qualities beginning with faith. It is called *maṇḍapeyya*:
"maṇḍa" in the sense of being the essence (*pasanna*), and "peyya" in the sense of being drinkable (*pātabba*).
For having drunk this, one falls unconscious in the middle of the street, becoming no longer the master even of one's own robes and so forth.
If it were [like that], even though one had faith, it should not be drunk; however, showing that my teaching is both thus faithful and drinkable, he said, "It is a *maṇḍapeyya*.

In this context, there are three kinds of *maṇḍa*: the *maṇḍa* of the teaching (*desanāmaṇḍa*), the *maṇḍa* of the recipient (*paṭiggahamaṇḍa*), and the *maṇḍa* of the holy life (*brahmacariyamaṇḍa*). What is the *maṇḍa* of the teaching?
The announcing, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, revealing, analyzing, and making plain of the Four Noble Truths; the announcing...
making plain of the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on] ...of the Noble Eightfold Path—this is the elixir of the teaching.
What is the elixir of the recipient? Monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, and gods...
Human beings or whoever else are capable of understanding—this is the essence of receiving. What is the essence of the holy life?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say: right view … [and so on] … right concentration. This is the essence of the holy life.
Furthermore, the essence of resolve is the faculty of faith; lack of faith is dregs. Lack of faith...

The meaning here should also be understood according to the method beginning with: "Having discarded the dregs, one drinks the essence of resolution for the faculty of faith; thus it is called 'the drink of the essence' (*maṇḍapeyya*)," and so forth.
"The Teacher is present" is the statement of the reason here. Because the Teacher is present, therefore, having applied energy, drink this essence. For the outsider...

Regarding the drinking of medicinal decoctions: when drinking them away from the physician, there is a suspicion that one does not know the proper measure, nor the time of their administration or their digestion.
However, when drinking in the presence of the physician, they drink without such suspicion, thinking, "The physician will know.
In the same way, thinking, "Our Teacher, the Master of Dhamma, is present," you should exert effort and drink [the medicine]. Thus it is with the drinking of the decoction.

Addressing them with these words, he said, "Therefore, monks... and so forth. In this context, "fruitful" (*saphalā*) means accompanied by benefits; "prosperous" (*saudrayā*) means accompanied by growth.
Now, pointing out the training to be practiced in accordance with that exhortation, he said, "For one's own sake, monks... and so forth.

In this context, "one's own welfare" (*attattha*) refers to Arahantship, which constitutes one's own true benefit. "To accomplish through diligence" (*appamādena sampādetuṃ*) means by means of heedfulness.
To perform all duties. "For the sake of others" means for the great fruit and benefit for those who provide the requisites. The rest is clear in every respect.
This is the second [sutta].
3. Commentary on the Upanisā Sutta.
23. Regarding the third [verse], in the passage beginning with “of one who knows” (*jānato*), “one who knows” (*jānato*) means of one who is knowing.
“One who sees” (*passato*) means of one who is seeing. Both words have the same meaning; only the phrasing (*byañjana*) differs.

Even so, the person is designated by the term “one who knows” by taking the characteristic of knowledge (*ñāṇalakkhaṇa*). For knowledge has the characteristic of knowing. The term “one who sees” is used by taking the radiance of knowledge (*ñāṇappabhāva*). For the radiance of seeing—
Knowledge (*ñāṇa*)—the person possessing knowledge (*ñāṇasamaṅgīpuggala*)—sees the phenomena revealed by knowledge through that knowledge, just as one with eyes sees forms with the eye.

Regarding the phrase "the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khaya*): here, the abandoning of the taints, their non-arising, the state of being exhausted, and the state of non-existence are all called "the destruction of the taints"; so too are their dissolution, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. This is seen in such passages as: "Through the destruction of the taints, the taintless liberation of mind... and so forth.

For the mode of exhaustion is called the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*). In the passage, “That which is the destruction, the passing away, the breaking up, the dissolution, the impermanence, and the disappearance of the taints,” it refers to dissolution. [As it is said:
“Of one in training, who is still practicing, following the straight path...”
“The first knowledge is regarding destruction; thereafter comes the subsequent higher knowledge. Herein, this refers to the Path.
For it arises as it expels and pacifies the taints (āsava); therefore, it is called the "destruction of the taints.
In the passage, “Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse,” this refers to the Fruit. For that arises at the moment the taints are destroyed; therefore—
"It is called the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya).
[It is said: ‘The taints increase for him; he is far from the destruction of the taints.
Herein, it is Nibbāna. For by resorting to that, the taints are destroyed; therefore it is called the destruction of the taints. Herein..."
However, the paths and fruits are intended here. "Not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see" means: "I do not speak to him who neither knows nor sees.
By this, those who claim that purification comes from the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and so forth even for one who does not know and does not see are refuted.
With the first two phrases, the means was stated; by this [phrase], he negates what is not the means.
Now, desiring to show that for which the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) occurs for one who knows, he began the inquiry:
"And what, bhikkhus, does one know? In this context, knowing is of many kinds.

For instance, a certain bhikkhu by nature is skilled in making a sunshade, while another is skilled in making any one of the robes and so forth; such works as these [are performed] by standing at the head of the duties (*vattasīsa*).
It should not be said that such knowledge, while performing [medical acts], is not the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the paths and fruits of heaven.
However, for one who has gone forth in the Dispensation and knows how to perform medical practices and the like, the taints (*āsava*) increase precisely for one who knows in this way.
Therefore, demonstrating that very thing by which the destruction of the taints occurs for one who knows and sees, he said: "Thus is form," and so forth.
"Thus, monks, for one who knows": this means for one who knows the arising and passing away of the five aggregates.
"The destruction of the taints occurs": because it is born at the time of the destruction of the taints, Arahantship receives the name "the destruction of the taints.
Having thus concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship, [the Buddha now describes] the preliminary path to be traversed by one whose taints are destroyed.

To show this, he said, "And as for that of his, monks," and so forth. Therein, "knowledge of destruction" (*khaye ñāṇa*) is the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*) when the fruit of arhatship—designated as the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*)—has been attained.

For that is called "knowledge of destruction" because it arises subsequently once the destruction designated as the fruit of arhatship has first arisen. "With its proximate cause" (*sa-upanisā*) means together with its cause.
"With condition" means that liberation—namely, the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship—is its condition by way of decisive support (upanissaya-paccaya).
In this manner, the status of being a condition for the subsequent factors should also be understood according to how they are applicable.
"Dispassion" refers to the Path; for it arises dispelling and casting out the defilements, and is therefore called "dispassion."
"Disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) means knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*). By this, he shows powerful insight (*balava-vipassanā*).

"Powerful insight" is a designation for four types of knowledge: knowledge of the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*), knowledge of contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*), knowledge of the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*), and knowledge of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).
"Knowledge and vision according to reality" (*yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana*) is vision consisting in the knowing of things according to their true nature. By this...
This shows nascent insight (*taruṇavipassanā*). For nascent insight is a condition for powerful insight.

"Nascent insight" is a designation for four knowledges: the knowledge of delimitation of formations, the knowledge of overcoming doubt, the knowledge of comprehension, and the knowledge of what is and is not the path.
"Concentration" refers to the concentration of the foundational jhāna; for that [concentration] is the basis for nascent insight.
It is a condition. "Happiness" (sukha) refers to the happiness prior to absorption (appanā). For that is a condition for the foundational jhāna.
"Tranquility" (passaddhi) refers to the subsiding of distress. For that is a condition for the happiness prior to absorption.
"Rapture" (pīti) refers to strong rapture. For that is a condition for the subsiding of distress. "Gladness" (pāmojja) refers to weak rapture.
For that [joy] is a condition for strong joy (*pīti*). "Faith" (*saddhā*) refers to faith arising repeatedly; for that is a condition for weak joy.
"Suffering" (*dukkha*) refers to the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*); for that is a condition for repeated faith.

"Birth" (*jāti*) refers to the birth of the aggregates along with their modifications; for that is a condition for the suffering of the round of existence. "Becoming" (*bhava*) refers to kamma-becoming. (It...)
For it is a condition for birth that is subject to change. By this same method, the remaining phrases should also be understood.
"Thullaphusitaka" means large raindrops. Regarding "pabbatakandarapadarasākhā":
here, a *kandara* is a mountain region split by water—that is, cleaved by water—obtaining the name "ka"; it is what is also called a "slope" (*nitamba*) or a "river-gorge" (*nadīkuñja*).
It is said thus. "A plateau" (*padara*) refers to a region of ground that has become fertile when the rain does not fall for eight months.

"Streams" (*sākhā*) refers to small watercourses leading toward the *kusumbha* river. "Pools" (*kusobbha*) refers to small reservoirs. "Large pools" (*mahāsobbha*) refers to large reservoirs. "Small rivers" (*kunnadī*) refers to minor streams. "Great rivers" (*mahānadī*) refers to the great rivers such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
In the same way, monks, regarding the statements "with ignorance as a condition, volitional formations arise," and so forth:

Ignorance (*avijjā*) should be regarded as a mountain; volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhārā*) as clouds; the cycle of existence beginning with consciousness (*viññāṇa*) as mountain clefts and the like;

and liberation (*vimutti*) as the ocean. Just as when rain falls upon the summit of a mountain and fills its clefts and other hollows, it gradually fills the great ocean, the sea—so too should the falling of the cloud of volitional formations upon the summit of the mountain of ignorance be understood.
For the uninstructed worldling, being ignorant through lack of true knowledge (*avijjā*) and having formed a longing through craving (*taṇhā*), accumulates wholesome and unwholesome kamma.

That wholesome and unwholesome kamma becomes the condition for rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*); the rebirth-linking consciousness and the subsequent factors become the conditions for name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*) and so forth.
Thus, it is like rain falling on the summit of a mountain filling the caves and other hollows until they reach the great ocean.

Just as when [a cloud] stands having struck [a mountain], so too is the period during which the whirlpool of consciousness and the rest is fulfilled and persists through the successive conditionality of the volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) that have arisen on the summit of the mountain of ignorance.
Furthermore, even though it is not explicitly mentioned in the Pāḷi, the word of the Buddha [is understood] by virtue of this passage:
"Here, a Tathāgata arises in the world; he goes forth from the home life into homelessness."
