It should be understood that this has indeed been included. For that birth which occurs in his family home is called "birth" (jāti) with its concomitant variations, conditioned by kamma-existence (kammabhava).

When he comes into the presence of Buddhas or Buddha-disciples and hears a discourse on the Dhamma brought forth by the [thirty-two] marks, which illuminates the defects of the round of existence (vaṭṭa), he becomes oppressed by the round; thus, for him, there is the birth of the aggregates (khandhajāti) with its concomitant variations.

It becomes a condition for the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*). Oppressed by that suffering of the round, he generates faith again and again and goes forth from the household life into homelessness; thus, the suffering of the round becomes a condition for his successive acts of faith.

Not satisfied with mere going-forth, while still less than five years old [in the Saṅgha], he takes formal dependence (*nissaya*) and, fulfilling the performance of duties, becomes proficient in the two Matikas.

Having determined what is to be done and what is not to be done, and having mastered the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) up to the stage of Arahantship, one dwells in the forest with the subject made free from tangles.
Therein, one begins the work upon the earth-kasiṇa and so forth; supported by that meditation subject, weak rapture (pīti) arises.
This is his joy (pāmojja) conditioned by faith, which becomes the condition for strong rapture. Strong rapture...
Through the subsiding of distress, there is that access-concentration (appanā-pubbabhāga-sukha); that happiness is the condition for the foundational jhāna-concentration.
Having produced mental pliancy by means of that concentration, he performs the work of nascent insight (taruṇa-vipassanā).
Thus, for him, the foundational jhāna-concentration is the condition for nascent insight; nascent insight is the condition for powerful insight (balava-vipassanā). Powerful insight...
The path [is the cause] for the liberation of the fruit; the liberation of the fruit [is the cause] for the knowledge of reviewing.

Thus, the time when the ocean of liberation is filled and established for one whose taints are destroyed should be understood as being like the time when the god’s ocean is gradually filled and established.
This is the third [section].
4. Commentary on the Aññatitthiyasutta 24.

In the fourth [verse], "he entered" (*pāvisi*) means he had already entered. However, although he had not yet actually entered, it is stated thus because he had set out with the intention, "I shall enter.
How so? Just as a man who has set out with the thought, "I shall go to the village," is described in that way even though he has not yet reached that village.
When it was asked, "Where is so-and-so?", it was replied, "He has gone to the village. Likewise, regarding the phrase "it is too early": it is said that on that day, the Elder departed very early;

likewise, the monks who had departed very early spent time in delay in these places—the Bodhi-terrace, the Cetiya-terrace, and the place for putting on and taking off their lower and upper robes—until the time for the alms-round arrived.

But as the Elder was thinking, "Until it is time for the alms-round, I shall engage in one or two discourses with these wanderers," the thought occurred to him: "What if I were to go there? He meant the Wanderers' Park;
it is said that this park was located between the Southern Gate and the Veḷuvana. "Here" refers to among these four doctrines. "What-doctrine-holders"?
"What does he proclaim? means: what does he say, what does he explain? They ask, "What is there to be seen here of the ascetic Gotama?
[The answer is: "We would explain in accordance with the Dhamma" means: we would speak of the reasons in conformity with the reason stated by the venerable Gotama.
"A reasoned discourse in accordance with the Dhamma" means: being possessed of reasons, [we would respond] to the reasons stated by others regarding the ascetic...
How could even the slightest reason for censure—any occurrence of a thesis or the pursuit of a doctrine by the ascetic Gotama—not come to be condemned by the wise?
This is what is meant: how could there not be, in every respect, a ground for censuring the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama?
"Thus they say: 'Suffering has contact as its condition'—this is the meaning of 'they say thus.
In that context, 'among those four doctrines,' the phrase 'surely those [feelings] are apart from contact' is a statement intended to prove the admission that 'even that has contact as its condition.
For since there is no experiencing of suffering without contact, it should therefore be understood that even that..."
"Conditioned by contact"—this is the intended meaning here.
"Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!"—this expression of approval was given to the Elder Sāriputta;
however, the Blessed One addressed it to him while together with the Elder Ānanda. In the phrase "at one time," *idha* is a mere particle; [it means] "on one occasion."
The meaning is as follows. This statement was spoken to show: "It was not only Sāriputta who entered Rājagaha; I too entered.
It was not only to him that this reflection arose; it also arose to me. It was not only with him that such a discussion with the sectarians took place; it has also occurred to me before."
“Wonderful! Marvelous!”—both of these terms merely indicate amazement. As for the meaning of the words here:
it is called *acchariya* because it is worthy of clapping one’s hands (*accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttaṃ*); it is called *abbhuta* because what had never occurred before has now occurred.
By the single phrase means by this single phrase: “With contact as condition, there is suffering. For by this, the sense of the refutation of all [other] doctrines is stated. This is the meaning.
"This very thing is suffering with contact as its condition"—this is the meaning of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

"May that itself appear here" means may that itself be present here. Now, the Elder, making that [meaning] both profound in its sense and profound in its appearance through a discourse on dependent origination beginning with aging-and-death, said, "If, venerable sir," and so forth, [introducing] the discourse that had arisen from that root.

Having grasped that very point and demonstrating the turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭa*), he spoke the words beginning with "But rather, when covered" (*channantveva*). The remainder is self-evident. This is the fourth [sutta]. 5.
Commentary on the Bhūmija Sutta (25–26).
In the fifth [sutta], "Bhūmija" is the name of that elder. The rest here also follows the same method as stated in the previous sutta.
This should be understood. However, this is the distinction: because this pleasure and pain do not arise solely from the condition of contact;
they are also produced when performed by the body, by speech, or by the mind;
they are produced when performed by oneself, or when performed by another; and they are produced when performed with full awareness, or even without full awareness.
Therefore, in order to show another specific condition for that [feeling], he said: "Or, Ānanda, when there is mindfulness regarding the body," and so forth.
"Caused by bodily volition" means caused by volition arisen at the door of the body. The same method applies to vocal volition and mental volition as well.
And here, twenty types of volition are found at the door of the body by way of wholesome and unwholesome states of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara); likewise at the door of speech.
In the mind-door, there are twenty-nine volitions together with nine types of volition pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial realms;
thus, across the three doors, there are sixty-nine volitions. The resultant pleasure and pain conditioned by them have been shown.

The phrase "and with ignorance as condition" is stated for the purpose of showing that those volitions, too, have ignorance as their condition. For it is because of that aforementioned classification of volitions...
Whether it be a bodily formation, a verbal formation, or a mental formation, he performs it himself with a volitional mind (*asaṅkhārika-citta*) even when not urged by others;
he performs it even with a volitional mind (*sasaṅkhārika-citta*) when being made to do so by others;
and he performs it even while knowing both the action and its result, thinking: "One performs such-and-such an action, and for that, such-and-such a result will come to pass."

Just as children imitate their parents when they perform such acts as worshipping at a cetiya, one performs action knowing only the act itself—even without knowing its result, thinking "this is the result of this action. Therefore, in order to demonstrate that, it was said:
"Or he himself, Ānanda, performs that bodily formation," and so forth.

“In these states, Ānanda”: those seventy-two hundred volitional states (cetanā-dhamma) which have been mentioned in these four places beginning with “either himself, Ānanda, that bodily formation,” etc.—in these states, ignorance (avijjā) has descended by way of decisive support (upanissaya-koṭi).
For all of them are included right here under the formula: “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations (saṅkhārā). Now...

Showing the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*), he said, "But as for ignorance," and so forth. "That body does not exist" means that the body, when which body exists, internal pleasure and pain arise conditioned by bodily volition (*kāyasañcetanā*), that body does not exist.
The same method applies to speech and mind as well. Furthermore, "body" refers to the body of volition;
"speech" is the speech of volition; and "mind" is precisely the mind of karma. Alternatively, "body" refers to the body of the sense-door (*dvārakāya*). The same applies to speech and mind.

The same principle applies here. When one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) pays homage at a shrine, recites the Dhamma, or attends to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), how is it that his body and the other aggregates do not exist?
It is because [his action] is without karmic result (avipāka). For an action performed by one whose taints are destroyed is neither wholesome nor unwholesome;
being without karmic result, it remains as mere functional activity (kiriyāmatta). Therefore, it is said that those aggregates—the body and so forth—do not exist for him.
In the phrases "that is not a field," and so forth: in the sense of growing, it is not a field;
in the sense of being a foundation, it is not a site; in the sense of being a condition, it is not a base; in the sense of being a cause, it is not a source.
For internal pleasure and pain would arise rooted in volition (*sañcetanā*); that volition is the cause for these [states] of growing and so on.
Because of the absence of a basis, that pleasure and pain has neither field, nor substance, nor sphere, nor foundation.
In this sutta, among feeling and the rest, only pleasure and pain are discussed, and those too are exclusively kamma-result (vipāka). The fifth [sutta] is finished.
The sixth, the Upavāṇa Sutta, is self-evident; however, here it is the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha) alone that is discussed. The sixth is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Paccayasutta* (Suttas 27–28).
In the seventh [sutta], taking the final phrase from those stated in successive order, it is said: "And what, bhikkhus, is aging-and-death? and so forth.
"Thus he understands the condition" means that he understands the condition by way of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). The arising of conditions and so forth are likewise understood.
It should be understood by way of the truth of origination and the others alone. "One endowed with right view" means one who is endowed with the view of the Path.
"Endowed with vision" is a synonym for that same term. "Has come to this True Dhamma" means he has come to the True Dhamma of the Path.

"He sees" means he sees precisely the True Dhamma of the Path. "By means of the knowledge of one in training" means by means of the knowledge of the Path itself. "By means of the clear vision of one in training" [means the same].
"Only by means of the knowledge of the path. "Has entered the stream of the Dhamma" means he has entered the very stream of the Dhamma known as the path.
"Noble" means one who has transcended the plane of the worldlings (*puthujjana*). "Possessing penetrative wisdom" means endowed with penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhika-paññā*).
"Standing knocking at the door of the Deathless" means that the Deathless is Nibbāna; standing knocking at its door, which is the Noble Path.
"It remains. The eighth [sutta] is self-evident. These are the seventh and eighth. 9.
Commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta (29–30).
The ninth was spoken with reference to the inclinations of monks who were reciters of the letter; for they are able to penetrate the meaning when it is spoken by adding the prefix *pari*. The ninth.
In the tenth [sutta], everything is quite clear. In these two suttas, only the penetration of the Four Noble Truths is discussed. The tenth [is finished].
The third chapter, the Chapter on the Ten Powers, is concluded.
4. The Chapter on the Kaḷāra Khattiya.
1. Commentary on the Bhūta Sutta 31.
Regarding the first question in the *Kaḷārakhattiya-vagga*, the "Question of Ajita": it refers to the questions asked by the young brahmin Ajita.

"Those who have measured the Dhamma" (*saṅkhātadhammā*) means those for whom the Dhamma has been measured, weighed, scrutinized, and fully determined. "Learners" (*sekkhā*) refers to the seven types of learners (*sekkhā*).
"Many" (*puthū*) is said with reference to those same seven persons. "Here" (*idha*) means in this teaching. "Clever" (*nipaka*):
"cleverness" (*nepakka*) is said to be wisdom; because he is endowed with that, he is clever. "Tell me, O wise one" (*pabrūhi*)—thus he requests.
"Conduct" (*iriyaṃ*) refers to livelihood, behavior, range, dwelling, and practice. "O Venerable One" (*mārisa*)—with this he addresses the Blessed One.
"O wise one, dear sir, please tell me the practice of those in training, of those who have mastered the Dhamma, and of those whose taints are destroyed"—this is the summary meaning here.
As for the statement "he remained silent": why did he remain silent even when asked up to three times? Was it because he was uncertain about the question, or rather because of his own inclination?
He was in doubt regarding the Teacher’s intention, not regarding the question itself. He thought to himself:

“The Teacher wishes me to explain the path leading to the attainment of the stages of training and beyond-training. That can be explained through many methods—by way of the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, and the structure of conditions.
How, then, shall I grasp the Teacher’s intention as I speak?”
“...will I be able to explain? Then the Teacher thought: “Aside from me, there is no disciple wandering with a bowl who is equal to Sāriputta in wisdom.
Even when asked this question by me, he has remained silent up to the third time.
Does he hesitate regarding the question, or rather regarding his own inclination? Then, knowing it was regarding his inclination, [the Teacher] spoke for the purpose of answering the question.

"Does he see this as 'it has come to be'?"— thus the Teacher gave the Elder Sāriputta a method, saying, "Sāriputta, explain this question by way of the five aggregates. By granting that method, the Elder [was enabled to proceed].
The answering of the question appeared to him through hundreds and thousands of methods, like the great ocean with its vast, open expanse revealed to a man standing on the shore.
Then, while explaining it to him, he said, "This, venerable sir, is what has come to be," and so forth. Therein, "this has come to be" (*bhūtam idam*) refers to this arisen pentad of aggregates.
"One sees with right wisdom" (*sammappaññāya passati*) means with the wisdom of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*).
He sees rightly. "He is practicing" means that from the stage of virtue up to the path of Arahantship, he is practicing for the sake of disenchantment and so forth.
Why was this begun? This pentad of aggregates exists dependent upon nutriment;
therefore, this was begun in order to show it by designating it as "arisen from nutriment. Thus, by this as well...
Thus, by way of this method, the practice of one in training (sekha) has been explained. "By the cessation of their nutriment" means by the cessation of those nutriments.

Why was this undertaken? Because that pentad of aggregates ceases through the cessation of nutriment; therefore, this was undertaken to show it by designating it as "arising from the cessation of nutriment.
Thus, even by this method, the practice of one in training alone has been explained.

It should be understood that all terms beginning with "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) are words expressing causes. "Liberated through non-clinging" (*anupādā vimutto*) means liberated without grasping at any phenomenon through the four types of clinging.
Having encouraged the Elder’s explanation with "Excellent, excellent!
(*sādhu sādhu*), the Blessed One himself, explaining in the same manner, spoke again the passage beginning with "This has come to be" (*bhūtam idam*). First.
2. Commentary on the Kaḷāra Sutta 32.
In the second [sutta], "Kaḷāra the Khattiya" is the name of that elder. His teeth, however, were black and unevenly shaped;
therefore, he is called "Kaḷāra. "Returned to the low life" means returned for the sake of the inferior state of a householder. "He obtained consolation" means...
This indicates that he surely did not obtain consolation, support, or a firm foundation; indeed, he surely did not obtain the three paths and the three fruits.
For if he had obtained those, he would certainly not have renounced the training and returned to the lower life—this is the elder’s intention.
"Indeed, friends, I do not doubt," means: "Friends, I do not doubt whether I have attained consolation or not."
For the Elder’s knowledge of the perfection of discipleship (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*) was his support; therefore, he did not doubt.

With the words, "But as for the future life, friend," he asks whether or not the attainment of Arahantship has been disclosed to him by the statement, "Rebirth in the future has been disclosed to you.
With the words, "I do not doubt it, friend," the Elder demonstrates the absence of doubt regarding that matter.
“He approached where the Blessed One was” means he approached thinking, “I will inform the Blessed One of this reason for hearing [this discourse].
“The final knowledge was declared” means the state of Arahatship was declared. “Birth is exhausted” was not declared by the Elder himself;
rather, this Elder, being joyful and full of faith, spoke thus after arranging the words and phrases. “He addressed a certain bhikkhu.”
Upon hearing this, the Teacher thought: "Sāriputta is wise and profound; he would not provide such an answer for any other reason.
This question must have been answered in brief. I shall summon him and have him explain the answer.
With this in mind, he addressed a certain bhikkhu.
“Sāriputta, if that is so,” the Blessed One asked this in order to have him declare his full enlightenment, thinking:
“He will not declare his enlightenment of his own accord; I shall ask him this question, and while he is answering it, he will declare his enlightenment.
“Friend, that which is the source of birth”: friend, this so-called “birth” is that for which there is a condition; when that condition is exhausted through its destruction...

It was known that the fruit designated as "birth" had been exhausted due to the condition of birth. Here too, the Elder did not hesitate regarding the question itself, but he hesitated regarding the underlying intention.

For it occurred to him: "It can be explained through many reasons, such as 'craving is exhausted,' 'clinging is exhausted,' 'existence is exhausted,' 'the condition is exhausted,' or 'defilements are exhausted. How [should I answer]?"
"However, while speaking, I shall be able to grasp the Teacher's intention.
Although he thus had doubts regarding the Teacher's intention, he nevertheless answered according to the formula of dependent origination (paccayākāra) without posing a question.
The Teacher also desired that he should answer precisely according to the formula of dependent origination; therefore, as he was answering, he grasped the [Teacher's] intention.
At that very moment, he realized, "I have grasped the Teacher’s intention. Then, the answering of his questions appeared to him by way of a hundred methods and a thousand methods.
However, because the Blessed One asked further questions, it should be understood that the latter approved of that explanation.
But why was this begun with the words, "How does one who knows...? It was in order to cause him to roar the lion’s roar within his own domain.

It is said that while the Elder was standing at the entrance of the Boar-Dug Cave, fanning the Teacher with a palm-leaf fan as the Paribbājaka Dīghanakha was being taught the *Vedanāpariggaha Sutta*, he attained the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*) by comprehending the three kinds of feeling.
This has been realized; this is his own domain. Standing within this domain, he will roar the lion’s roar—it was with reference to him that the Teacher asked this question.
"Impermanent" means impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having existed.
Regarding the statement, "What is impermanent is suffering," although pleasant feeling is pleasant in its persistence and painful in its change, and painful feeling is painful in its persistence...
Pleasures of change, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling], knowledge as pleasure, and ignorance as pain— all these,
at the limit of change, are indeed called suffering. "Known" means that because this triad of feelings has been known as suffering,
it shows that craving for them does not arise.
"Excellent, excellent!"—this was the Blessed One’s encouragement of the Elder regarding his knowledge of the delimitation of feelings (*vedanā-pariccheda-jānana*).
For the Elder, even though it had not been stated whether there were one, two, three, or four feelings, understood their delimitation as "three" according to the method already explained;
therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus while encouraging him. "In suffering"—the Blessed One said this with the following intention:
He said: “Sāriputta, that which you declared—‘For this reason, craving did not arise toward feelings’—was well-declared.
However, by analyzing them as ‘three kinds of feeling,’ you have made it overly prolix;
for even had you declared them simply as ‘in suffering,’ it would have been well-declared. For when one merely knows that whatever is felt is suffering...”
"Indeed, craving does not abide in feelings.
What is meant by "by what liberation"? Which liberation? By what liberation was your final knowledge (aññā) declared?
"By internal liberation" means by means of internal liberation—that is, having comprehended internal formations and attained Arhatship.
The meaning. In this regard, a tetrad should be understood: internal misapprehension with internal emergence;
internal misapprehension with external emergence; external misapprehension with external emergence;
and external misapprehension with internal emergence. For having misapprehended internally, one must indeed also see external phenomena.
Having focused externally, one also [focuses] on internal phenomena. Therefore, a certain bhikkhu, having applied knowledge to internal formations and defined them, applies it externally;
and having comprehended them externally, he again applies it internally.
At the time of his full comprehension (*sammasana*) of internal formations, the emergence of the Path occurs. Thus, internally...
Internal fixation is called emergence within. Someone, having introduced knowledge into internal formations and defined them, introduces it externally;
for him, at the time of comprehending external formations, there is emergence via the Path.
Thus, internal fixation is called emergence externally. Someone [fixes] upon external formations...
Having applied knowledge and defined those [external formations], he applies it internally; having discerned them internally as well, he again applies it externally.
At the time of comprehending external formations, his emergence occurs via the Path.
Thus, the application of attention to external formations is called "emergence externally. Someone else, having applied knowledge to external formations...
Having defined them, he brings them inward; at the time of comprehending the internal formations, the emergence of the Path occurs for him.
Thus, external fixation is what is called "emergence within.
In this context, the Elder, demonstrating that "by discerning the internal formations and defining them, I attained Arahantship through the emergence of the Path," said:
"I have indeed attained internal liberation, friends," he said.
"By the destruction of all clinging" means by the destruction of all four kinds of clinging.
"I dwell mindful in that manner" means I dwell endowed with mindfulness in that way. "As one dwelling mindfully" means in whatever manner I am mindful...

Dwelling thus endowed [with these qualities], the taints do not flow forth: "from the eye, taints flow, flow forth, stream out, and proceed toward forms"—thus, through the six doors and with respect to the six objects, the taints such as the taint of sensual desire, which are by nature prone to flow, do not flow forth and do not increase;
the meaning is that they do not arise in me. And I do not despise myself.
"And I do not despise myself. By this, the abandoning of self-contempt is stated. For when it is thus, understanding becomes clear.

"By a recluse" means by a recluse who is a Buddha. "I have no doubt regarding them" means that regarding those [taints], I have no doubt as to which is the taint of sensual desire, which is the taint of existence, which is the taint of views, and which is the taint of ignorance—thus even according to their specific distinctions—and "the four..."
Regarding the phrase "the taints," I have no doubt even as to this numerical limitation.
"They have been abandoned by me" means that I do not give rise to doubt, thinking, "They have been abandoned by me. The Blessed One said:
"Even if you were to answer thus, it would be well-explained; however, when you say such things as, 'Friend, I am inwardly liberated,' etc.," [he spoke].
Showing that "too much elaboration has been made," he said this.

"Rising from his seat, he entered the monastery" means that having risen from the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, he entered the monastery—the interior of the Great Fragrant Chamber—while the assembly remained undispersed.
Why? Because Buddhas [do not depart] until the teaching is finished and the assembly is dispersed.

When rising from his seat and entering the Fragrant Chamber after the assembly has departed, the Teacher enters either for the purpose of praising an individual or for the purpose of praising the Dhamma.
On such occasions, when entering for the purpose of praising an individual, the Teacher reflects thus:
"The monks who have received this Dhamma from me—briefly recited as a summary but not yet analyzed in detail—will [entrust it] to Ānanda..."
Or if they approach Kaccāyana and ask him, he will explain it to them by reconciling it with my own knowledge;
and those who receive the Dhamma from him will in turn ask me about it. To them I shall say: "Well spoken, monks, by Ānanda!
Well spoken, monks, by Kaccāyana! If you had asked me this matter, I too would have explained it in exactly the same way."
“I shall praise those persons in such a way that they would answer me thus: ‘It is even so.
Then, having conceived reverence for them, the monks will approach them; and those monks will direct them toward the goal and the Dhamma.
Directed by them, they will fulfill the three trainings and make an end of suffering.”
Or else, it occurs to him: "When I have departed, he will display his own power; then I too shall praise him in that same way.

Hearing my praise, the monks, having conceived a sense of reverence, will think that they ought to approach him, listen to his words, and place their trust in them; this will be for their long-term welfare."
Entering for the sake of praising the Dhamma with the thought, "for their welfare and happiness," he reflected just as he had reflected in the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta*.

For there, it occurred to him: "When I have entered the monastery, while censuring those who are heirs to material things and praising those who are heirs to the Dhamma, Sāriputta, sitting right here in this assembly, will teach the Dhamma; thus both of us..."
“Taught with a mind that shares our single intention, this teaching will become supreme and weighty, like a stone parasol.

Then, wishing to exalt and proclaim the Venerable Sāriputta and establish him [in his position], he rose from his seat and entered his dwelling for the purpose of honoring the individual. In such instances, the Blessed One, while still at his sitting place, vanished by means of the movement of his mind.
It should be understood that he enters the monastery. For if he had gone by means of his physical movement, the entire assembly would have followed surrounding the Blessed One;
thus, once broken up, it would be difficult for them to gather again. Therefore, the Blessed One entered by means of the movement of his mind alone, with his body remaining invisible.

When the Blessed One had thus entered, the Venerable Sāriputta—desiring to let out a lion’s roar in accordance with the Blessed One’s own intention—addressed the bhikkhus there shortly after the Blessed One had departed:
"Previously unknown" means that this was not previously informed to me, nor was it understood by me, thinking, "He will ask this question. Regarding the phrase "the first question": "If he..."
"Sāriputta, they might ask this first question: 'But friend Sāriputta, knowing what and seeing what have you declared final knowledge—that birth is exhausted?
[In this context] 'hesitation' (*dandhāyitatta*) means slowness or lack of speed for the purpose of discerning the Teacher's intention.
He approved of the first question with the words: 'But friend Sāriputta, what is the source of birth?'"
By asking this second question, he expressed his approval of the first question, which had been answered thus: “Friend, that from which birth has its source.

“It occurred to him” means that because the Blessed One had approved [the answer] through hundreds and thousands of methods, such that the single-pointedness of the question became manifest, it occurred to him.
“I could explain this matter to the Blessed One even for an entire day” means throughout the whole day.
“If asked about this meaning of dependent origination by the Blessed One, I could explain it with various words and phrases for an entire day.

Thinking, “The Elder is letting out a sublime lion’s roar; this is a good opportunity—I shall report this to the One of Ten Powers,” he approached the Blessed One. Thus it was that he went to where the Blessed One was.
Regarding the phrase "for that, O Bhikkhu, is the Dhammadhātu of Sāriputta":

here, "Dhammadhātu" refers to the disciple’s knowledge of mastery (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*), which is capable of demonstrating the manifestation of the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). For the disciple’s knowledge of mastery follows the same course as the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*);
just as past, future, and present phenomena are manifest to the omniscience of the Buddhas, so too [are they] to this.
The Elder’s knowledge of the perfection of a disciple's knowledge knows all the phenomena that are within the range of a disciple's knowledge. This is the second [section].

3. Commentary on the Sutta on the Bases of Knowledge (Ñāṇavatthusutta): In the third [section], "Listen to that" means listen to this exposition of the bases of knowledge. And here, "bases of knowledge" refers to knowledge itself.
It should be understood as "bases of knowledge" (*ñāṇavatthu*). Regarding the four [knowledges] beginning with "knowledge of aging-and-death," the first [knowledge] consists of four types:
knowledge consisting of hearing, knowledge of comprehension, knowledge of penetration, and knowledge of review. The second is likewise.
However, the third consists of only three types, excluding knowledge of comprehension; the fourth is likewise. This applies to supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*) as well.
For there is no such thing as "comprehension" (sammasana) [without this]. The same principle applies to such phrases as "knowledge of birth" and so forth.
"By this Dhamma" means either by this Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths or by the Dhamma of the knowledge of the Path (maggañāṇa).
Regarding the terms "seen," etc.: "seen" means seen by the eye of knowledge (ñāṇacakkhu); "known" means known by wisdom (paññā); "timeless" (akālika) means...
Without allowing even a short time to pass, immediately after the penetration itself, by means of that which bestows the fruit. *Pattena* means by what has been attained.
*Pariyogāḷhena* means by what has been thoroughly penetrated, having entered into it by means of wisdom (*paññā*).

"He leads the method regarding the past and the future" means that he leads the method regarding both the past and the future by way of the formula beginning with "Whatever [monks]... And here, it is not by means of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths...
Or, by means of the knowledge of the path (maggañāṇa), it is possible to apply the method to the past and the future;

however, when the Four Truths have been penetrated by the knowledge of the path, there subsequently arises what is called the knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa). It should be understood that one applies the method by means of that [reviewing knowledge].
"They directly knew" (abbhaññaṃsu) means they fully understood (abhi-aññaṃsu) or knew. "Just as I do now" (seyyathāpāhaṃ, etarahī) means just as I [do] now by way of the Four Truths.

"I know. "Knowledge by way of inference" (*anvaye ñāṇaṃ*) means knowledge following after; it is knowledge that follows upon the knowledge of the Dhamma. This is a name for the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).
"Knowledge regarding the Dhamma" (*dhamme ñāṇaṃ*) is the knowledge of the Path (*maggañāṇa*). In this sutta, the stage of the trainee (*sekkhabhūmi*) of one whose taints are exhausted is described.
Third. 4. Commentary on the Second Sutta on the Bases of Knowledge.
34. "In the fourth [section], 'seventy-seven' means seven and seventy. It is said that those monks were reciters of the letter (*byañjanabhāṇaka*);
they were able to penetrate the teaching when it was spoken with many words. Therefore, this sutta was spoken according to their inclination.

'Knowledge of the stability of phenomena' (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is knowledge regarding the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). For the mode of conditions is the cause for the persistence of the occurrence of phenomena."

It is called "the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhiti*); knowledge regarding this is "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), which is a designation for these six kinds of knowledge.
"Subject to destruction" (*khayadhamma*) means having the nature of going to destruction. "Subject to vanishing" (*vayadhamma*) means having the nature of going to vanishing.
"Subject to fading away" (*virāgadhamma*) means having the nature of fading away. "Subject to cessation" (*nirodhadhamma*) means having the nature of ceasing. "Seventy-seven" (*sattasattarī*)...
By making seven for each one, there are seventy-seven in eleven locations. In this sutta, insight (*vipassanā*) and further insight (*paṭivipassanā*) are explained. This is the fourth [section]. 5.
Commentary on the Sutta on the Condition of Ignorance (*Avijjāpaccayasutta*):
In the fifth [sutta], the Teacher concluded the teaching right here with the words, "there is an origination. For what reason? Because of the one who holds wrong views (*diṭṭhigatika*).
For the purpose of granting him an opportunity. For in that assembly there was a person holding wrong views who intended to find fault;
thinking, "He will ask a question, and then I shall answer it," [the Blessed One] concluded his teaching in order to grant him that opportunity.
"An improper question" means an unsuitable question; the sense is that this is a bad question. But is it not the case that [he asked]: "Venerable sir, what now is aging-and-death?"?

"This was well asked. Although it was indeed well asked, nevertheless, just as when a fine meal worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold is served in a golden bowl, yet even a single lump of excrement the size of an *āmalaka* fruit is placed upon it, the entire meal becomes foul food that must be discarded—so too, by this phrase expressing the doctrine of the apprehension of a sentient being, "And to whom does this aging-and-death belong? [the question is rendered futile].
"Just as that food is like a lump of excrement and thus bad food, so too has all this become a foolish question.
"Living the holy life" (*brahmacariyavāsa*) means dwelling in the Noble Path. Regarding the view that "the soul is the same as the body," one who holds this view thinks:
"When the soul perishes, the body perishes; when the body perishes, the soul perishes."
He grasps it. For one who grasps in this way, that view is called the "view of annihilation" because of the grasping that "the being is annihilated.
However, if one were to grasp that "only conditioned phenomena arise and cease," it would be what is called right view within the dispensation.
And this noble path, while bringing about the cessation of the round of existence, completely cuts off the round.

When that very cycle arises, if it is possible for it to cease even without the cultivation of the path—because its form has been grasped through the view of annihilationism—then the cultivation of the path becomes useless. Therefore it is said: "There is no living of the holy life.
According to the second method, one who holds the view that the soul is one thing and the body another thinks: "The body is annihilated right here; [the soul is not]."
"Life does not [remain]; rather, life goes as it pleases, like a bird from its cage.
For one who grasps in this way, that view is called the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), because of the apprehension that "life has gone from this world to the next world.
And this Noble Path arises turning away from the round of existence in the three realms; it [does not arise] even with respect to a single conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*).

If [the self] were permanent, stable, and eternal, then even one who has arisen [in the world] would not be able to turn the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) away; thus, the cultivation of the path (maggabhāvanā) would be useless.
Therefore it was said: "Monk, if there is the view that 'the soul is one thing and the body is another,' there is no living of the holy life (brahmacariyavāsa).

The terms "quibbling" (*visūkāyika*) and so forth are all synonyms for wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*). For that [wrong view] is, in the sense of piercing through, the opposite of right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
It is called "visūkāyika" because it conceals itself like a deceptive trick; it is called "visevita" because it proceeds by opposing right view rather than following it;
and it is called "virūpaṃ phanditaṃ vipphanditaṃ" because its wavering and floundering grasp at annihilationism at one time and eternalism at another.
"Tālāvatthukatāni" means they have been made like the stump of a palmyra tree, in the sense that they will not grow again.
The meaning is that they have been uprooted like a palmyra tree with its head cut off, and their place of standing has been made [empty] like the site where that tree stood.
"Reduced to non-existence" means they have been brought to a state of subsequent non-existence. The fifth [sutta].
6. Commentary on the Second Sutta on the Condition of Ignorance (Avijjāpaccaya).
36. "Or again, monks, if one should say thus," [the Teacher spoke] as follows. In that assembly, there was a holder of views (diṭṭhigatika) who desired to ask a question;
however, being of a timid nature, he was unable to rise and ask the One of Ten Powers (dasabala).
Therefore, the Teacher, having himself asked in accordance with his intention, answered him. This is the sixth.
7. Commentary on the *Natumhasutta* 37.
Regarding the seventh [verse], "Not yours": for when there is a self (*atta*), there is what belongs to a self (*attaniya*).
But since the self itself does not exist, he said, "Not yours. Nor "of others": another is indeed the self of others; when that exists, [there is what belongs to] others.

It might be so; however, that too does not exist, which is why he said, "nor from others. "Monks, this is an old karma"—this is not merely old karma itself, but rather this body is produced by old karma;
therefore, it is spoken of thus by way of the conventional expression for its condition (*paccaya-vohāra*).

The passage beginning with "wrought" (*abhisaṅkhata*) and so forth is stated by way of the conventional expression for karma (*kamma-vohāra*), because of the similarity in their prior characteristics and nature.
The meaning here, however, is as follows: "conditioned" (abhisaṅkhataṃ) should be understood as "made by conditions.

"Volitionally produced" (abhisañcetayitaṃ) should be understood as "having volition as its basis" and "rooted in volition. "To be felt" (vedaniyaṃ) should be understood as "the basis for what is to be felt. This is the seventh [sutta]. 8.
Commentary on the Cetanā-sutta.

38. "And what it intends, monks": whatever volition it intends; the meaning is that it sets it in motion. "And what it plans": whatever planning it plans; the meaning is precisely that it sets it in motion.

"And what it underlies": whatever underlying tendency it underlies; the meaning is precisely that it sets it in motion. And herein, "it intends" refers to wholesome and unwholesome volitions belonging to the three planes of existence.
"Seized" (*gahitā*) and "plans" (*pakappeti*): among the eight types of greed-accompanied consciousness, the conceptualizations of craving and views are seized. "Underlies" (*anuseti*):
the latent tendency (*anusaya*) is seized both by way of co-nascence and by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) in relation to the twelve types of volition (*cetanā*).

"This becomes its object" (*ārammaṇam etaṃ hoti*): because there is no obstruction to the arising of kamma-consciousness when these classes of phenomena such as volition exist, this class of phenomena consisting of volition and so forth [becomes the object].
It is a condition. For here, "condition" is intended in the sense of an object (*ārammaṇa*).
"For the stability of consciousness" means for the sake of the stability of kamma-consciousness. "When the object exists" means when that condition exists.
"There is a foundation for consciousness" means there is a foundation for that kamma-consciousness. "When that consciousness is established" means when that kamma-consciousness is established.
When the root has arisen through the activation of karma by means of the volition "Virūḷha," it possesses the capacity to draw forth rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"The production of renewed existence" (*punabbhavābhinibbatti*) refers to the production designated as renewed existence.
By the phrase "If, monks, one does not intend," the moment when volition belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka-cetanā*) is not operating is stated. If...
"Formulates" (*pakappeti*) refers to the moment when the formulations of craving and views (*taṇhā-diṭṭhi-kappa*) do not yet operate.

"If it still underlies" (*atha ce anuseti*)—here, by the phrase "in the resultant states of the three planes and in limited functional states" (*tebhūmaka-vipākesu paritta-kiriyāsu rūpe*), the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) is taken in its sense as that which has not yet been abandoned.

"This becomes the object" (*ārammaṇam etaṃ hoti*): since the arising of karmic consciousness is not obstructed when an underlying tendency exists, this class of underlying tendencies serves as a condition (*paccaya*).
In the phrases beginning with "nor does he intend," in the first clause, wholesome and unwholesome volitions of the three planes are excluded;

in the second clause, craving and views within the eight types of consciousness are excluded; and in the third clause, that underlying tendency which lies latent as an unabandoned state among the aforementioned phenomena is excluded.
Furthermore, for the sake of non-confusion, one should understand this tetrad here: "one intends, plans, and underlies; one intends but does not plan, yet underlies;
one neither intends nor plans, yet underlies; one neither intends nor plans, nor underlies.
Among these, the first method shows the classification of phenomena (*dhamma*). In the second method, "one intends" refers to wholesome volition (*cetanā*) belonging to the three planes of existence.

And the four unwholesome volitions (*akusalacetanā*) are included. "He does not intend" (*na pakappeti*): in the eight [types of] consciousness, craving and views have ceased. "Latent tendency" (*anuseti*):

in the wholesome states of the three planes, the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) is grasped by way of decisive support (*upanissaya-koṭi*); in the four unwholesome volitions, it is grasped by way of both co-nascence (*sahajāta-koṭi*) and decisive support.
In the third method, "he does not will" (*na ceteti*) refers to the wholesome and unwholesome [states] of the three planes.
"Ceased, it does not form intentions": in the eight types of consciousness, craving and views have ceased;

having excluded what is mentioned in the Sutta as "underlying tendencies" (*anusaya*), the decisive support (*upanissaya*) is taken here in its unabandoned state within the wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional states of the three planes, as well as in material phenomena.
The fourth method is the same as the previous one.

"In that which is not established" means in that which has not taken root. "Not grown" means having failed to produce roots capable of drawing forth rebirth-linking after the impulse of karma has been given.

What, then, is being stated here? It is appropriate to say either the function of the path of Arahantship, the performance of the task by one whose taints are exhausted, or the nine supramundane states. And herein, regarding consciousness and future renewed existence:
And between [consciousness and name-and-form] there is one link; between feeling and craving there is one; between existence and birth there is one.
This is the eighth. 9. Commentary on the Second Cetanā Sutta:
In the ninth, between consciousness and name-and-form there is one link; between feeling and craving there is one; between existence and birth there is one. This is the ninth.
10. Commentary on the Third Cetanā Sutta 40.
In the tenth [verse], *natī* means craving (*taṇhā*). For that [craving] is called "inclination" (*natī*) in the sense of inclining toward agreeable forms and so forth.
"There is going according to coming" means there is going in accordance with what has come; that is, when the karma or the sign of karma has appeared.
Or, there is a destination for consciousness by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) toward a gross sign (gahinimitta). Regarding "passing away and reappearing" (cutūpapāta):

when there is such a destination of consciousness toward the object of rebirth-linking from which it has come, there is "passing away" (cuti), defined as falling away from here, and "reappearing" (upapāta), defined as arising there;
this is what is called "passing away and reappearing. Thus, in this discourse, [it refers] to both inclination (nati) and coming-and-going (āgatigati).
In the interval, only one connection has been stated. The tenth [chapter].
The fourth section, the Kaḷārakhattiya-vagga.
5. The Gahapati-vagga.
1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Five Terrors and Fears (Pañcaverabhayasuttavaṇṇanā) 41.

In the first discourse of the Chapter on Householders (*Gahapativagga*), the phrase "when" (*yata*) means "at which time. "Fears and terrors" (*bhayāni verāni*) refers to the volitions (*cetanā*) of fear and enmity.

"By means of the factors of stream-entry" (*sotāpattiyaṅgehi*) refers to the two kinds of factors for stream-entry: that which is a factor for stream-entry, and that which is a factor *of* stream-entry—namely, that which exists in the prior stage for the attainment of stream-entry.
It is stated thus: "Association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, careful attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
Furthermore, it is a factor for one who has acquired these qualities and stands having attained stream-entry; it is also called a factor of a stream-enterer.
This is a designation for the forms of verified confidence in the Buddha and so forth; this is what is intended here.

"Noble" (*ariya*) means blameless and beyond reproach. "The method" (*ñāya*) refers both to the knowledge established by knowing what has arisen dependently (*paṭiccasamuppanna*) and to dependent origination itself.
As it is said: "The method is called dependent origination; the Noble Eightfold Path is also the method.

"By means of wisdom" (*paññāya*) means by means of the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) that arises again and again. "Well seen" (*sudiṭṭha*) means well seen by way of seeing [it] as it repeatedly arises.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Hell is exhausted" (*khīṇanirayo*), hell is "exhausted" for me because it will not arise there again in the future; thus, "I am one whose hell is exhausted. This same method applies in all cases.

A "stream-enterer" (*sotāpanna*) is one who has entered the stream of the Path. "One of a nature not subject to falling away" (*avinipātadhammo*) means one whose nature is not to undergo a miserable rebirth.

"One who is fixed" (*niyato*) means fixed by the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*), which is designated as the first Path. "One whose ultimate goal is full enlightenment" (*sambodhiparāyano*) refers to the three higher Paths.
"Full enlightenment is my supreme goal"—thus I am "one whose supreme goal is full enlightenment"; the meaning is that I shall certainly awaken to that full enlightenment.
"On account of the taking of life" means by reason of performing the action of taking life. "Fear and enmity" are one and the same in meaning.
This enmity is of two kinds: external and internal. For instance, by one person another's father might have been killed, and he [the son] thinks:
Thinking, "It is said that my father was killed by this man; I too shall kill him," he wanders about carrying a sharpened weapon.
That volition of the mind which arises within him is called external enmity (*bāhira-vera*).
Furthermore, in the other person, there arises the volition: "It is said that he wanders about thinking 'I shall kill him'; I myself shall kill him first."
This is what is called internal enmity. Both of these, for the time being, pertain only to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*).

However, when the warder of hell sees one born there and thinks, "I shall strike him," and seizes a flaming club, the volition that arises in that warder of hell is his external enmity pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*).
And as for his [volition] thinking, "This person [is striking] me who am innocent..."
When the thought arises, "He is coming to strike me; I myself shall strike him first," this is his internal enmity pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*).
As for that external enmity, it is called "personal enmity" (*puggalavera*) in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
Suffering (*dukkha*) and mental distress (*domanassa*) are identical in meaning. And just as it is here, so it is in the remaining phrases with regard to "by this... [and so forth].

The arising of enmity should be understood through such modes as: "My goods were stolen," "My wife has been unchaste," "Having spoken falsely, my wealth is ruined," or "This was done by one intoxicated with liquor.
By "unshakable confidence" (aveccappasāda) is meant the confidence attained that is immovable.
By "virtues dear to the Noble Ones" (ariyakanta) are meant the five precepts; for these are indeed dear and beloved to the Noble Ones (Ariyas), even when they have passed into other existences.
The Noble Ones do not abandon these; therefore, they are called "beloved by the Noble Ones.
Whatever else might need to be said here has all been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition on the recollections (*anussati*). First.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Fear of the Five Enmities.
42. In the second [sutta], the distinction consists merely in the fact that it was spoken to the bhikkhus.
This is the second. 3. Commentary on the Dukkha Sutta 43.

In the third [sutta], "of suffering" (dukkhassa) means of the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha). "Origination" (samudaya) refers to two types of origination: momentary origination (khaṇikasamudaya) and...
And there is the arising by way of conditions. A bhikkhu who sees the arising by way of conditions also sees the momentary arising;
one who sees the momentary arising also sees the arising by way of conditions.
Cessation is twofold: absolute cessation and cessation as dissolution. One who sees absolute cessation also sees cessation as dissolution; one who sees cessation as dissolution...
Even while passing by, one sees its ultimate cessation. "I shall teach":
this means, "I shall teach the arising and the cessation of the suffering of the round of existence—that is, its production and its dissolution; listen to that. "Dependent upon" (*paṭicca*):
having made it a condition by way of support and by way of object. "The meeting of the three is contact" (*tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso*): contact is the coming together of the three.
"Monks, 'this is the origin of suffering'—this refers to the arising of the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). 'Cessation' means its dissolution.
For in this way, the suffering of the cycle of existence is dismantled so that there is no further rebirth. Third.
4. Commentary on the *Lokasutta*."
44. "In the world" (loka) in the fourth [verse] means the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*). This is the distinction here. The fourth [section]. 5.
Commentary on the Ñātika Sutta 45.
In the fifth [sutta], "at Ñātika" refers to the village of two kinsmen. "At the Brick Hall" (*giñjakāvasatha*) refers to the great palace constructed with bricks.
*Dhammapariyāya* means a discourse on the Dhamma, that is, a teaching on the Dhamma. *Upassuti* means a place of eavesdropping;
the meaning is that he stood at such a place where, having approached it, one is able to hear the Blessed One’s voice.

It is said that he had come for the purpose of sweeping the courtyard around the Gandhakuṭī, but having set aside his own work, he stood there listening to the Blessed One’s sound of the Dhamma. *Addasa* (he saw) refers to that time.
It is said that as the Blessed One was attending to the mode of conditions from the very beginning, reflecting, "This arises through this condition;
this [arises] through that," everything up to the peak of existence became a single expanse.

The Teacher, setting aside his mental attention and reciting the text aloud, brought the teaching to its conclusion according to the sequence of the discourse, and then [thought], "Now, regarding this exposition of the Dhamma..."
While reflecting, "Has anyone heard it?", he saw that bhikkhu. Therefore it is said: "The Blessed One saw. *Assosi no* means "did he hear?
Alternatively, *assosi no* means "did he hear us as we were speaking? Regarding the words "learn" (*uggaṇhāhi*) and so forth:
having heard [the teaching], one who makes it proficient while remaining silent is said to "learn. Having joined word by word, it becomes familiar through speech.
"Making it one's own" means mastering it. "Bearing it in mind" means making it proficient and reaching the stage of mastery in both ways.
"Connected with the goal" (atthasaṃhita) means dependent on the cause. "The beginning of the holy life" (ādibrahmacariyaka) means being the beginning and the foundation for the holy life of the Path.
Thus, in these three suttas, only the cycle of existence and its cessation (vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa) are explained. Fifth.
6. Commentary on the Discourse to a Certain Brahmin (Aññatarabrāhmaṇasutta). 46.
"A certain" (aññatara) refers to a certain brahmin who was not well-known by name. This is the sixth. 7.
Commentary on the Discourse to Jāṇussoṇi.
47. In the seventh [discourse], Jāṇussoṇī is the name obtained by virtue of his office; he was a great domestic chaplain with a wealth of eight hundred million.
This is the seventh. 8. Commentary on the Lokāyatika Sutta: 48.
In the eighth, "Lokāyatika" refers to one who has gained proficiency in the Lokāyata, the science of caviling. "This Lokāyata is the eldest... [etc.]
First, the Lokāyata. "Lokāyata" means extended (*āyata*) for the world itself;

it should be understood as a view-position (*diṭṭhigata*) that is vast and profound, yet of limited nature. "Unity" (*ekatta*) means having a single nature, namely, a permanent nature—this is what he asks about.
"Plurality" (*puthutta*) means having a diverse nature compared to its previous nature, by way of states such as gods, humans, and so forth.
"Having been first, it does not exist afterwards"—this he asks with reference to annihilationism (*uccheda*).

Thus, in this context, it should be understood that "everything exists" and "everything is a unity" are these two eternalist views (*sassataditthi*), while "nothing exists" and "everything is a plurality" are these two annihilationist views (*ucchedaditthi*). Eighth.
9. Commentary on the Ariyasāvaka Sutta 49.
In the ninth [sutta], "kiṃ nu kho" (what indeed) is a demonstration of the manner in which doubt arises. "Samudayati" means it arises.
This is the ninth. 10. Commentary on the Second Ariyasāvaka Sutta
50. In the tenth [chapter], even two methods are stated together. This alone is the distinction from the preceding; the rest is exactly the same. Tenth. The fifth section:
The Chapter on Householders. 6. The Chapter on Suffering (Dukkhavagga).
1. Commentary on the Parivīmaṃsana Sutta 51.
In the first sutta of the Dukkhavagga, "parivīmaṃsamāno" means investigating. If it is asked:
why is aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) alone mentioned as "of many kinds and various aspects" when it has been grasped [as the primary object]? Because when that is grasped...
Because all suffering is included [within it]. For just as when a man is seized by his crest-lock, that man is indeed seized, so too when aging and death are grasped, all suffering is indeed grasped.
Therefore, having understood that "this manifold, variously categorized suffering which arises in the world," one sees all suffering as like a man standing [therein].
Having shown it, as if grasping it by the crest, he seized old age and death.

"Leading to what is appropriate for the cessation of old age and death" means that, being similar—by virtue of its being free from defilement and its purity—to the cessation of old age and death, it leads [to it]. And he practices accordingly, just as...

"He is said to be 'practicing' (paṭipanna) because he practices in this way. "One who lives in accordance with the Dhamma" (anudhammacārī) means he practices the Dhamma of practice that follows the Dhamma of Nibbāna;
the meaning is that he fulfills it. "Practicing for the destruction of suffering" means practicing, beginning with virtue, for the sake of the cessation of the suffering of aging and death.
"For the cessation of formations" means for the cessation of the suffering of formations.
"For the sake of cessation. Up to this point, the teaching has been explained as far as arahantship.
Now, one might expect the teaching to conclude after demonstrating the reviewing of the fruit of arahantship and the constant abiding;

why, then, does it take up the phrase "one who is immersed in ignorance"? It is for the purpose of showing that even for one whose taints are destroyed, the cycle of existence and suffering have been transcended.
Furthermore, when the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) has been introduced and the process of its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) is being explained, there is a sentient being capable of awakening here;

it should be understood that this [teaching] is also grasped by him according to his own disposition (*ajjhāsaya*). In this context, "one who has gone into ignorance" (*avijjāgata*) means one who has gone to, approached, or is possessed of ignorance.
"A person, a man" (*purisapuggala*) means a man who is himself a person. By both of these terms, he speaks in terms of conventional designation (*sammuti-kathā*).
For the Buddhas there are two kinds of discourse: conventional discourse (*sammuti-kathā*) and ultimate discourse (*paramattha-kathā*).

Among these, that which proceeds as “a being, a man, a person, an individual, Tissa, Nāga,” and so forth, is called conventional discourse. That which proceeds as “aggregates, elements, sense bases,” and so forth, is called ultimate discourse.
Even when speaking of the ultimate, they speak without abandoning the conventional.
Whether they speak of conventional truth or ultimate truth, they speak only what is true. Therefore it is said:
“The Fully Enlightened One, the best among speakers, proclaimed two truths:
The conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found.”
“Conventional speech is true as the cause for worldly consensus;
ultimate speech is true as the actual characteristic of phenomena.
If one forms a meritorious formation, it refers to the meritorious volitional formation consisting of the thirteen types of volition. “One forms” means one performs.
"Consciousness fares on to merit" means that kamma-consciousness is approached by, or associated with, meritorious kamma;

and resultant consciousness is [approached] by resultant merit. "If he performs a formation that is demeritorious" means he performs a demeritorious formation consisting of the twelve types of volition.
"If he performs a formation that is imperturbable" means a formation of imperturbability consisting of the four types of volition. "Fares on to the imperturbable."
"Consciousness comes to be": by means of the imperturbability of karma, karmic consciousness is approached; by means of the imperturbability of result, resultant consciousness is approached.
And here, because the threefold formative action of karma is included, the twelve-linked mode of conditionality is indeed included.
To this extent, the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) has been shown.
Now, demonstrating the process of turning away (*vivaṭṭa*), he said, "From the time, monks... and so forth. In this context, *avijjā* (ignorance) is non-knowing regarding the Four Truths.
*Vijjā* (true knowledge) is the knowledge of the path to Arhatship. And here, true knowledge arises precisely when ignorance has been abandoned.
Just as darkness is dispelled by the lighting of a lamp even during a night of four-fold darkness, so too...

With the arising of true knowledge, the abandoning of ignorance is to be understood. "He does not cling to anything in the world" means he does not grasp at or misapprehend any phenomenon in the world.

"Not clinging, he does not tremble" means that by not clinging and not grasping, he does not tremble with the trembling of craving nor with the trembling of fear; he does not crave and he does not fear.
The meaning is as follows. "By himself alone" means that he attains final nibbāna by his own self, not through the power of another.

Why was it begun with the words, "If he feels a pleasant feeling"? It was begun in order to show the constant abiding after having shown the reviewing knowledge of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
"Not adhered to" means not grasped by being swallowed and finalized by craving (*taṇhā*).
Now, why is painful feeling mentioned? Is there anyone who delights even in that? Yes, there is.

For it is precisely by delighting in pleasure that one is said to delight in suffering, because one seeks pleasure upon encountering suffering, and because pleasure itself is subject to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*).
"Ending with the body" means delimited by the body, as far as the five-sense-door body extends.
The meaning is: "occurs" refers to the five-door feeling that occurs as long as [the life-faculty] proceeds.
"Lasting until the end of life" means delimited by life; the meaning is: it is the mind-door feeling that occurs for as long as life proceeds.
In this regard, the five-door feeling arises later and ceases first, whereas the mind-door feeling...
Having arisen first, it ceases later. For at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it establishes itself precisely upon the physical basis (*vatthurūpa*).

During the course of existence (*pavatta*), when functioning through the five doors, it becomes excessive and powerful—arising as lust, hatred, and delusion—at the prime of life, during the age of twenty; it remains stable at the age of fifty.
From the time of sixty years of age onwards, it begins to decline; at eighty or ninety years of age, it becomes dull.
For at that time, even when beings say, "We have sat together or lain down together for a long time," they say, "I do not recognize you.
Even when presented with intense objects such as forms and so forth, they say, "We do not see them, we do not hear them," or "We do not perceive pleasant or unpleasant odors, or sweet tastes..."
They say, “We do not know whether it is unpleasant, stiff, or soft. Thus, their five-door sensations have ceased, and only those of the mind-door continue.
Even that, gradually diminishing, continues at the time of death supported by the heart-base alone.
As long as this continues, so long is the being said to live. When it no longer continues, [the being is dead].
Then it is said that the mind has ceased.
This meaning may be illustrated by means of a pond:
Suppose, for example, a man were to construct a pond provided with five water-inlets; when it has rained for the first time, [the water from] the five...

Suppose one were to enter through water channels and fill a basin within a reservoir; then, as it rains again and again, the water would fill the channels and remain standing, overflowing for half a *gāvuta* or a *yojana*, trickling away from here and there;
then, when the outlets and drains are opened while work is being done in the fields, the water flows out during the time of the crop harvest.
When water is flowing out, one might say, "The water has diminished;

let us catch fish," yet after a few days, the water will settle back into the very same pits. As long as that water remains in those pits, it continues to be reckoned as "there is water in the great reservoir.
But when it is cut off there, then [it is no longer so reckoned] in the reservoir.
"there is no water," so too should this be understood.
For just as when it first rains and water enters through five channels, it is the time when the ponds are filled;
even so, at the very first moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it is the time when the mind-door feeling becomes established in the physical basis (*vatthurūpa*). Again and again...
The time when the five paths are filled while it is raining from the sky is like the time when the five-door sensory experience occurs;

the overflowing for a distance of half a *gāvuta* or a *yojana* is like the state of that experience being exceedingly powerful through passion and so forth during the first stage of life at twenty years of age;
and as long as the water does not flow out from the irrigation trench once planted, so long is the trench full.
The period of its stability is like the time when it stood for fifty years;
from the age of sixty onwards, its decline is like the time when water begins to flow out once the drainage-pipes have been opened while work is being done;

and at the age of eighty or ninety, the state of the sensory consciousnesses (pañcadvārika-vedanā) is like the time when only a small amount of water remains in the water-channels after the water has mostly run away.
The "slow time" is like the time when water remains settled in wells; it is the period during which mind-door feeling occurs in dependence upon the heart-base.

Just as one can say, "There is water in the reservoir," even when there is only a small amount of water in the wells, so long as that feeling continues to occur, one says, "the being lives. However, when the water in the wells has been cut off...
"Just as it is said, ‘there is no water in this well,’ so too, when feeling does not arise at the mind-door, one is said to be ‘dead.
It is with reference to this feeling that it was said: ‘experiencing a feeling that has its limit in life.
‘With the breaking up of the body’ means by the dissolution of the body. ‘After the exhaustion of life’ means after the passing away of life."
"Right here" (*idheva*) means not going elsewhere after death, but remaining right here by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

"They will become cool" (*sītībhavissanti*) means they will become cool—free from the agitation and distress of active flux—and subject to non-occurrence. "Bodies" (*sarīrāni*) refers to the bodies of the elements (*dhātu-sarīra*). "Will remain behind" (*avasissantī*) means they will be left over as remnants.
"From a potter's kiln" (*kumbhakārapākā*) means from the place where a potter bakes his vessels. "He would set aside" (*paṭisisseyya*) means he would put them away. "Potsherds" (*kapallāni*)...
The clay pots are bound together with the mouth-covering. "They would remain" means they would stay. "In the same way" refers here to this application of the simile:
the three realms of existence (bhava) are to be seen as like the kiln where the potter’s wares are fired;
the practitioner (yogāvacara) is like the potter; and the knowledge of the path to Arhatship is like the stick used to remove the pots from the kiln once they have been fired.
The unconditioned plane of Nibbāna is like a level stretch of ground;
the time when one has dragged a hot pot along with a stick and placed it on that level ground is like the time when a practitioner of insight (vipassanā),

while contemplating the sevenfold set of material phenomena and the sevenfold set of immaterial phenomena, finds the meditation subject familiar and clearly manifest, and encounters such favorable conditions as a suitable climate.

It should be understood that after obtaining [the fruit], while seated on a single seat, he developed insight, attained the supreme fruit of Arahantship, uplifted his own being from the four lower realms, and remained in the unconditioned plane of Nibbāna by means of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
However, one whose taints are destroyed does not pass away like a heated pot on the very day he attains Arahantship; rather, he remains for as long as his life-span lasts.
But, maintaining the continuity of the Dispensation, he remains for fifty-six years;
then, upon reaching his final consciousness, with the breaking up of the aggregates acquired through clinging, he attains final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
Then, like the shards of a pot, only the non-clinging physical remains are left behind. Thus one understands: "The bodily remains are left behind."
This, however, was stated for the purpose of applying the inquiry to one whose taints are exhausted.
"Consciousness might be discerned" means that rebirth-linking consciousness might be discerned. "Excellent, excellent!"—this is the encouragement of the Elder’s explanation.
"It is so"—this refers to the fact that when these three kinds of volitional formations are absent, rebirth-linking consciousness [does not arise].
"Without clear knowledge," and so forth; it is exactly thus. "Be resolved" means: obtain resolution (*adhimokkha*), which is characterized as a definitive conclusion (*sanniṭṭhāna*).
"This alone is the end of suffering": this very thing is the end of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*), this is its limit, namely, Nibbāna.
First. 2. Commentary on the *Upādāna-sutta*.
52. "In the second [simile], 'in things conducive to clinging' means in the phenomena belonging to the three planes that serve as conditions for the four kinds of clinging.

'One who observes gratification' means one who contemplates gratification. 'Therein' refers to that mass of fire. 'Its nutriment' means its condition. 'Its fuel' is a synonym for the same thing. 'Just so,' etc.:
here, the three realms of existence are like the mass of fire, and the cycle of existence belonging to the three planes is likewise."
This very point is as follows: the foolish worldling who depends on the cycle of existence is like a man who tends a fire;

the performance of wholesome and unwholesome kamma through the six sense-doors by means of craving in that worldling who contemplates gratification is like the throwing of dry grass, cow dung, and so forth into the fire.
Just as the mass of fire increases by repeatedly throwing more of that grass and dung once the previous supply is exhausted, [so does the worldling increase his own suffering].
The production of the suffering of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭadukkha) again and again by a foolish worldling through the accumulation of the aforementioned kamma as he repeatedly rises up.
"He should not from time to time throw in dry grass"—for someone wishing his welfare might say this:
"Sir, why do you rise up again and again, bind them into bundles, and [place] dry grass and wood in a basket?"
“Having filled [the vessel], do you kindle this fire by throwing in dried cow dung? Is there any increase for you on account of this?
“This is our family tradition, sir,” he replied. “But on account of this, I suffer only loss; where is there any increase?
For while tending this fire, I am unable to bathe, eat, or lie down. Because of that...
"Indeed, sir, what is the use of this futile fanning of the fire? Come, place these grasses and other materials you have brought here;
they will burn by themselves. However, there is a lotus pond with cool water in such-and-such a place;
bathe there, adorn yourself with garlands, perfumes, and ointments, and being well-clad and properly robed—"
"Having entered the city on foot, having ascended the excellent palace and opened the window, sit resplendent in the great street, one-pointed and established in happiness;

while you are sitting there, this fire will, through the exhaustion of the grass and other fuel, spontaneously reach a state of non-manifestation. He would do exactly so. And while he was sitting there in that very manner—
That fire would reach a state of non-manifestation through the exhaustion of its fuel. It is with reference to this that it was said, "not from time to time," and so forth.
As for the phrase "even so," the application of the simile here is as follows:
the great mass of fire burning forty loads of wood should be seen as the round of existence in the three planes; and the man tending the fire should be seen as one dependent upon that round.
The practitioner of yoga is like a man seeking his own welfare, and the Fully Enlightened One is like that man;

the time when the Tathāgata spoke of the meditation subject regarding the phenomena of the three planes—saying, "Come, bhikkhu, become disenchanted with the phenomena of the three planes, and thus you shall be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra"—is like the time when that man was given instruction by the other man. As for that man...
Just as one who has sat upon a palace after practicing according to the instructions, so too for the yogi:
having received the Sugata’s counsel and entered an empty dwelling, he establishes insight (*vipassanā*) regarding phenomena belonging to the three planes;

then, gradually obtaining suitable nutriment and other requisites, the time comes when, while seated in a single session, he is established in the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*). For him, [the attainment] through bathing, ointments, and so forth—
For one seated there, with his body exquisitely adorned, it is as if the time has come for the yogi to be absorbed in one-pointed bliss within the lotus pond of the Noble Path—

having bathed thoroughly in the water of path-knowledge so that the stains of the defilements are washed away, having put on the garments of moral shame and dread, having anointed himself with the ointment of virtue,
having adorned his person with the ornament of Arahatship, having donned the garland of flowers of liberation, and wearing the sandals of the bases of psychic power.

This is the time when, having ascended and entered the city of Nibbāna, he has mounted the palace of the Dhamma and, shining upon the great street of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), has attained and is seated in the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti) which has Nibbāna as its object.

For that person seated there, it is like the time when the mass of fire reaches its cessation due to the exhaustion of the grass and other fuels; so it is for the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).
Having remained for the duration of his lifespan, with the breakup of the aggregates subject to clinging, he has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue;
thus should the great quenching of the cycle of existence be understood. This is the second.
3. Commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta.
53. "In the third [verse], 'in the conditions for the fetters' (*saṃyojaniyesu*) means in the conditions for the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*).

'One should meditate' (*jhāyeyya*) means one should kindle [the lamp]. 'One should pour oil and provide a wick' (*telaṃ āsiñceyya vaṭṭiṃ upasaṃhareyya*) means that for the purpose of maintaining the lamp, one should take a vessel of oil and a large wick-holder and, standing constantly nearby, pour oil when the oil is exhausted and provide a wick when the wick is exhausted."
One should apply [this]. The rest here, together with the comparison, is to be understood in the same manner as before. This is the third. 4.
Commentary on the Second Saṃyojana Sutta:
In the fourth [sutta], the simile is stated first and the meaning afterwards. The rest is exactly the same. This is the fourth.
5. Commentary on the Mahārukkhasutta 55.
In the fifth [verse], "carrying up the essence," they bring up the essence of earth and the essence of water to the top.
Because the essence has been brought up, a moisture like drops and droplets appears on the tips of the sprouts of the tree that is a hundred cubits high.
It remains. Herein, this is the correlation with the simile: the round of existence in the three planes is like the great tree;
the sense bases are like the roots; the ascent of the sap through the roots is like the ascent of karma through the six doors;

and because the sap has ascended, the persistence of the great tree for as long as the aeon is like the persistence of the karma of the foolish worldling who relies on the round through the six doors.
