The "long-standing" refers to the state of remaining for a long time by way of increasing the cycle (*vatta*) through repeated effort.
"A spade and a basket" means both a spade and a carrying-basket.
"He should cut it into pieces" means he should cut it, making small and large fragments. This, however, is the application of the simile here: for even here, there is a great tree.
The round of existence in the three planes is like a tree; the practitioner is like a man wishing to destroy that tree;
knowledge is like a spade; concentration is like a basket; knowledge is like an axe for cutting down the tree;

wisdom is like the time when the practitioner, having received the meditation subject from his teacher, attends to it while at the root of the tree; [and it is] like [the tree being cut] into pieces and fragments.
In brief, the attention directed toward the four great elements is like the time of cutting; the detailed attention directed toward the forty-two parts is like the splitting [of the wood];

and the discernment of name-and-form by way of these—the secondary materiality, the consciousness that has the aggregate of material form as its object, and the consciousness itself—is like the time of making it into individual chips; this is the severing of the roots.
It is like the search for the conditions for that very name-and-form; it is like the time of drying [the body] in the wind and sun and burning it with fire.

It is the attainment of the highest fruit by one who, having gradually increased insight, obtained some suitable condition and sat cross-legged while the meditation subject was clearly manifest, performing the duties of a recluse; it is the making of the paste.

The period during which one remains for the duration of one's lifespan—without attaining final Nibbāna on the very day of reaching Arahantship—is like being blown away by a great wind or swept away by a river;

this should be understood as the cessation of the round (*vaṭṭa*) for one who has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) through the breaking up of the aggregates of clinging (*upādiṇṇakakkhandha*). This is the fifth.
6. Commentary on the Second Mahārukkha Sutta (The Great Tree Discourse) 56.
In this sixth discourse as well, the simile is stated first and the meaning afterwards; this alone is the distinction.
The sixth [discourse] is concluded. 7. Commentary on the Taruṇarukkha Sutta (The Young Tree Discourse)
57–59. "In the seventh [year], 'young'" means one that has not yet borne fruit. "One should clear it" means one should clean it.
"One should add soil" means that after removing hard and coarse soil, one should put in sweet soil mixed with soft cow-dung powder.

"Having attained growth" means that having reached growth, one that is intended for flowers would take flowers, and one intended for fruit would take fruit. Here, however, is the application of the simile:
For the round of existence in the three planes is like a young tree; the worldling dependent on that round is like the man who tends the tree;
the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome kamma through the three doors is like the roots, fruits, sapwood, and so forth;
and the continued occurrence of the round for the worldling as he accumulates kamma through the three doors is like the growth and development of the tree. The turning away from the round (vivaṭṭa).
It should be understood in the same manner already stated. The eighth and ninth [suttas] have their meanings obvious. Regarding the seventh and following:
10. Commentary on the Nidāna Sutta.
In the tenth [sutta], "he dwells among the Kurus" means he dwells in that country which, by way of the plural form, has acquired the conventional designation "the Kurus."
"Kammāsadhamma, a market town of the Kurus": this is the name of a market town belonging to the Kurus; the meaning is that he made it his alms-residence village.
"Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of affection and a term of respect. "Ānanda" is the name of that elder. "Sat down to one side":
avoiding the six faults of sitting, he sat in the place facing the right knee, [upon the ground] of the six colors...

Having entered into the rays of the Buddha as if plunging into clear lac juice, as if donning a golden robe, or as if entering the center of a canopy of red woolen cloth, the Venerable Ānanda, the treasurer of the Dhamma, sat down.
Therefore it is said: "He sat down to one side."
At what time and for what reason did this venerable one approach the Blessed One?

It was at the evening hour, for the purpose of asking a question concerning the nature of conditions (*paccayākāra*). It is said that on that day, while wandering for alms in Kammāsadhamma, this venerable one—acting as if he were depositing a thousand coins at every door—was engaged in gathering a following of families.
Having returned from his alms round and performed the duties toward the Teacher, when the Teacher had entered the Fragrant Chamber,
he paid homage to the Teacher and went to his own daytime resting place. After performing the duties toward his pupils and they had departed,
he swept the daytime resting place, spread out his leather mat, and cooled his hands and feet with water from his water-pot.
Having arranged his cross-legged posture and sat down, he entered the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala-samāpatti*).

Then, emerging from that attainment after a predetermined period of time, he applied his knowledge to the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). Starting from the beginning with "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," he proceeded to the end;
starting from the end, he proceeded to the beginning; starting from both ends, he proceeded to the middle; and starting from the middle...
Avoiding both extremes, he comprehended the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) three times by way of twelve steps.
As he was thus comprehending it, the mode of conditions became clear and appeared to him as plain as anything on the palm of his hand. Then he thought:
"This mode of conditions has been described by all the Buddhas as profound and appearing profound; yet for me, while my knowledge is only partial..."
"Since this appears to my mindful disciple as something shallow, manifest, and clear—as if it were right before his eyes—I shall ask the Teacher about the reason for its appearing thus to me:
'Is it only to me that this appears so shallow, or does it appear the same way to others as well?
Having risen from his seat, he shook out his leather mat, took it with him, and set out in the evening.
He approached the Blessed One. Therefore it was said: "Approaching in the evening time for the purpose of asking a question on the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*).
Regarding the phrase "as deep as": here the word *yāva* indicates the exceeding of a measure. The meaning is: "deep beyond measure," that is, "extremely deep.
"Appearing deep" means that it appears and is seen as being indeed deep. For one thing may be merely superficial...
One [lake] appears deep; due to the taste of decaying leaves, it is black in color like stagnant water.
For even though it is only knee-deep, it appears as if it were a hundred fathoms deep. One [lake] is deep but appears shallow, like clear water reflecting the luster of jewels.
For even though it is a hundred fathoms deep, it seems as if it were only knee-deep. One [lake] is shallow and appears shallow.
It is like water in a bowl or similar vessel. One [kind] is deep and appears deep, like the water in the great ocean at the base of Sineru.
Thus, water itself receives four names. However, this is not the case with dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
For this receives only one name: "deep and appearing deep. Even though it is of such a nature, nevertheless...
"Yet to me it appears as if it were something quite obvious. This is wonderful, venerable sir! This is marvelous, venerable sir!
Thus, expressing his own amazement, he asked the question and sat down in silence.
Having heard his words, the Blessed One [replied], "Ānanda is like one stretching out his hand to grasp the peak of existence, or like Mount Sineru..."

Thinking, “He speaks of this question within the Buddha’s domain as if it were something very shallow, like one who strives to extract the marrow after breaking open a bone, or like one who wishes to cross the great ocean without a ship,
or like one who strives to take the essence of the earth by overturning the earth itself;
well then, I shall explain its profound nature,” he said, “Do not say so,” and so forth.
In this context, *mā heva*—the syllable *ha* is merely a particle; the meaning is "do not speak thus.
Furthermore, the Blessed One speaks these words both while encouraging the Venerable Ānanda and while discouraging him. Therein, "encouraging" means:
"Ānanda, you possess great wisdom and lucid knowledge; therefore, even dependent origination, though profound, is as if clear to you."
It appears so, yet one should not perceive it as shallow for others; rather, it is indeed deep and appears deep.

Regarding this, they cite four similes: it is said that when a great wrestler, who had been nourished on the essence of fine food for six months and had practiced wrestling with stones, was going to the battlefield after having trained with wrestling-stones during a festival, there was a wrestling-stone [in his path].
They showed it to him. He asked, "What is this? "It is a wrestler’s stone," they replied. "Bring it here," he said.

When they said, "We cannot lift it," he went there himself and asked, "Where is the heavy part of this? Having lifted two stones with his two hands and thrown them like play-balls, he departed. In that case, for the wrestler, the wrestler’s stone was light.

It should be said that for others as well, it is "light. For the Venerable Ānanda, who was endowed with a resolution spanning one hundred thousand aeons, was like a wrestler accustomed to the flavors of fine food for six months;

just as a wrestling stone is light to a wrestler because of his great strength, so too dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) should be called "shallow" because of the Elder’s great wisdom. But it should not be said that it is shallow for others.
In the great ocean there are four types of fish measuring four thousand yojanas each: the great fish named *timi*, two hundred yojanas long;
the *timiṅgala*, three hundred yojanas long; the *timirapiṅgala*, five hundred yojanas long; and the *ānanda*, *timindara*, *ajjhāroha*, and *mahātimi*.
Among these, they usually refer to it by the name *timirapiṅgala*. It is said that when he moves his right ear, [the water] flows for five hundred yojanas.
In one place the water moves; likewise the left ear, likewise the tail, and likewise the head.

But when he has moved both ears, struck with his tail, and tossed his head back and forth, beginning to play, the water at a distance of seven or eight hundred yojanas boils as if it were placed in a vessel on a stove, even at a distance of a hundred yojanas.
In that place, the water cannot even cover its back. He would say: "They say this great ocean is deep;
how can it be deep when we cannot find water enough to cover our backs?
In this regard, for the *timirapiṅgala* fish born there, the great ocean is shallow, as it is for other small fish.
It should not be said that it is shallow; likewise, for an elder endowed with wisdom, dependent origination is not shallow, nor should it be said to be shallow for others.
Furthermore, the king of the *supaṇṇas* is one hundred and fifty *yojanas* long.
His right wing is fifty *yojanas*, his left wing is likewise, the circle of his tail feathers is sixty *yojanas*, and his neck is thirty *yojanas*.
Its mouth is nine yojanas wide, and its feet are twelve yojanas long. When it begins to display the wind from its wings, even a space of seven or eight hundred yojanas is not sufficient.
It would say: "They say this space is infinite; how can it be infinite when we cannot even find room for the expanse of the wind from our wings?
In that regard, [this refers to] the king of the supaṇṇas who has attained such a body.
Just as space cannot be said to be "limited" because it is limited for other small birds, so too,
the fact that dependent origination is shallow for an elder endowed with wisdom does not mean it is shallow for others.
Furthermore, Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, measures four thousand eight hundred yojanas from the tips of his feet to the ends of his hair.
They exist. Between his two arms, it is twelve hundred *yojanas* in extent; in thickness, six hundred *yojanas*;
the palms of his hands and feet are three hundred *yojanas*; likewise his mouth; a single joint of a finger is fifty *yojanas*, as is the space between his eyebrows;
his forehead is three hundred *yojanas*; and his head is nine hundred *yojanas*. For him, the great ocean—
For one who has entered deep water, it becomes as shallow as the knee. He might say: "They say this great ocean is deep;
how can it be deep? We do not even find water enough to cover our knees.
In that case, for Rāhu, who is situated within the body, the great ocean is shallow, and for others as well, it is shallow.

It should not be said [that it is shallow]. In the same way, although dependent origination is shallow for an elder endowed with knowledge, it should not be said that it is shallow for others as well.
It was with reference to this matter that the Blessed One said, "Not so, Ānanda! Not so, Ānanda!

For to this elder, dependent origination—which is profound—appeared shallow due to four reasons. What are these four? Because of his excellence in past supportive conditions, because of his dwelling at a sacred ford (tittha), because of his attainment of stream-entry, and because of his great learning.
It is said that one hundred thousand aeons ago, a Teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world.
His city was called Haṃsavatī; his father was King Ānanda, and his mother was Queen Sumedhā. The Bodhisatta was a prince named Uttara.
On the very day his son was born, he made the Great Renunciation, went forth into homelessness, and devoted himself to the supreme effort.
Having attained omniscience in due course and uttered the inspired utterance, “Through many a round of births,” he spent seven days on the seat of enlightenment.
Then, thinking, “I shall set my foot upon the earth,” he extended his foot.
Thereupon, the earth split open and a great lotus rose up; its central petals were ninety cubits long, and its filaments thirty cubits.
The central hub was twelve cubits in size, and the dust was as much as nine water-jars.

The Teacher, however, was fifty-eight cubits in height; the distance between his two arms was eighteen cubits, his forehead five cubits, and his hands and feet eleven cubits each. With his eleven-cubit foot, he [reached] the twelve-cubit [hub].

As soon as his heel touched the center of the lotus, dust the size of nine water-jars rose up and, having ascended to a height of fifty-eight cubits, overspread the area like a scattering of powdered *manosilā*.
From that time on, the Blessed One became known as "Padumuttara. His two chief disciples were Devila and Sujāta, and his two chief female disciples were Amitā and Asamā.

His chief female disciple was named Sumana, and his attendant was named Upaṭṭhāka. The Blessed One Padumuttara, providing for his father, dwelt in the capital city of Haṃsavatī with a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.
His younger brother was Prince Sumanakumāra. To him, the king [granted] wealth from Haṃsavatī at a distance of two hundred yojanas.
He gave [it]. Sometimes he would come and see both his father and the Teacher. Then one day, the border region rose in revolt.
Sumana sent a message to the king. The king replied, "My dear son, why have you been dismissed by me?
He suppressed the bandits and sent word to the king, "The country has been pacified, Your Majesty. The king was pleased and said, "Quickly..."
“Let my son come,” he said. He had about a thousand ministers, and while on the road with them, he consulted with them:
“If my father, being pleased, grants me a boon, what should I take?
Then some of them said to him, “Take an elephant; take a horse; take the kingdom; take the seven treasures.”
They said: "Others [said], 'You are the sons of the Lord of the Earth; wealth is not difficult for you to obtain.
Even all that has been acquired must be abandoned when departing; only merit is that which one takes with one when departing.
Therefore, while the gods are offering a boon, choose the boon of attending upon the Blessed One Padumuttara for three months. He [replied], 'You are my true friends...'"
“Indeed, this mind is not mine; rather, it has been produced by you, and thus I shall act.

Having gone and paid homage to his father, and being embraced by his father and kissed on the head, when the father said, “I grant you a boon, my son,” he replied, “Great King, I wish to make my life fruitful by attending upon the Blessed One for three months with the four requisites.”
“Grant me this boon,” he said. “It is not possible, dear one; choose another boon. “Your Majesty, for kshatriyas there are indeed no two ways about it:
grant me only this, for I have no need of anything else. “Dear one, the minds of Buddhas are difficult to fathom;
if the Blessed One does not wish for it, what will become of it even if it is given by me? “Very well, Your Majesty.”
“I shall know the mind of the Blessed One,” he thought, and went to the monastery.
At that time, having finished his meal, the Blessed One had entered the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī).
He approached the monks who were seated in the pavilion (maṇḍalamāḷa). They said to him, “Prince, why have you come?”

“I wish to see the Blessed One; please let me see the Blessed One. “Prince, we do not obtain permission to see the Teacher at our own will whenever we desire. “But who, venerable sir, does obtain it? “The Elder named Sumanatthera, prince. “Where is the elder, venerable sir? Having asked for the place where the elder was sitting and having gone there, he paid homage and said: “I wish, venerable sir, to see the Blessed One. “Prince, you may see the Teacher at your own will whenever you desire. “Venerable sir, I am very busy with my royal duties; how can I see him at my own will whenever I desire? “If that is so, prince, go to the monastery at dawn tomorrow morning and wait at the gate. Then you will see the Teacher at your own will whenever you desire. He went and waited at the gate. At that time, the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the assembly. When the Blessed One saw him waiting at the gate, he stopped his discourse and said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the gate and say: ‘Prince, the Teacher calls you. The Venerable Ānanda went and said: “Prince, the Teacher calls you. He went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then taught him the Dhamma. When the Blessed One had taught him the Dhamma, he rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the gate and say: ‘Prince, the Teacher has finished teaching the Dhamma; you may now depart. The Venerable Ānanda went and said: “Prince, the Teacher has finished teaching the Dhamma; you may now depart. He paid homage to the Blessed One and departed. As he was going along the road, he thought: “I have seen the Teacher, but I have not heard the Dhamma. He turned back, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then taught him the Dhamma in detail. When the Blessed One had taught him the Dhamma in detail, he rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the gate and say: ‘Prince, the Teacher has finished teaching the Dhamma in detail; you may now depart. The Venerable Ānanda went and said: “Prince, the Teacher has finished teaching the Dhamma in detail; you may now depart. He paid homage to the Blessed One and departed. As he was going along the road, he thought: “I have seen the Teacher and have heard the Dhamma, but I have not received the Teacher’s blessing. He turned back, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, he said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One grant me his blessing. The Blessed One granted him this blessing: “May you live long, prince; may you be free from illness; may you maintain yourself in comfort. “Venerable sir, what is the meaning of this blessing? “Prince, when a noble disciple possesses these three things, he lives long, is free from illness, and maintains himself in comfort: he is possessed of faith, he is virtuous, and he is wise. “Venerable sir, I am already possessed of faith and virtue; but as for wisdom, I am still lacking. “Prince, if you were to develop the perception of impermanence, you would become wise. “Venerable sir, how should I develop the perception of impermanence? [The Blessed One explained: “Prince, you should develop the perception of impermanence thus: ‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all things are non-self. “Venerable sir, I shall do so. Then the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed. Prince Jayasena followed the Blessed One for a short distance, then turned back, entered the city, and went to his own residence. There he summoned his ministers and said: “Sirs, from today on, I shall give alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Prepare the requisites. “Very well, prince,” they replied and did as instructed. On the following day, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha entered the city for alms. Prince Jayasena, having prepared the seats and set out water for washing the feet, stood waiting at the gateway. When the Blessed One arrived, he paid homage to him, took his bowl and robe, led him into the inner chamber, seated him on the prepared seat, and washed his feet. Then he personally served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with various kinds of excellent food until they were satisfied. When the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, Prince Jayasena took a low seat, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I wish to go forth under the Blessed One; I wish to receive the full admission. “Prince, have you obtained your parents’ permission? “No, venerable sir, I have not. “Prince, the Tathāgatas do not grant the going-forth to anyone who has not obtained his parents’ permission. “Venerable sir, I shall obtain their permission. Prince Jayasena then rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed. He went to his parents, prostrated himself at their feet, and said: “Mother and father, I wish to go forth under the Blessed One; I wish to receive the full admission. “Son, you are our only child, dear and beloved. We cannot bear to let you go forth. A second and a third time he made the same request, and received the same answer. Finally, he said: “Mother and father, if you do not permit me to go forth, I shall starve myself to death right here. His parents, fearing death, gave their permission, saying: “Son, since you speak thus, we give you our permission to go forth. Prince Jayasena paid homage to his parents, kept them to his right, and returned to the Blessed One. He paid homage to the Blessed One, stood to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, I have obtained my parents’ permission; may I go forth under the Blessed One; may I receive the full admission. Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, ordain Prince Jayasena. The Venerable Ānanda took Prince Jayasena to a secluded spot, shaved his head and beard, dressed him in the yellow robes, and helped him to don the saṅghāṭi. Then he brought him before the Blessed One and said: “Venerable sir, Prince Jayasena has come to the Blessed One; may the Blessed One grant him the going-forth and the full admission. The Blessed One said: “Come, bhikkhu,” and that was enough for Prince Jayasena to be ordained and to become a bhikkhu. The newly ordained bhikkhu Jayasena paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then taught him the Dhamma. When the Blessed One had taught him the Dhamma, he rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the gate and say: ‘Bhikkhu Jayasena, the Teacher calls you. The Venerable Ānanda went and said: “Bhikkhu Jayasena, the Teacher calls you. He went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then taught him the Dhamma in detail. When the Blessed One had taught him the Dhamma in detail, he rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the gate and say: ‘Bhikkhu Jayasena, the Teacher has finished teaching the Dhamma in detail; you may now depart. The Venerable Ānanda went and said: “Bhikkhu Jayasena, the Teacher has finished teaching the Dhamma in detail; you may now depart. He paid homage to the Blessed One and departed. As he was going along the road, he thought: “I have seen the Teacher and have heard the Dhamma, but I have not received the Teacher’s blessing. He turned back, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, he said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One grant me his blessing. The Blessed One granted him this blessing: “May you live long, bhikkhu; may you be free from illness; may you maintain yourself in comfort. “Venerable sir, what is the meaning of this blessing? “Bhikkhu, when a noble disciple possesses these three things, he lives long, is free from illness, and maintains himself in comfort: he is possessed of faith, he is virtuous, and he is
“Venerable sir, I wish to see the Blessed One; please let me see the Blessed One,” he said.
The Elder took him by the hand, saying, “Come, Prince,” and having placed him in the courtyard surrounding the Perfumed Chamber, he ascended into the Perfumed Chamber.
Then the Blessed One asked him, “Suman, why have you come? “Venerable sir, I have come to see the Blessed One. “In that case, monk—”
“Prepare a seat,” he said. The Elder prepared a seat. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, the prince offered him hospitality, asking, “When did you arrive, Prince?
“Venerable sir, when you had entered the fragrant chamber, the monks said, ‘We do not wish to see the Blessed One at every moment we desire.’”
“They sent me to the presence of the Elder, saying, ‘Please grant him [permission]. Yet the Elder showed himself with but a single word.
‘Venerable sir, I think this Elder is a favorite in your dispensation. ‘Yes, prince, this bhikkhu is indeed a favorite in my dispensation.
‘Venerable sir, by doing what in the dispensation of the Buddhas does one become a favorite? ‘By giving gifts and by undertaking the precepts of virtue.’”
“Having performed the Uposatha ceremony, O Prince,” [the Prince said], “I too, like an elder, desire to be a beloved one in the Buddha’s dispensation;
please consent to spend the three-month rains retreat with me.
The Blessed One, having looked to see whether there was purpose in going, and seeing that there was, said, “O Prince, Tathāgatas indeed delight in empty dwellings. The Prince—
Having said, “It is understood, Blessed One; it is understood, Sugata,” he took a promise, saying, “Venerable Sir, I shall go first and have a monastery built;
when I have sent word, please come together with a hundred thousand bhikkhus.
Then, having gone into his father’s presence, he said, “Sire, I have been granted permission by the Blessed One; when I have sent for you, you must [go] to the Blessed One.”
"Let them be sent," he said; then, having paid homage to his father and departed, he traveled a journey of one hundred and twenty *yojanas*, establishing a monastery at every *yojana*.
Having arrived, while searching for a site for a monastery in his own city, he saw the garden of a householder named Sobhana.
Having purchased it for a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and expended another hundred thousand, he had a monastery built there. In that place...

Having had a fragrant chamber built for the Blessed One and huts, caves, and pavilions for the other monks to serve as night-quarters and day-quarters, and having completed the surrounding wall and the gateway, he sent word to his father:
"My task is finished; please send for the Teacher."
After the king had fed the Blessed One, he said, "The Blessed One’s business with Sumanas is finished; he awaits your arrival.
The Blessed One, accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand monks, proceeded along, staying at monasteries every yojana.
When the prince heard that the Teacher was coming, he went out to meet him for a yojana, honoring him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and having led him into the monastery—
“It was bought by me for a hundred thousand, and built for a hundred thousand;
accept this garden named Sobhana, O Great Sage.
Thus he presented the monastery. On the day of entering the rains retreat, having given alms, [he gave it] to his own sons, wife, and ministers.
Having summoned them, he said: “The Teacher has come from afar to our presence; for Buddhas indeed hold the Dhamma as their primary weight, not material gifts.
Therefore, for these three months, I shall dwell right here wearing only two robes and undertaking the ten precepts.
You, however, should give alms for these one hundred thousand who have destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) according to this very same manner.”
Living in a place very similar to the dwelling of the Elder Sumanas, he observed everything the elder did as his service for the Blessed One;
thinking, "In this place, this elder is uniquely beloved;
it is fitting to aspire to that very same position," he entered a village when the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) was approaching and gave a great almsgiving for seven days.
On the seventh day, having placed the triple robe at the feet of one hundred thousand bhikkhus and paid homage to the Blessed One, he said:

"Venerable Sir, this merit that I have performed, beginning from the construction of monasteries at intervals of one *yojana* along the road, was not done aspiring for the excellence of Sakka, nor for the excellence of Māra or Brahmā; rather, it was for the sake of the Buddha..."
"This was done by one who aspired to the state of being an attendant. Therefore, O Blessed One, may I too in the future become the attendant of a Buddha, just like the Elder Sumana.
Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself with the five-pointed salutation, paid homage, and lay down.
The Blessed One, observing whether the great mind of this noble youth would succeed or not, [saw that] "in the future, after one hundred thousand [aeons] from now..."
Knowing that "in this kappa, a Buddha named Gotama will arise, and you shall become his attendant," he said:
"May everything you desire and aspire to be fulfilled;
may all your intentions be realized, like the moon on the fifteenth day."
The prince said: "Having heard that those called Buddhas speak without duplicity," on the very second day he acted as if following closely behind the Blessed One, taking his bowl and robe.
Having given alms for a hundred thousand years during that appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in heaven; and even during the time of Kassapa Buddha, while [the Buddha] was wandering for alms—
Having given his upper robe to the Elder for the purpose of receiving his alms-bowl, he made an offering.
Having been reborn again in heaven and passing away from there, he became the King of Bārāṇasī.
He had leaf-huts constructed for eight Paccekabuddhas, provided them with jeweled water-vessels, and served them with the four requisites for ten thousand years. These are the well-known sites.
Having given gifts for a hundred thousand eons, our Bodhisatta was reborn together with him in the Tusita heaven;

passing away from there, he took conception in the house of the Sakyan Amitodana, eventually went forth, attained perfect enlightenment, and returned to Kapilavatthu on his first journey. When the Blessed One was departing from there—
When the princes were going forth to become members of the Blessed One’s retinue, he went out together with Bhaddiya and the others;

having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One and shortly thereafter heard a discourse on the Dhamma from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Thus this Venerable One was endowed with a prior spiritual support.
Due to this excellence of his prior supportive conditions (*pubbūpanissaya*), even the profound dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) appeared to him as if it were shallow.
Furthermore, "dwelling at a ford" (*titthavāsa*) refers to learning from, listening to, questioning, and retaining [the teachings] in the presence of the teachers;
this was exceedingly pure for the Elder. Therefore, even this profound [doctrine] appeared to him as if it were shallow. And of those who have attained the stream-entry (*sotāpanna*)...
The mode of conditionality (paccayākāra) presents itself clearly, and this venerable one is a stream-enterer (sotāpanna).
To those of great learning, the delimitation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) becomes as manifest as a bed and chair in a four-cubit room when a lamp is burning;
and this venerable one is the foremost among those of great learning. Thus, by virtue of his vast erudition, even the profound mode of conditionality [is clear to him].
It appeared as clear as if it were lying on its back. Dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is profound by way of four kinds of profundity;
that profundity has indeed been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. All of that appeared to the Elder as if it were clear.
Therefore, the Blessed One, encouraging the Venerable Ānanda, said, "Do not [think] thus," and so forth. This is the intended meaning here.
“Ānanda, you possess great wisdom and lucid knowledge; therefore, even dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), though profound, appears to you as if it were shallow.
For this reason, do not say: ‘Does this appear to me alone as if it were shallow, or does it appear so to others as well?
As for what was said regarding ‘disparaging,’ this is the intended meaning: Ānanda, ‘And yet, to me, it appears utterly shallow...’”
“...appears as if shallow,” do not speak thus.

For if this appears to you as if shallow and shallow indeed, why did you not become a stream-enterer by your own natural disposition, instead of penetrating the path of stream-entry by standing upon the method given by me?
Ānanda, it is Nibbāna itself that is profound; but the mode of conditionality has become shallow, so why [do you say] it is coarse?

Having eradicated these four defilements—the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the gross underlying tendency to sensual lust, and the underlying tendency to aversion—you do not realize the fruit of once-returning;
and having eradicated those same four defilements when they have become subtle, you do not realize the fruit of non-returning; [as well as] the five fetters beginning with lust for the form realm.

Having eradicated these eight defilements— the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance— why do you not realize Arhatship? Or why,

like Sāriputta and Moggallāna who fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable aeon plus a hundred thousand aeons, do you not penetrate the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple, having likewise fulfilled the perfections for more than a hundred thousand aeons?
For two incalculable eons, having fulfilled the perfections like the Paccekabuddhas, why did you not penetrate the knowledge of Paccekabodhi?
Or if that [knowledge] appeared to you in its entirety as something superficial,
then why, like the Buddhas who have fulfilled the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons, did you not [attain] the knowledge of omniscience?
Do you not realize it? Are you indifferent to these special attainments? Behold how far you have failed:
though you stand within the sphere of knowledge of a disciple, you say that the extremely profound mode of conditionality appears to you "as if shallow.
These words of yours contradict the teaching of the Buddhas. By such a monk as you...
It is not fitting to speak in opposition to the discourse of the Buddhas.
Indeed, Ānanda, four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons have passed while I was striving to penetrate this very structure of conditions (paccayākāra).
And for the sake of penetrating the structure of conditions, there was no gift I did not give, nor were any perfections (pāramī) left unfulfilled by me.

There was no [such] name. However, as I was dispelling the host of Māra as if it were effortless while thinking, "Today I shall penetrate the principle of dependent origination," this great earth did not shake even by the measure of two finger-breadths;
likewise when I was accomplishing the recollection of past lives in the first watch and the divine eye in the middle watch. But in the last watch, at the time of the powerful dawn, for me—
“‘Ignorance is a condition for volitional formations in nine ways’— at the mere sight of this,
the ten-thousandfold world system shook like drops of water on a lotus leaf struck by the wind, emitting hundreds and thousands of cries, like a bronze bowl beaten with an iron rod.
And so profound, Ānanda, is this dependent origination, and so profound its appearance.”
And, Ānanda, it is through not having fully awakened to this Dhamma... [as before] ...that one does not transcend [suffering].
"To this Dhamma" means to this Dhamma of conditions (*paccaya-dhamma*). "Not having fully awakened" means not awakening by way of the full understanding of the known (*ñāta-pariññā*).
"Not having penetrated" means not penetrating by way of the full understanding of investigation and abandonment (*tīraṇa-pahāna-pariññā*). "Become like a tangled skein" means a skein...

They have become as if confounded. Just as a weaver’s thread that has been poorly laid out and gnawed by mice becomes tangled here and there, making it difficult to join the end with the end or the beginning with the beginning—saying, "This is the end" or "This is the beginning"—even so, beings who stumble over this system of conditions become confused and utterly bewildered; they do not...

They are able to straighten the pattern of conditions (*paccayākāra*). In that regard, while it might be possible to straighten a tangled thread by applying personal effort (*paccatta-purisakāra*), there is no other being besides the two Bodhisattvas who is capable of straightening the pattern of conditions through their own inherent nature (*dhammatā*).
Just as a tangled thread, when treated with sour gruel and carded with a comb...
Just as that which is struck here and there becomes knotted and bound into balls, so too these beings,
having stumbled among the conditions and being unable to make the conditions straight, become knotted and bound into balls by way of the sixty-two types of views.
For whatever views there are that people rely upon, they all arise precisely because those individuals are unable to make the conditions straight.
“Kulāgaṇṭhikajāta” means that which is called a “kulāgaṇṭhika,” namely, a weaver’s yarn. Some say that *kulā* is a bird, and its nest is also [called] *kulā*.
Just as it is difficult to bring either of these two together—end with end or root with root—in a confused state, it should be applied according to the previous method.
“Become like muñja grass and pabbaja grass” means they have become such as those two kinds of grass.

For just as when ropes made from those two kinds of grass have worn out and one picks up a piece fallen somewhere, it is difficult to match the tip with the tip or the root with the root, saying, “This is the tip; this is the root,” so too—

Standing upon one's own personal effort (*paccatta-purisakāra*), it would be possible to make [the causal process] straight; however, with the exception of the two Bodhisattvas, there is no other being capable of making the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) straight by means of their own inherent nature (*dhammatā*).
Thus, this generation, unable to make the condition straight, becomes knotted by way of dogmatic views (*diṭṭhigata*) and falls into the states of loss and miserable destinies.
One does not transcend the ruinous cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

In this context, "the state of loss" (*apāya*) refers to hell, the animal womb, the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*), and the host of asuras. Indeed, all of these are called "the state of loss" because of the absence of the "wealth" (*aya*) known as prosperity;
likewise, they are called "bad destinations" (*duggati*) because they are the destination of suffering, and [they are called] "a heap of misery" because of the lack of happiness.
Because of falling down, it is called "falling" (*vinipāta*).
But the other [type of suffering] is described thus: "The uninterrupted succession of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as they proceed is called *saṃsāra*."
All of this does not exceed or go beyond that; rather, from death to rebirth-linking and from rebirth-linking to death,
thus repeatedly undergoing deaths and rebirth-linkings within the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations,
the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings— like a ship tossed by the wind upon the great ocean— it revolves upon the wheel.
"And like a bullock yoked [to a cart], he merely wanders about. Thus the Blessed One spoke, expressing his displeasure with the Venerable Ānanda.
The rest here is exactly as previously stated. The tenth [sutta].
The sixth chapter, the Chapter on Suffering (*Dukkhavagga*), is concluded.
7. Mahāvagga 1.
Assutavāsutta Commentary 61.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the Mahāvagga: "The uninstructed" refers to those who are unskilled in the aggregates, elements, sense bases, the principle of dependent origination, the foundations of mindfulness, and so forth.

One who lacks proficiency in learning, inquiry, and discernment. A *puthujjana* (worldling) is so called because he is a "generator" (*puthu-jana*) of various kinds of defilements and other such things through his causes.
For this has been said: "They generate many defilements, thus they are worldlings"—all of which should be expanded in detail.
Furthermore, [he is so called] because he is turned away from the noble Dhamma and is beyond the reach of calculation for the multitude.
He is called a *puthujjana* because he is included among those people who practice base qualities;
or alternatively, he is a *puthujjana* because he has gone separately (*puthu*) and alone, being dissociated from the Noble Ones who are endowed with virtues such as moral discipline and learning.
Thus, by these two terms—“the uninstructed worldling” (*assutavā puthujjano*)—those who are...
“Two types of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:

one is the blind worldling, and the other is the noble worldling.”—Of these two worldlings mentioned, it is the blind worldling who is taken here. In this [context], it refers to the present, directly perceptible body.

[The text] shows. "In that which consists of the four great elements" means in the body made of the four great elements; the meaning is: produced by the four great elements, consisting of the four great elements.
"One should become disenchanted" means one should feel weary. "One should become dispassionate" means one should not be attached. "One should be liberated" means one should desire to be released.
"Accumulation" means increase. "Dissipation" means decrease. "Grasping" means production. "Laying down" means dissolution.
"Therefore" means because these four distinctions—growth, decline, and production—are discerned; thus, it means "for that reason.
In this way, the Blessed One, having made it inappropriate for them to comprehend form within the body composed of the four great elements, makes it appropriate for them to comprehend the formless.
Why? Because those monks have a powerful and excessive attachment to form. Therefore...
Having shown that for them form is something to be grasped and encompassed, he spoke thus in order to expel them and establish them in the formless.

"Mind," and so forth—all this is a name for the mind-base (*manāyatana*) alone. For it is called "mind" (*citta*) because it is the basis of consciousness, because it is the range of consciousness, and because it is the consciousness associated with mental states;
it is called "mentality" (*mano*) in the sense of cognizing; and it is called "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) in the sense of discerning. "Not able" means not capable.

*Ajjhositam* means that which has been swallowed, finalized, and grasped by craving (*taṇhā*). *Mamāyitam* means that which has been grasped as "this is mine" through the conceit of craving (*taṇhāmama*).
*Parāmaṭṭham* means that which has been grasped after being misapprehended by views (*diṭṭhi*). "This is mine" is the grasping of craving;
by this, the eight hundred modes of craving’s wandering (*taṇhāvicarita*) are included. "I am this" is the grasping of conceit (*māna*); by this, the nine types of conceit are included.
They are grasped. The grasping of views, thinking "This is my self," means that by it, the sixty-two views are grasped.
Therefore—because it has been grasped in this way for a long time—one is not able to become disenchanted with it.
Why did he say, "It would be better, monks..."? Because at first, it was improper for him to discern form.

It was spoken [regarding] form and appropriate form; then, having understood that "the perception of those bhikkhus has emerged from form and gone toward the formless," he began this teaching in order to expel it.
In that context, "one might approach as a self" means one might grasp it as a self.
"Even more" means even beyond a hundred years. But why did the Blessed One speak thus? Is it because of more than a hundred years?
Is there such a thing as matter that remains stationary? Indeed, matter occurring in the first stage of life does not reach the middle stage of life;

matter occurring in the middle stage of life [does not reach] the final stage of life; matter occurring before the meal [does not reach] after the meal; matter occurring after the meal [does not reach] the first watch of the night;
matter occurring in the first watch of the night [does not reach] the middle watch of the night; matter occurring in the middle watch of the night...
Does it not reach the final watch [of the night]? Likewise, it does not reach standing while engaged in walking;
sitting while engaged in standing; or lying down while engaged in sitting. Even in a single mode of conduct (*iriyāpatha*), there is shifting while engaged in lifting the foot;
moving forward while engaged in shifting; moving backward while engaged in moving forward; and releasing while engaged in moving backward.
Is it that the occurrence [of formations] does not reach the point of being laid down, nor does the laying down reach the point of cessation;
rather, right there, each limit (odhi) becoming a limit and each section (pabba) becoming a section, the formations break apart with a *paṭapaṭa* sound like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan?
This is true. However, just as when a lamp is burning, the [wick] produced at each respective part of the wick—
Without transcending its limits, it breaks up right there; nevertheless, by virtue of its continuity in the lineage (*paveṇi*), it is called "a lamp that has burned all night.
So too here, by way of this lineage, this body is shown as if it were enduring for such a long time.
"Of night and day" means both during the night and during the day. This genitive case is used in the sense of the locative. "Quite another... [etc.]
"One arises, another ceases" means that what arises and ceases at night is indeed different from what arises and ceases during the day.
However, the meaning should not be taken as "one arises while another, which has not yet arisen, ceases.
This phrase, "of the night and of the day," is a minor elaboration following the previous sequence.
This was stated by way of the traditional lineage (*paveṇi*); however, there is no such thing as a single mind capable of remaining for even one night or one day.
For within a single *accharā-khaṇa* (the blink of an eye), many hundreds of thousands of millions of mental states arise.
And this has also been said in the *Milindapañha*:

“O Great King, a hundred cartloads of rice, thirty-seven and a half cartloads, seven bushels of rice, and two measures—this much rice, if used as a stake for a single moment of consciousness occurring in the blink of an eye, would be exhausted and brought to its end.
“In the forest” means in the great forest. By the phrase “releasing that and taking another, releasing that and taking another,” [it is shown].

He does not descend to the ground without having found a branch to grasp; rather, as he wanders through that great forest, he continues to wander while grasping this or that branch—this is the meaning shown.
"In the same way" refers here to the following application of the simile: for the great forest in the wilderness is like the forest of mental objects (*ārammaṇa*).
This should be understood: the mind arising in the forest of objects is like a monkey roaming in that forest;

its greed for objects is like its grasping at branches. Just as that monkey wandering in the wilderness abandons one branch and seizes another, so too this mind wandering in the forest of objects sometimes [seizes] a visible-form object.
Having grasped [an object], it arises; sometimes it is one among sound and the rest, sometimes it is past, future, or present, and likewise, sometimes it is internal, sometimes external.
And just as that monkey wandering in the forest cannot be said to have descended and sat on the ground because he could not find a branch, but rather [seized] a single leafy branch...

Just as one sits down only after having grasped [something], even so, it should not be said that the mind, while wandering in the forest of objects, arises without having obtained a single clung-to object;
rather, it should be understood that it arises only after having grasped an object of a single class.
And at this point, the Blessed One, having extracted [the mind] from the material, established its grasp upon the immaterial.
Having removed [the perception] from form by means of the formless;
now, desiring to expel that [perception] from both, the Blessed One began the teaching: "In this regard, monks, the instructed noble disciple...
This meaning, however, should be illustrated by the simile of the man bitten by a venomous snake: it is said that a certain man was bitten by a venomous snake.
Then, thinking, "I shall remove his poison," a skilled physician arrived; having induced vomiting, he recited a mantra—"Garula below, Naga above"—and caused the poison to rise upward.
When the snake-king realized it had reached as far as the region of his eyes, he thought, "I will not allow it to ascend further;
I shall place it right where it was bitten. Thus, [he became] Garula above...
Having recited the *nāga* mantra from below, he fumed [the snake's] ear, struck it with a stick, and introduced the antidote (*visa*) so that it remained right at the site of the bite.
Knowing that the poison was staying there, he neutralized the venom by applying an ointment of anti-venom (*agada*),
bathed the man, and said, "Be well," before departing wherever he pleased.
In this context, the time when these bhikkhus grasped at form is like the settling of venom in the body of one bitten by a poisonous snake;

the Tathāgata is like a skilled physician; and the time when the Tathāgata, having extracted their grasp of form, established them in the formless, is like the time when, after reciting a mantra, the physician causes the venom to rise upward. As far as...
Just as one might prevent poison that has ascended to the eye from rising further upward by using the power of a mantra to bring it back down and settle it right at the site of the bite,
so too did the Teacher, having extracted the grasping of those bhikkhus from the formless (arūpa), establish them in form (rūpa).
This was for the purpose of extracting the grasping from both sides, like the rubbing out of poison situated at the site of the bite with the application of an antidote (agada).
The time at which this teaching was commenced should be understood. Therein, by the phrase "becoming disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate," the Path is explained;
by "through dispassion, one is liberated," the Fruit is explained; and by "when liberated," etc., the reviewing knowledge is explained. First. 2.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Unlearned.
62. In the second [phrase], "to be experienced as pleasant" means the condition for pleasant feeling.
"Contact" refers to eye-contact and so forth. But is it not the case that eye-contact is not a condition for pleasant feeling?

It is not so by way of a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), but it is a condition for the feeling of the impulsion (*javana*) by way of a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*); it is with reference to this that this was said. This applies to ear-contact and the others as well.
The same method applies here. "Corresponding" (*tajjātikaṃ*) means suitable for that, appropriate to that contact; such is the meaning.

"To be experienced as painful," and so forth, should be understood according to the manner already stated. "By striking together and by coming together" (*saṅghaṭṭanasamodhānā*): by both striking together and by coming together;
the meaning is "by the conjunction of striking together. "Heat" (*usmā*) is the mode of warmth. "Fire is produced" (*tejo abhinibbattati*) means a flame and embers.
"It emerges" is not to be taken literally; rather, this is a synonym for the manifestation of heat. In that context, "of two pieces of wood" means of two fire-drills.

Therein, the lower drill is like the physical basis (*vatthu*), the upper drill is like the object (*ārammaṇa*), the friction is like contact (*phassa*), and the element of heat is like feeling (*vedanā*). Second.
3. Commentary on the *Puttamamsūpama Sutta* (The Simile of the Son’s Flesh). 63.
In the third sutta, the passage beginning with “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of nutriment” is exactly as previously explained.

However, since its presentation is based on a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppattika*), I shall first demonstrate that and then provide a word-by-word commentary on the sequence of terms. But by which [occasion]...?
Was this established on the basis of an occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*)? It was on account of gain and honor (*lābhasakkāra*).

It is said that great gain and honor arose for the Blessed One, as befits one who has fulfilled the accumulation of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) over four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*).
For, just as a great flood arises when twin great clouds pour rain in all directions, so too did the fruits of all the perfections (*pāramī*) ripen within a single lifetime.

Thinking, “We shall give,” they gathered together as if one and produced a great flood of gain and honor. From here and there, Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and others arrived with food, drink, vehicles, clothing, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth in their hands, seeking the Blessed One, asking, “Where is the Buddha?
Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of Gods, the Bull among Men, the Lion among Men?
Even after bringing provisions by the hundreds of carts, they were unable to find a place to enter.
For a distance of a *gāvuta* all around, they stood and moved along, wheeling against wheel, just as happened with the Brahmins of Andhakavinda and others.
All this should be understood according to the method set forth in various Suttas and in the Khandhaka.
As it was for the Blessed One, so it was for the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus. And this has been said:
Now at that time, the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, and he received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The community of monks also was honored... [as before] ...and received medicinal requisites for the sick.

Likewise: "Cunda, as far as any Saṅgha or group has arisen in the world today, Cunda, I do not see any other single Saṅgha that has attained such a pinnacle of gain and a pinnacle of fame as this Bhikkhu Saṅgha, Cunda.
Thus, the gain and honor that had arisen for both the Blessed One and the Saṅgha became immeasurable when combined, like the waters of two great rivers.
Then the Teacher, having gone into seclusion, reflected: "Great gain and honor have arisen even for past Buddhas..."

“Such was it in the past, and such will it be for those yet to come. Are the bhikkhus now able to consume food with mindfulness and clear comprehension, being equanimous and free from desire and lust, or are they not?
He saw some recently ordained sons of good family consuming food without reflecting upon it.
Having seen this, it occurred to him: "While I was fulfilling the perfections for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons, I did not do so for the sake of robes and such;
rather, I fulfilled them for the sake of the supreme fruit, arahantship.
These monks also, having gone forth in my presence, have not gone forth for the sake of robes and such, but for the sake of arahantship alone."
“Those who have gone forth are now treating what is essence-less as essence, and what is harmful as beneficial. Thus, a sense of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma arose in him.

Then he thought: “If it were possible to prescribe a fifth *pārājika* offense, then the consumption of food without due reflection could have been made the fifth *pārājika*. But it is not possible to do so, for this is a matter that must be constantly practiced.”
"Of beings. But as it has been stated, they will see this as being like the fifth *pārājika*.

Thus I shall establish the mirror of Dhamma, the restraint, the boundary, which the monks of the future, having repeatedly brought it to mind and having reflected upon the four requisites, will partake of them.
On account of this occasion, [the Buddha spoke] this sutta on the simile of the son's flesh.
He set it down. In this regard, "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of nutriment," and so forth, has already been explained in meaning below.

Having now elaborated upon the four nutriments, [the Buddha] spoke the passage beginning with, "And how, bhikkhus, is physical nutriment to be regarded? in order to show the danger (*ādīnava*) inherent in them.
In that context, *jāyampatikā* means both wife and husband. *Parittaṃ*...
"Sambala" refers to a small amount of provisions for the journey, such as one of these: a wrapped meal, *sattu* (flour), or sweetmeats.
"A wilderness path" (*kantāramagga*) means a path that is a wilderness, or a path within a wilderness. A wilderness (*kantāra*) is fivefold:

the wilderness of robbers, the wilderness of wild beasts, the wilderness of non-human beings, the wilderness lacking water, and the wilderness lacking food. Among these, where there is danger from robbers...
That which is a forest of thieves is a *corakantāra*. That where there are wild beasts such as lions, tigers, and so forth, is a *vāḷakantāra*.
That where there is danger due to non-human beings such as powerful *mukha-yakkhinīs* and others, is an *amanussakantāra*.
That where there is no water for drinking or bathing is a *nirudakakantāra*. That where there is nothing whatsoever to eat or consume...
There is not even any presence of roots, tubers, and so forth; that is what is called a "desert with little food.

However, where these five kinds of danger exist, that is simply a "wilderness" (*kantāra*). Furthermore, there are such wildernesses that can be crossed in one, two, or three days and so on, but those are not intended here.
Here, however, it refers to a hundred-yojana desert that is waterless and has little food.

This is the intended meaning. "Would set out on a path through such a wilderness" means that, being afflicted by the fear of hunger, the fear of disease, and the fear of kings, they would set out thinking:
"Having crossed this wilderness, we shall dwell happily in the kingdom of a righteous king, free from affliction."
"An only son" refers to one who has been taken up after being lifted [from his mother's lap], one who is worthy of compassion, and whose body is not yet firm—an only son.

"Dried meat and the marrow" means: having taken it from the thick, solid parts, it is dried meat (*vallūra*); having taken it from the places where the sinews adhere to the bones, it is the "sinew-meat" (*sūlamaṃsa*).
"They would grind it up" means they would strike it. "Where is the only son?"—this [is the question].
Such was their manner of lamentation.
Now, setting aside the literal meaning here, this is a brief commentary on the significance from the beginning:
it is said that a husband and wife, taking their son with them and provided with meager provisions for the journey, set out upon a wilderness path eight hundred leagues long.
When they had traveled fifty yojanas, their provisions were exhausted; afflicted by hunger and thirst, they sat down in the sparse shade.
Then the man said to his wife: "My dear, for fifty yojanas all around from here there is neither village nor town.
Therefore, whatever work must be done by a man—be it much plowing, cattle-tending, or the like—"
"Now I am no longer able to do that; come, kill me, eat half my flesh, make the other half into provisions for the journey, and cross the wilderness together with your son. Again she said to him:
"Master, now I am no longer able to perform even the many tasks a woman ought to do, such as spinning thread and so forth; come, [kill me]."
“Kill her, eat half the flesh, and making the other half into provisions for the journey, cross the wilderness together with your son.
Again, he said to her: “Bhadde, by the death of a woman, the death of two is brought about.
For the dull-witted boy cannot live without his mother. But if we survive, then [we may look after] the child again.”
“Let us obtain [some meat]. Come now, my dear son, let us kill him, take his flesh, and cross the wilderness.
Then the mother said to her son, “Dear child, go to your father,” and he went.

Thereupon his father said, “I have endured no small suffering through plowing, cattle-herding, and other such labors with the thought, ‘I will nourish my son,’ yet I am not able to [provide for] my son.”
Having said, "To kill him, you yourself must kill your own son," she added, "Dear child, go to your mother.
He went there. Then his mother also said, "When I longed for a son, I experienced no small amount of suffering through the cow-vow, the dog-vow, supplications to deities, and so forth;
what need is there to mention the time I carried him in my womb? I cannot..."
Saying, "I shall kill my son," he replied, "Dear father, go right to your father. Thus, while passing between the two of them, he died.
Seeing him, they lamented; then, taking the flesh in the manner described, they departed while eating it.
For those people, that food of their son’s flesh—being repulsive for nine reasons—was neither for sport nor for intoxication.
It is not for the sake of adornment, nor for the sake of beautification; it serves solely for the purpose of crossing over the wilderness.

If you ask by what nine reasons it is repulsive: because it is the flesh of one born with oneself, because it is the flesh of a kinsman, because it is the flesh of a son, because it is the flesh of a beloved son, because it is the flesh of the young, because it is raw flesh, because it is unseasoned flesh, because it is unsalted, and because it is unfumigated. For in this way, you...

For nine reasons they ate that putrid flesh of their sons; they did not eat it being full of passion or with greedy minds, but rather they ate it while remaining in a state of equanimity, free from desire and attachment.
They did not remove the parts connected to the bones, sinews, and skin to eat only the choice, thick pieces of meat; rather, they ate only the flesh that came directly into their hands.
They did not eat until they were full, nor did they eat up to the point of their throats; rather, they ate only a little each day, just enough to sustain themselves for that single day.
They did not eat while being stingy with one another; rather, they ate with a mind entirely pure, free from the stain of avarice.
They did not think, "Let us eat some other kind of meat, such as the flesh of deer or peacock."
They ate while utterly deluded; indeed, they ate even though they knew it was the flesh of their own beloved sons.
They did not eat having made the aspiration, "O, may we eat such son-flesh again," but rather they ate having already transcended such aspirations.
It was not as if, after eating this much in the wilderness, they thought, "Having passed through the remainder of the wilderness..."
Thinking, "We shall eat it after mixing it with salt, sour gruel, and other condiments," they made a store of it.
But at the end of the wilderness journey, thinking, "The great multitude might see us," they either buried it in the ground or consumed it by fire.
They did not harbor pride or arrogance, thinking, "No one else should ever get to eat the flesh of their own son as we have. Thus, they humbled their pride.
But having subdued their pride, they ate. They did not eat while disparaging it, thinking, "What is the use of this saltless, unsour, unspiced, and foul-smelling food?";
rather, having transcended all disparagement, they ate. Nor did they look down upon one another, saying, "This portion is yours, this portion is mine;
this child is yours, this child is mine. Instead, they remained united and harmonious.

They ate it. Perceiving this kind of enjoyment by them—devoid of desire, passion, and so forth—the Teacher, in order to authorize that practice for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus as well, said: "What do you think, bhikkhus, would they take food for sport? and so on.
In that context, the phrases beginning with "for sport" have already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. Regarding the word "of the wilderness":
"Of one who has crossed over the remainder of the wilderness.

In the same way, the meaning is that [the flesh of a dear son] should be viewed as being like [the flesh of a dear son], by means of the nine kinds of repulsiveness. Which nine? Those beginning with repulsiveness of movement (*gamanapaṭikkūlatā*). Even when reflecting on repulsiveness of movement...

One takes hold of physical nutriment by reflecting on the repulsiveness of the search for it, and also by reflecting on the repulsiveness of its consumption, its storage, its receptacle, its digestion—whether digested or undigested—and its excretions.
Furthermore, these [other] repulsivens, beginning with the repulsiveness of the journey, have already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the repulsiveness of nutriment.
Thus, by means of these nine kinds of repulsiveness, one should consume food after treating it as being like the flesh of one’s own son.

Just as those husband and wife did not eat the flesh of their beloved son out of passion or with greedy minds, but ate it while remaining in a state of equanimity, established in consumption free from desire and lust;
so too, one should consume [the food] by making it an act of consumption free from desire and lust. And just as they did not remove the large pieces of bone, sinew, and skin...
They ate only the choice meat, and they ate only what came directly into their hands; likewise, one should eat in regular succession like a lion,
not picking out only the excellent food mixed with ghee, meat, and so forth from here and there— without using the back of the hand to reject dry rice, thin curry, and the like,
and without leaving a gap as if with a ring or a chicken— but rather eating everything presented in due order.
And just as they did not eat until their throats were full, but rather ate only a little each day,
just enough for sustenance, even so the General of the Dhamma did not eat until his belly was full like some other brahmins such as Āḷāra Kālāma, but left space for four or five morsels.
It should be consumed like that. It is said that while he was living for forty-five years, he uttered this lion’s roar, saying:
"I have not taken food even for a single day without first causing a sour eructation after my meal," and spoke this verse:
"Without having eaten four or five morsels, one should drink water; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
“It is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute.

Just as they ate without being stingy with one another, but rather ate with a mind that was utterly pure and free from the stain of stinginess, even so, having obtained almsfood, one should not be stingy, thinking: “If he takes all of this...”
“I will give it all away; if someone takes half, I will give half; if there is anything remaining after it has been taken, I myself shall consume it.
Thus, one who abides in the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (duties of courtesy) should consume [the meat].
And so that they do not consume it in confusion, thinking, “Let us eat some other kind of deer meat, or perhaps the flesh of peacocks and so forth,” [one should act accordingly].

However, they ate while knowing that the flesh was that of their own beloved son; in the very same way, having received alms-food, one should not give rise to the delusion of self-apprehension by thinking, "I am eating," or "I am consuming.

Rather, having abandoned such delusion, one should understand: "The edible food does not know, 'I am nourishing this body composed of the four great elements,' and the body does not know, 'Edible food is nourishing me. Thus, having abandoned delusion—
It should be consumed. Furthermore, it should be consumed by one who remains undeluded through mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*).

And just as those [in the past] did not consume it while making the wish, "O, may we eat such flesh of a son again," but rather consumed it having transcended all wishing, even so should one consume exquisite food.

Having received [food], one should not form a wish or lament, thinking, "Oh, may I receive such as this again tomorrow, on the next day too," nor, having received coarse food, think, "Today I have not received fine food as I did yesterday. Without craving, one should remain thus:
"I do not lament for the past, nor do I long for the future."
“I subsist on what is present; thereby my complexion brightens.
Recalling this instruction, one should consume [food] with the thought: “I shall subsist on what is present alone.
And just as those [travelers] do not think, “Having eaten this much in the wilderness, we will cross the remainder of the wilderness with salt, sour gruel, and so forth,”...

Having prepared them, they thought, "We shall eat them," and so they stored them away. But at the end of the desert journey, thinking, "The great multitude will see it before long," they either buried them in the ground or consumed them by fire. In just this way:
"Of foods and also of drinks..."
“Having obtained solid foods or even robes,
one should not make a store;
nor should one be distressed when not obtaining them.”
Recalling this exhortation, one should consume whatever of the four requisites one receives by taking only what is sufficient for one's own maintenance from each,
distributing the remainder among fellow practitioners of the holy life, and avoiding hoarding. Furthermore,
one should not harbor pride, thinking, "No one else is permitted to eat such 'son-flesh' as we do."
Or they did not act with pride; rather, having subdued their conceit and subdued their arrogance, they ate.
In the same way, having obtained exquisite food, one should not give rise to conceit or arrogance, thinking, "I am a recipient of robes, almsfood, and so forth.
Reflecting, "This going-forth is not for the sake of robes and such things, but this going-forth is for the sake of Arahantship," one should consume it only with conceit and arrogance subdued.

Just as they did not eat those [foods] after disparaging them, saying, "What is the use of this saltless, sourless, unseasoned, foul-smelling thing?", but rather ate them once they had overcome their contempt;

even so, having received alms-food, one should not disparage that alms-food by saying, "What is the use of this coarse and tasteless food, like the fodder for horses and oxen? Throw it into a dog's trough!", nor should one think, "Who will eat this?"?
"Give [the food] to crows, dogs, and the like"— thus, without disparaging the donor:
"Wandering with bowl in hand, though not mute yet considered mute,
one should not despise a small gift, nor should one look down upon the giver."
One should consume [the almsfood] while recollecting this exhortation. Just as they did not despise one another, thinking, "This is your portion, this is my portion;

your son, my son," but rather ate together in harmony and with mutual affection—even so, having received almsfood, one should not think, "Who would give to those like you without cause?"... [and so forth].
“Even a woman who has just given birth does not think that you should give anything to those who stumble and wander about in the marketplaces;
yet we obtain fine robes and other requisites wherever we go,” thus he despises his virtuous fellow-celibates—
referring to whom it was said:

“Thus, overcome by that gain, honor, and fame, with his mind consumed by them, he holds other virtuous bhikkhus in contempt. For that, O bhikkhus, leads to the misfortune and suffering of that foolish man for a long time.
Thus, without holding anyone in contempt, one should enjoy [the requisites] in harmony and in mutual amity with all fellow practitioners of the holy life.

“Fully understood” means fully understood by means of these three kinds of full understanding: full understanding as the known (*ñāta-pariññā*), full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*), and full understanding as abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*).
How so? Here, a bhikkhu reflects: "This so-called 'edible food' consists, by way of its basis, of the eightfold materiality that has nutritive essence as its eighth factor.

Where does this eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence encounter resistance? In the sensitivity of the tongue. On what is the sensitivity of the tongue dependent? It is dependent on the four great elements.
Thus, these phenomena—the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence, the sensitivity of the tongue, and the great elements which are their conditions—constitute the aggregate of form."
The mental states consisting of contact as the fifth factor that arise for one grasping at that [name] are the four immaterial aggregates.
Thus he understands: "All these five aggregates, in brief, are merely name-and-form.
Having defined those phenomena by way of their individual intrinsic characteristics, he seeks their conditions and contemplates dependent origination in both forward and reverse order.

He sees. To this extent, because he has seen name-and-form together with its conditions as they truly are by way of the door of physical nutriment, physical nutriment is fully understood through full understanding by knowledge (*ñātapariññā*).
He then subjects that very same name-and-form together with its conditions to the three characteristics—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—and investigates it by means of the seven contemplations.
To this extent, it is fully understood by him through the full understanding of scrutiny, which is termed the knowledge of comprehension that penetrates the three characteristics.

Furthermore, by means of the path of non-returning, as one who understands that very same name-and-form through the drawing away of desire and lust, it is fully understood through the full understanding of abandoning.
"Consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure" means that the lust arising from the five strands of sensual pleasure is fully understood. Herein, there are three kinds of full understanding.

The single full understanding is the full understanding of all; it is the root full understanding. What is this single full understanding? When a bhikkhu fully understands the craving for a single flavor at the door of the tongue, by that very act, lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is indeed fully understood.

Why? Because that [lust] arises precisely from that [craving]. For that same craving, when it arises at the door of the eye, is called "lust for forms," and likewise at the doors of the ear and so forth.

The sensual lusts for sounds and so forth have arisen. Thus, just as when a single thief is being executed on one of five roads, once he is caught on one road and his head is cut off, all five roads become safe;

in the same way, when craving for tastes at the door of the tongue is fully understood, the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is also fully understood. This is called "single full understanding" (*ekapariññā*).
What is "full comprehension of all"? For when alms-food has been placed in a bowl, only one kind of lust—lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure—is found there.
How so? First, as he gazes upon its pure color, there is lust for visible forms.
When warm ghee is poured onto it, a crackling sound arises; likewise, as he eats such solid food...
The sound of "murmurūti" arises; for one who relishes that, there is lust for sound. For one relishing the scent of cumin and other spices, there is lust for odor.
Through the quality of deliciousness, there is lust for flavor. For one relishing soft food as being possessed of tactile sensation, there is lust for the tangible.
Thus, when this nutriment has been taken up with mindfulness and clear comprehension and consumed with enjoyment free from desire, [it is properly digested].
"When all of that has been fully understood," this is what is called "full understanding of the whole" (*sabbapariññā*).
What is "full understanding of the root" (*mūlapariññā*)? For edible food is the root of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. Why? Because when that exists, it arises.
It is said that during the time of the Brahmin Tissa’s terror, for twelve years, the minds of husbands and wives were filled with longing for one another.

There was no [fear] at all. Why? Because of the meagerness of food. But when the danger had subsided, the island of Tambapaṇṇi, extending for a hundred yojanas, became as one festival through the birth celebrations of the children.
Thus, when the root-condition, food, is fully understood, the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is also fully understood;
this is what is called "full understanding of the root."
“There is no such fetter”: because it has been abandoned along with that lust, being something to be abandoned together with it, it does not exist.
