Thus this teaching has been explained up to the stage of the non-returner path. However, thinking, “Let them not fall into complacency with just this much,” it is appropriate to continue the explanation up to the stage of Arahantship by increasing insight into the five aggregates by means of those very same forms and so forth.
The first nutriment is finished.
In the second [simile], "skinless" means that from the skin onwards, up to the roots of the horns, the entire body has had its skin stripped away, being the color of a *kiṃsuka* tree trunk.
But why is the simile of the skinless cow taken instead of taking another simile such as an elephant, horse, ox, or the like? It is for the purpose of enduring.
This is for the purpose of illustrating a state of incapacity. For a woman is unable to endure or tolerate arisen painful feeling;
likewise, it is to show that the nutriment of contact (*phassāhāra*) is weak and feeble that this very simile was brought forward.
"Wall" (*kuṭṭa*) refers to any one of the various types such as stone walls and so forth. "Creatures dependent on a wall" (*kuṭṭanissitā pāṇā*) refers to spiders, crickets, mice, and the like.
"Those dependent on trees" refers to creatures such as large centipedes. "Those dependent on water" refers to fish, crocodiles, and so forth.
"Those dependent on the air" refers to gadflies, mosquitoes, crows, hawks, and so forth. "They might devour them" means they might tear them off and eat them.
Seeing the danger of being devoured by various creatures in those respective places—each rooted in its particular habitat—she did not consider her own honor or respect.

Just as one does not desire back-massage, body-shampooing, or warm water, even so a bhikkhu, seeing the danger of being devoured by the vermin of the defilements rooted in the nutriment of contact, becomes disinterested in contact belonging to the three planes.

"When the nutriment of contact has been fully understood," bhikkhus, means when it has been fully understood by means of the three kinds of full understanding. Here too, there are three kinds of full understanding.

In this context, the thorough knowledge through understanding (*ñātapariññā*) is the seeing of name-and-form together with its conditions as they truly are, as follows: "Contact is the aggregate of formations; the feeling associated with it is the aggregate of feeling; perception is the aggregate of perception; consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness;
and their bases and objects are the aggregate of form. Having applied the three characteristics to those very things, for the seven...

The full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*) is the weighing [of phenomena] as impermanent and so forth by way of the contemplations (*anupassanā*). However, the full understanding by abandoning (*pahānapariññā*) is the path of Arahantship which draws out desire and lust for that very same name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Thus, when the nutriment of contact (*phassāhāra*) has been fully understood by these three kinds of full understanding, the three feelings are also fully understood, because they are rooted in it and associated with it. Thus, by way of the nutriment of contact...
The teaching is explained up to the stage of *arahantship*.

This is the second nutriment. Regarding the third, "a pit of embers" (*aṅgārakāsū*): it is a pit of burning coals. "Pit" (*kāsū*) refers to both a heap and a hollow. "Others scatter a pit of embers..."
"Men are weeping, their limbs scorched;
O charioteer, fear seizes me upon seeing this.
I ask you, Mātali, the divine charioteer."
In this context, a heap is called "kāsu.
In the verse, "Why do you dig a *kāsu* while hurrying, O charioteer?"—here it refers to a pit.
Here too, this same meaning is intended. "Exceeding a man's height" means more than a man's height, measuring five *ratana*s.
"Of those whose flames are extinguished and whose smoke has vanished"—by this he shows its state of great feverish heat (*pariḷāha*).
For when there is a flame or smoke, the wind arises and the feverish heat is not great; in the absence of those, due to the absence of wind, the feverish heat becomes great.
"It should be far away indeed"—it should remain at a distance.
"Even so," it is said; here is the application of the simile: the round of existence in the three realms is to be regarded as the pit of glowing embers.
The foolish worldling dependent on that round is like the man who desires to live. The two strong men are like wholesome and unwholesome karma.
The time when those two seize the man by his various limbs and drag him toward the pit of glowing embers is like [the time] for the worldling.
This is the time for the accumulation of kamma. For it is only when kamma is being accumulated that it is said to "draw" rebirth-linking.
Just as suffering arises from the cause of glowing embers and ashes, so too should the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭa-dukkha) be understood to arise from the cause of kamma.

"Fully understood" means fully understood by way of the three kinds of full understanding (pariññā). As for the application of full understanding here, it is to be understood in the same manner as explained in the section on contact (phassa).
They are to be understood. "The three kinds of craving" refers to craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*);
these are fully understood. Why? Because mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) is rooted in craving. For when the cause is not abandoned, the fruit is not abandoned.
Thus, by way of the nutriment of mental volition, the teaching has been explained up to the stage of Arahantship. This is the third nutriment.

In the fourth [verse], "one who behaves wickedly" (*āgucārī*) means one who acts evilly, a doer of harm. "How is that man? asks: what kind of person is he, and does he subsist or not subsist? "He lives just as before, O King" means he lives now exactly as he did previously.
"Even so indeed" (*evameva kho*)—here too, this is the application of the simile: action (*kamma*) is to be seen like the king;

the foolish worldling dependent on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭasannissito bālaputhujjano*) is like the man who behaves wickedly; and the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*) is like the three hundred spears.

Just as when a king issues the command, "Strike this man who has committed a crime with three hundred spears," and the executioners seize the culprit and cast him upon the whetting stone, so too does the karma-king seize the ordinary person (*puthujjana*) dependent on the cycle of existence and cast him into rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
In that regard, although the rebirth-linking consciousness is like the three hundred spears, there is no pain in the spears themselves;
rather, the pain arises from the wound caused by being struck by the spears. Even so it is with rebirth-linking.
There is no suffering [in the act of giving itself]; however, once rebirth has been granted, the suffering of the process (pavatta) is like the pain rooted in a wound struck by a spear.

"Thoroughly understood" means thoroughly understood by means of the three kinds of full understanding (pariññā). Here too, the application of full understanding should be understood in the same manner as explained in the section on contact as nutriment (phassāhāra).
"Name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) refers to name-and-form conditioned by consciousness; for when consciousness is thoroughly understood, that [name-and-form] is also thoroughly understood.

It exists because it is rooted in that and because it arises together with it. Thus, by way of the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*), the teaching has been explained up to the stage of Arhatship.
This concludes the fourth nutriment. Third [chapter].
4. Commentary on the Atthirāga Sutta.
64. In the fourth [verse], "lust" (*rāga*) and so forth are synonyms for greed (*lobha*). For it is called "lust" by way of coloring; "delight" (*nandi*) by way of rejoicing;
and "craving" (*taṇhā*) by way of thirsting. "Consciousness is established and grown there":

it is both "established" and "grown" because, having impelled the kamma, it possesses the capacity to draw in rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Wherein" refers to the round of existence consisting of the three planes.
This is the locative case; or rather, in all instances, this is the locative case for each preceding word.

"Therein there is the growth of formations" (saṅkhārānaṃ vuddhi) is said with reference to the formations that are the causes for the cycle of the future for one who is situated within this cycle of kamma-result (vipākavaṭṭa).
"Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future" (yattha atthi āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti) means in whatever place there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
"Even so," it is said; here is the application of the simile:
for action together with its concomitant equipment is like the dyer and the painter, while the round of existence in the three realms is like the wooden plank, the wall, and the cloth.
Just as the dyer and the painter produce forms upon clean planks and such surfaces, even so action together with its equipment produces form within the various states of existence.
In this regard, just as matter produced by an unskilled artisan is deformed, ill-shaped, and unpleasant, even so,
when a certain person performs an action with a mind dissociated from knowledge, that action— while producing matter—
does not grant excellence to the eyes and other faculties, but results instead in ugliness, deformity, and even for one's parents.
It produces an unpleasant form. However, just as a form produced by a skilled painter is beautiful,
well-proportioned, and pleasing, even so, when a certain person performs an action with a mind associated with knowledge,
that action, while producing form, bestows excellence upon the eyes and other faculties, resulting in beauty.
It produces a well-formed material form as if it were adorned and prepared.
Herein, by condensing nutriment together with consciousness, there is one junction between nutriment and name-and-form;

and by condensing the process of kamma-result together with name-and-form, there is another junction between the formations of name-and-form and the formations [of volition]. And of those formations...
And it should be understood that there is one link (sandhi) between future existence and this life.
A "gabled house" (*kūṭāgāra*) is a house built using a single beam-end (*kaṇṇikā*). A "hall with a gabled roof" (*kūṭāgārasālā*) is a hall built using two beam-ends.
"In the same way," in this context, the karma of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) should be understood as being like the rays of the sun. The rays of the sun...

However, it does exist; it is merely called "without a basis" (*appatiṭṭhā*) due to the absence of a foundation. For one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), karma is "without a basis" precisely because of its non-existence.
Indeed, his body and so forth do exist, but the karma performed by them—whether wholesome or unwholesome—does not occur;
remaining in mere functional activity (*kiriyamatta*), it is without result. Thus, for him, karma is "without a basis" precisely because of its non-existence.
...is called "birth. This is the fourth [section].
5. Commentary on the *Nagarasutta*. 65.

Regarding the fifth [sutta], in the passage "When there is name-and-form, there is consciousness," and [the parallel] "When there are volitional formations, there is consciousness," and "Due to ignorance..."
One might have said, "When there is ignorance, there are volitional formations," yet neither of these was stated. Why?

Because ignorance and volitional formations constitute a third existence (*bhava*), and this insight (*vipassanā*) does not coincide with them. For the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) has become established by way of the present five-aggregate existence.
But is it not the case that if ignorance and volitional formations were not seen, it would be impossible for him to be a Buddha? True, it would be impossible.
However, you have seen this only by way of existence, clinging, and craving.

Therefore, it is just as if a man pursuing a lizard, seeing it enter a well, were to descend, dig up the place where it entered, seize the lizard, and depart, rather than digging further toward the other side.
Why? Because there is nothing more to be found there. In the same way, the Great Man also—
Like a man pursuing a lizard, he sat upon the Bodhi throne and, beginning from aging and death, sought their conditions—thinking, "This is the condition for this;
this is the condition for that"—until he saw the condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Seeking the condition for that as well, he saw consciousness (*viññāṇa*) itself. Then [he realized]: "To this extent, by way of the five-aggregate existence..."

He turned back from insight with the thought, "This is the range of comprehension. Beyond that, there exist the two factors of ignorance and formations, which are like an unbroken section of a hollow mast;
however, because these were already grasped by the preceding insight, they do not constitute a separate object for comprehension, and thus he did not grasp them.
"It turns back" means it returns. But what consciousness here turns back? Both the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) and the insight consciousness (*vipassanā-viññāṇa*).
Therein, the rebirth-linking consciousness turns back from its condition, while the insight consciousness turns back from its object.
Neither of them transcends name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); neither goes beyond name-and-form. To this extent—

If consciousness were a condition for name-and-form in cases such as "one is born," or if name-and-form were a condition for consciousness, or if both were conditions for one another—then by that much alone one would be born or reborn.
Beyond this, what else could be born or reborn? Is it not the case that precisely this is what is born and what is reborn?
Having thus shown the five factors along with the successive processes of death and rebirth-linking, he then concludes the meaning already stated by saying, "In this way, namely:
with name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form.
Following that, by way of the forward order of conditions, he shows future aging and death rooted in name-and-form with consciousness as its condition.
In order to demonstrate this, he said: "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense-bases," and so forth.

*Añjasam* is a synonym for the Path (*magga*) itself. *Uddhāpavantam* means possessed of a rampart and a moat; it is so called because it has risen above the moat (*āpata*), having acquired the conventional designation of being thus equipped with a wall and a foundation.
*Ramaṇīyam* means [pleasant] both within and on all sides of the four gates.
It is delightful with an abundance of various goods. "Have it built" means: having sent forth the great multitude, cause them to dwell there.

"He would have it built" means: he would cause them to dwell there. And while causing it to be built, he would first send forth eighteen koṭis of people and, having asked, "Is it complete?", when told, "It is not yet complete," he would send forth another five clans. Having asked again...
When it was said, "It is not yet complete," he would send another fifty-five families.

Having asked again, when it was said, "It is not yet complete," he would send another thirty families. Having asked again, when it was said, "It is not yet complete," he would send another thousand families.
Having asked again, when it was said, "It is not yet complete," [he would send] another...
He would send eleven hundred thousand families. When asked again and told, "It is not yet full," he would send another eighty-four thousand families.
When asked again and told, "It is full," [the king] said, "Great King, what are you saying?
This is a vast city, free from congestion; it is impossible to fill it by sending families in this manner. [Strike] the drum!"

But having had it circulated, he might say: “Proclaim the praises of our city and announce to the world that it shall receive these various benefits: ‘Our city is endowed with such-and-such prosperity;
let those who wish to dwell there go at their pleasure, and they shall receive this and that benefit. He would do so. Then—

When people, having heard of both the virtues of the city and the benefits of its protection, would gather from all directions and fill the city, it would at a later time become prosperous and flourishing.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "At a later time, that city would be prosperous and flourishing," and so forth.
In this context, "iddha" means prosperous with abundant food; "phīta" means blossomed with all kinds of excellences;
"bāhujañña" means that which is to be known by many, or that which is beneficial to many people (alternatively, the reading "bahujana" is also found);
"ākiṇṇamanussa" means crowded with people, filled without any gaps; and "vuḍḍhivepullappatta" means having attained both growth and vastness.
The meaning is that he has attained both the state of excellence and vastness, and was born in the foremost city within the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*).
"In the same way" (*evameva kho*)—herein this is the application of the simile:

the Great Man (*mahāpurisa*) fulfilling the perfections (*pāramī*) starting from the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha should be regarded as being like the man wandering in the forest wilderness; of that man...
Just as a man following a single footpath might later see a great highway, so too,
for the Great Being who was seated at the seat of enlightenment after having gradually practiced the eightfold path of insight (vipassanā) during his preliminary stage;
and just as one following that solitary path might later see a great highway, so it was for the Great Being while he was engaged in higher insight (uparivipassanā).
The vision of the supramundane path is like a person traveling along that very road seeing the city ahead;

the Tathāgata’s vision of the city of Nibbāna is likewise. However, in this case, the city outside was seen by one person and inhabited by another, whereas the Teacher himself saw the city of Nibbāna and himself made his dwelling there. For that person, of the four...
The time when the Tathāgata saw the four paths is like the time when [the king] saw the city gates;
the time when the Tathāgata entered Nibbāna by means of the four paths is like the time when he entered the city through the four gates;
and the time when the Tathāgata [attained] reviewing knowledge is like the time when he [the king] arranged his goods within the city.
This was the time for defining the fifty-one wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). It was like the time when a man seeks a family to build a house for his city;
it was the time when the Teacher, having emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), surveyed the beings to be converted (*veneyyasatta*).
It was like the king, when requested by that man, seeing one great householder; it was like the Blessed One, when requested by Mahābrahmā, [seeing] the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña.
It was as if the time had come for the King to summon the great householder and send him forth with the command,
"Dwell in the city. It was the moment when the Blessed One, having traveled eighteen yojanas after his single meal,
entered Isipatana in Bārāṇasī on the full-moon day of Āsāḷha and taught the Dhamma, making the Elder a bodily witness, while the great householder—

Just as when the Tathāgata had set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, the time when he took eighteen koṭis of men and entered the city, so too was it when the Elder, together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, was established in the fruit of stream-entry;
thus the city of Nibbāna was first inhabited. Then, having been asked, "Is the city now full?", he replied, "Not yet."
When this was said, starting from the five families up to the sending of eighty-four thousand families,
the Tathāgata— beginning from the fifth day— taught the *Anattalakkhaṇa-sutta* and other discourses to the group of five,
beginning with Yaśas and the fifty-five noble sons, the thirty Bhaddavaggiyas, the thousand former matted-hair ascetics, and those headed by Bimbisāra.

At that time, eleven hundred thousand men and eighty-four thousand others were led to enter the Noble Path and dispatched to the City of Nibbāna by means of this expression of appreciation beyond the walls; then, as the city was not yet filled by that method,
he had the drum beaten throughout the month, like a proclamation of the city's excellence and a proclamation of the exemptions and gains for the families.
For eight days, sitting here and there, he proclaimed the praise of Nibbāna and the benefits of crossing over the wilderness of birth and so forth to those who preach the Dhamma;
then, like people coming from all directions to gather in a city after hearing the Dhamma discourse here and there, they departed from their respective places and went forth into homelessness.
Taking this as the beginning, the convergence in Nibbāna of immeasurable clansmen who have entered upon the progressive path should be seen.

"The ancient path" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path. For this Noble Path is called "the unarisen path" in the *Pavāraṇā Sutta* by way of its not having occurred [previously], whereas in this sutta it is called "the ancient path" by way of its having been traversed. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*)...
The entire teaching is comprised of the three trainings. "Prosperous" (*iddha*) means well-provided with the relish of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).

"Flourishing" (*phīta*) means blossomed with the ornaments of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). "Extended" (*vitthārika*) means widespread. "Well-known among many" (*bāhujañña*) means intelligible to many people.
"Well-expounded as far as gods and humans" means it is defined by its reach as far as the gods and humans throughout the ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
"In this interval, it has been well-expounded and well-taught by the Tathāgata. This is the fifth. 6.
Commentary on the *Sammasa Sutta*. 66.
Regarding the sixth [sutta], why did he address [the bhikkhus]? Because his teaching of the Dharma was subtle and struck at the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*).
He attended upon him. It is said that in that country the people were endowed with causes and possessed of wisdom. The food there was indeed succulent;
by partaking of it, the wisdom of the people increased, and they became capable of penetrating the profound discourse on the Dhamma struck by the three characteristics.
For this very reason, the Blessed One taught the Great Foundations of Mindfulness and the Great Causality in the *Dīgha Nikāya* and *Majjhima Nikāya*.
"He spoke other profound suttas right there, such as the *Āneñjasappāya* and the *Cūḷanidāna* and other suttas from the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.
'Sammasatha no' means 'do you comprehend? 'Antaraṃ sammasanti' means they comprehend the internal, namely, the comprehension of conditions (*paccaya-sammasana*).
That bhikkhu did not satisfy the Blessed One's mind" [refers to] the Blessed One who wished to have him explain by way of the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*).
Thus, having not given a categorical answer, he was unable to grasp the intention while explaining by way of the thirty-two marks.
“He said this” means that the teaching had not yet reached its proper conclusion; he said this for the purpose of bringing the teaching to its proper conclusion.
Therefore, Ānanda, listen—this is a phrase found nowhere else in the Buddha’s word consisting of the Three Piṭakas. For elsewhere it is thus:
It has not been said [otherwise]. "With clinging as its source" means with the clinging of the aggregates (*khandha*) as its source.
Here, the "clinging" intended is the pentad of aggregates. "Arises" means it is born. "Settles down" means it establishes itself by way of recurring occurrence.
"Whatever in the world is of a lovely nature and pleasant nature" refers to that which in the world is both of a dear character and of a sweet character.
Regarding the passage beginning "The eye surveys the world," etc.: for in this world, beings who are obsessed with a sense of "mine" toward the eye and other faculties,
when established in prosperity, imagine their own eye to have fivefold translucent clarity—
like a jeweled lion-lattice opened within a golden palace— and the ear to be like a silver tube.
They imagine the feet to be like anklets; they imagine the nose—known by the designation "high-bridged"—to be like a stalk of green palmyra placed upright;
they imagine the tongue to be like a piece of red woolen cloth, soft, smooth, and giving off a sweet flavor;
they imagine the body to be like a sal tree trunk or a golden archway; and they imagine the mind to be sublime, unlike the minds of others.
"They saw it as permanent" means they perceived it as permanent. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
"They were not liberated from suffering" means they were not liberated from the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). "They will see" means they will perceive.
"A bronze cup for drinking water" is a name for a *saraka* (a drinking vessel); however, because one drinks water (*āpa*) in it, it is called "āpānīya."
“Āpānīyakaṃso” means a bronze vessel for drinking; this is the name for the scum of fermented liquor (*surāmaṇḍasara*).
However, because of the statement beginning with “endowed with color,” it is said that only the drink contained within the bronze vessel is thus described.

“Ghammābhitatto” means scorched by heat. “Ghammapareto” means touched by heat; the meaning is “overcome” by it. For [the thought] “while he drinks, it will refresh him” refers to one who is drinking it.
The water will be pleasing because of its excellence of color and other qualities, or it will remain pervading the entire body, producing satisfaction.
"Without reflection" means without reviewing.
"In the same way" refers here to this application of the simile: for in the world, that which is lovely in form is like the bowl of drinking water.
The object of a pleasant nature is to be seen as follows: the worldling dependent on the cycle of existence is like a man tormented by the heat;
the people inviting him with objects that are dear and pleasant in the world are like the people inviting him with a vessel of drinking water;
and the teacher, preceptor, and others are like the person at the tavern who announces both the excellence and the danger regarding the vessel of drinking water.

He has a virtuous friend. Just as that man’s trusted person informs him of both the advantages and the dangers regarding the drinking vessel, even so does the teacher or the preceptor explain to the bhikkhu the gratification and the escape in regard to the five cords of sensual pleasure.
In this context, just as when the advantages and dangers of the drinking vessel have been explained, that man [focuses] only on the excellence of its beautiful color and so forth...

Just as one who has developed a craving for it, thinking, "If death should occur, I shall know it later," drinks it impulsively without reflection and meets with death or suffering equal to death; even so, bhikkhu, regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure,
there is only the mere gratification consisting of the joy that arises through seeing them and so forth, while the danger is both pertaining to the present life and to future lives.
"Sense pleasures are manifold and of various kinds, but they provide little gratification and involve much suffering and much despair"—

having thus explained both the benefits and the dangers by way of his teachers and preceptors, and having further exhorted him, saying, "Enter upon the path of the recluse; guard the doors of your senses, be moderate in eating, and be devoted to wakefulness"— even so, because his mind was bound to gratification...
Thinking, "If there will be such a danger as described, I shall know it later," he reviles his teacher and preceptor;

having abandoned the recitation of texts, questioning, and the performance of duties, he engages in talk about worldly gain; desiring to enjoy sensual pleasures, he renounces the training and returns to the low life.
Then, while fulfilling his misconduct, at the time of breaking into houses and so forth—

Having seized him, saying, “This is a thief,” he was shown to the king; having undergone the cutting off of his hands, feet, and so forth right here, he experiences great suffering in the four states of misery in the future life.
“To remove [the thirst] with water” means to carry it away with cool water. “With whey” means with a mere measure of whey.

"With salt-water" means with sour gruel mixed with salt. "With salt-vinegar" (loṇasovīraka): they prepare what is called salt-vinegar by adding all kinds of grains, fruits, shoots, and so forth; [the monk drinks] with that.
As for the application of the simile here: the practitioner at the time he is dependent on the round [of existence] is like the man oppressed by the heat.

It should be seen as follows: just as that man’s reflection leads him to abandon the drinking vessel and quench his thirst with water and other drinks, so too does a bhikkhu—who stands by the instruction of his teacher and preceptor, guards the six sense doors, and gradually increases his insight—attain the fruit of Arahantship;
for the four [types of] drink are like the four [types of] nutriment.
Just as those who have drunk one or another of these drinks dispel their thirst for liquor and travel happily wherever they wish,

so too should the time be understood when the one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), having drunk the drink of the four paths, dispels craving and proceeds toward the direction of Nibbāna, which has never been reached before. This is the sixth [simile].
7. Commentary on the Naḷakalāpī Sutta 67.
Regarding the seventh [question], why does he ask, "But how is it, friends"? He asks, "Being asked thus, how indeed would one answer?
This is for the purpose of knowing the elder's underlying intention. Furthermore, in the past, two Chief Disciples resolved this very question.
He asks, "The monks will understand in the future," thinking that they might not grasp it immediately. When the Elder says, "Right now indeed we...
he does so because it has been stated that consciousness is the condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and thus he asserts that this very name-and-form is the condition for consciousness.

As for the phrase "like a bundle of reeds": here, rather than employing a comparison such as a bundle of iron, this simile is brought forward in order to demonstrate the weak and fragile nature of both consciousness and name-and-form.
The teaching is presented up to the point "there is cessation" by way of the five-aggregate existence that has arisen through conditions.
"By thirty-six bases" means by way of thirty-six reasons, three for each of the twelve sections answered below.
And herein, the first is the quality of the preacher of the Dhamma, the second is the practice, and the third is the fruit of the practice.
Therein, by the first method, the perfection of the teaching is explained; by the second, the stage of the trainee (*sekha*); and by the third, the stage of the one beyond training (*asekha*).
This is the seventh [section]. 8. Commentary on the Kosambī Sutta: 68.
Regarding the eighth [verse], "except in another case": for some, having placed faith in another, think that whatever this person says is true.
One person accepts it by way of conviction (*ruci*): having sat down and reflected, they accept whatever reason pleases them, thinking, "This exists.
Another accepts it by way of oral tradition (*anussava*): "There has been such a tradition for a long time; this is what actually happened.
Yet another accepts it by way of reasoning (*ākāraparivitakka*): as one person reflects, a certain reason presents itself, and he accepts it, thinking, "This must exist."

As another reflected, a certain view arose, by which that reason was acceptable to him as he contemplated it; he grasped it through the acceptance resulting from contemplation of the view, thinking, "It exists.
But the Elder, having rejected all five of these reasons, asked about the state of being penetrated by direct knowledge: "Friend Musīla, apart from this..."
He said, "By faith," and so forth. Therein, "except for" means setting aside the causes such as faith; the meaning is "without these causes.
"The cessation of existence is Nibbāna" means that the cessation of the five aggregates is Nibbāna.
"He remained silent": the Elder was one whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava), yet he remained silent, neither saying "I am one whose taints are destroyed" nor "I am not."
[The text] says: "The Venerable Nārada said this to the Venerable Paṭissava. Why did he say it? It is said that he thought:
"This question—that 'the cessation of existence is called Nibbāna'—is something that even those in training (sekha) ought to know.
Yet this elder is making this elder act as if he were on the stage of one beyond training (asekha). I shall make him understand this point," and so he spoke.
"Clearly seen with right wisdom" means it has been well-seen by means of the path-wisdom together with insight (*vipassanā*).
"And I am not an Arahant" indicates that because he stands on the path of the Non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*), he is not yet an Arahant.
Furthermore, the knowledge he now possesses that "the cessation of existence is Nibbāna" is the reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) freed from the nineteen types of reviewing-knowledge.
"A well" (*udapāna*) is a water cistern thirty-two cubits deep. "A water-dipper" (*udakavāraka*) is a vessel for pouring out water.
"He has knowledge of the water" means that while standing on the bank and looking down, such knowledge would arise [in him].
"But without touching it with his body" means that he would not be able to draw out the water and dwell having touched it with his body. Regarding the well:
For the seeing of Nibbāna by a non-returner (anāgāmin) is like the sight of water; the non-returner is like a man tormented by heat;

the path of arahantship is like a water-pipe. Just as a man tormented by heat sees water in a well, so too the non-returner, through the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa), knows: "There is a time for the fruit of arahantship above this."
Just as that man, due to the absence of a water-vessel, is unable to bring out water and touch it with his body,
so too the non-returner, due to the absence of the path to arahantship, is unable— having made Nibbāna the object and having entered the attainment of the fruit of arahantship—
to remain seated therein. This is the eighth [simile].
9. Commentary on the *Upayantīsutta* 69.
In the ninth [verse], "upayanto" means going upwards at the time when the waters increase. "Mahānadiyo" refers to the great rivers such as the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and others.
"Upayāpeti" means he causes them to go upwards; the meaning is that he increases and fills them. "Avijjā upayantī" means ignorance is going upwards.
Ignorance (*avijjā*), as it moves upward, is able to become a condition for the volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*).

"It causes the volitional formations to go upward" means it causes them to proceed upward and increases them. The meaning in all such instances should be understood in this way. "Going away" (*apayanto*) means departing or receding.
"Ignorance going away" means ignorance, while departing and receding, [serves] as a condition for the volitional formations above.
The meaning is that they are unable to come into being. "He causes formations to depart" means he causes formations to go away.
This same method applies to all the phrases. The ninth [sutta].
10. Commentary on the Susīma Sutta.
70. "Venerated" (garukato) means he is honored in mind by all gods and humans like a stone parasol.

"Honored" (mānito) means he is loved with the heart. "Worshipped" (pūjito) means he is worshipped with the worship of the four requisites. "Revered" (apacito) means he is revered by acting in a humble manner.
Indeed, upon seeing the Teacher, people descend from the backs of elephants and so forth, clear the path, and [remove their ornaments] from their shoulders.
They removed their upper garments, rose from their seats, and paid him homage. In this way, he was honored by them.
Susīma was the name of a wise wanderer (paribbājaka) skilled in the Vedangas. "Come, you!"—for it seems they thought thus:
"The ascetic Gotama did not attain the pinnacle of gain by virtue of his birth or lineage; rather, he is a preeminent poet because of his supreme poetic skill."
He composes books for his disciples and gives them to them;

having mastered them, they deliver discourses while sitting with their supporters, recite verses of thanksgiving, and perform public recitations, and so forth. Those who have faith in them provide them with material gains.
If we were to know even a small portion of what the ascetic Gotama knows, we could [establish] our own doctrine therein.
“Having included ourselves among the attendants, we shall speak [of this] to them; thus we shall become even more successful than they.
Who, having gone forth in the presence of the ascetic Gotama, will be able to learn it quickly?
Having thought thus, and seeing that Susīma was capable, they approached him and spoke as follows.
“He approached the Venerable Ānanda”—for what reason did he approach him? It is said that this thought occurred to him:
“To whom should I go so that I might be able to obtain this Dhamma quickly? Then he reflected:
“The ascetic Gotama is venerable, possessed of great spiritual power, and devoted to his regimen; it is not possible to approach him at an improper time. There are others...”
Many kṣatriyas and others approach the ascetic Gotama; therefore, at that time as well, it is not possible to approach him.

Among his disciples, Sāriputta is of great wisdom and is ranked foremost in the discernment of the characteristics of insight (vipassanālakkhaṇa); Mahāmoggallāna is ranked foremost in the characteristics of concentration (samādhilakkhaṇa);
Mahākassapa is foremost among those who maintain the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and Anuruddha is foremost among those with the divine eye (dibbacakkhu).
Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta was established as the foremost among those who preach the Dhamma, and the Elder Upāli as the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya;
but this Ānanda is one of great learning, a bearer of the Tipiṭaka, who recites the Dhamma by bringing forth what the Teacher spoke on various occasions,
and he was established as the foremost in five respects, being a recipient of eight boons and endowed with four wonderful and marvelous qualities.
“Being endowed with such qualities, having gone into his presence, I will be able to quickly obtain the Dhamma.
Therefore, he approached the Venerable Ānanda.
As for why he approached [the Buddha] without ordaining himself first: it is said that this thought occurred to him:
“This man wanders about in the time of the heretics, individually claiming, ‘I am the Teacher. Having gone forth, he might even seek to bring harm to the Dispensation.
However, I do not know his underlying intention; the Teacher will know it.
Therefore, taking him with him, he approached the Blessed One. “Therefore, Ānanda, let Susīma go forth,” said the Teacher.
He thought: “This wanderer lives proclaiming in the doctrine of the sectarians, ‘I am a teacher distinct [from others],’ yet he says, ‘I wish to practice the holy life under you here.
Is it because he has faith in me, or in my disciples, or perhaps in the Dhamma discourse of myself or my disciples?”
Then, perceiving that he lacked even a single point of faith, [the Buddha thought], "This man has gone forth thinking, 'I shall deceive the Dhamma in my teaching.
Thus his coming is impure; what will his accomplishment be like? Observing him, [the Buddha] knew:
"Although he has gone forth thinking, 'I shall deceive the Dhamma,' yet after only a few days of striving, he will attain arahantship."
“Therefore, Ānanda, let Susīma go forth,” he said. “The answer was given”:

it is said that those monks, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher and dwelling for the three months of the rains retreat, attained Arahatship while striving and exerting themselves within that very same period. They [reported] the quality they had attained...
"We shall inform the Teacher. Having thus invited one another and having settled the lodgings, they came into the presence of the Teacher and reported the qualities they had attained.
It was with reference to this that it was said. "Aññā" is a name for Arahatship. "Byākatā" means announced. "Assosi" (he heard):
it is said that he, having lent his ear, went to the places where those various bhikkhus were standing.
He went here and there, desiring to hear this or that [teaching]. As for why he approached those bhikkhus:
having heard reports concerning them, it occurred to him, "I believe there must be some other supreme measure, the very essence of this Dispensation, which is like a teacher’s closed fist;
I shall go and find out. Therefore, he approached them.
"Aneka-vihitaṃ" means of many kinds. "Iddhividhaṃ" means a portion of psychic power (*iddhi*).
By saying "making manifest and making invisible," he asks whether you are able to make yourself invisible after having become manifest, or to make yourself manifest after having become invisible.
"Tiro-kuṭṭaṃ" means through another wall. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "Ummujja-nimujjaṃ" means emerging and submerging.
"And diving. "By means of a cross-legged posture" (*pallaṅkena*) means by binding the legs in the cross-legged position. "Are you able?"—he asks this to see whether one is able to sit or to go.
"A winged bird" (*pakkhī sakuṇo*) means a bird possessed of wings. This is the summary here;

however, the method of explanation for this supernormal power (*iddhividha*), as well as for the divine ear and so forth that follow, should be understood according to the manner set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Peaceful liberations" means that the formless liberations are peaceful both by virtue of the peace of their factors and the peace of their objects.

"Having touched with the body" means having touched and attained them with the mental body (*nāmakāya*). "'Friends, we are liberated by wisdom'—friend, this shows that we are dry-insight practitioners devoid of jhāna, liberated by wisdom alone. Or, "You should understand [this]."
"Friend Susīma, why did they say, 'Perhaps you do not understand'? It was because it occurred to them:
"Having taken up his intention, we will not be able to explain it; however, by asking the One of Ten Powers, he will become free from doubt.
"Knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) refers to insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*); that arises first.
"Knowledge regarding Nibbāna" refers to the knowledge of the path that arises while one is practicing insight meditation; that arises subsequently. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus.
Why did he say, "You should understand," and so forth? It was said for the purpose of showing that such knowledge can arise even without concentration.
For this is what is meant: Susīma, neither the path nor the fruit is the outflow of concentration, nor is it the benefit of concentration.
It is not the accomplishment of concentration, but rather the outflow of insight, the benefit of insight,
and the fruition of insight. Therefore, whether you know it or do not know it, first there is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena,
and afterwards there is the knowledge of Nibbāna.
Now, having recognized his capacity for penetration (*paṭivedhabhabbatā*), the Buddha taught him the Dhamma in three rounds, beginning with:
"What do you think, Susīma? Is form permanent or impermanent? At the conclusion of that three-round teaching, the Elder attained Arahantship.
Now, applying further inquiry to him, the Buddha said: "Susīma, do you see that aging and death have birth as their condition? and so forth.
But why did he begin with the words, “But you, Susīma”?

It was for the purpose of making it clear to those bhikkhus who were dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka) and devoid of jhāna. This is the intention here: “It is not only you who are devoid of jhāna and a dry-insight practitioner;
these bhikkhus, too, are exactly like that. The rest is clear everywhere. The tenth [chapter].
The Seventh Chapter: The Great Section (Mahāvagga). 8.
The Section on Ascetics and Brahmins (Samaṇabrāhmaṇavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Old Age and Death, etc. (Jarāmaraṇasuttādivaṇṇanā).
71–72. In the *Samaṇabrāhmaṇa-vagga*, eleven suttas are spoken by taking each single term from among aging, death, and so forth, one by one; these have already been explained.
This concludes the eighth chapter, the *Samaṇabrāhmaṇa-vagga*.
9. The Intermediate Series (*Antarapeyyāla*).
1. Commentary on the *Satthusutta* and others. 73.
From this point onward, there are twelve intermediate sub-chapters (antarapeyyālavagga) proceeding in the manner beginning with "A Teacher is to be sought.
All of these are [taught] according to the inclinations of those individuals to be trained (*veneyyapuggala*) who are to be awakened in various ways.

Thus it was said. Therein, "the Teacher" (satthā) refers to either the Buddha or a disciple; whoever one relies upon to obtain knowledge of the Path is called the Teacher, and he is to be sought after.
"The training is to be practiced" means that the threefold training is to be undertaken.
Regarding "exertion" (yoga) and the rest: "exertion" (yoga) is application. "Zeal" (chanda) is the wholesome desire to act. "Exertion" (ussoḷhi) is supreme energy that endures everything.
“Unyielding” means not turning back. “Ardor” is precisely the energy that burns away the defilements. “Constancy” is continuous practice.
“Mindfulness” is the mindfulness that comprehends the Four Noble Truths by way of aging, death, and so forth. “Clear comprehension” is knowledge of exactly that same kind.
“Diligence” is diligence in the cultivation of the Truths. The rest is clear everywhere.
The ninth intermediate recitation section is finished.
The commentary on the Nidāna Saṃyutta is completed.
2. The Abhisamaya Saṃyutta.
1. Commentary on the *Nakhasikhā-sutta* (74).
In the first discourse of the *Abhisamaya-saṃyutta*, the phrase "on the tip of a fingernail" refers to the very edge of the nail, which is free from the flesh.
Now, while for worldly people the tip of a fingernail may be large, for the Teacher it is like the tip of a red lotus petal.

"Subtle. But how, in this case, is the dust settled there? By the power of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-bala*). For the Blessed One, desiring to make the meaning known, settled it there by the power of resolve.
"A hundredth part of a hair's breadth": having divided the dust of the great earth into a hundred portions, [this refers to] one portion from among them.
The same method applies to what follows as well. "Those who have fully realized" (*abhisametāvino*).

"For one who stands having fully realized the Noble Truths through wisdom": "In comparison with the previous mass of suffering that has been exhausted and consumed"—this very [present] suffering is more abundant; that is to say, it is "exhausted.
Thus, in comparison with the mass of suffering mentioned first, when it is being examined by placing it in proximity to that [previous mass] through knowledge (*ñāṇa*), [it is seen as follows].
The meaning is as follows. But what herein is called "prior suffering"? That which has been exhausted. And what is exhausted?
That which would have arisen had the first path not been cultivated. Compared to what, however?
To all that might arise anywhere within seven personal existences in the woeful states, beginning with the eighth rebirth-linking. All of this—
That should be understood as "completely exhausted. "Seven times" means seven occasions; the meaning is "in seven individual existences.
"At most" indicates that this is his maximum limit. "Of great benefit" means one who accomplishes a great purpose.
First. 2. Commentary on the *Pokkharaṇī-sutta*.

75. In the second [simile], "lotus pond" (*pokkharaṇī*) means a large pond (*vāpī*). "In depth" refers to its profundity. "Level with the brim" means equal to the edge of the mouth. "Drinkable by a crow" means it is possible for a crow standing on the bank to drink by simply inserting its beak.
This is the second [simile]. 3. Commentary on the *Saṃbhejjaudaka-sutta* and others. 76–77.
In the third [simile], "where these [rivers] meet" means in that place where they converge. "Flowing together" means they come together and flow.
*Samantīti* means they come together. *Dve vā ti vāti* means two or three. *Udakaphusitānīti* means water droplets.
*Saṃbhejjaudakanti* means the water at the place where it has merged with other rivers. The fourth [sutta] is clear in meaning. [This concludes] the third and fourth [sections].
5. Commentary on the *Pathavīsutta* and others.
78–84. "In the fifth [case], 'having lifted up from the great earth' means having lifted them from the great earth within the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
'The size of a kola-fruit' means the measure of a stone used for leveling the ground. 'A pellet' means a pellet of clay. 'Should set down' means should place it in one spot.

The meaning in the sixth and subsequent cases should be understood in the same manner as stated previously. At the conclusion, however, [there is mention] of the ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of other sects."

"Attainment" means that even the entire attainment of virtues by outsiders does not approach even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousandth part of the virtues attained through the first path. [The fifth and subsequent sections.
The commentary on the *Abhisamayasaṃyutta* is finished.
3. Saṃyutta on the Elements (Dhātusaṃyutta) 1.
The Chapter on Diversity (Nānattavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Diversity of Elements (Dhātunānattasutta-vaṇṇanā)

85. In the first [chapter] of the *Dhātusaṃyutta*, "diversity of elements" (*dhātunānatta*) refers to the diversity of the intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) of those phenomena which have received the name "element" (*dhātu*) in the sense of their individual essence (*sabhāvaṭṭha*), as defined by the meaning of "insentient-ness" (*nissattaṭṭha*) and "emptiness" (*suññataṭṭha*). In such cases as "eye-element" (*cakkhudhātu*) and so forth:

the sensitivity of the eye is the eye-element; the visible object as its objective field is the form-element (*rūpadhātu*); and the consciousness based upon that sensitivity of the eye is the eye-consciousness-element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*).
The ear-sensitivity is the ear-element; sound as an object is the sound-element; the consciousness based on the ear-sensitivity is the ear-consciousness-element.
The nose-sensitivity is the nose-element; odor as an object is the odor-element; the consciousness based on the nose-sensitivity is the nose-consciousness-element.
The tongue-sensitivity is the tongue-element; taste as an object is the taste-element; the consciousness based on the tongue-sensitivity is the tongue-consciousness-element.

The body-sensitivity is the body-element (*kāyadhātu*); the tangible object is the tangible-element (*phoṭṭhabbadhātu*); and the consciousness based on the body-sensitivity is the body-consciousness-element (*kāyaviññāṇadhātu*).
The three mind-elements (*manodhātu*) are the mind-element; the three aggregates beginning with feeling, subtle material phenomena, and Nibbāna are the mental-object-element (*dhammadhātu*);
and all mind-consciousness is the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*). And herein, there are sixteen...
The elements are those of the sense-sphere; at the end, two are of four planes. First. 2.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Diversity of Contact (Phassanānattasutta). 86.
In the second [discourse], "the diversity of contact arises" means that contact of various natures arises. Therein, visual-contact and so forth...
[It arises] associated with eye-consciousness and so forth; mental contact is associated with the first impulsion in the mind-door. Therefore:

"Dependent on the mind-element" means that dependent on the functional mind-consciousness-element (kiriyā-manoviññāṇadhātu) which is the adverting of the mind-door, contact of the first impulsion arises—this is the meaning here. Second.
3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Diversity of Contact (Nophassanānattasuttavaṇṇanā) 87.

Regarding the third [discourse]: "Dependent on mental contact, the mind-element does not arise. This should be understood to mean that dependent on the contact associated with the first impulsive consciousness in the mind-door, the functional mind-consciousness-element of adverting does not arise. The third [is concluded].
4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Diversity of Feelings (Vedanānānattasutta) 88.
Regarding the fourth [sutta], "feeling born of eye-contact": all feelings at that sense-door would proceed starting from the receiving mind-element (*sampaṭicchana-manodhātu*);
however, for the sake of facilitating its arising, only the immediately preceding feeling of reception (*sampaṭicchana-vedanā*) is mentioned.

"It is appropriate to grasp" is what was stated. "Dependent on mind-contact": the intention here is that dependent on the advertence-contact at the mind-door there is the feeling of the first impulsion;
dependent on the contact of the first impulsion there is the feeling of the second impulsion. Fourth. 5.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Diversity of Feeling.
89. In the fifth [sutta], the method explained in the third and fourth is taught by combining them together.

Thus, in the four suttas beginning with the second, instead of taking "mind-element" (*manodhātu*) as "mind-element," "mind-door adverting [consciousness]" (*manodvārāvajjana*) is taken as "mind-element.

All of these were taught according to the inclinations of those who would understand them when explained in such various ways. This same principle applies to the subsequent ones as well. The fifth [sutta].
6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Diversity of External Elements (Bāhiradhātunānattasutta-vaṇṇanā) 90.
In the sixth [discourse], however, five elements belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), while the mental-object element (dhammadhātu) belongs to four planes. This is the sixth.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Diversity of Perceptions (Saññānānattasutta-vaṇṇanā)
91. "In the seventh [case], 'the form element' (rūpadhātu) refers to a visible-object base that has entered the field of vision, such as the clothing or head-coverings of oneself or another.
'Perception of form' (rūpasaññā) is the perception associated with eye-consciousness.

'Intention regarding form' (rūpasaṅkappa) is the intention associated with the three types of consciousness beginning with the receiving consciousness. 'Desire for form' (rūpacchanda) is desire in the sense of being desirous of form. 'Fever of form' (rūpapariḷāha)..."
In the case of form, burning (*pariḷāha*) is in the sense of its being consumed.
"The quest for form" is the search for the acquisition of that form after having taken hold of what is seen and gathered when burning has arisen.

And here, perception (*saññā*), intention (*saṅkappa*), and desire (*chanda*) are found both in a single impulsion-moment (*javana-vāra*) and in various impulsion-moments; however, burning and the quest are found only in various impulsion-moments.

"Thus, monks, is the diversity of elements (*dhātunānatta*). In this context, the meaning should be understood according to this method: "Depending on an element whose diverse intrinsic nature consists of form and so forth, there arises a perception whose diverse intrinsic nature consists of the perception of form and so forth. This is the seventh [sutta].
8. Commentary on the Sutta on the Diversity of Non-Seeking Higher [States] (*Nopariyesanānānattasutta*).

92. In the eighth [sutta], the phrase “fever for the Dhamma does not arise on account of the search for the Dhamma” is stated; this is merely a negation of what has been previously mentioned. This is the eighth. 9.
Commentary on the Suttas beginning with the *Bāhiraphassanānatta-sutta*. 93–94.

In the ninth [sutta], the phrase “perception of forms arises” means that perception arises with respect to an object of the kind already described. “Intention regarding forms” (rūpa-saṅkappa) means...
In that very object, there is the volition associated with the three types of consciousness.
"Contact with form" is the contact that touches that same object. "Feeling" is the feeling that experiences that same object. Desire and the others are exactly as previously explained.
"Acquisition of form" refers to the object acquired after searching, together with craving; this is what is called "acquisition of form. This...
Thus far, the method of universal inclusion has been explained by way of the arising of all phenomena within a single object. Another method involves a mixture with adventitious objects:
first, these four factors—perception of form, intention regarding form, contact, and feeling—occur in relation to a fixed object during constant enjoyment.
For a fixed object is one that is desirable, lovely, and pleasing.
Whatever appears as dear seems as if it were real, yet whatever is merely an adventitious object remains even when it agitates the mind. Here is an illustration:
it is said that a certain son of a minister, surrounded by country folk, was standing in the middle of a village performing some work.
At that time, a female lay devotee, having gone to the river and bathed, returned adorned and prepared, surrounded by a group of her kinsmen.

He goes to his house. Seeing her from afar, he forms the perception that "this must be a visiting woman" and sends a man, saying, "Go, my good man, find out who she is. Having gone and seen her, the man returns;
when asked, "Who is she? he reports the matter exactly as it is. In this way, one agitates the mind with respect to a visiting object. [The defilement] arisen therein...
Desire for form is called "desire for form"; the fever that arises taking that very thing as its object is called "fever for form";
the pursuit of it by gathering companions is called "pursuit of form"; and what is obtained after the pursuit, together with craving, as an object is called "acquisition of form."

But the Elder Cūḷa-Tissa, a resident of Uruvelā, said: "Although contact and feeling were taken by the Blessed One as the middle term in the text, yet by turning the text around, perception arising with respect to an object of the kind described is 'perception of form' (rūpa-saññā);

the intention toward that same [object] is 'intention regarding form' (rūpa-saṅkappa); the desire for that same [object] is 'desire for form' (rūpa-chanda); and the fever for that same [object] is 'fever for form' (rūpa-pariḷāha)."
“Seeking is the seeking for form; having sought it, what is obtained together with craving is the acquisition of form as an object.

When the object has been thus acquired, there is contact as the touching [of that object], and feeling as the experiencing [of it]. Thus, this dyad—the contact with form and the feeling born of contact with form—is obtained.
They also take another section called the “unmanifested” (avibhūta). For the object—

Whether it is enclosed by a fence of hemp-cloth or concealed by grass, leaves, and so forth, the perception that arises toward that object when one looks at it with the thought, "Half of my object has been seen; now I shall see it clearly," is called the perception of form (*rūpasaññā*).
It should be understood that the intentions and so forth arising toward that very same object are called the intention regarding form (*rūpasaṅkappa*) and so forth. Here too—

Furthermore, perception (*saññā*), intention (*saṅkappa*), contact (*phassa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and desire (*chanda*) are found both in a single impulsion-moment (*ekajavana-vāra*) and in multiple impulsion-moments (*nānājavana-vāra*);
whereas fever (*pariḷāha*), seeking (*pariyesanā*), and gain (*lābha*) are found only in multiple impulsion-moments. The tenth [sutta] is self-evident. These are the ninth and tenth.
This is the first chapter on Diversity (*Nānatta-vagga*).
2. Second Chapter. 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Seven Elements (Sattadhātusutta). 95.

In the first [sutta] of the second chapter, "the light element" (*ābhādhātu*) means the element of illumination (*ālokadhātu*). Regarding illumination as well, there is the preliminary work (*parikamma*) for the illumination-kasina (*ālokakasiṇa*).

Having done so, this is the name for the jhāna that has arisen together with its object, even for one who has attained jhāna. "The beautiful element" (*subhadhātu*) refers specifically to the jhāna that has arisen together with its object by way of the jhāna produced in the beautiful kasiṇa.
The base of infinite space itself is the "space-infinity-element" (*ākāsānañcāyatanadhātu*).

The cessation of perception and feeling itself is the "cessation-of-perception-and-feeling-element" (*saññāvedayitanirodhadhātu*). Thus the Blessed One [spoke] to one skilled in the sequence of connections.
Having sat down there, he brought his teaching to a conclusion, granting an opportunity for the bhikkhu who wished to ask a question.
"In dependence on darkness": for darkness is delimited by light, and light by darkness;
it is made manifest by means of darkness. Therefore, he said, "It is manifested in dependence on darkness. "In dependence on the foul": [the same applies].
The same principle applies here as well. For the unattractive is delimited by the attractive, and the attractive by the unattractive;
when there is the unattractive, the attractive is discerned. Therefore he spoke thus. "Dependent on form" means dependent on the fine-material-sphere attainment (*rūpāvacara-samāpatti*).

For when there is the fine-material-sphere attainment, there arises what is called the attainment of the base of infinite space, or the transcendence of form. Therefore he spoke thus. This also applies to the base of infinite consciousness element and so forth.
The same method applies here. "In dependence on cessation" means in dependence on the non-occurrence of the four aggregates through their analytical cessation.
For it is in dependence on the cessation of the aggregates that what is called the attainment of cessation is discerned, not in dependence on the occurrence of the aggregates;
therefore, he spoke thus. And herein, it should be understood that the attainment of cessation is simply the cessation of the four aggregates.
"How is attainment to be reached? means: how, being of what nature, are these attainments to be reached?
"The attainment of perception is to be reached" means that because of the presence of perception, they are called "attainments of perception" and are thus to be reached as such.
"The attainment with residual formations is to be reached" means because of the remaining of subtle formations.

It must be attained by becoming what is called the attainment with a residue of formations (*saṅkhārāvasesa-samāpatti*). "The attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is to be attained" means that cessation itself is the attainment of cessation;
the sense is that it must be attained by becoming what is called the attainment of cessation. First.
2. Commentary on the *Sanidāna-sutta*.
96. In the second [instance], *sanidāna* is a neuter noun in the locative case; the meaning is: "having arisen with a cause and with conditions.

Regarding the phrase, "Bhikkhus, dependent on the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*)," here the sense-sphere refers to sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*), the phenomena of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*), and specifically all unwholesome states. As it has been said:

“In this context, what is the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*)? Whatever thought, applied thought, intention, absorption, sustained application, mental projection, and wrong intention associated with sensual desire—this is called the sense-sphere element.
From the Avīci hell below as its limit, up to including the Paranimmitavasavatti devas above, whatever lies within this interval...”

"Whatever is included within this sphere, whatever is comprised within this sphere—the aggregates, elements, and bases: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is called the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, all unwholesome states are also the sense-sphere element.
Here, there are two ways of explaining [the term] "inclusive" (*sabbasaṅgāhika*) and "unmixed" (*asambhinna*). How so? For by the inclusion of the sense-sphere element...
The elements of ill will (*vyāpādadhātu*) and cruelty (*vihiṃsādhātu*) are included; thus, this is the inclusive [definition].

However, because those two elements are mentioned separately, the remaining phenomena are the "sense-sphere element" (*kāmadhātu*); this is the non-confused [definition]. This is what should be understood here:
depending on this sense-sphere element either by way of its object (*ārammaṇa*) or by way of association (*sampayoga*), that which is called "perception of sensual desire" (*kāmasaññā*) arises.

"Dependent on the perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*)" means that, depending either by way of association (*sampayoga*) or by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) upon the perception of sensual desire, what is called "sensual intention" (*kāmasaṅkappa*) arises.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood for all the following phrases.
"By three grounds" means by three causes. "He practices wrongly" means he practices an untruthful practice, a practice that does not lead to liberation.
"‘The element of ill will, monks’—here, both the thought of ill will (*byāpādavitakka*) and ill will itself (*byāpāda*) are the element of ill will.
As it is said: ‘In this context, what is the element of ill will? It is the thinking, the initial application of thought, associated with ill will... this is called the element of ill will.
It is the resentment, the hostility, the anger, the intense anger... the dissatisfaction of the mind toward the ten grounds for malice.’"
“This is called the element of ill will.
Based on this element of ill will—by way of the condition of co-arising and so forth—the perception of ill will arises. The rest should be understood in the same manner as before.
Regarding the phrase “the element of cruelty, monks,” here both the thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsā-vitakka*) and cruelty itself (*vihiṃsā*) are the element of cruelty. As it has been said:
“In this context, what is the element of cruelty (*vihiṃsā-dhātu*)? It is the reasoning and applied thought associated with cruelty... [as above] ...this is called the element of cruelty.
Here, someone harms beings with the hand, or with a clod, or with a staff, or with a sword, or with a rope, or with one thing or another.
Whatever such harming, injuring, hurting, cruelty, provocation, or assault there is—”
“This is called the element of cruelty.

Based on this element of cruelty by way of the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so forth, what is termed the perception of cruelty arises. The rest here should also be understood according to the previous method.
“In a thicket of grass” means in a dense forest of grass. “Calamity and ruin” means lack of growth and destruction. “Even so” refers here to—
The object should be regarded as a dry grass forest; unwholesome perception as a grass torch;

and these beings as the creatures dependent upon that grass and wood. Just as those creatures meet with ruin and disaster if a grass torch placed in a dry grass forest is not quickly fanned out so as to prevent it from burning down, even so, those recluses or brahmins who [fail to do so] when unwholesome perception has arisen...
They do not abandon [it] through suppression, through its being a factor [of the path], or through eradication; thus they dwell in suffering.

"Unbalanced" refers to unwholesome perception accompanied by the imbalance of lust and so forth. "Does not quickly abandon it" means he does not swiftly abandon it by means of suppression and the other methods.
"Does not dispel it" means he does not remove it. "Does not bring it to an end" means he does not leave even its mere dissolution without remainder.
It does not make it disappear; "it does not lead to non-existence" means it does not cause it to go to non-existence. In this way, the negative particle *na* is to be supplied in all instances.
"To be expected" (*pāṭikaṅkhā*) means it is to be expected or desired.

Regarding the phrase "the element of renunciation, monks": here, both the thought of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*) and the element of renunciation (*nekkhammadhātu*) refer to all wholesome states (*kusala-dhammā*). As it has been said:

“In this context, what is the element of renunciation (*nekkhammadhātu*)? Thought (*takka*), initial application (*vitakka*) … [and so on] … right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) associated with renunciation—this is called the element of renunciation.
Here too, the exposition is twofold. For by the inclusion of the element of renunciation, the other two elements are also included because they are comprised within wholesome states;
thus, this is a comprehensive definition. However, those elements should be explained individually.
Excluding those [three], all remaining wholesome states are the element of renunciation (*nekkhammadhātu*); this is the undifferentiated [classification].

Depending on this element of renunciation by way of such conditions as co-nascence (*sahajāta*), the so-called "perception of renunciation" (*nekkhammasaññā*) arises; and depending on perception and the other [mental factors], thought (*vitakka*) and the rest arise accordingly.

“Bhikkhus, the element of non-ill will”: here, both the thought of non-ill will (*abyāpādavitakka*) and non-ill will itself (*abyāpāda*) are the element of non-ill will. As it is said: “In this context, what is the element of non-ill will?

Thought associated with non-ill will... this is called the element of non-ill will. That which is loving-kindness toward beings, the state of being loving, the state of having been loving, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called the element of non-ill will.
Depending on this element of non-ill will, the perception of non-ill will arises in the manner already described.

Regarding the phrase "the element of non-harming, monks": here too, both the thought-conception associated with non-harming (*avihiṃsā-vitakka*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) are the element of non-harming.
As it is said: "In this context, what is the element of non-harming? It is the thought-conception associated with non-harming... [and so on]... this is called the element of non-harming.
That which is compassion toward beings, the state of being compassionate, the quality of being compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion—this is called the element of non-harming."

In dependence upon this element of non-harming (*avihiṃsā-dhātu*), the perception of non-harming (*avihiṃsā-saññā*) arises in the same manner already described. The remainder is to be understood everywhere according to what has been stated. Second. 3.
Commentary on the Giñjakāvasatha Sutta (The Brick House Discourse) 97.
In the third [discourse], with the words "The element, monks," he begins from here to illustrate that the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) is the "element. It arises.
"Perception": perception arises, a view arises, and a thought arises depending upon one's underlying intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Here too, thinking "Kaccāna will ask a question," he brought the teaching to a conclusion at this point in order to grant him an opportunity.
"Among those who are not perfectly enlightened ones" refers to the six teachers. "We are perfectly enlightened ones" means, "We are indeed perfectly enlightened ones."
"Depending on what is it discerned? When what exists does it come to be?"—with this he asks about the view arisen among teachers.
By saying "among those who are not Fully Enlightened Ones, these are the Fully Enlightened Ones," he likewise asks about the view arisen even among the disciples of the heretics.
Now, since that view arises depending on the element of ignorance (*avijjādhātu*) for them, and the element of ignorance is indeed vast...
“Element (*dhātu*); therefore, in order to show that its arising depends upon a great element, he said: ‘Indeed, this is great,’ and so forth.
‘Depending on a low element, Kaccāna’ means depending on a low inclination (*ajjhāsaya*). ‘Aspiration (*paṇidhi*)’ is the fixing of the mind.
This [aspiration] arises in one who longs for the female state or for the state of an animal such as a monkey, etc. Low…”
"A person" means that whoever these inferior qualities arise in, that person too is called "inferior.
"Inferior speech" means that whatever speech he has, that too is inferior. "He proclaims what is inferior" means that even when he proclaims, he proclaims only what is inferior;
even when he teaches, he teaches only what is inferior—all the phrases should be construed in this way. "Rebirth" means two kinds of rebirth: acquisition and [rebirth in a state].

And there is "arising" (*nibbatti*). Arising should be understood by way of birth in low families and so forth; acquisition (*paṭilābha*) is by way of the inferior triad at the moment of the arising of consciousness.
How so? For his arising is inferior because of being born into one of the five low families; it is middling because of being born into the Vaiśya or Śūdra families;
it is superior because of being born into the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa families. Furthermore, regarding the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness...
Inferior by way of attainment is the attainment of the states belonging to the three planes; middling by way of attainment is the attainment of the nine supramundane states;
and sublime by way of attainment is the attainment of [the higher stages]. However, in this context, only actual rebirth is intended. This is the third. 4.
Commentary on the *Hīnādhimuttika Sutta*.

98. "In the fourth [verse], *saṃsandanti* means they become one. *Samenti* means they come together; they become without interval. *Hīnādhimuttikā* means those with inferior inclinations (*hīnajjhāsaya*). *Kalyāṇādhimuttikā* means those with noble inclinations (*kalyāṇajjhāsaya*).

This is the fourth [verse]. 5. Commentary on the Caṅkama Sutta 99. In the fifth [verse], *passatha no* means "look indeed. "All these" refers to the Elder Sāriputta being addressed by the Blessed One.
“Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus, of great wisdom, namely Sāriputta.

Thus, thinking, “We shall ask him a profound question struck by the three characteristics—a question concerning the distinction between aggregates, the distinction between elements, the distinction between bases, and the distinction between the foundations of mindfulness and the factors conducive to enlightenment,” those of great wisdom alone surround him. And he, for their sake...

As if stretching out the earth, as if scooping up sand from the foot of Mount Sineru, as if splitting the Cakkavāḷa mountains, as if lifting up Mount Sineru, as if expanding the sky, and as if raising up the moon and sun, he answers every question that is asked.
Therefore it was said: "All these bhikkhus, monks, are of great wisdom."

Mahāmoggallāna too was placed by the Blessed One in the foremost position among those possessing psychic power, saying: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus, in psychic power, namely Mahāmoggallāna.

Thus, thinking, “We shall ask him about the preliminary work, the benefits, the resolve, and the transformations,” those possessing psychic power themselves surrounded him. He, for his part, [addressed them] in the manner already described.
He speaks whatever is asked. Therefore it was said: “All these bhikkhus, monks, are of great psychic power.

Mahākassapa too was placed by the Blessed One at the forefront of those who preach the ascetic practices (dhutavāda), with the words: “Monks, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who preach the ascetic practices, namely Mahākassapa.
Thus, [he spoke] regarding the maintenance of the ascetic practices and their benefits.
Thinking, “We shall ask about their convergence, their resolve, and their distinctions,” those who advocate the ascetic practices (dhutavāda) surrounded him.
He, for his part, answered each of their questions exactly as they were asked. Therefore it was said: “All these monks, bhikkhus, are advocates of the ascetic practices.
And the Elder Anuruddha was declared by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the monks, who possess the divine eye.”

Because Anuruddha was thus ranked as the foremost among those with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), those who possessed the divine eye surrounded him, thinking, "We shall ask him about the preliminary practice, the benefits, and the defilements of the divine eye.
He, for his part, explained each question they asked to them exactly as it was asked. Therefore it is said: "All these monks, bhikkhus, possess the divine eye."

The Elder Puṇṇa was also placed by the Blessed One in the foremost position among preachers of the Dhamma, as it was said: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who preach the Dhamma, namely Puṇṇa, son of Mantāṇī.

Thus, thinking, "We shall ask him about various aspects of his preaching—the concise and the detailed, the profound and the superficial, the diverse modes of discourse, and so forth"—the preachers of the Dhamma approached him.
They surround him. He too explains to them, according to the method of each discourse on the Dhamma:

"Friends, it is fitting for one who is a preacher of the Dhamma to praise the assembly at the beginning, to reveal emptiness in the middle, and to reach the climax by way of the Four Noble Truths at the end.
Therefore it was said: "All these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, are preachers of the Dhamma."

The Elder Upāli was also established by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya, with the words: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost of my bhikkhu disciples in the mastery of the Vinaya, namely Upāli.

Thus, thinking, “We shall ask him about what is heavy and light, what is curable and incurable, and what constitutes an offense and what does not,” those who uphold the Vinaya surround him. And he, for his part, [answers] whatever they have asked.
He speaks in that very same way. Therefore it was said: “All these monks, bhikkhus, are masters of the Vinaya.

The Elder Ānanda was also placed by the Blessed One at the head of those who are learned, as it was said: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus, who are learned, namely Ānanda.
Thus, [he possessed] the tenfold intelligence regarding the phrasing (*byañjana-buddhi*).
