Thinking, "We shall ask about the origin, the connection, and the sequence," those who are well-versed in the scriptures surround him.
He, for his part, explains everything to them, saying, "This is how it should be spoken; this is how it should be understood. Therefore it was said:
"All these monks, bhikkhus, are well-versed in the scriptures."

But Devadatta, being of evil desire and overcome by craving, was surrounded by those of evil desire who thought, "We shall ask him about various kinds of hypocrisy regarding the maintenance of family connections. He, too, explained to them each such method.
Therefore it was said: "All these monks, bhikkhus, are of evil desire."

But why did these two walk back and forth nearby? It was for the purpose of providing protection, thinking, "Devadatta, with a mind corrupted toward the Teacher, might even attempt to do him harm. And why did Devadatta walk back and forth?
It was for the purpose of concealing the evil he had committed, thinking, "This man is not the doer; if he were the doer, he would not have come here. What...
But was Devadatta capable of doing harm to the Blessed One, or was there a need for the Blessed One’s protection? No.
Therefore it was said: "It is impossible, Ānanda, it is out of the question, that the Tathāgata should pass away through an external assault.
However, the monks had come out of reverence for the Teacher. For this very reason, having spoken thus, the Blessed One—
“Dismiss the community of monks, Ānanda,” he said, and so he was dismissed. This is the fifth [sutta].
6. Commentary on the Suttas with Verses (Sagāthāvagga) 100.
Regarding the sixth [sutta]: “Excrement mingles and meets with excrement” means in the midst of the ocean, in the midst of a country, and in the midst of a world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
Even when standing, not undergoing any differentiation in color, fragrance, or flavor, it blends, harmonizes, and becomes one and the same, continuous throughout.

The same method applies to the others as well. However, this comparison of undesirable things is brought forward for the purpose of showing the similarity between those of inferior disposition and one of inferior disposition;
whereas the comparisons of milk and so forth are for those of noble disposition.
This is for the purpose of showing the similarity of dispositions.
"Associations" refers to the moisture of craving based on seeing, hearing, and other forms of association. "The thicket has grown" means the forest of defilements has grown.
"It is cut by non-association" means by not associating—that is, by not seeing—when one does not engage in standing, sitting, and so forth together with others.
It is destroyed. “One who lives well” means one living a pure life. “May he dwell together” means he should live in common residence.
This is the sixth [sutta]. 7. Commentary on the *Assaddhasaṃsandana-sutta* (Sutta 101).
Regarding the seventh [verse], in the phrases “the faithless with the faithless,” etc., it refers to those who are devoid of faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha.

Persons devoid of vigor and devoid of essence, standing on the near shore of the ocean, are indistinguishable and continuous with those faithless ones standing on the far shore because of that very lack of faith.
Likewise, shameless persons who have broken the bounds of propriety are [indistinguishable] from the shameless;
those lacking moral dread, fearing no evil deed, are [indistinguishable] from those lacking moral dread; and those of little learning...

Those devoid of learning are with those of little learning; the indolent, lazy persons are with the indolent; those of muddled mindfulness—like crows that have dropped their food or jackals that have dropped their meat—are with those of muddled mindfulness;
the unwise, being devoid of the wisdom that discerns the aggregates and so forth, are with those likewise unwise;
those endowed with faith, who are devoted to duties such as worshipping at shrines, are with those of faith; and those possessing a sense of shame are with persons of conscience.

Those who possess a sense of shame were together with those possessing a sense of shame; those who are modest, fearful of evil, and possessed of moral dread were together with those possessed of moral dread;

those who are learned, retainers of what they have heard, retainers of the Āgamas, guardians of the texts, and protectors of the lineage were together with those who are learned; those who have aroused energy and are perfected in exertion were together with those who have aroused energy;

those established in mindfulness, endowed with the mindfulness that encompasses all duties, were together with those established in mindfulness; and those possessed of wisdom were together with those of great wisdom.
Even those standing at a distance come together and unite with those possessed of wisdom through their diamond-like knowledge by virtue of that perfection of wisdom. This is the seventh [sutta].
8–12. Commentary on the Suttas Beginning with "Rooted in Lack of Faith" (102–106):
The eighth and following [suttas] teach those same states, such as lack of faith, by way of triads. Therein, in the eighth...
Five triads based on lack of faith (*assaddha*) and so forth have been taught according to the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*) and the bright side (*sukkapakkha*);

in the ninth [triad], four based on moral shamelessness (*ahirika*); in the tenth, three based on lack of dread of wrongdoing (*anottappa*); in the eleventh, two based on little learning (*appassuta*);
and in the twelfth, one triad based on laziness (*kusīta*). Thus, there are fifteen triads in total across these five discourses (*suttanta*). And these fifteen—
They also say "suttantas. This is called the Tikapeyyāla (The Triplet Series). [The sections] beginning with the eighth.
The second chapter.
3. The Chapter on Courses of Action (Kammapathavagga).
1–2. Commentary on the *Asamāhita-sutta* and others. 107–108.
In the following [suttas], the first is stated by way of the pentad beginning with lack of faith (*assaddha*), and likewise the second.

However, in the first, the term "unconcentrated" (*asamāhita*) is the fourth [term], while in the second, it is the term "immoral" (*dussīla*). When they are spoken of in this way, for persons who gain understanding [thereby]...

For these were spoken according to their underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*). Here, "unconcentrated" means devoid of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
"Immoral" means lacking virtue (*nissīla*). [This concludes] the first and second [sections]. 3–5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Five Training Precepts, etc.
109–111. The third [section] is spoken according to the inclination of those who awaken by way of the five courses of action; the fourth, by way of the seven courses of action;

and the fifth, by way of the ten courses of action. Therein, in the third, the phrase "those who stand in the heedlessness of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants" refers to that fermented liquor known as *surā*, *meraya*, and *majja* which they drink with a state of mind characterized by negligence; that is called "the heedlessness of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants."
They are called *surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhāyino* because they stand upon that [intoxicant]; this, first of all, is the meaning of the uncommon term here.
In the fifth [precept], those who destroy living beings are *pāṇātipātino*; the meaning is "killers of living beings.

Those who take what is not given are *adinnādāyino*; the meaning is "stealers from others. Those who engage in sexual misconduct through the defilement of desire regarding sensual objects are *kāmesumicchācārino*.
They speak falsely, thus they are "false-speakers" (*musāvādino*); the meaning is that they are speakers of empty, untrue speech that destroys the welfare of others.
They have malicious speech, thus they are "malicious-tongued" (*pisuṇavācā*). They have harsh speech that cuts to the quick, thus they are "harsh-tongued" (*pharusavācā*).
They prattle idle chatter, thus they are "frivolous-talkers" (*samphappalāpino*). They covet, thus they are "covetous" (*abhijjhāluno*).
The meaning is: those whose nature is to covet the property of others. Those whose minds are corrupted and putrid are "corrupted-minded" (*byāpannacitta*).
Those whose views are wrong, evil, and censured by the wise are "wrong-viewed" (*micchādiṭṭhika*);

that is, they are possessed of a view included within the courses of action, having as its basis such [denials] as "there is no giving," which is comprised within wrongness (*micchatta*) and is non-leading to liberation.

The meaning [of *sammādiṭṭhikā*] is as follows: those whose views (*diṭṭhi*) are right (*sammā*), beautiful (*sobhana*), and praised by the wise (*viññūpasattha*) are "those with right view" (*sammādiṭṭhikā*).

This means they are endowed with the view of the ownership of action (*kammassakata-diṭṭhi*)—beginning with "there is what is given" (*atthi dinnaṃ*)—which is included within the paths of action, and with the path-view (*magga-diṭṭhi*) which is included within the state of rightness (*sammatta*).
This, then, is merely a word-by-word commentary on the terms here that have not been previously explained.

Now, the tenfold dark-side category consists of: killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.

Among these, "the destruction (atipāta) of a living being (pāṇa)" is "killing living beings" (pāṇātipāta); it is said to mean the slaying or the killing of a living being. And here, in common parlance, "living being" (pāṇa) refers to—
A "being" (*satta*) is, in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

When one perceives a living being as a living being, the volition (*cetanā*) of killing—which arises through either the door of body or the door of speech and instigates an effort that severs the life-faculty—is the taking of life (*pāṇātipāta*).
This is less blameworthy when the living beings are animals and the like devoid of special qualities, and it is more blameworthy when the being has a large body. Why is this?
It is light in degree due to the greatness of the application, even when the application is equal, because of the greatness of the object.

Among humans and others who possess qualities, it is less blameworthy when they have few qualities and more blameworthy when they have great qualities. However, when there is equality in the bodily qualities, it should be understood that it is less blameworthy when the defilements and the effort are mild, and more blameworthy when they are intense.
For this [offense], there are five constituent factors: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the intention to kill, the means employed, and death by that means.
There are six modes of application: by one's own hand, by command, by relinquishing, by stationary means, by means of knowledge, and by means of psychic power.
However, if this matter were to be explained in detail, it would become excessively prolix; therefore, we shall not elaborate on it, nor on other matters of a similar nature.
However, those who seek the truth should take this from the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
"Taking what is not given" (*adinnādāna*) means seizing what has not been given; it is said to be the taking of another’s property, theft, or robbery.

In this context, "what is not given" (*adinna*) refers to that which is possessed by another, where another person, if they were to exercise their will over it, would be subject to punishment and blame.
It exists. However, when something is owned by another, the volition of theft—which originates from the act of taking it—arises in one who perceives it as being owned by another;
this constitutes taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*). This is less blameworthy when the property of another is inferior, and more blameworthy when it is superior.
Why? Because of the superiority of the object (*vatthu*). When the objects are equal, it is more blameworthy in the case of the property belonging to those who possess superior virtues.
Taking each successive item as being superior in quality, compared to the object belonging to one of inferior quality, there is less offense.

For that [offense], there are five constituent factors: the object is possessed by another, the perception that it is possessed by another, the intention to steal, the preparatory effort, and the carrying away by means of that effort.
There are six modes of application, beginning with "by one's own hand" (sāhatthika) and so forth; and these, according to their respective nature, constitute the act of stealing.
It occurs by way of these types of theft: open theft, concealed theft, theft by artifice, and theft by fraud;
this is the summary here, while the detailed explanation is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
Regarding "sexual misconduct" (*kāmesumicchācāra*): here, "in sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) refers to sexual intercourse. "Misconduct" (*micchācāra*) means that which is entirely censured.

It is base conduct. By way of its characteristic, however, sexual misconduct is the volition of transgressing against an improper place, proceeding through the door of the body with the intention of an unrighteous state.

In this context, an "improper place" for men refers to those protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both mother and father, protected by a brother, protected by a sister, protected by relatives, protected by their clan, or protected by the Dhamma.

"Guarded and subject to punishment" refers to the ten types beginning with those protected by their mother; "bought for wealth" refers to the ten types beginning with the *dhanakkītā*—namely, the *chandavāsinī*, *bhogavāsinī*, *paṭavāsinī*, *odapattakinī*, *obhatacumbaṭā*, a female slave who is also a wife, a female servant who is also a wife, one captured under a banner, and a momentary wife.
Thus, there are twenty women. Among these women, however, of the two...
Other men [commit sexual misconduct] with twelve kinds of women: those who are protected by relatives, those who are protected by punishment, and the ten types beginning with those bought for money.

This is what is called an "unapproachable object. Furthermore, this sexual misconduct is less blameworthy when directed toward an unapproachable object that lacks qualities such as virtue (sīla), but it is greatly blameworthy when directed toward one endowed with such qualities. It has four constituent factors: the unapproachable object, and so forth.

In that case, there is the intention to engage in sexual misconduct, the actual effort of engaging in it, and the acceptance of proceeding along a path that is not the proper path. There is one type of effort, namely, that which is performed by one's own hand.
"Lying" (*musā*) is either a verbal or bodily effort that destroys another's purpose when one has the prior intention to deceive;

or, according to another method, it is the volition (*cetanā*) that, with the intent to deceive, originates the bodily or verbal effort intended to deceive another. This is false speech (*musāvāda*). Another method [of definition]: [omitted for brevity as per instructions]
"Lying" (*musā*) refers to a matter that is non-existent and untrue. "Speaking" (*vāda*) is the making known of that [matter] as being existent and true.
By way of its characteristic, however, lying is the volition that originates the communication of a matter as being thus, by one who desires to make another understand an untrue matter as being thus.
It is slight in its degree of blame when the object it destroys is small, and it is greatly blameworthy when that object is great.
Moreover, for householders, speaking in the manner of "there is nothing" and so forth out of a desire not to give away what belongs to oneself is slightly blameworthy;
however, speaking as a witness for the purpose of destroying another's welfare is greatly blameworthy.

For those who have gone forth, having obtained even a small amount of oil or ghee, to speak with a motive of jesting according to the method of exaggerated talk, such as "Today in the village the oil flows like a river," [is blameworthy].

When it occurs in accordance with the facts, it is a minor offense; however, for those who speak according to the method of saying "I have seen" what has not been seen, and so forth, it is a major offense.
It has four constituent factors: an object that is not as it appears, a mind intent on deception, the corresponding effort, and another's understanding of that meaning.
There is one mode of application, which is solely by means of oneself—either by body, or by something connected to the body, or by speech.
Or it should be understood as the performance of an action intended to deceive another.
If the other person understands that matter because of that action, this person is bound by the kamma of false speech at the very moment of the volition that originates that action.
Regarding "slanderous speech" (*pisuṇavācā*) and so forth: by whatever speech one speaks to someone, there arises in that person's heart the perception of oneself as being dear...
That which creates a state of emptiness in another is malicious speech (*pisuṇavācā*).
But that speech by which one makes both oneself and another harsh, or which is itself harsh—neither pleasant to the ear nor heart-stirring—is harsh speech (*pharusavācā*).
That by which one prattles nonsense and what is useless is idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*). The volition (*cetanā*) that is the root of these [actions] is also [to be understood in the same way].
It receives the name "malicious speech" (*pisuṇavācā*) and so forth; and it is precisely this that is intended here.
In this context, malicious speech is the volition that, arising from a defiled mind, initiates bodily or vocal effort for the purpose of dividing others or out of a desire for one's own favor.
That [volition] is less blameworthy when the person whom it divides possesses few virtues, and more blameworthy when that person possesses great virtues.
It is highly blameworthy. Its four constituent factors are: another person who is to be divided;
the intention to cause division, thinking, "In this way they will become divided" or "they will become separated"; the desire for intimacy, thinking, "In this way I will become dear and trustworthy";
the corresponding effort; and the recognition of that purpose.
Harsh speech is an exclusively cruel volition that originates from bodily and verbal undertakings intended to cut another’s vital parts.
To illustrate this, there is the following account: It is said that once a certain boy was going into the forest, disregarding his mother’s words.
Unable to turn him back, the mother cursed him, saying, "May a fierce buffalo pursue you!"
Then, right there in the forest, a female buffalo rose up. The boy performed an act of truth, saying: "May that which my mother spoke with her mouth not come to pass;
may that which she thought in her mind come to pass. The buffalo stood right there as if it were bound.
Thus, even an action that would normally cause a mortal wound does not become harsh speech if there is gentleness of mind. [This was said regarding] parents.
For sometimes parents say to their children, “May thieves cut you into pieces,” yet they do not wish even a single lotus leaf to fall upon them.
And sometimes teachers and preceptors say to their dependents, “What are these shameless and fearless ones doing?
Drive them out! Yet they [the parents and teachers] nevertheless desire the excellence of their [children and dependents'] mastery of the scriptures and spiritual attainments.
They desire it. And just as harsh speech does not occur because of gentleness of mind, so too, gentle speech does not occur because of gentleness of speech.
For the words "Lay this person down comfortably" spoken by one wishing to have them killed are not gentle speech;
rather, it is harsh speech due to the harshness of the mind. That [speech], however, is [considered gentle] because of the incompetence of the person toward whom it was directed.

It is slightly blameworthy when it is of great merit, and greatly blameworthy when it is of great demerit. It has three constituent factors: another person who is to be reviled, a mind of anger, and the act of reviling itself.
Idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*) is unwholesome volition that communicates what is useless and originates from bodily and verbal application.

It is slightly blameworthy due to weak habituation, and greatly blameworthy due to great habituation. It has two constituent factors: a preoccupation with useless talk such as the Battle of the Bhāratas or the Abduction of Sītā, and [the actual speech].
And likewise, the telling of such talk.
It is called *abhijjhā* because one covets (*abhijjhāyati*). The meaning is that it proceeds by being directed toward another’s property and inclining toward it.
Having the characteristic of coveting another’s property in the form of thinking, “O, may this be mine,” it is slightly blameworthy, like the taking of what is not given.
And it is a great offense. It has two constituent factors: another's property and one's own appropriation.
For even when greed arises with regard to another's property, there is as yet no breach of the course of action (kamma-patha) until one appropriates it for oneself, thinking, "Oh, may this be mine!"
It is called *vyāpāda* because it intends the destruction of what is beneficial and pleasant. Its characteristic is mental malice directed toward the ruin of others.
Like harsh speech, it is less blameworthy [in its initial impulse] but greatly blameworthy [in its result]. It has two constituent factors: another being and the thought of their destruction.
For even when anger arises with another being as its object, there is as yet no breach of the path of action (*kammappatha*) until one thinks, "Oh, that this person..."
"He might be cut off or perish"—thus one contemplates his destruction.
Because it lacks the apprehension of things as they truly are, it sees wrongly; thus it is wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*).
Its characteristic is a perverted vision, such as "there is no giving," and so forth. Like frivolous chatter (*samphappalāpa*), it is both slightly blameworthy and greatly blameworthy. Moreover...
Furthermore, those that are indeterminate are less blameworthy, while those that are determinate are more blameworthy. It has two constituent factors:
the object itself, which is contrary to the mode of apprehension, and its appearing in such a manner as it is grasped.
Now, regarding these ten unwholesome courses of action, [they are to be analyzed] by way of their intrinsic nature, their classification, their objects, and their associated feeling.
The analysis should be understood in five ways, beginning with "as root.

Therein, "as phenomena" (*dhammato*) means that, in their respective order, these consist of seven volitional phenomena (*cetanā-dhamma*) alone, while the three beginning with covetousness (*abhijjhā*) are associated with volition.

"As factors" (*koṭṭhāsato*) means that, in their respective order, these eight—namely, the seven and wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*)—are indeed courses of action (*kamma-patha*), but they are not roots; for covetousness and ill-will (*byāpāda*) [are not roots].
They are both courses of kamma and roots. For when covetousness becomes a root, greed is an unwholesome root; ill will, being hatred, is an unwholesome root. As for the object:
killing living beings has the life-faculty as its object, which is a formation; taking what is not given has either a being or a formation as its object;
sexual misconduct has formations as its object by way of the tangible, and it may also have a being as its object.
Some [teachers] say: False speech has either beings or mental formations as its object; likewise for malicious speech. Harsh speech has only beings as its object.
Frivolous chatter has either beings or mental formations as its object, by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized;
likewise for covetousness. Ill will has only beings as its object. Wrong view has mental formations as its object, by way of the phenomena belonging to the three planes.

Killing living beings is painful feeling (*dukkha-vedanā*). For even though kings, upon seeing a thief, may say with a smile, "Go, kill him," their decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*) is nevertheless associated only with pain.
Taking what is not given possesses all three feelings. Sexual misconduct possesses two feelings by way of pleasure (*sukha*) and neutrality (*majjhata*); [this refers to] the decisive mind...
However, there is no neutral feeling [associated with them]. False speech has three feelings; likewise, malicious speech and harsh speech have painful feeling;
frivolous chatter has three feelings; covetousness has two feelings, by way of pleasure and neutrality; likewise, wrong view. Ill will has painful feeling.

Regarding the roots: killing living beings has two roots, being rooted in hatred (*dosa*) and delusion (*moha*). Taking what is not given is rooted either in hatred and delusion or in greed (*lobha*) and delusion.
Sexual misconduct is rooted in greed and delusion. False speech is rooted either in hatred and delusion or in greed and delusion;
the same applies to malicious speech and frivolous talk. Harsh speech is rooted in hatred and delusion. Covetousness is rooted in delusion.
Ill will has the same single root. Wrong view has two roots, through greed and delusion.
Regarding the phrases "abstaining from taking life" and so forth, the meanings of taking life and the other offenses are as already explained.
As for the abstinence by which one is said to abstain from these, it is threefold when classified: abstinence by encounter, abstinence by undertaking, and abstinence by eradication.

In this context, the abstinence that arises in those who have not formally undertaken the training rules (sikkhāpada), who—having reflected upon their own birth, age, learning, and so forth—do not transgress a situation encountered [with the thought], "It is unbecoming for us to do such a thing," should be understood as *sampattavirati* (abstinence by encounter).
This is like the case of the lay follower Cakkana in the island of Siṃhala. It is said that when he was still a child, his mother fell ill.
[The meat] appeared. And the physician said, "Fresh hare-flesh must be obtained.
Thereupon, Cakkana’s brother sent Cakkana, saying, "Go, dear one, and search the field. He went there.
At that moment, a certain hare had come to eat the young grain. Seeing him, [Cakkana] ran with speed toward a creeper.
Bound, he made the sound "kiri kiri. Hearing that sound, Cakkana went to him, seized him, and thought, "I shall prepare medicine for my mother.
Then he thought again: "It is not fitting for me to deprive another of life for the sake of my mother's life.
He then said to him, "Go to the forest and subsist on grass and water with the deer."
He released it. When his brother asked, "Father, was a hare caught? he explained what had happened. Then his brother rebuked him.

He went to his mother and stood there, speaking the truth: "Since I was born, I do not recall ever intentionally depriving a living being of life. At that very moment, his mother became free from her ailment.

Furthermore, the abstinence that arises in those who have undertaken the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), who—having sacrificed their own lives both at the time of undertaking the training rules and thereafter—do not transgress the basis [of the precept], should be understood as "abstinence by undertaking" (*samādānavirati*). This is like the case of the lay follower who lived on Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna.
It is said that he received the training rules from the Elder Piṅgala-Buddharakkhita, who resided at the Ambaṭṭha Monastery.
Having taken it, he ploughed the field. Then his ox went astray; searching for it, he climbed Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna, where a great serpent seized him.
He thought, "I shall cut off its head with this sharp axe.
Then he thought again, "This is not fitting for me, that I should [break] the precept in the presence of my venerable teacher who is to be honored..."

"Having taken it, I shall break it. Having thought this up to three times—"I would rather give up my life than the training rule"—he cast away the sharp wooden axe he had placed on his shoulder in the forest. At that very moment, the great beast released him and departed.

However, the abstinence associated with the Noble Path should be understood as "abstinence through eradication," from the moment of its arising onwards, even the thought "I shall kill a living being" does not arise in the minds of Noble Persons.

And just as it was for the unwholesome courses of action, so too for these wholesome courses of action, the exposition should be understood by way of five modes: as to the nature of the phenomena (*dhamma*), as to their components (*koṭṭhāsa*), as to their objects (*ārammaṇa*), as to their feeling (*vedanā*), and as to their roots (*mūla*). In that regard, "as to the nature of the phenomena":
among these, the first seven may consist either of volition (*cetanā*) or of abstinences (*virati*); at the end, however, the three are associated only with volition.
Regarding the "divisions": in sequence, there are only seven courses of action (kamma-patha), not roots; at the end, there are three that are both courses of action and roots.
For when non-covetousness reaches the state of a root, it becomes the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha); non-ill-will becomes the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa);
and right view becomes the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha).
"By way of object" refers to killing living beings and so forth. Their objects are indeed those very things. For abstention is defined precisely by way of the basis that is to be transgressed.

However, it should be understood that just as the Noble Path, having Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too these courses of kamma—having the life-faculty and so forth as their objects—abandon the unwholesome conduct of killing living beings and the rest.
Regarding "from feeling": all [feelings] are either pleasant or neutral; for when one has attained the wholesome, there is no such thing as painful feeling.
Regarding "from the roots": in successive order, for one abstaining with a consciousness associated with knowledge, they have three roots by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion;
for one abstaining with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, they have two roots. Non-covetousness occurs with a consciousness associated with knowledge...

For one who abstains [from unwholesome deeds], it has two roots; when associated with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, it has one root. However, non-greed (*alobha*) does not have itself as its own root.
The same principle applies to non-hatred (*abyāpāda*). Right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) has two roots by way of non-greed and non-hatred. Thus ends the third [section]. 6.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Eightfold Path (*Aṭṭhaṅgikasutta-vaṇṇanā*).
112. The sixth [sutta] was spoken according to the inclination of those who awaken by way of the eight factors of the path. This is the sixth. 7.
Commentary on the *Dasaṅgasutta* 113.
The seventh is by way of the ten wrongnesses and rightnesses. Therein, "those with wrong knowledge" refers to those with wrong reflection.
The meaning is "endowed with. "Those of wrong liberation" refers to those who have adopted and stand by a wholesome liberation that does not lead to emancipation.
"Those of right knowledge" refers to correct reflective discernment. "Those of right liberation" refers to being endowed with the liberating fruit of deliverance that leads to emancipation.
This is the seventh [section].
The Third Chapter on the Paths of Action (Kammapathavagga).
4. The Fourth Chapter. 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Four Elements (Catudhātusutta).
114. In the first [sutta] of the fourth section: "The earth element" is the supporting element;
"the water element" is the binding element; "the fire element" is the maturing element; "the air element" is the distending element. This is the summary here;
however, in detail, these should be explained by way of the twenty parts and so forth. First.
2. Commentary on the Pubbe-sambodha Sutta 115.
In the second [sutta], "this is the gratification of the earth element" means this is the gratification based upon the earth element.
This [gratification] occurs when one raises the body, stretches out the belly, and says, "Exert yourselves here to insert even a finger! or...
Or he says, "Stretch out your hand; try to bend this," and it should be understood by way of such occurrences. Regarding the terms "impermanent" and so forth:
they are impermanent (*anicca*) in the sense of existing and then ceasing to be; they are suffering (*dukkha*) in the sense of oppression;

and they are subject to change (*vipariṇāmadhamma*) in the sense of the disappearance of their own-nature. This is the danger (*ādīnava*) of the earth element: the manner in which it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
This aspect means "the danger in the earth element. The "subduing of desire and lust" and the "abandoning of desire and lust" refer to Nibbāna;
for by resorting to Nibbāna, desire and lust for the earth element are both subdued and abandoned, and therefore Nibbāna is its escape.
This is the gratification in the water element; this is the gratification based upon the water element. And this [gratification] is distinct from that which is afflicted by the water element.
Having seen this, [he thought]: "Why is it that from the moment he lies down, he keeps going out and coming back toward the place for urination;
even when he performs a slight task, his sweat-soaked garment reaches the point where it must be wrung out;
and even when he speaks a mere word of thanksgiving, he has to take up a palm-leaf fan? Yet we lie down in the evening..."

This should be understood by way of those who speak thus: "We rise early; our bodies are like full jars of sesame; while performing great work, not even a drop of sweat arises upon us; and while preaching the Dhamma, there is not even the slightest warmth in our bodies, as if we were struck by a thunderbolt."
"This is the gratification of the fire element" means this is the gratification based upon the fire element. Having seen those afflicted by cold, [he thinks]:
"Why is it that these people, having swallowed only a little gruel, rice, or food, sit with stiffened bellies and search for a brazier all night long?
Even when a mere drop falls upon their bodies, they search for a brazier."
This should be understood by way of those who say: "Do they lie down after merely spreading out [the bedding] and putting on their robes?
But we eat even very tough meat or cakes, and we consume food until our bellies are full; yet at that very moment it all dissolves for us like a lump of foam.
Even when a seven-day heatwave is occurring, there is not even the slightest burning sensation of cold in our bodies. It is by such people as these that this should be known.
"This is the gratification of the air element" means that this is the gratification consisting in reliance upon the air element. For instance, seeing others who are afraid of the wind, one might say:
"Even when these people perform only a slight task, or merely speak with approval, the wind pierces their bodies;
when they have traveled even a distance of a *gāvuta*, their hands and feet grow weary, their backs ache, and [they suffer] from abdominal winds, head-winds, ear-winds, and so forth."
"Those who are constantly afflicted spend their time merely using oil, molasses, and the like as remedies for wind-disorders;

but for us, even while performing great work, preaching the Dhamma throughout the three watches of the night, or traveling ten yojanas in a single day, there is not so much as a cramp in our hands or feet, nor even a backache.
It was by virtue of those who lived in such a manner [that he spoke].
It should be understood thus. For when these elements proceed in this way, they are said to provide gratification (*assādenti*).

"I directly knew" (*abbhaññāsim*) means I knew by means of distinguished knowledge (*abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena*). "Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" (*anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhim*) refers to the supreme, most excellent, and perfectly self-awakened state;
or alternatively, to the praised and beautiful awakening. "Awakening" (*bodhi*) also refers to the tree.
The path, omniscient knowledge, and Nibbāna are all [called] Bodhi.
For in passages such as “the first fully enlightened one at the foot of the Bodhi tree” and “between the Bodhi and Gayā,” the tree is called Bodhi.

In the passage “Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four paths,” it refers to the path. And in the passage “the one of excellent and vast wisdom attains Bodhi,” [it refers to omniscient knowledge].

In the passage where it says "all-knowing wisdom," it refers to omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). In the passage where it says "having attained enlightenment, the deathless, the unconditioned," it refers to Nibbāna.
But here, the path of arahantship of the Blessed One is intended.
Is the path of arahantship of the disciples the unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttarā bodhi*)? It is not. Why? Because it does not bestow all qualities.

For among them, for some it bestows only the path to arahantship and the fruit of arahantship; for some, the three types of higher knowledge (tisso vijjā); for some, the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā);
for some, the four analytical insights (catasso paṭisambhidā); and for some, the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa).
For the paccekabuddhas as well, it bestows only the knowledge of pacceka-enlightenment. But for the Buddhas, it bestows the attainment of all qualities, just as a consecration does for a king.
The state of sovereignty over the entire world. Therefore, for no one else whatsoever does there exist unsurpassed enlightenment.
"I have fully awakened" means I acknowledged it thus: "I am fully awakened; having attained and penetrated [the truth], I stand firm.
And the knowledge and vision arose within me means the reviewing-knowledge capable of seeing the qualities already realized.
"Unshakable is my liberation"—thus the knowledge arose in me: "This liberation of mine, the fruit of Arahantship, is unshakable.
In this regard, its unshakability should be understood in two ways: by way of its cause and by way of its object.

For it is unshakable by way of its cause because the defilements, having been eradicated by the four paths, do not return; and it is unshakable by way of its object because it is an unshakable state (*akuppa-dhamma*).
It is "unshakable" (*akuppa*) even in terms of its object (*ārammaṇa*), because it proceeds having made Nibbāna its object. "Last" (*antima*) means final.
"Now there is no further becoming" (*natthi dāni punabbhavo*) means that now there is no further existence whatsoever.
In this sutta, the Four Truths are explained. How so? For among the four elements, gratification (*assāda*) is the Truth of Origination (*samudayasacca*).
The danger is the truth of suffering; the escape is the truth of cessation; and the path that understands cessation is the truth of the path.

It is indeed appropriate to explain this according to the detailed method as well. For herein, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence upon the earth element—this is the gratification of the earth element—and the penetration of its abandonment is the truth of the origin. As for that...
The earth element is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; this is the penetration by full understanding of the danger in the earth element, which is the truth of suffering.
The removal of desire and lust for the earth element, the abandoning of desire and lust for the earth element—this is the escape from the earth element;
this is the penetration by realization, which is the truth of cessation. Whatever view and intention there is regarding these three points...
Speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration—this penetration through cultivation is the Truth of the Path. This is the second [section]. 3.
Commentary on the *Acariṃ* Sutta 116. Regarding the third [verse]:

“I have traveled” (*acarim*) means I have traveled by way of the range of knowledge; the meaning is, by way of experiencing. “As far as” (*yāvatā*) means to whatever extent. This is the third [section].
4. Commentary on the Noceda Sutta 117.
In the fourth method, the terms beginning with "nissaṭā" (escaped) should be understood by connecting them with the negations stated at the outset:
"They did not escape, they were not dissociated, they were not liberated, they did not dwell with a mind whose boundaries were not transcended. This is according to the second method.

"By that which has made an end of boundaries" means by that which is without boundaries. In this context, there are two kinds of boundaries: the boundary of defilements (*kilesa-mariyādā*) and the boundary of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-mariyādā*).

Now, when someone has abandoned half of the defilements while half remain unabandoned, or has abandoned half of the round of existence while half remains unabandoned, their consciousness is said to have "made an end of boundaries" with reference either to the abandoned defilements or to the round of existence.
This was not spoken with reference to one who has not abandoned the defilements or to the round of existence;

rather, here it is said, "with a mind that has made no boundary," because both have been abandoned. The meaning is: with a mind that stands without having made a boundary, a mind that has transcended all boundaries.
Thus, in these three suttas, only the Four Noble Truths are taught. Fourth.
5. Commentary on the Ekantadukkha Sutta 118.
In the fifth [sutta], "entirely painful" (*ekantadukkha*) means that for one who has transcended [the world], it is entirely painful, like the sound of a hot iron ball.

"Assailed by suffering" (*dukkhānupatita*) means beset by suffering. "Overcome by suffering" (*dukkhāvakkanta*) means entered into or submerged in suffering. "Pleasurable" (*sukha*)... [text continues]
They are the conditions for pleasant feeling. In this way, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. In this sutta, the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇa*) is explained.
The fifth [sutta]. 6–10. Commentary on the *Abhinanda* Sutta and others, 119–123.
In the sixth and seventh [suttas], turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) is taught; in the final three, the Four Noble Truths (*catusacca*) themselves. These are the sixth and following.
The Fourth Chapter.
The commentary on the *Dhātusaṃyutta* is finished.
4. The *Anamataggasaṃyutta*.
1. First Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Sutta on Grass and Wood. 124.
In the first [sutta] of the *Anamatagga Saṃyutta*, "anamatagga" means that its end is not known; [it refers to] a hundred years, a thousand years...
Even though one has pursued it with knowledge, its beginning—the end of the deathless—is unknown;
it is not possible to know its summit from this side or that, meaning its prior and subsequent limits are undivided. "Saṃsāra" is the uninterrupted succession of the aggregates and so forth.
"The prior limit is not discerned" means that its initial boundary is not seen. To the extent that its prior limit...
It is not perceived; even the end is not perceived by that very tip, but beings transmigrate only in the middle.
"It would reach exhaustion"—this was said because the illustration is small. For in an external system, the meaning is limited while the illustration is vast:
"This ox is like an elephant; a pig is like an ox; [the world] is like the ocean."
For when "a pond" is mentioned, they do not conceive of such a vast measure. However, in the Buddha's time, the simile was small while the meaning was great.

For although only one Jambudīpa is taken in the text, even with hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of such Jambudīpas, the grass and so forth would be exhausted by that effort; yet it would not be enough for a single person.
"Mother, mother!"—you have experienced suffering; "intense" is a synonym for that very same thing.

"Calamity" refers to the manifold kinds of misfortune, such as the loss of kinsmen. "Kaṭasī" means a cemetery, or simply the earth itself, for it is increased by the repeated casting down of corpses of those who die. "It is indeed enough"—this is quite appropriate. First.
2. Commentary on the *Pathavī-sutta* 125.

"The great earth" (*mahāpathavim*) refers to the great earth bounded by the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). "He would set it aside" means that having split that earth and made pellets of the stated size, he would place them to one side. This is the second [sutta]. 3.
Commentary on the *Assu-sutta*
126. "Of those weeping" means of those crying out with sound. "Flowing" means streaming forth.
"In the four great oceans" refers to the four great oceans as demarcated by the rays of Mount Sineru.
For the eastern face of Sineru is made of silver, the southern face is made of beryl, the western face is made of crystal, and the northern face...

It is made of gold. The silver and jewel rays issuing from the eastern and southern sides merge together, travel across the surface of the great ocean, and remain striking against the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.

The jewel and crystal rays issuing from the southern and western sides, the crystal and gold rays issuing from the western and northern sides, and the [gold and jewel] rays issuing from the northern and eastern sides—[merge together and proceed in the same manner].
The rays of gold and silver, having come together, travel across the surface of the great ocean and stand striking against the Cakkavāḷa mountain.
Between those rays are the four great oceans. It is with reference to these that it was said, "in the four great oceans.
Regarding the phrase "misfortune concerning kinsmen" and so forth: *byasana* means *viasana*, which signifies destruction.
The misfortune of relatives is "relative misfortune" (*ñātibyasanam*); the misfortune of wealth is "wealth misfortune" (*bhogabyasanam*).

Illness, however, is called "misfortune" because it itself withers away and destroys health; thus, illness itself is the misfortune, which is "illness-misfortune" (*rogabyasanam*). This is the third [section]. 4.
Commentary on the *Khīrasutta* (The Discourse on Milk)
127. Regarding the fourth [nutriment], *mātuthañña* means the milk of a human mother who shares the same name.
For among these beings—whether born as gadflies, ants, and so forth, or as fish, turtles, and so forth, or among the species of birds—there is no mother’s milk at the time of birth;

however, there is milk when they are born as goats, cattle, buffalo, and so forth, and likewise among humans. In that regard, both during the time of being goats and so forth, and also among humans, [one is called] "Devī" (O Goddess).
It should be understood that the milk drunk by one who is conceived in the womb of a mother with the single name "Tissā"—
rather than those conceived in the wombs of mothers with various other names such as "Sumanā"— is greater in volume than the water in the four great oceans.
This is the fourth [section].
5. Commentary on the Pabbata Sutta 128.

Regarding the fifth [verse], "But it is possible, venerable sir": it is said that the monk thought, "The Teacher merely says, 'It is not easy, it is not easy,' regarding the extreme length of this beginningless saṃsāra; how does he cut it off?"
"Is it possible to provide a simile?"—it was for this reason that he spoke thus.
"With Kāsika cloth" means with a very fine fabric made of thread spun from three cotton fibers twisted together. When rubbed with that, how much would be worn away?
"The size of a mustard seed. The fifth [chapter].
6. Commentary on the Sāsapasutta 129.

Regarding the sixth [verse], "an iron city" (āyasaṃ nagaraṃ) should be understood as a city surrounded by an iron wall, but not one filled inside with single-storied palaces and the like made of iron. This is the sixth.
7. Commentary on the Sāvakasutta.

130. Regarding the seventh [case], "they would recollect": if one person were to recollect one hundred thousand aeons, another would recollect another hundred thousand from that person's point of reference, and yet another would recollect another; in this way, all four together would recollect four hundred thousand aeons.
This is the seventh. 8–9. Commentary on the Gaṅgā-sutta and others.

131–132. In the eighth [sutta], "the sand in this interval" refers to the sand within this interval measuring five hundred yojanas in length. In the ninth, there is nothing to be said. These are the eighth and ninth. 10.
Commentary on the *Puggala-sutta* (Sutta 10). 133.
In the tenth, the three terms beginning with "a skeleton" (*aṭṭhikaṅkala*) are synonyms for a heap. However, from the time these beings possess bones...
The time when there are no bones is much more frequent. For among these beings, such as earthworms and the like, there are no bones at all;

whereas for those that are fish, turtles, and so forth, bones are more numerous. Therefore, setting aside both the time when there are no bones and the time when there are many bones, one should take only the time when there are an equal number of bones.
"To the north of Vulture Peak" means standing on the northern side of Vulture Peak. "Of the Giribbaja of the Magadhans."
The meaning is: "standing on Giribbaja, the mountain-enclosure of the Magadha country. The rest is entirely obvious throughout.
The tenth [sutta]. The first chapter. Chapter Two.
1. Commentary on the Duggata Sutta (Sutta 134).
In the first sutta of the second chapter, "duggata" means poor and destitute. "Durūpeta" means endowed with hands and feet that are deformed. This is the first [sutta]. 2.
Commentary on the Sukhita Sutta.

135. In the second [verse], "happy" means endowed with happiness; "possessing great wealth and great enjoyments. "Well-adorned" means decorated and prepared, mounted upon the back of an elephant, and accompanied by a large retinue. This is the second [section]. 3. Commentary on the *Tiṃsamatta-sutta* (The Thirty): 136.

In the third [verse], "Pāveyyakas" refers to those dwelling in the Pāvā region. Regarding the phrases "all were forest-dwellers," and so forth, it is by way of undertaking the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) that they are described.
Their status as forest-dwellers (*āraññika*) and so forth should be understood. "All with fetters" (*sasaṃyojana*) means all are bound;

some are stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), some are once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), and some are non-returners (*anāgāmin*). For among them, there is neither an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) nor one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

In the phrases beginning with "of those with qualities" (*guṇṇaṃ*), when there are colors such as white or black, only the time of a single color should be taken. "Highwaymen" (*pāripanthaka*) are those who stand at a crossroads or ambush.
"Highwaymen and robbers. "Adulterers" refers to those who engage in sexual misconduct with the wives of others. This is the third [section]. 4–9.
Commentary on the Suttas beginning with "The Mother": 137–142.
Regarding the fourth and subsequent sections, the meaning should be understood through both the restriction of gender and the restriction of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). For, among men...
"Female time" and "male time for females"—such is the fixed rule regarding gender here.
Beings transmigrate from this world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) to another world-system, and from other world-systems back to this one.

Among them, showing that even during the female time in this world-system she was indeed a mother, he said: "She who has not previously been a mother," and likewise in the cases of "she who has not previously been a father," and so forth.
The same method applies to the fourth and subsequent [suttas].
10. Commentary on the Vepulla-pabbata Sutta: 143.

In the tenth [sutta], the phrase "In the past" (*bhūtapubbaṃ*) indicates that he brings forward and shows a particular account (*apadāna*) from a time gone by. "A designation arose" (*samaññā udapādi*).
There was a proclamation. "They ascend in four days"—this was said with reference to those of medium strength. "The foremost" means the most excellent.

"A blessed pair" means a beautiful couple. Regarding "they ascend in three days": it is said that during the interval between two Buddhas, the earth swelled by one *yojana*, and thus that mountain became three *yojanas* in height.
"Or a little more" means slightly more than a hundred years—perhaps ten or twenty years.
Furthermore, there is no one who lives for exactly a hundred years; at most, people live sixty or eighty years.
However, many die before reaching a hundred years, such as at the age of five or ten. And herein, the Blessed One Kakusandha...
It is said that Koṇāgamana was born during a time when the lifespan was thirty thousand years, whereas [Kakusandha] was born during a time when the lifespan was forty thousand years;
this is presented as if there were a gradual decline, yet it is not actually a continuous decline. Rather, it should be understood that after increasing again and again, the lifespan declined.
How so? First, the Blessed One Kakusandha appeared in this very eon during a time when the lifespan was forty thousand years.
Having been reborn, he lived for five portions of the lifespan; having completed four portions and while the fifth was still remaining, he attained final Nibbāna.

That lifespan, after decreasing until it reached the time of ten-year human life, increased again to become incalculable, and then, as it decreased once more, it remained at a time when the lifespan was thirty thousand years;
at that time, Koṇāgamana was reborn. In that [lifespan] also...

Likewise, when that [Buddha] had attained final Nibbāna, the human lifespan, having reached the ten-year period, increased again until it became incalculable, and then, after decreasing, remained at twenty thousand years;
at that time, the Blessed One Kassapa was born.
When he too had likewise attained final Nibbāna, the lifespan again reached the ten-year period and increased once more until it became incalculable.
After the lifespan had decreased for a period of one hundred years, our Sammasambuddha was born.
Thus, it should be understood that [the Buddhas] appear after the lifespan has gradually decreased, increased, and then decreased again.
And in that regard, whatever the measure of the lifespan may be when the Buddhas are born during periods of decline, their own lifespan will be exactly that same measure. The tenth [chapter].
The Second Chapter.
The Commentary on the *Anamatagga Saṃyutta* is finished.
5. The *Kassapa Saṃyutta*.
1. Commentary on the *Santuṭṭha-sutta* (144).
In the first sutta of the *Kassapa-saṃyutta*, "santuṭṭhāyaṃ" means "this one is contented. Regarding "with whatever [is obtained]" (*itarītarena*):

it does not mean content with just anything—whether coarse or fine, rough or refined, firm or worn-out—but rather the meaning is that he is content with whatever is obtained, such as what has been received, and so forth.
For regarding robes, there are three kinds of contentment: contentment with what is obtained, contentment with what is suitable to one’s strength, and contentment with what is appropriate.
The same method applies to almsfood and the other requisites.
This is their detailed explanation: here, a bhikkhu receives a robe, whether it be beautiful or ugly.
Or, he sustains himself with that very [robe], does not long for another, and even if he obtains one, he does not accept it.

This is his contentment regarding robes as they are obtained (*yathālābha-santuṣṭi*). Furthermore, if he is naturally weak, or overcome by illness or old age, and finds it exhausting to wear a heavy robe, he exchanges it with a fellow monk of similar standing and sustains himself with a light one; even so, he remains truly content.
This is his contentment with robes according to his ability. Another person obtains superior requisites;
having received one of the costly robes such as a robe made of fine cloth (*paṭṭacīvara*) or many robes, he gives them to others, saying: "Let this be for the elders who have long been gone forth;
let this be suitable for those of great learning; let this be for the sick; let this be for those who receive little. Having given them to these, [he himself uses what remains].
Or, having gathered rags from an old garment or from a heap of refuse and made a *saṅghāṭī* robe from them, he remains content even while wearing it.
This is his contentment with robes as is appropriate.
Furthermore, in this case, a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined; he subsists on that alone and does not seek another.
He does not long for it, and even if he obtains it, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever almsfood is obtained.

However, if he receives almsfood that is contrary to his natural constitution or contrary to his illness—such that by consuming it he would suffer discomfort—he gives that to a fellow monk of similar condition and, having eaten suitable food from that monk's hand, [proceeds].
Even while performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), he remains content. This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength.

Another person receives much and excellent almsfood; like [the one who gives] robes, he gives that to those who have long been ordained, those who are learned, those of little gain, and the sick, or else, having given what remains to them, he remains content even when eating mixed food after wandering for alms himself.
This is his contentment with almsfood as it is appropriate.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives a lodging that is either pleasing or unpleasing;
he gives rise to neither joy nor aversion because of it, but is satisfied even with what is obtained as little as a mere grass mat. This is his...

Contentment with whatever dwelling-place one obtains is as follows: if, however, one obtains a dwelling-place that is naturally unsuitable for oneself or incompatible with one's illness, such that living there causes discomfort, one should give it to a fellow monk of similar standing and remain content even while living in a suitable dwelling belonging to that monk.
This is one’s contentment with regard to the dwelling-place according to one’s strength.
Another person of great merit obtains many excellent lodgings, such as caves, pavilions, and gabled houses;
yet, having given these away like robes and other requisites to those who have been long ordained, to the learned, to those of little gain, and to the sick, he remains content wherever he dwells.
This is his contentment with a lodging appropriate to his state. As for that which is called "the supreme lodging":

Reflecting, "This is a basis for negligence; lethargy and drowsiness descend upon one sitting there, and when one who is overcome by sleep awakens, evil thoughts manifest," he does not accept even such a lodging when offered.
Having rejected it, he dwells in open spaces, at the foot of trees, and so forth, and remains contented. This too is [contentment] with respect to lodgings.
Contentment with what is appropriate.
Here, however, a bhikkhu receives medicine that is either coarse or refined;

he is content with whatever he receives, does not long for another, and even if he finds it, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained regarding the requisite of medicine.
But one who needs oil and receives molasses may give that to a fellow monk, take oil from his hand, or seek something else entirely, and even while preparing medicine in this way, he remains content.
This is his contentment with medicinal requisites according to his strength. Furthermore, another person of great merit [receives] abundant, high-quality medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses.
Having obtained it, he gives that robe-like [gain] to those who have long been ordained, those who are learned, those who receive little, and those who are ill;
even while subsisting on whatever they bring back, he remains truly content.
But suppose someone were told, "Venerable sir, take whichever you wish," with *muttaharītaka* placed in one vessel and the four sweet substances (*catumadhura*) in another; if, among those two...

If a disease is cured by one thing or another, yet he refuses the "four sweets"—thinking, "The so-called *muttaharītaka* has been praised by the Buddha and others"—and instead prepares his medicine with *muttaharītaka*, he remains supremely content.

This is his contentment with what is appropriate regarding the requisite of medicine. Thus, with reference to these three kinds of contentment, [the Blessed One said]: "Bhikkhus, this bhikkhu is content..."
“Kassapa [is content] with whatever robe [he receives],” it is said.
Regarding “one who speaks in praise”: one person is contented but does not speak in praise of contentment;
another is not contented but speaks in praise of contentment; and another is neither contented nor speaks in praise of contentment.
He is content with one thing and speaks in praise of contentment. To show that he is such a person, it is said: "one who speaks in praise of contentment with whatever robe-material is obtained.
"Improper search" refers to various kinds of improper search, such as engaging in the business of acting as a messenger or a go-between.
"Not having obtained" means not having acquired. And just as some [person] thinks, "How indeed shall I obtain a robe?"...
Being together with virtuous monks, he acts with hypocrisy and is terrified and anxious;
yet, when he has not obtained a robe in this way, he is not anxious. "Having obtained" means having acquired it through lawful and equitable means.
"Unattached" means free from the greed of craving. "Uninfatuated" means not having fallen into a swoon of excessive thirst (*taṇhā*). "Unconsumed" means...
“Not submerged in craving” means not enveloped by it. “Seeing the danger” means seeing the peril in the fault of improper search and in the enjoyment of what is attached to.
“Possessing the wisdom of escape” means that he partakes [of food] knowing precisely that escape which has been described as, “only for the warding off of cold,” and so forth.
In the phrases beginning with “with whatever alms-food [he may receive],” etc., [it refers to] that which is obtained as it comes, and so on.
The meaning should be understood as follows: "with whatever almsfood, with whatever lodging, and with whatever medicinal requisites for the sick.

Regarding the phrase, "Bhikkhus, I will exhort you by means of Kassapa," it refers to how the Elder Mahākassapa, in four [respects]— [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated here.*
He is said to "exhort by means of Kassapa" when he exhorts, saying, "May you also become like him, being content with three kinds of contentment regarding the four requisites.
Or, regarding the phrase "or whoever else is like Kassapa," it means:
"Or whoever else, like Kassapa—that is, like the Elder Mahākassapa—should be content with three kinds of contentment regarding the four requisites, may you also [be so]."
When advising, "Become such as this," he is said to advise by way of being like Kassapa. "One should practice for the sake of becoming thus" means:
"It is indeed a burden to speak of this practice of the austere conduct (*sallekhācāra*) described in this *Santuṭṭhi-sutta* of the Perfectly Enlightened One;
it is likewise a burden for us to fulfill this practice completely. For [Kassapa] has come..."
"But the burden must be taken up. Having reflected thus, he said: "Just as I have spoken, so too should you practice for the sake of becoming such and for the sake of being such. First.
2. Commentary on the *Anottappī-sutta*.
145. "In the second [case], 'without ardor' (*anātāpī*) means devoid of that energy which heats up (*ātapati*) the defilements.

'Without moral dread' (*anottappī*) means fearless—devoid of fear regarding the arising of defilements and the non-arising of the wholesome. 'For the sake of full awakening' (*sambodhāya*) means for the purpose of awakening. 'For the sake of Nibbāna' (*nibbānāya*) means for the realization of Nibbāna.
'Of the unsurpassed security from bondage' (*anuttarassa yogakkhemassa*) refers to Arahantship, for that is indeed unsurpassed."
And it is secure from the four bonds.

Regarding the phrases "not yet arisen" and so forth: when someone has previously obtained requisites such as robes—or a pleasant object—from any one of their attendants, co-residents, or pupils, and then grasps that thing unreasonably as "beautiful" and "pleasant," [that is what is meant].

Or else, when one attends inappropriately to some object never experienced before, in whatever manner it may be, unwholesome evil states such as greed arise; these should be understood as "not yet arisen.
For otherwise, throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there are no evil states that have not already arisen at some time. And even regarding an object previously experienced—
Or, when certain states— whether by way of their natural intelligence regarding an object, or through questioning and inquiry, or through study, new undertakings, or wise attention—
do not arise previously but subsequently arise suddenly due to a corresponding condition,
these too should be understood as "unarisen states that, if they were to arise, would lead to harm. And in those very same bases and objects:
Arising again and again, they are said not to be abandoned; it should be understood that "if these arisen states are not abandoned, they will lead to harm.

This is the summary here; however, the detailed classification of the arisen and the unarisen, as well as the method for abandoning and not abandoning, is all explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the purification of knowledge and vision.
"Wholesome states not yet arisen" refers to blameless states—namely virtue, concentration, the path, and the fruits—which have not yet been attained.
"Arisen" refers to those very same states that have been attained. "If they were to cease, it would lead to harm":
it should be understood that if those states of virtue and so forth were to cease through decline and fail to arise again, it would lead to what is disadvantageous.
And herein, those who are mundane fall away, whereas for those who are supramundane there is no falling away.
Furthermore, this teaching was given with reference to this right striving: "for the stability of wholesome states that have arisen.
Or else, if the second path were not to arise quickly while the first path is ceasing, it would lead to harm; thus it is here.
The meaning should be understood. Thus, in this sutta, these four right efforts are explained by way of preliminary insight (*pubbabhāga-vipassanā*). Second. 3.
Commentary on the Moon-like Sutta (Candūpama-sutta) 146.
In the third [sutta], "being like the moon" means being similar to the moon. Not because of its circularity; rather, it is as follows:
Just as the moon, when ascending into the vault of the sky, forms no intimacy, affection, attachment, craving, longing,
or obsession with anyone, yet remains dear and pleasing to the great multitude; so too,
by not forming such intimacy and the like with anyone, you are dear and pleasing to many people.
The meaning is: "Having become like the moon, approach the four castes, beginning with the khattiya clan.

Furthermore, the meaning here should be understood through such methods as: "Just as the moon dispels darkness and spreads light, so too, by dispelling the darkness of the defilements and spreading the light of knowledge, you have become like the moon. And so forth.
"Having withdrawn the body and withdrawn the mind": by not engaging in intimacy with those very people, one has withdrawn and removed both body and mind;
this is the meaning. For a monk who neither dwells in the forest nor reflects upon sensual thoughts and the like does not withdraw his body, nor does he withdraw his mind.
But he who indeed dwells in the forest, yet [reflects upon] sensual thoughts and the like...
But he who dwells near a village and does not give rise to thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, this one withdraws the mind, not the body.
He who dwells in the forest and does not give rise to thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, this one withdraws the mind, not the body.
But he who dwells both in the forest and does not give rise to thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, this one withdraws both. Having become such as this, [he visits] families...
Pointing out that one should approach [the teacher], he said: "Having drawn back the body, having drawn back the mind.
"Always like novices" means always remaining as if they were newcomers;
for a newcomer, having entered the house reached in due order, if the masters of the house see him, [thinking] "our sons and brothers are away..."
"Having gone thus, they wandered," thinking thus with compassion, she had them sit down and fed them;
as soon as they had finished eating, she would rise and depart, saying, "Take your bowls," neither forming intimacy with them nor arranging for their business affairs.
In the same way, you too, having entered a house in due order, [should act] regarding whatever postures...
He points out: "People give with confidence; having taken that, you should depart without being occupied with their social ties or their business and duties.
To illustrate this state of being a constant novice, the story of the two brothers from the village of Vasāḷa should be told. From the village of Vasāḷa...
It is said that two brothers went forth and were ordained; they became known as the Elder Cūḷanāga and the Elder Mahānāga.
Having lived on Cittala Mountain for thirty years and attained *arahantship*, they thought, "We shall see our mother," and returned.
They stayed at the Vāsāla city monastery and, on the following day, entered among the womenfolk for alms. Their mother, too—
Having ladled out some gruel with a spoon, she poured it into the bowl of one of them. As she gazed at it, maternal affection arose within her.

Then she said to him, "Dear son, you are my great-nephew. The Elder replied, "Ask the last Elder, laywoman," and departed. After giving gruel to the last Elder as well, she said, "Dear son, you are my..."
“Is it your son Cūḷanāga? he asked. The Elder said, “Why do you not ask about the previous elder, lay follower?
and having said this, he departed. In this way, a bhikkhu who has severed his intimacy even with his mother is called “always new.
*Appagabbhā* means not impudent; [not impudent] by way of the eight bases of bodily impudence and the four bases of verbal impudence.
The meaning is that one is devoid of immodesty of mind in its many forms. "Immodesty of body" refers to improper physical conduct in eight situations:
within the Saṅgha, in a group, before an individual, in a dining hall, in a sauna, at a bathing place, on the path for almsround, and when entering a house.
For example, here someone sits with their legs crossed in the midst of the Saṅgha.

Placing foot upon foot while walking, and so forth. Likewise, in the midst of a group (*gaṇa*). "In the midst of a group" means either in an assembly of the fourfold assembly or in an assembly of those belonging to the Suttanta-group and so on.

Likewise, toward persons who are senior. Furthermore, in the dining hall, he does not give a seat to the seniors, nor does he yield his seat to the juniors. Likewise, in the sauna (*jantāghara*). And here, [if he sits] without asking permission from the seniors...

He performs acts such as lighting fires and making noise. Furthermore, disregarding what was stated regarding bathing places—that "one should bathe according to the order of arrival, without making the criteria of 'young' or 'old' a factor"—he arrives later, enters the water, and displaces both the elders and the juniors.
On the path of alms-round, however, he stands in front for the sake of the best seat, the best water, and the best alms-food.
He walks along striking arm against arm. Regarding entering a house:
he enters before the elders and engages in physical play with the youths, and so forth.
Verbal audacity in four instances refers to the utterance of improper speech within the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or a house.
For example: here someone speaks on the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha without having asked for permission.
Likewise, in the midst of a group of the kind previously described, or in the presence of an individual, when questioned by people there, he answers without asking permission from one who is senior.
Furthermore, within a house, [he asks]: "So-and-so, what is there? Is there rice-gruel, or rather solid food?"
He speaks such things as, "What food? "What will you give me? "What shall we eat today? "What shall we consume? "What shall we drink? and so forth.

Mental immodesty (*manopāgabbhiya*) in various matters means that even without committing transgressions through body or speech in those respective instances, one mentally indulges in thoughts of sensual desire and the like.
Furthermore, while being actually immoral, one thinks, "People call me virtuous."
“May he know”—thus, even such evil desire as this constitutes mental immodesty (*manopāgabbhiya*). Therefore, he says:
“Having become free from immodesty (*appagabbhā*) by the absence of all these forms of immodesty, approach.
“An old well” (*jarudapāna*) means a dilapidated well. “A mountain precipice” (*pabbatavisaṃ*) means a steep, dangerous place on a mountain. “A river difficult to cross” (*nadīvidugga*)...
A river’s difficult place where the banks have crumbled away. One who is devoted to play and the like should pull back the body from such places;

without making the body one-sidedly heavy, without letting it be supported by the wind, and without withdrawing the mind—failing to see the danger that "falling here will result in broken hands, feet, and so forth"—he should not be negligent.
If he looks with affection, he falls and meets with misfortune such as the breaking of hands and feet.
However, one who desires water or wishes to look for some other purpose should withdraw the body to one side, make it heavy, and take hold of the support of the wind;
he should also withdraw the mind and arouse a sense of spiritual urgency by seeing the danger.
He looks down, he does not fall; having looked as he pleases, he departs happily wherever he wishes.
"In the same way" refers here to this application of the simile: the four families are like the old well and so forth, and the man who looks down is like the bhikkhu.
Just as that man, looking at them with his body and mind unwithdrawn, [remains there]...
Just as one falls [into a pit], so too a bhikkhu who approaches families with his body and other faculties unguarded becomes entangled among those families;
from that, he encounters various kinds of misfortune, such as the breaking of the foundation of virtue (*sīla*).
But just as a person whose body and mind are withdrawn does not fall there, so too, by means of a guarded body, guarded minds, and well-established guarded speech, [he does not fall].
When a bhikkhu approaches families with his body and mind withdrawn through mindfulness, he is not fettered by those families.
Then, just as the feet of a man who has not fallen there do not break, so too his foot of virtue does not break.
Just as his hands do not break, so too his hand of faith does not break. Just as his belly does not break...
In this way, the interior of the concentration does not break. Just as the head does not break, so too the head of knowledge (*ñāṇasīsa*) does not break;
and just as that [head] is not pierced by stumps, thorns, and the like, so too this [mind] is not pierced by the thorns of lust and the like.
Just as he, being free from affliction, looks about as he pleases and departs happily wherever he wishes, so too does the bhikkhu [visit] families.

Relying upon requisites such as robes and so forth, he cultivates his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), comprehends conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), and having attained *arahantship*, being made happy by supramundane bliss, he goes wherever he wishes toward the direction of *nibbāna*, which he had never gone to before.
Now, one of inferior inclination who practices wrongly might say: "The Perfectly Enlightened One [taught] the threefold impudence..."

Having cut off his line of argument by saying, "He places [the monks] in an impossible position, imposes an unbearable burden, and makes them do what cannot be done," Kassapa said, "Bhikkhus, it is indeed possible to do so;
there are such monks," and began with the words, "Bhikkhus... and so forth, demonstrating that this was indeed possible.
"He waved his hand in the air" means that, as if emitting twin flashes of lightning within the blue expanse of the sky, he moved his hand through the lower part, the upper part, and both sides.
Furthermore, this is known as "unmixed phrasing" (*asambhinnapada*) within the Buddha’s word consisting of the Three Pitakas.
"With a joyful mind" (*attamano*) means with a contented heart; it is a mind grasped without being severed by dejection (*domanassa*). [This was said] concerning Kassapa.
"O monks"—this too was spoken in the same manner as before for the purpose of showing that such monks do exist, having refuted the opposing argument.
"They would show a sign of confidence" means they would provide requisites such as robes and so forth. "They would practice accordingly" refers to the training in virtue (*sīla*).

In the place where virtue has arrived, they should fulfill it; in the place where concentration, insight, the path, and the fruit have arrived, they should accomplish each of those for the sake of becoming such [as they are].
"Anudayanti" means the state of protecting. "Anukampanti" means the softness of heart.
Both of these are synonyms for compassion (*kāruñña*). "Kassapo, bhikkhave," this too is according to the previous method.
This was said for the purpose of cutting off the arguments of opponents and demonstrating that there indeed exists such a bhikkhu.
Regarding the phrase "by Kassapa," the meaning should be understood in the same manner as before, by applying the analogy of the moon and so forth. The third [sutta].
4. Commentary on the *Kulūpaka Sutta*.

147. “One who frequents families” (*kulūpaka*) means one who approaches family households. “Let them give to me” (*dentu yeva me*) means “let them give to me. “He is distressed” (*sandīyati*) means he is troubled or oppressed. The rest here should be understood according to the method already explained. This is the fourth [sutta]. 5. Commentary on the *Jiṇṇa-sutta* (The Old Man Sutta) 148.

In the fifth [sutta], “old” (*jiṇṇa*) means an elder (*thera*), one who is advanced in years. “Heavy” (*garukāni*) refers to [the requisites] from the time they were received from the presence of the Teacher.
