Starting from the places where they were torn and split, through the sewing together of threads and the application of patches, they became many layers and grew heavy.
"Worn out" (Nibbasanāni) means they received that name because they had previously been worn by the Blessed One and then discarded.

"Therefore" (tasmā) means because you are both old and possess a heavy rag-robe (paṃsukūla). "Householder's wife" (gahapatānī) refers to one who has abandoned the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes.
He says, "Wear robes given by householders. Regarding "invitations": he says, "Abandoning the practice of eating only almsfood, accept invitations such as meals provided by ticket.
Regarding "in my presence": he says, "Abandoning the practice of dwelling in the forest, dwell only in lodgings within the village."
But surely, just as a king, having appointed a general to the position of commander-in-chief,
would act improperly if he were to take that very office away from one who has pleased him by performing his own duties such as attending upon the king, and give it to another—
even so did the Teacher travel three *gāvutas* along the road to meet the Elder Mahākassapa at Rājagaha.
And while sitting at the foot of the Bahuputtaka tree between Nālandā and Pāṭaligāma, he ordained him by means of the three exhortations;
having exchanged his own robe with him, he made the elder a forest-dweller (*araññika*) by birth and a wearer of rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*) by birth.
Through his desire to perform those duties, even as he was pleasing the Teacher’s mind, [he acquired] rag-robes and so forth.
If one were to say that by urging someone to accept householders' robes and so forth after having them relinquish them, one is doing what is improper—that is not the case. Why?
Because it is according to his own inclination. For the Teacher does not wish to cause the relinquishing of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas);
rather, just as drums and other instruments do not emit sound unless struck, so too such individuals do not roar the lion's roar unless they are prompted.
Desiring to cause [the others] to roar, and with the intention of making a lion’s roar, he spoke thus.
The Elder, likewise, in accordance with the Teacher’s own intention, let out a lion’s roar in this manner: “Venerable sir, for a long time I have been a forest-dweller,” and so forth.
As for the phrase “a happy dwelling in this very life”: such a happy dwelling in this very life is obtained only by one who is a forest-dweller, not otherwise.
Those who dwell within a village: for while living within a village, one hears the sounds of children, sees unsuitable forms, and hears unsuitable sounds;

because of this, dissatisfaction arises in him. But the forest-dweller, having gone beyond a *gāvuta* or half a *yojana* and having plunged deep into the forest, dwells there hearing the sounds of leopards, tigers, lions, and so forth, of which—
Through the condition of seclusion, a non-human delight in seclusion arises. With reference to this it was said:
“For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is peaceful, there is a non-human delight as he correctly discerns the Dhamma.”
“Whenever one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates,
one finds rapture and gladness— that which is the deathless for those who understand it.
Whether in front or behind, if no other is found...”
“Right there one finds comfort, delighting alone in the forest.
Thus, this [comfort] is obtained only by one who lives on alms-food, not by one who does not live on alms-food.
For one who does not live on alms-food wanders at improper times, goes with hurried steps, turns back, and goes with obstacles; and therein he is full of many doubts.
But one who lives on almsfood does not wander at the wrong time, does not go with hurried pace, does not turn back, goes unhindered, and is not greatly troubled therein. How so?
For one who does not live on almsfood, while dwelling in a monastery far from a village, must set out very early for [the sake of] rice-gruel or leftover food.
"Perhaps I will receive something from the alms-food distribution or other offerings in the assembly hall.
Thinking thus, he went out early in the morning, cutting through the fences of the monkey-orchards and rousing the cattle that were lying down; thus he became one who wanders at an improper time.
He followed after the deer in order to reach it just as the people were leaving their homes for the sake of field-work and other tasks.

Moving with speed as if in haste, he becomes one who acts with urgency. Seeing something along the way, he asks, "Is such-and-such a lay follower or such-and-such a lay follower at home or not at home?
Upon hearing, "Not at home," he trembles like one scorched by fire, thinking, "Now, where shall I obtain [alms]?
He is like one wishing to go toward the western direction, yet having received a ticket for the eastern direction, [seeks] another...
Approaching the one who had received the voting-ticket from the western direction, he exchanged the tickets, saying: "Venerable sir, I am going to the western direction;
please take my ticket and give yours to me.
Or, while eating a single ticket-meal that had been brought, he [thinks]: "The bowl for another ticket-meal..."
When people said, "Give it here," he replied, "Venerable sir, give me your bowl; I will put the food into my own bowl and then give your bowl back to you.
Having thus had another's bowl given to him, and once the food was brought, he placed it into his own bowl.
Returning the bowl, he is said to be "exchanging bowls. [This occurred when] kings, royal ministers, and others were in the monastery...
They give great gifts, and because of this, voting tickets (salākā) are obtained even in distant villages;

thinking, "If I do not go there, I will not receive a ticket again for another seven days," he goes out of fear of not receiving one. Going in such a manner, he is said to go while being "obstructed" (palibuddho).
Furthermore, regarding the person for whose sake he goes—whether for the purpose of rice distributed by voting ticket or otherwise—he wonders: "Will they indeed give it to me, or will they not?"
"Will they give? Will they give something choice, or rather something coarse? Will it be little, or rather much?
Will it be cold, or rather warm?"—thus there is much uncertainty in that regard.
However, the alms-collector, having risen early, performed his duties and services, and attended to his body, [proceeds] to his dwelling place...
Having entered [the village], he attends to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), observes the time, and goes at a time sufficient for giving alms such as a ladleful of food to the multitude;
thus, he is not one who wanders at the wrong time. Walking while practicing insight by dividing each step into six parts, he is not one who walks hurriedly.
Because of his own dignity, [he does not inquire] whether "so-and-so is in the house" or "not in the house."
He does not ask; he does not even accept tickets for meals and the like. Since he does not accept them, what would he have to exchange? He is not hindered by others;
attending to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he goes wherever he pleases. Unlike the other, he does not have many doubts.
If he fails to obtain [alms] in one village or street, he wanders elsewhere. Even there, he...
Having failed to obtain [alms] elsewhere, he wanders about, gathers mixed rice, and goes on after consuming it as if it were the Deathless.
This is obtained only by one who is a rag-robe wearer (*paṃsukūlika*), not by one who is not a rag-robe wearer.

For one who is not a rag-robe wearer wanders about seeking a rainy-season robe (*vassāvāsika*), and does not seek what is suitable for his lodging. But a rag-robe wearer does not wander about seeking a rainy-season robe...
He practices; he seeks only what is suitable for his lodging. This applies only to one who possesses the three robes, not to another.
For one who does not possess the three robes has many belongings and many requisites; therefore, there is no comfortable living for him.
This applies only to those with few desires and so forth, not to others. Hence it was said: "Considering his own comfortable dwelling in this very life. This is the fifth.

6. Commentary on the Ovāda Sutta 149. Why did he say, "I am [the one]" in the sixth [verse]? It was for the purpose of establishing the Elder in his own proper place. Was it because Sāriputta and Moggallāna were not there?
They were indeed there. However, this thought occurred to him: "These two will not remain for long; Kassapa, however, has a lifespan of one thousand years."
“Thus, after I have attained final nibbāna, he will sit in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave and compile the Dhamma and Vinaya, ensuring that my teaching shall endure for a period of five thousand years.
I establish him in his proper place, so that the bhikkhus will think, ‘One must listen respectfully to Kassapa.
Therefore he spoke thus. “Difficult to speak with” (*dubbaca*) means difficult [to deal with].
They should be addressed. "By means of being difficult to speak with" (*dovacassakaraṇehi*) means by means of making oneself difficult to address.

"Those who do not grasp what is favorable" (*appadakkhiṇaggāhino*) means that having heard the instruction, they do not grasp it favorably; they do not practice according to what was taught. This shows that by not practicing, they have become known as those who grasp what is contrary.
"Speaking excessively" (*accāvadante*) means speaking beyond [the bounds]; relying on their learning and mastery of the scriptures, they speak too much.
The meaning is "engaging in debate. "Who will speak more? means: while preaching the Dhamma, who will speak more—will it be you, or shall it be me?
"Who will speak more beautifully? refers to this: one person, though speaking much, speaks what is disconnected and unpleasant, while another speaks what is connected and pleasant;
with reference to that, he asks, "Who will speak more beautifully? Furthermore, one [person] speaks much...
One who speaks beautifully does not speak for long; he rises quickly; he carries a single person on a journey—it is with reference to him that [the Buddha] said, "Who stays longer? This is the sixth.
7. Commentary on the Second Ovāda Sutta.
150. Seventh: "Faith" means faith of conviction (*okappana-saddhā*). "Energy" refers to physical and mental energy. "Wisdom" is the wisdom that knows wholesome phenomena.
"There are no monks who give exhortation" means that for this person there are no instructors, teachers, or spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitta*);
this, venerable sir, he shows to be decline. This is the seventh.
8. Commentary on the Third Discourse of Advice (Tatiya-ovāda-sutta) 151.
Regarding the eighth [phrase], "for thus" (*tathā hi pana*): this particle is used to establish the reason for his former ease in speaking and his present difficulty in speaking.
"Therein" (*tattha*) means among those elders. "What is the name of this bhikkhu? (*ko nāmāyaṃ bhikkhu*) means what is the name of this bhikkhu? Is it the Elder Tissa?
"Is it not the Elder Nāga? "Therein" means while such honor was being performed. "For the sake of being thus" (*tathattāya*) means for the state of being so;

the meaning is: for the state of being a forest-dweller and so forth. "One who desires fellow-celibates" (*sabrahmacārikāmo*): he desires, wishes, and longs thus, "May these [companions] move about surrounding me"—thus he is one who desires fellow-celibates. "For the sake of being thus" means for the purpose of producing gain and honor.

"By the affliction of fellow celibates" (*brahmacārupaddavena*): that which is called the "affliction" consisting of excessive desire and lust for the four requisites of fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*), by that they are afflicted.
"Longing" (*abhipatthanā*): excessive longing. "By the longing of fellow celibates" (*brahmacāriabhipatthanena*):
by way of the state of the four requisites, which is reckoned as the excessive longing of fellow celibates. The eighth [chapter].
9. Commentary on the *Jhānābhiññā Sutta* 152.
In the ninth [sutta], the phrase "as far as I wish" (*yāvadeva ākaṅkhāmīti*) means "as far as I desire.

Furthermore, those four fine-material-sphere jhānas which follow this, according to the method beginning with "quite secluded from sensual pleasures," and those beginning with "by completely surmounting perceptions of form," etc., [are described].

By way of method, the four formless attainments are stated; likewise, the attainment of cessation is stated as "having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the cessation of perception and feeling";
and the five mundane direct knowledges are stated by way of method such as "the various kinds of psychic power," and so forth.
Regarding this, whatever needs to be said has all been provided in the word-by-word commentary and in the exposition of the method of development.
This has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. Regarding "the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khaya*), it means by means of the destruction of the taints.
"Taintless" (*anāsava*) means that which has become a non-condition for the taints. "Liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) refers to the concentration of the fruit of arahantship.
"Liberation through wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) refers to the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship. This is the ninth [chapter].
10. Commentary on the Upassaya Sutta (153).
Regarding the tenth [sutta], as for the request, "Come, venerable sir," why does he ask to go to the nuns' residence? It is not for the sake of gain or honor;
rather, there are nuns there who require a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and he thinks, "I shall encourage them and teach them the meditation subject."
He requests [permission]. But surely he himself is one who has mastered the Three Piṭakas and is learned; why is it that he cannot speak for himself? It is not that he cannot.
However, he requests it thinking, "How will they believe the words of a disciple who is like a Buddha? [The other asks:
"You have many duties and much to do"—does this mean the Elder is occupied with building work or similar tasks, such that he speaks thus? No.

But when the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, the four assemblies approached the Elder Ānanda and, weeping and lamenting, cried out: "Venerable sir, whom shall we now follow with his bowl and robes?
Whose cell shall we sweep? To whom shall we offer water for rinsing the mouth?
The Elder said: "Conditioned things are impermanent; even toward a body grown old, the King of Death is indeed shameless."
"Strike! This is the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*); do not grieve, do not lament. Thus he reassured the assembly. This was his many tasks;
it was with reference to this that the Elder spoke thus. "He instructed" means he showed the quality of the practice (*paṭipatti*).
"He incited" means he caused them to take it up. "He inspired" means he roused them. "He gladdened" means he caused them to rejoice in the qualities they had attained.
*Thullatissā*: she was stout in body (*sarīrena thūlā*) and named Tissa. *Vedehamunino*: of the wise sages (*paṇḍitamunino*).
For a wise person (*paṇḍito*) acts upon all duties by means of what is called knowledge (*veda*), and therefore is called "Vedeha.
Being both Vedeha and a sage (*muni*), he is a "Vedehamuni. He thought that the Dhamma should be spoken [to him]—[referring to] the keeper of the Dhamma-treasury who upholds the Tipiṭaka.
Being himself a forest-dweller and a wearer of rag-robes, he thinks, "I am a preacher of the Dhamma," and thus considers it appropriate to speak on the Dhamma.
"What is this, and how is this?"—she speaks while being ignorant. "He heard"—this refers to having heard it by means of another person coming and informing him.
"Wait, friend"—that is, "stay, friend. "Do not let the Saṅgha [deal] further with you..."
"Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus not examine him in this excessive manner. This is what is meant: "The Saṅgha should not think thus:
'Ānanda has rejected a disciple who was a counterpart to the Buddha, yet he did not reject a single bhikkhunī;
there must be some intimacy or affection between them.'"
Now, demonstrating his own likeness to a Buddha, he said, "What do you think, friend," and so forth.

"Seven cubits" (*sattaratanam*) means seven *hattha*s in measure. "An elephant" (*nāgam*) means a male elephant. "Or eight and a half cubits" (*aḍḍhaṭṭharatanam vā*) means seven and a half *hattha*s less by half a *ratana*;
the meaning is that from the forefeet up to the frontal globes, it is seven *hattha*s plus one span (*vidatthi*) in height. "Of palm leaves" (*tālapattikāya*).

With a young palm leaf. "Cavitthā" means she has departed—not dead, nor lost—but because she had spoken ill of a disciple who was the Buddha’s equal, while the Elder Mahākassapa was roaring his lion’s roar with the six supernormal powers, her yellow robes began to gnaw at her body like thorny branches or itch-grass stalks; having removed them, [she departed].
At the very moment he was clothed in the fine linen robes, a delight in his mind arose. The tenth [sutta].
11. Commentary on the Cīvara Sutta (The Discourse on Robes) 154.
In the eleventh [sutta], "at Dakkhiṇāgiri" means on the southern side of the mountain that stands surrounding Rājagaha.
The meaning is that he was wandering on a tour in a country named Dakkhiṇāgiri. Now, this "tour" (cārikā) is of two kinds: the hurried tour and the unhurried tour.

In that regard, when someone, having put on one saffron robe and draped another over his shoulder, with bowl and robes hanging from his shoulder, takes up a sunshade while sweat is pouring from his body—

He travels seven or eight *yojanas* in a single day; or else, whenever the Buddhas see even a single being capable of being enlightened, they travel a hundred or a thousand *yojanas* in an instant—this is called a "hurried journey" (*turitacārikā*).
However, on an ordinary day, he travels a distance of one *gāvuta*, half a *yojana*, three *gāvutas*, or one *yojana* for the sake of an invitation for that very day.
When he accepts [the invitation] and makes his journey while gathering the people, this is called a "non-hastening tour. This is what is intended here.
But surely the Elder had followed behind the One of Ten Powers for twenty-five years like a shadow, never even giving the opportunity for the words "Where is Ānanda?
to arise; at what time then did he [depart] with the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus?
"Does he receive permission to go on a journey together [with the Teacher]? "In the year of the Teacher’s final nibbāna.

It is said that when the Teacher had attained final nibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus assembled at the Teacher’s final nibbāna, selected five hundred bhikkhus for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya, saying: "Friends..."
"I shall spend the rains retreat at Rājagaha and rehearse the Dhamma and Vinaya;
you, before the commencement of the rains, should sever your own impediments and assemble at Rājagaha," he said, and then he himself went to Rājagaha.
The Elder Ānanda, taking the Blessed One’s bowl and robe and instructing the great multitude, went to Sāvatthī.
Having departed from there, he went to Rājagaha and wandered on tour in Dakkhiṇāgiri; it was with reference to this that it was said.

"For the most part, those who were still youths" means that those known as "those who have returned to the lower life" were for the most part young boys—tender and youthful monks of one or two years' standing, as well as unordained boys. But why did these [boys] go forth?
Why did they return to the lower life? It is said that their parents thought: "The Elder Ānanda is trusted by the Teacher;
having requested eight boons, he attends upon him. He is able to take the Teacher wherever he wishes to go.
Let us have our children ordained in his presence; he will then take the Teacher back with him. In him...
“Now that he has arrived, we shall be able to perform a great honor for him. For this reason, their relatives first ordained them.
However, when the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, their aspiration was cut off; then they disrobed all at once.
“According as they pleased” means according to their liking or according to their inclination. “The threefold meal was established” refers to [the rule against] eating in a group.
"Except on an occasion, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). This was said with reference to this.
For in that case, there is no offense even for those who accept an invitation to an improper meal while three people are eating together; therefore, it is called "eating in a group of three.
"For the sake of restraining wicked individuals" means for the purpose of subduing persons of immoral conduct. [And] for the sake of [protecting] well-behaved monks...
"For the sake of living in comfort" means that through the restraint of those who are difficult to manage, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies proceed for those who are well-behaved;

there is communal living, and this constitutes their "living in comfort. It is for the purpose of this living in comfort, so that those with evil desires might not, by relying on a faction, cause a schism in the Saṅgha—just as Devadatta did when he, together with his followers, requested food from families and ate it.
The meaning is that it was laid down for this reason: "Lest others with evil desires, by relying on him, should split the Saṅgha;
and lest others with evil desires, by forming groups and requesting [food] from families, should increase their faction and, relying on that side, split the Saṅgha.
And [it was laid down] out of compassion for the families. Regarding the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā within the Bhikkhu Saṅgha...
When people live in harmony, they become destined for heaven by giving alms-food on tickets and other offerings;
thus, this rule was established out of compassion for families—this is the meaning.
"I think you wander about destroying the crops" means you roam about as if you were destroying the harvest. "I think you wander about destroying families" means...
"You wander about as if destroying and killing families. 'It falls apart' means it especially crumbles and breaks down.

'Your novices, friend, are falling apart,' friend, means these novices of yours—for the most part, for the majority—being young, having been ordained for one or two years, both youths and *śrāmaṇeras*, are falling apart and breaking down. Or rather, this boy..."
"You took me for a mere child" means he spoke thus to rebuke the Elder, implying, "This boy does not know his own measure.
"We are not released from the charge of being called 'children'" means we are not freed from the accusation of being called children. "For indeed, you...
is said for the purpose of showing the reason why he should be addressed in this way. This is the intended meaning here: because of these... you.
"You wander together with young bhikkhus who lack restraint over their sense faculties;
therefore, as you wander with children, you deserve to be called a 'child'.
Regarding the phrase "one who was formerly a member of another sect," this is because, in this teaching, there is neither a teacher nor a preceptor for the Elder.
It is evident that he himself had gone forth after taking up the saffron robes; therefore, out of dissatisfaction, she attributed his former status as a member of another sect to him and said:
"Sahasā" (suddenly/impulsively); here, while "sahasā-cāra" (acting impulsively) can refer to the practice of passion or delusion, this is stated by way of the practice of hatred.
"Appaṭisaṅkhā" means without reflection; now, purifying his own going-forth, he said: "In that regard, friends," and so forth. Therein—
"To acknowledge another teacher" means: I do not know how to acknowledge anyone other than the Blessed One as "another teacher of mine.

Regarding such passages as "household life is cramped," even if a husband and wife live in a house sixty cubits square or a hundred leagues apart, their household life is still "cramped" in the sense that it is possessed of belongings and possessed of obstacles.
“Rājāpatha” means the place where the dust of passion (*rāga*) and so forth arises; this is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
It is also appropriate to say it is the “path of arrival. Because it is unattached, it is like open space (*abbhokāsa*).

For one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*), even while dwelling in gabled houses, palaces made of jewels, celestial mansions (*devavimāna*), and the like—places that are enclosed with doors and windows closed—he is neither attached, nor clinging, nor bound.

Therefore it was said: “The life of renunciation is open space. Furthermore, household life is crowded because there is no opportunity for the performance of wholesome deeds, like a place of uncovered rubbish where dust collects, as it is a place where the dust of the defilements gathers;
whereas the life of renunciation is open space because there is every opportunity to perform wholesome deeds with ease.
"This is not easy... [and so on] "...one should go forth"—herein, this is the brief explanation:
this holy life of the three trainings must be practiced as entirely complete, because it must be carried out until the final moment of consciousness without being broken for even a single day;
and it must be practiced as entirely pure, because it must be carried out until the final moment of consciousness without being stained by the impurity of the defilements for even a single day.
It should be practiced as smooth as a polished conch shell, resembling a washed conch shell;
this is not easy for one living in a household, dwelling in the midst of a home, to practice perfectly fulfilled... [as before] ...in its entirety.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, and, having donned the saffron robes that are dyed with astringent juice and suitable for those leading the holy life, [go forth]?
Having clothed themselves and put on robes, they would go forth from the home life into homelessness.

And here, since the work beneficial to the home—such as farming, trade, and so forth—is called "the state of the householder" (*agāriya*), and that does not exist for one who has gone forth, therefore it should be understood that going forth is "homelessness" (*anagāriya*);
that is the state of homelessness. "They would go forth" means they would practice [the religious life].
"Of rags from cloth" (*paṭapilotikānaṃ*) means of worn-out rags; for even a new garment of thirteen cubits is called a "rag" (*pilotikā*) from the time its fringes are cut off.
Thus, referring to a *saṅghāṭī* robe made by cutting up costly fabrics, it is said:
"a *saṅghāṭī* of rags from cloth. "Set out on a journey" (*addhānamaggappaṭipanno*) means from the point of having set out for half a *yojana*.
The "path" is called the "road"; he has set out upon that road of the journey, meaning he has set out upon a long road.

Now, in order to clarify this matter—namely, how he went forth and how he set out upon the road of the journey—a gradual discourse (anupubbikathā) should be told, beginning from his initial resolution (abhinīhāra).
It is said that in the past, at the limit of one hundred thousand aeons ago...
A Teacher named Padumuttara arose; while he was dwelling in the Khema Deer Park in dependence upon the city of Haṃsavatī,
a householder named Vedeha, possessing a wealth of eighty koṭis, ate a fine meal early in the morning,
undertook the precepts of the Uposatha, took perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, went to the monastery, and worshipped the Teacher.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. At that moment, the Teacher placed the Elder Mahānisabha as the third disciple among his monks, declaring:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost of my disciples, the monks who are exponents of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), namely Nisabha.
When the lay follower heard this, he was filled with faith; at the conclusion of the Dhamma talk, when the great multitude had risen and departed, [he remained].
Having paid homage to the Teacher, he said, "Venerable sir, please accept my almsfood tomorrow. "The community of monks is large, lay follower," [the Teacher replied].
"How many are there, Blessed One? "Six million eight hundred thousand monks.
"Venerable sir, please accept my almsfood without leaving even a single novice behind in the monastery. The Teacher consented. The lay follower [then went] to the Teacher...
Having understood the Teacher’s acceptance, he went home, prepared a great almsgiving, and on the following day announced the time to the Teacher.
The Teacher took his bowl and robe, went to the lay follower’s house surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and sat upon the seat prepared for him.
At the conclusion of the water-offering, receiving the rice gruel, the meal, and other offerings, he performed the distribution of the food. The lay follower, too—
He sat down in the presence of the Teacher.
In the meantime, while the Elder Mahānisabha was wandering for alms, he entered that very street.
Seeing him, the lay follower rose, went toward him, paid homage to the Elder, and said, "Venerable sir, please give me your bowl. The Elder gave him his bowl.
“Venerable sir, please enter right here; the Teacher is sitting at home. “It will not do, lay follower.
The lay follower took the elder’s bowl, filled it with almsfood, brought it out, and gave it to him.
Then, having followed the elder and returned, he sat down in the presence of the Teacher and said: “Venerable sir, the Elder Mahā-Nisabha said, ‘The Teacher—’”
Even when told, "He is sitting in the house," he did not wish to enter, thinking, "Does he perhaps possess some quality that surpasses yours?
Now, Buddhas have no such thing as "miserliness regarding praise. Then the Teacher said:
"Lay follower, we sit in the house waiting for alms; that bhikkhu does not sit like that while looking out for alms."
“We live in lodgings within a village, while he lives only in the forest. We live under cover, while he lives only in the open air.
Such are his various virtues,” he said, speaking as if filling the great ocean.
The lay follower, who was already like a lamp burning naturally, became even more deeply inspired—like a lamp doused with oil—and thought: “What...?”
“With this attainment of mine, I shall make a resolution that in the future, in the presence of a certain Buddha, I will become the foremost among those who preach the ascetic practices (dhutavāda).
Having again invited the Teacher and given alms for seven days according to that same method, on the seventh day—
On that day, having given sets of the three robes to six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus,
he prostrated at the feet of the Teacher and said: "Venerable Sir, whatever bodily, verbal, and mental acts of loving-kindness I have performed while giving alms for seven days—
by this merit, may I not seek the attainment of any other divine state, nor the attainment of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā."

“...or I aspire for this: may this deed of mine become a condition for attaining the foremost rank among those who observe the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), reaching the position attained by the Elder Mahānisabha in the presence of a future Buddha.
The Teacher, observing whether this great position aspired for by him would be fulfilled, perceived that it would indeed be so.
Having seen him, he said: "A delightful state has been aspired to by you.
In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand kappas, a Buddha named Gotama will arise; you will become his third disciple, the Elder Mahākassapa.
Upon hearing this, the lay follower thought, "There are no two kinds of speech from Buddhas," and on the following day, it was as if that very thing had already been attained.
He considered this a great attainment. Having observed moral virtue for as long as he lived, he passed away there and was reborn in the heavenly realms.

From that time on, experiencing prosperity among gods and humans, ninety-one aeons ago, while the Sammasambuddha Vipassi was dwelling in the Khema Deer Park near the city of Bandhumati, he passed away from the world of the gods and [was reborn] in a certain...
He was reborn into a family of Brahmins that had long been in decline. At that time, there was a great clamor, for it was said: "The Blessed One Vipassī will preach the Dhamma every seventh year.
Deities throughout the entire Jambudīpa proclaimed, "The Teacher will preach the Dhamma!
The Brahmin heard this message, and he had only a single lower garment.
The same was true for the brahmin woman; however, the cloak worn by both was one and the same. Throughout the entire city, he was known as the "Brahmin with a Single Garment.

Whenever there was an assembly of brahmins for some business, he would leave his wife at home and go himself; whenever there was an assembly of brahmin women, he would remain at home while the brahmin woman took that garment [and went].
She went away after having put on her robe. On that day, however, the brahmin said to the brahmin lady:
"Madam, will you listen to the Dhamma in the evening or during the day? "We women by nature cannot listen at night;
we shall listen during the day. Having thus left the brahmin at home, she put on her robe and [went] during the day together with the female lay devotees.
Having gone and paid homage to the Teacher, she sat to one side; after hearing the Dhamma, she returned together with the female lay followers.
Then the brahmin, having left his wife at home and put on his upper garment, went to the monastery.
At that time, the Teacher was seated upon a decorated Dhamma-throne in the midst of the assembly, holding a fan of peacock feathers.
He delivered a discourse on the Dhamma as if causing the Ganges to descend from the sky, or as if churning the ocean with Mount Sineru as its churning-stick.

As the brahmin sat at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, in that very first watch of the night, five-colored rapture arose, filling his entire body. He gathered up his wrapped garment and [said]: "Of the Ten-Powered One..."
"I shall give it," he thought. Then, as it were displaying a thousand dangers, avarice arose within him; thinking, "The brahmin woman and I have but this one garment;
we have no other upper robe, and it is impossible to go outside without wearing one," he became entirely unwilling to give it.
Then, after the first watch had passed, during the middle watch...
In that very same way, rapture arose within him; and having thought in that same manner, he remained unwilling to give it.
Then, when the middle watch had passed and during the last watch as well, rapture arose in him just as before.
He said, "Whether it be crossing over or death, I shall know later," and folding the cloth, he placed it at the feet of the Teacher. Then, having folded his left hand, he—
Having clapped his right hand three times, he cried out three times, "Victory! Victory!
At that moment, King Bandhuma was sitting behind the Dhamma throne within the curtain, listening to the Dhamma.
The sound "Victory! was unpleasant to the king, so he sent a man, saying, "Go and ask him this."
“What are you saying? When he had gone there and was asked by him, he replied:
“The rest [of the people] mount elephant-vehicles and the like, take up swords, shields, and so forth, and conquer the enemy army; that is not wonderful.
But I, having crushed the mind of stinginess as if crushing the head of a rogue ox coming up from behind with a mallet and driving it away, [discarded] the cloth I was wearing...”
“I gave it to the One of Ten Powers; thus has my stinginess been conquered,” he said. The man went and reported this matter to the king.
The king said, “Indeed, we did not know what was appropriate for the One of Ten Powers, but the brahmin knew;
and he sent a pair of garments as well. Seeing that, the brahmin thought: “While I sat here in silence...”
Without first giving anything himself, he gave [the cloth] to the Teacher while praising his virtues, thinking, "What need have I for that which has arisen based on the Teacher's virtues?
He then gave even that pair of cloths to the One of Ten Powers. The King asked, "What was done by the brahmin?
and having heard, "He too gave that pair of cloths to the Tathāgata," he gave two other pairs of cloths.
He sent them. The brahmin gave those as well. The king sent four more, and in this manner he sent up to thirty-two pairs of garments.
Then the brahmin thought, "If I accept these, it will seem as though I am increasing my own gain.
Therefore, taking two pairs of garments—one for himself and one for his wife—he gave thirty pairs to the Tathāgata alone. From that time on...
And he became one who was trusted by the Teacher.
Then one day, seeing him listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher during the cold season, the king gave him his own red woolen cloak worth a hundred thousand pieces and said:
"From now on, listen to the Dhamma wearing this."
Thinking, "What use have I for this blanket brought to this putrid body?

he went away after making it into a canopy over the Tathāgata’s bed inside the Fragrant Chamber. Then one day, the king went to the monastery early in the morning and sat down in the presence of the Teacher inside the Fragrant Chamber. At that time, the six-colored rays of the Buddha...
They struck against the blanket, and the blanket shone exceedingly. The king, looking upward and recognizing it, said:
"Venerable sir, this is our blanket; it was given by us to a single-garmented brahmin.
"Great king, you honored the brahmin; the brahmin has honored me. The king thought, "The brahmin understood what was appropriate."

Thinking, "I shall not [neglect this]," he was filled with faith; having made everything that was beneficial to people into groups of eight, he gave a gift called the "All-Eight" (*sabbaṭṭhaka*) and appointed him to the position of royal chaplain.

He too, thinking, "A group of eight times eight is sixty-four," had sixty-four sets of daily meals (*salākabhatta*) prepared, and having given alms for as long as he lived and guarded his virtue, he passed away.
Passing away from there, he was reborn in heaven.

Passing away again from there, in the interval between two Buddhas—namely, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana and the Fortunate One Kassapa—he was reborn in Bārāṇasī in the house of a householder. Having reached maturity, he entered the life of a householder.
One day, Vāsava was walking for exercise in the forest. At that time, a Paccekabuddha was making robes by a riverbank;
when the wind did not blow favorably, he began to fold them up and set them aside.
Seeing this, Vāsava asked, "Venerable sir, why are you folding them up and setting them aside? He replied, "The wind does not blow favorably. "Venerable sir, use this [cloth] instead," he said.
Having given him a garment, she made this aspiration: "In whatever place I am reborn, may I never suffer any decline.
While his wife was quarreling with her sister-in-law at home, the Paccekabuddha entered for alms.
Then his sister-in-law, having given alms-food to the Paccekabuddha, said, referring to his wife: "Such a one..."
“I would rather avoid a fool for a hundred leagues,” she made this aspiration. Standing at the door of her house, she heard this and thought, “May he not eat the meal given by this woman!
Taking her bowl, she threw away the alms-food, filled it with mud, and gave it to him.
Seeing this, the other [woman] said, “Foolish girl, you may as well insult me or strike me! To one such as this...”
"But it is not fitting to discard the food from the bowl of one who has fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable eons by giving him mud," he said.
Then his wife reflected; she cried out, "Wait, venerable sir!
and instead of discarding the mud, she washed the bowl, rubbed it with fragrant powder, and [filled it] with excellent fourfold honey.
Having filled it and placed it in the hand of the Paccekabuddha—shining with the ghee poured on top, which was the color of the interior of a lotus—he made this aspiration:
"Just as this alms-food has become radiant, may my body likewise become radiant.
After the Paccekabuddha had expressed his appreciation, he soared into the sky. And those husband and wife...
Having performed wholesome deeds for the duration of his lifespan, he was reborn in heaven;

then, passing away from there, he was reborn as the son of a merchant in Bārāṇasī who possessed a fortune of eight hundred million, while the other woman was reborn as the daughter of a merchant of similar means.
When he reached maturity, they brought that very merchant’s daughter to him as a wife. Because of the ripening of a deed previously committed by her...

By the power of that karma, as soon as she had entered her husband’s family home, her entire body became foul-smelling within the threshold, like a latrine with its lid opened. When the merchant’s son asked, “Whose smell is this?
and heard it was the merchant’s daughter, he sent her back to her own family home by means of a formal decree, crying out, “Take her away! Take her away!”
Having been turned back at seven places by that very same obstacle, she thought: "I have been turned back at seven places.
What is the use of my life? She had her own jewelry and ornaments broken up and had a gold tablet made—one cubit long, one span wide, and four finger-breadths high.
Then, [she prepared] a lump of yellow orpiment and realgar.
Taking eight handfuls of blue lotuses, she went to the site where the stupa for Kassapa, the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, was being built.
At that moment, a row of bricks being laid around the perimeter was short by one jar-brick.
The merchant’s daughter said to the mason, “Place this brick here. “Mother, you have arrived at a most auspicious time; [place it] yourself.”
"Let her place it. Having climbed up, she mixed yellow orpiment and red arsenic with oil; using that as an adhesive, she set the brick in place.
She then made an offering of eight handfuls of blue lotuses upon it, paid homage, and made this aspiration:
"In every place where I am reborn, may the fragrance of sandalwood waft from my body and the fragrance of blue lotuses from my mouth. Having thus worshipped the Cetiya, she departed.
Having performed a circumambulation, she departed.
Then, at that very moment, mindfulness arose in the merchant’s son to whom she had first been led into his house.
Since the festival of the constellations was proclaimed throughout the city, he said to his attendants: "At that time, here..."
“The merchant’s daughter has been brought here; where is she? “She is at her family home, Master. “Bring her back; we shall celebrate the festival.
They went, paid their respects to her, and stood there. When she asked them, “What brings you here, dear ones? they explained the matter to her.
She said, “Dear ones, I have already worshipped the Cetiya with my jewelry; as for the jewelry—”
“I have none. They went and informed the merchant’s son. “Bring her here; we shall obtain her ornaments,” they said.
So they brought her. As soon as she entered the house, the entire dwelling was filled with the fragrance of sandalwood and the scent of blue lotuses.
The merchant’s son asked her: “Previously, a foul odor issued from your body, but now from your body—”
"The scent of sandalwood comes from her body, and the fragrance of blue lotuses wafts from her mouth. What is this?

She then related the deeds she had performed from the very beginning. The merchant’s son, gaining confidence that "the teaching of the Buddhas is indeed leading to liberation," wrapped a golden stupa one *yojana* in height with a fine woolen cloak and adorned it here and there with golden lotuses the size of chariot wheels.
He adorned them; their pendants were twelve cubits long. Having remained there for the duration of his lifespan, he was reborn in heaven.
Passing away from there, he was reborn in a family of ministers at a place one *yojana* from Bārāṇasī.
A merchant’s daughter, having descended from the world of the gods, was reborn as the eldest daughter in the royal family.
When they had reached maturity, a festival was proclaimed in the village where the prince lived. He said to his mother, "Mother, give me a garment; I shall play at the festival.
She brought out a washed cloth and gave it to him. "Mother, this is too coarse," he said.
She brought out another and gave it to him, but he rejected that as well. She brought out yet another and gave it to him, but he rejected that too.
Then his mother said to him, "Dear son, in such a household as we were born into, there is no merit for us to obtain anything more refined than this.
"I am going to a place where I may find gain, Mother," he replied. "Son, I desire nothing less than your obtaining the kingdom in the city of Bārāṇasī this very day!
Having paid homage to his mother, he said, "I am going, Mother. "Go then."
“Father! Such was the thought that occurred to her: “Where will he go? Will he sit here or there within the house?
But he, having departed according to the course of his merit, went to Bārāṇasī and lay down in the park upon the auspicious stone slab with his head covered.
And it was the seventh day since the death of the King of Bārāṇasī.
After the ministers had performed the funeral rites for the king, they sat in the royal courtyard and deliberated:
"The king has only one daughter and no son. A kingdom cannot endure without a king. Who shall be king?
Having thus deliberated, they said, "You be it! You be it! The chaplain said, "It is not right to look about too much; let us send forth the Phussa-chariot."

Having yoked those four horses, white as water-lilies, and having placed the fivefold royal insignia and the white parasol upon the chariot itself, they let the chariot go forth and had musical instruments played behind it.
The chariot departed through the eastern gate and headed toward the park; because of his familiarity with the place, he proceeded toward the park.
"Let us turn back," some said. The chaplain said, "Do not turn back. The chariot, having circumambulated the prince, stood ready for him to mount.
The chaplain, pulling back the corner of his upper garment and looking at the soles of the prince's feet, thought, "Let this island suffice;
he is fit to rule over the four continents surrounded by two thousand islands."
Having said this, he had the musical instruments played three times, saying, "Play them again! Play them again!
Then the prince opened his mouth and looked out, asking, "For what purpose have you come?
They replied, "Your Majesty, the kingdom has come to you. "Where is the king? "He has gone to the state of the gods, Sire. "How many days have passed?"
“Today is the seventh day,” they said. “There is neither son nor daughter. “There is a daughter, Your Majesty, but no son.

“In that case, I shall rule the kingdom. They immediately prepared a consecration pavilion, adorned the princess with all her ornaments, brought her to the pleasure garden, and performed the consecration for the prince.
Then, after he had been consecrated, they brought him a garment worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
He asked, "What is this, dear sirs? They replied, "It is a lower garment for Your Majesty. "Is it not, dear sirs, too thick?
"There is nothing finer than this among the garments used by humans, Your Majesty. "Does your king wear such a garment? "Yes, Your Majesty."
“I do not think your king is meritorious; bring a golden pitcher! We shall surely obtain clothing. They brought a golden pitcher.
He rose, washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, took water in his hand, and sprinkled it toward the eastern direction.
Piercing through the solid earth, eight *kappa*-trees appeared.
They arose. Taking water again, they sprinkled it toward the south, west, and north;
thus, in the four directions, thirty-two wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*) arose, eight in each direction.
He put on one divine cloth as an undergarment and another as an upper robe, thinking, "Let not the women who spin thread in King Nanda’s realm spin any more thread."

Having said, "In this manner, have the drum beaten," he raised the royal parasol, adorned himself, mounted the back of a noble elephant, and entering the city, ascended the palace and enjoyed great prosperity.
As time passed in this way, one day the queen, seeing the king's splendor, exclaimed with an expression of compassion, "Oh, what an ascetic! and [fell ill].
She showed it to him. When asked, "What is this, O Queen? she replied, "O King, it is a very great prosperity.
In the past, having placed faith in the Buddhas, you performed wholesome deeds; now, however, you do not perform the wholesome acts that serve as a condition for the future.
[The King said,] "To whom shall I give? There are no virtuous ones. [She replied,] "O King, Jambudīpa is not empty of Arahants; you should simply give alms."
“Let it be prepared; I shall obtain the Arahants,” he said. On the following day, the king had alms-food prepared at the eastern gate.
Early in the morning, the queen, having resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha, lay down on her chest facing eastward on the upper terrace of the palace and said:
“If there are Arahants in this direction, let them come and accept our alms.”
In that direction there were no Arahants; they gave that honor to the poor, the destitute, and the beggars.
On the following day, having prepared alms at the southern gate, he acted in the same manner; on the next day, at the western gate.
But on the day it was prepared at the northern gate, while the Queen was likewise inviting [the monks], Padumavatī, who was dwelling in the Himālayas—
The eldest of the five hundred sons who were Paccekabuddhas, Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha, addressed his brothers:
"Sirs, King Nanda invites you; please accept his invitation.
Having accepted, they washed their faces at Lake Anotatta on the following day, came through the air, and descended at the northern gate. People went out to meet them.
“Your Majesty, five hundred paccekabuddhas have arrived,” they reported to the king.
The king, together with the queen, went forth, paid homage, took their bowls, and had the paccekabuddhas ascend the palace.

After giving them alms-food, at the conclusion of the meal, the king prostrated himself at the feet of the senior elder of the Saṅgha, and the queen prostrated herself at the feet of the youngest member of the Saṅgha, saying, “Venerable sirs, you are not lacking in the four requisites.”
“They will become weary; we shall not be deprived of merit. Grant us your promise that we may dwell here for as long as we live.
Having thus obtained their promise, they prepared a complete dwelling place in the park, including five hundred leaf-huts and five hundred walking-paths, and settled them there.
As time passed in this way, the king’s border region rose in revolt. Having exhorted the queen, saying, “I am going to pacify the border;
you must not neglect the Paccekabuddhas,” he departed. Even before his return, the life-force of the Paccekabuddhas was exhausted.
After spending three watches of the night sporting in meditative absorption, the Paccekabuddha Mahāpaduma, at the rising of the dawn—
Having taken hold of the support-slab, he attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue while still standing;

by this same method, the others did as well, so that all were completely extinguished. On the following day, the queen had the place where the paccekabuddhas had sat smeared with green cow dung, scattered flowers, and offered incense; she sat waiting for their arrival, and [beheld] their coming.
Not seeing him, she sent [a messenger], saying: "Go, dear one, and find out whether the noble ones are unwell in any way.
He went, opened the door of Mahāpaduma’s leaf-hut, and not seeing him there, he went to the walkway;
seeing him standing leaning against the support-board, he paid homage and said, "It is time, Bhante. [He saw] the body that had attained final Nibbāna.
"What will he say? Thinking, "He must be sleeping," he went and touched the elder's foot with his hand.
Perceiving through the coldness and stiffness of the feet that he had attained final Nibbāna, he went to the second one; likewise to the third.
Having thus ascertained that all had attained final Nibbāna, he went to the royal palace. "Where are the Paccekabuddhas, dear father? he asked.
When asked, he replied, "The queen has attained final Nibbāna. The queen, weeping and wailing, went out and, together with the citizens, went there.
She had a grand festival performed, carried out the funeral rites for the Paccekabuddhas, took their relics, and established a stupa.
When the king had returned after suppressing the border regions, he went out to meet the queen who had come to welcome him and asked, "My lady, did you not neglect the Paccekabuddhas?
Are the masters free from illness? "They have passed away, O King," she replied.
The king thought, "If death comes even to such wise ones as these, what escape can there be for us? Without entering the city, he...
Having entered the very garden, he summoned his eldest son, prepared the kingdom for him, and himself went forth into the ascetic life.
The queen also thought, "Now that he has gone forth, what shall I do? and she likewise went forth right there in the garden.
Both of them developed the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and, passing away from there, were reborn in the Brahma-world.
While they were living right there, our Teacher appeared in the world and, having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, eventually entered Rājagaha.
This young brahmin Pippali was reborn in the Magadha country, in the brahmin village of Mahātittha, in the womb of the chief queen of the brahmin Kapila;
this Bhaddā Kāpilānī [was reborn] in the Madda country, in the city of Sāgala, in the womb of the wife of a brahmin of the Kosiya clan.
They were born from the womb of the chief queen.

As they grew up in due course, when Pippali the youth was twenty years old and Bhaddā reached her sixteenth year, his parents looked at their son and pressed him very hard, saying, "Dear, you have reached maturity; one must establish the family lineage. The youth said:
“Do not speak such words within my hearing. I will look after you as long as you remain;
once you have departed from here, I shall go forth into the homeless life. After a few days had passed, they spoke again, but he likewise refused.
They spoke yet again, and he refused once more. From that time on, his mother spoke of it incessantly.
The young man, thinking, "I shall persuade my mother," gave a thousand gold *nikkhas* to the goldsmiths and had them fashion a female figure.
When the work of bathing, polishing, and so forth was finished, he had her dressed in red garments,
adorned with flowers of exquisite color and various ornaments, and [presented her] to his mother.
Having summoned her, he said: "Mother, when I obtain such an object as this, I shall live at home;
when I do not obtain it, I shall not live here. The wise Brahmin woman thought: "My son is meritorious, a giver of gifts, and one who has made a firm resolve.
He did not perform his merit alone; surely there must be someone who performed merit together with him, appearing like a golden statue."
Having summoned eight brahmins and gratified them with all desirable things, he placed a golden image upon a chariot and dispatched them, saying:
"Go, dear sirs; wherever you see a girl of a family equal to ours in birth, lineage, and wealth, give her this very golden image as a gift."
Thinking, "This work is ours," they departed. Reflecting, "Where shall we go?
they decided, "There is a place called the Madda country; let us go to the Madda country. They went to the city of Sāgala in the Madda country.
There, having placed that golden image at a bathing ford, they sat down to one side. Then Bhaddā’s nurse—
Having bathed Bhaddā, adorned her, and seated her in the bedchamber, she was returning to bathe herself when she saw that image.
Thinking, "My noble daughter has come here," she rebuked it, saying, "You ill-behaved girl, why have you come here?
Raising her palm-leaf fan, she struck it on the side of its cheek, saying, "Go away quickly! Her hand struck against the stone.
She trembled as if struck by lightning. Stepping back, she said, "Having seen such a stiff-necked person as this, I formed the perception that he was my noble daughter's husband;
yet even for my noble daughter, it would be improper to have him as the one who receives her lower garment.
Then those men surrounded her and asked, "Is such a person your husband's sister? She replied, "What is she? Is there anyone a hundred times her worth?"
“My noble lady is a thousand times more beautiful than I; when she sits within her twelve-cubit chamber, there is no need for a lamp, for she dispels the darkness with the radiance of her own body.

“In that case, come,” they said, and taking the hunchback, they placed her upon a chariot adorned with golden figures, stopped at the door of the house of the Kosiya clan, and announced their arrival.
The brahmin, having offered a hospitable welcome, asked, "From where have you come? "From the house of the brahmin Kapila in the village of Mahātittha in the kingdom of Magadha," they replied.
"For what purpose have you come? "For this reason," they said. "Excellent, dear ones!
Our brahmin is of equal birth, lineage, and wealth; I shall give you my daughter. Thus he accepted their gift.
They sent a message to the brahmin Kapila, saying: "The girl has been obtained; do what must be done.
Having heard that message, they informed the young man Pippali: "It seems the girl has been obtained. The young man thought:
"I thought I would not obtain her, yet they say she has been obtained. Without desiring her, I shall send a letter."
Going into seclusion, he wrote a letter: “May Bhaddā obtain a household life befitting her own birth, clan, and wealth;
as for me, I shall go forth and take ordination, so that you do not later feel regret.

Hearing that he intended to give her to such-and-such a man, Bhaddā also went into seclusion and wrote a letter: “The noble son [intends to give me] to one befitting his own birth, clan, and wealth...”
“Let him obtain a householder’s life. I shall go forth and renounce the world; do not have regrets later. Thus they spoke.
On the way, the two letters met. “Whose letter is this? “It was sent by the young man Pippali to Bhaddā. “Whose letter is this?
“It was sent by Bhaddā to the young man Pippali. When this was said, both [letters]...
Having had them read it, [the king] said, "Behold the karma of these children! He had them split open and discarded in the forest;
then, having written identical letters, he sent them hither and thither. Thus, even though they did not desire it, their meeting took place.
On that very same day, the young man had one flower garland woven, and Bhaddā also had one woven.
Having placed them in the middle of the seat, both of them, having finished their evening meal, gathered together thinking, "We shall go to bed.
The young man climbed onto the bed on the right side. Bhaddā, having climbed onto the left side, said:
"On whichever side the flowers wither, we shall know that a mind of lust has arisen in that person; [do not remove] this flower garland..."

“They should associate with one another. However, out of fear of physical contact with each other’s bodies, they spent their time without descending into sleep even for three watches of the night; by day, there was not even a mere smile.
Unmixed with worldly pleasures, as long as their parents lived, they did not manage the household estate; but when they had passed away, they began to manage it.
Great indeed was the youth’s prosperity: it sufficed for him to obtain, on a single day after bathing his body, twelve measures of Magadha gold dust alone;
sixty great reservoirs equipped with water-lifting machines, a plantation twelve leagues in extent, fourteen slave villages equal in size to Anurādhapura, and fourteen elephant corps.
There were fourteen divisions of cavalry and fourteen divisions of chariots.
One day, having mounted a decorated horse and being surrounded by a great multitude of people, he went to his place of work;
standing at the edge of a field, he saw crows and other birds, as well as insects such as earthworms, picking up and eating the soil torn open by the ploughs.
Having seen this, he asked, "Sirs, what are these people eating? "Earthworms, noble sir. "To whom does the evil committed by these belong?
"To you, noble sir. He thought: "If the evil committed by these belongs to me, what use will eighty-seven million pieces of wealth be to me?
What use will twelve leagues of agricultural lands be? What use will the water-mills be?"
“Having bestowed these sixty great ponds and fourteen villages upon Bhaddā Kāpilānī,
I shall go forth and renounce the world.
At that moment, Bhaddā Kāpilānī had three jars of sesame seeds spread out within her inner apartments.
Surrounded by her nurses, she sat watching crows eating sesame seeds and asked, "Mother, what are these eating?
"Seeds, noble lady. "Who would incur demerit for this? "You would, noble lady.
She thought, "It is enough for me to receive four cubits of cloth and a measure of boiled rice; yet, if by so much as this..."
“Whatever unwholesome deed has been committed by this person will remain mine; even in a thousand existences, it will not be possible for me to lift my head from the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa).
As soon as the noble son arrives, I shall hand over everything to him, depart, and go forth into homelessness.
When the young man arrived, he bathed, ascended the palace, and sat upon a magnificent couch; then, [the wheel-turning monarch] of his—
They prepared suitable food. After both had eaten and the attendants had departed, they sat down in a secluded and comfortable place.
Then the young man said to Bhaddā: "Bhaddā, when you came to this house, how much wealth did you bring?
"Fifty-five thousand carts, my lord. "All of that, and whatever else is in this [house]..."
“In my home there are seven hundred and eighty million [pieces of gold], along with wealth consisting of sixty reservoirs bound by machinery and other such assets;
I shall hand all of this over to you alone. “But what about you, noble lady? “I shall go forth into the religious life.
“Noble lady, I too have been sitting here waiting for your arrival; I too shall go forth into the religious life. To them, it was as if their leaf-hut were on fire.
Three states of existence appeared to them. Saying, "We shall go forth," they had garments dyed with astringent juice and earthen bowls brought from the marketplace;

having shaved one another's hair, they went forth, saying, "Our going forth is for the sake of those who are Arhats in the world. Having placed their bowls in bags and slung them over their shoulders, they departed.
They descended from the palace. Among the household slaves and laborers, no one recognized them.
Then, as they departed from the Brahmin village and proceeded through the gate of the slave village, the residents of the slave village recognized them by their deportment and gestures.
Weeping, they fell at their feet and said, "Noble sirs, why do you leave us behind as if we were helpless? They replied.
“Friends, we have gone forth because we thought, ‘The three realms of existence are like a thatched hut on fire.
If we were to set even one of you free, it would not suffice for even a hundred years; therefore, wash your own heads yourselves and live as free men.
Having said this, they departed while those [slaves] were still weeping. As the Elder walked on ahead, he turned back...
Looking back, he thought: "This Bhaddā Kāpilānī, the most precious woman in all of Jambudīpa, is coming behind me.
It is indeed possible that someone might think: 'Even though they have gone forth, these two cannot exist apart;
they are doing what is unbecoming,' or else someone might become corrupted in mind."
"I would fill the states of misery. Having abandoned this, it is right for me to go," he thought, and his mind was thus resolved.
As he went forward, seeing a forked path, he stood at its head. Bhaddā also came up, paid homage, and stood there.
Then he said to her, "Bhaddā, having seen such a woman as you coming behind me..."
"Thinking, 'Even though they have gone forth, these people cannot exist without women,' the great multitude would become malevolent toward us and fill the states of misery.
At this forked path, you take one way and I shall go by the other.
"Yes, noble sir; women are indeed a stain upon those who have gone forth. Thinking, 'Even after going forth, they cannot exist without them,' the multitude..."
“Seeing the fault, you take one path; we shall go without you.
Having thus spoken, he circumambulated him three times, prostrated at four places with the five-fold salutation, and raising his hands in a radiant *añjali* with the ten nails joined together, said:
“The friendship cultivated over the course of a hundred thousand aeons is broken this day.”
“You are of a right-hand birth; a right-hand path is suitable for you. We are women, of a left-hand birth;
a left-hand path is suitable for us. Having said this, they paid homage and set out on their respective paths.
At the moment they had split apart, this great earth thought: “Although I am able to support the Cakkavāḷa mountains and Mount Sineru, I am not able to support your virtues.”
Crying out as if saying, "I cannot," she trembled; a sound like a thunderclap resounded in the sky, and the Cakkavāḷa mountain roared.

Sitting in his fragrant chamber within the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana, the Perfectly Enlightened One heard the sound of the earth’s trembling and wondered, "Whose [deed] is it that the earth is shaking?
As he reflected, he perceived: "It is the young brahmin Pippali and Bhaddā Kāpilānī."
"Having renounced immeasurable prosperity for my sake and gone forth, this earthquake has occurred at the place of their separation due to the power of the virtues of both;
it is fitting that I too should provide them with support.
Having spoken thus, he emerged from the Gandhakuṭi, took his own bowl and robes, and without informing any of the eighty great elders, [traveled] three gavutas...

Having gone out to meet him on the road between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, he sat down cross-legged at the foot of the Bahuputtaka banyan tree. But when he sat down, he did not do so like some mere rag-robe wearer;

rather, assuming the full appearance of a Buddha, he sat emitting eighty cubits of dense, radiant Buddha-rays. Thus, at that moment, [the rays] were as large as palm-leaf umbrellas, cartwheels, or gabled houses.
The Buddha’s rays, flashing and streaming hither and thither, made that forest region one mass of light,
as if it were the time when a thousand moons and a thousand suns had risen together. Through the splendor of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
the forest appeared like the sky filled with a host of shimmering stars, or like water in which lotuses and water-lilies are in full bloom.
It shone forth. The trunk of the tree named Nigrodha was white, its leaves were blue, and its fruits were red.
On that day, however, the hundred-branched Nigrodha tree became the color of gold.
Having thus explained the meaning of the phrase "who had set out on the road," [the text continues]: "Now, as to how he went forth..."
And as it was said: "In order to clarify this matter, this progressive account (anupubbikathā) should be told starting from the initial resolution," that [account] is to be understood as follows:
"Between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā" means between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā. And the Teacher...
"May I indeed see the Blessed One; may I see only the Blessed One. If I were to see a Teacher, it would be this very Blessed One that I would see.
For it is not possible for me to have a Teacher other than him. "May I indeed see the Sugata; may I see only the Blessed One.
If I were to see one who has gone well (*sugata*) because of having gone perfectly through right practice, it would be this very Blessed One that I would see.
"If I were to see one named 'Sammāsambuddha,' I would see this very Blessed One. For it is not possible for there to be another Sugata other than him.
"If I were to see a 'Sammāsambuddha'—one who has awakened perfectly and fully to the truths—I would see this very Blessed One."
"I would have passed by [him]. For it is not possible for me to become a Perfectly Enlightened One other than him"—this is the intended meaning here.

Thus, by that very act of seeing, he demonstrates: "Friend, regarding the Blessed One, I became free from doubt, thinking: 'This is the Teacher; this is the Sugata; this is the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Although the phrase "He is my Teacher, venerable sir" has occurred twice, [it is stated here again for emphasis].
However, it should be understood that this was said three times. For by this he indicates: "Friends, thus did I announce my discipleship three times.
"Ajānaññeva" means "while not knowing. The same method applies to the second phrase as well.
"Even his head would split apart" refers to any other external teacher who, while not knowing, makes the claim, "I know," and who is thus possessed of such [arrogance] with his whole heart.

A disciple with a serene mind might perform such a supreme act of prostration that his head would fall from his neck like a palm fruit severed from its stalk, or rather, it would split into seven pieces—this is the meaning. What need is there to say more?
If the Elder Mahākassapa were to perform this supreme act of prostration upon the great ocean with such a state of mental serenity, [the result would be even greater].
If he were to place it on a potsherd, it would dissolve like a drop of water. If he were to place it on the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), it would scatter like a handful of husks.
If he were to place it on Mount Sineru, it would crumble like a handful of flour struck by a crow’s beak.
If he were to place it on the great earth, it would disperse like a heap of ash blown away by the wind.
Yet, even such prostration by the Elder was unable to disturb so much as a single hair on the Teacher’s gold-colored insteps.
Let alone Mahākassapa— were there even a thousand or a hundred thousand monks equal to Mahākassapa,
their display of prostration would not be able to disturb so much as a single hair on the ten-powered One’s insteps, nor even his rag-robe.
Or he is able to move even that which possesses rays. Such is the great power of the Teacher.

Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: because I speak "I know" only when I actually know, and "I see" only when I actually see, therefore, Kassapa, you must train yourself in this way. *Tibba* means thick, abundant, or great. *Hirottappa* means...
"Shame and fear of wrongdoing": "will be present" means it will be established even earlier.
For if one approaches [elders, etc. having established shame and fear of wrongdoing toward them, the elders and others also approach him with shame and fear of wrongdoing;
this is the benefit here. "Connected with the wholesome" means dependent upon the wholesome.
"Making it a bone" means making oneself a bone by means of that Dhamma, or making that Dhamma a bone [to one's heart], thinking, "This is my purpose.

"Applying the mind" means placing it in the mind. "Attending with the whole mind" means attending with a mind of total application, not allowing the mind to go even slightly outward. "With ear pricked up" means...
"Having stilled the ear and having directed both the stream of knowledge and the stream of confidence, you should train yourself thus: 'I will listen attentively to the Dhamma taught by me.
And as for the phrase 'mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by pleasure':

this refers to mindfulness directed to the body associated with pleasure by way of the first jhāna in relation to the foul (aśubha) and to mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna). Furthermore, this [mindfulness] is threefold..."
This very instruction was the elder’s going-forth and his full ordination. "With taints" means being possessed of defilements.
"Eating the country's alms-food" means eating what is given out of faith. For there are four kinds of enjoyment:
enjoyment by theft, enjoyment as a debt, enjoyment as an inheritance, and enjoyment as an owner. Among these—
Even for one who is immoral and sits in the midst of the Saṅgha to eat, his consumption is called "consumption by theft. Why?
Because of his lack of mastery over the four requisites. For one who possesses virtue, consumption without due reflection is called "consumption as a debt.
The consumption of the seven trainees is called "consumption as an inheritance. The consumption of one whose taints are destroyed is...

"Enjoyment by the owner" means this: only one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), being the owner, enjoys [the requisites] free from debt. The Elder, having himself been an ordinary person (puthujjana), spoke thus while treating the enjoyment of what he had used as a mere enjoyment under debt.
"On the eighth day higher knowledge arose" means that on the eighth day the fruit of Arhatship (arahattaphala) arose.
Then, friends, when the Blessed One "stepped off the path," his stepping off the path occurred earlier on that very day, whereas the attainment of Arahantship occurred later.
However, because the section of the teaching has come down in this way, the attainment of Arahantship is shown first.
But why did the Blessed One step off the path? It is said that he thought thus: "This bhikkhu is one who dwells in the forest by birth..."
“I shall practice the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes and the ascetic practice of eating only from a single alms-bowl.
For this reason, he stepped down. “They are soft indeed; this one of yours is soft.

And while speaking these words, the Blessed One touched that robe with his hand, which was the color of a lotus flower, stroking it from edge to edge. Why did he speak thus? Because he wished to exchange robes with the Elder.
Why did he become desirous of exchanging [the robes]? Because of his desire to establish the Elder in his own place.

But since it was the proper custom for the Elder that when the praise of a robe or an alms-bowl was spoken, he would say, "Take this for yourselves," he therefore said, "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept from me. "But will you wear them for me, Kassapa?"
"Kassapa," he said, "these are hempen rag-robes that have been worn out; will you be able to wear these rag-robes that are worn from use?
This was not said with reference to physical strength, but rather with reference to the fulfillment of practice.
This is the intended meaning here: "I [shall give] this robe to the slave-girl named Puṇṇā."
Having put it on, I entered that cemetery where it had been discarded;
there, surrounded by creatures as large as water-jars, I shook off those creatures and, standing in the Great Noble Lineage, took hold of it.
On the day I took this robe, the great earth in the ten thousand world-systems trembled with a great roar, and the sky thundered.

The deities of the world-system gave their approval, saying, "It is fitting for a monk who accepts this robe to be one born of refuse-rags, born of the forest, born of the single-seat practice, and born of the alms-round;
will you be able to act in a manner worthy of this robe? The Elder, too, [possessed] the strength of five elephants himself...

He maintains it; without having speculated on it, with the resolve, "I shall fulfill this practice," and desiring to make something worthy of the Sugata’s robe, he said, "Venerable sir, I shall wear it. "I am practicing" means "I have entered upon the practice.
Having thus exchanged robes, the Blessed One put on the robe worn by the Elder, and [the Elder put on] the Teacher's robe.
At that time, the great earth, bounded by the waters, thundered and shook.
Regarding the phrases "the son of the Blessed One" and so forth: the Elder is the "son of the Blessed One" because, depending upon the Blessed One, he was born of the noble birth.
By means of the instruction issued from the mouth [of the Buddha] after dwelling in his presence, he attained both the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Because he is established [in the Dhamma], he is "born from the breast," born from the mouth. Because he is born from the nature of the exhortation and fashioned by the nature of the exhortation, he is "born of the Dhamma" and "fashioned by the Dhamma.
He is worthy of the inheritance of the Dhamma of exhortation, or rather, the inheritance of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma itself; thus, he is an "heir to the Dhamma.
"Rags from a dust heap that have been accepted" refers to the rag-robe worn by the Teacher.
"It was accepted for the purpose of wearing [the robe].

"One speaking rightly would say" means that one who would speak rightly of a person by way of qualities such as "a son of the Blessed One" and so forth—speaking rightly of me, he would say, "I am of such a nature. By this much, the Elder's going-forth [is established].
And it has been thoroughly purified. This is the intended meaning here:

"Friends, how could one who has no preceptor known and no teacher—being shaven-headed like a barber, wearing saffron robes taken by himself, and reckoned as 'one who has gone over to the sect of the heretics'—receive such a three-league journey to meet him, or the going-forth through the three exhortations?"
"Does she receive the higher ordination (*upasampadā*), or does she receive the exchange of robes body-to-body? Behold how ill-spoken are the words of the nun Thullanandā!
Having thus cleared up her going-forth (*pabbajjā*), he now said, "I, friends... and so forth, in order to roar the lion’s roar with the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
The remainder should be understood in the same manner as before. The eleventh [section].
12. Commentary on the Paraṃmaraṇa Sutta 155.
In the twelfth [sutta], "Tathāgata" refers to a being. "Friend, this is not connected with the goal" means, friend, that this speculative view is not based upon the goal.
"Not conducive to the fundamental holy life" means it is not even conducive to the preliminary practice of the path of the holy life.
"It does not exist. For this, friends, is "conducive to welfare"; that is, friends, this meditation subject on the Four Noble Truths is based on welfare.
This is "the beginning of the holy life"; that is, it is the beginning of the holy life of the Path, the preliminary practice.
The twelfth [chapter]. 13. Commentary on the *Saddhammappatirūpaka-sutta*.
156. "In the thirteenth [verse], 'having understood, they stood firm' means they were established in Arahatship.
Regarding 'counterfeit true Dhamma,' there are two kinds of counterfeit true Dhamma: the counterfeit true Dhamma of realization and the counterfeit true Dhamma of the scriptures. In that regard:
"He wavers in radiance, in knowledge, and in rapture;..."
“Through tranquility and through pleasure, the mind trembles;
it wavers in resolution, exertion, and establishment;
and also in the adverting of equanimity, in equanimity itself, and in attachment.”
“He who has cultivated these ten points through wisdom is skilled in the agitation regarding the Dhamma and does not fall into delusion.
