This is the set of defilements of insight-knowledge, which is called a counterfeit of the true Dhamma of attainment. Furthermore, the three...

Not included in the formal recitations (saṅgīti) are these five bases of discourse: the Discourse on Elements (Dhātukathā), the Discourse on Objects (Ārammaṇakathā), the Discourse on Foulness (Asubhakathā), the Discourse on the Bases of Knowledge (Ñāṇavatthukathā), and the Casket of Wisdom (Vijjākaraṇḍaka).
Excluded from these are the Guḷhavinaya, the Guḷhavessantara, the Guḷhamahosadha, the Vaṇṇapiṭaka, the Aṅgulimālapiṭaka, the Raṭṭhapālagajjita, the Āḷavakagajjita, and the Vedallapiṭaka.
That which is not the word of the Buddha is called a counterfeit of the true Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-saddhamma-patirūpaka*).
A counterfeit of gold is an ornament made of brass that has been treated with a golden solution and possesses a golden color.
For during festive occasions, people go to the marketplace thinking, "We shall take some jewelry. Then them—
The shopkeepers said, “If you need ornaments, take these; for they are both solid, beautiful, and inexpensive.
Having heard this from them, [the people] thought, “These men speak the truth;
by wearing these one can enjoy the festival, and they are both splendid and cheap. Thus, having taken them, they—
They depart. Just as gold trinkets, when not being sold, must be set aside and stored away, so too, when that which resembles the true gold has arisen, it is said to disappear.
Then, "the disappearance of the True Dhamma" refers to the disappearance of the True Dhamma of realization and the True Dhamma of practice.
Regarding "the disappearance of the true Dhamma of the scriptures": there occurs the disappearance of the threefold True Dhamma.
For during the first dispensation (Buddhism), the monks attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Then, as time passed, they were no longer able to attain the analytical knowledges;
they attained the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*). After that, being unable to attain the six direct knowledges, they attained the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*).
Now, as time passes, those who are unable to attain the threefold knowledge (tisso vijjā) will reach at least the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya).
Those unable to reach even that will reach the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala); those unable to reach even that, the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala);
and those unable to reach even that, the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). As time continues to pass, they will not even be able to attain the fruit of stream-entry. Then, for them—
When insight, defiled by these secondary corruptions, remains merely undertaken,
then the True Dhamma of realization will be said to have disappeared.
For at the time of the First Enlightenment, the monks fulfilled the practice appropriate for the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
As time passes, being unable to achieve that, they will strive for the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*); being unable to achieve even those, they will strive for the three true insights (*vijjā*);
being unable to achieve even those, they will strive for the fruit of arhatship alone.
Furthermore, as time passes, being unable to fulfill the practice appropriate for arhatship, they will fulfill the practice appropriate for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Being unable even to achieve that, they will fail to attain the fruit of once-returning; being unable even to achieve that, they will fail to attain the fruit of stream-entry.

But when, being unable to fulfill even the practice appropriate for the fruit of stream-entry, they remain at the mere level of purity of virtue, then the true Dhamma of practice may be said to have disappeared.
As long as the word of the Buddha consisting of the Tipiṭaka continues to exist, it is not appropriate to say that the Dispensation has disappeared.
Let alone the three Piṭakas; even when the Abhidhamma Piṭaka has disappeared, although the other two remain, it cannot be said that the Dispensation has disappeared.
Even when those two have disappeared and only the Vinaya Piṭaka remains, and even within that, when only the Khandhaka and Parivāra remain—
When the two Vibhaṅgas alone have disappeared, and the Mahāvinaya has disappeared—even though the two Pātimokkhas are still extant—the Dispensation (sāsana) has not yet disappeared.
However, when the two Pātimokkhas disappear, then there will be the disappearance of the True Dharma of the scriptures (pariyatti-saddhamma).
When that has disappeared, the Dispensation is said to have disappeared. Regarding the scriptures...
For when practice disappears, realization disappears; when practice disappears, attainment disappears.
Why is this? Because this study is the condition for practice, and practice is the condition for attainment.
Thus, even in relation to practice, study alone is the measure.
Now, during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, there was a monk named Kapila who was not one to fulfill his duties.
Taking up a fan, he sat upon his seat intending to recite the Pātimokkha and asked, "Is there anything occurring in this assembly?
Then, out of fear of him, even those for whom the Pātimokkha was actually being recited did not say, "We are reciting it," but instead said, "We are not reciting it."
Did the Dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One decline when he rose from his seat and departed after setting aside the fan?
Although it did indeed decline, the scriptures (*pariyatti*) remain an absolute authority.

For just as one cannot say that the water in a great reservoir will not remain because its embankment is firm, nor can one say that lotuses and other flowers will not bloom while the water is present.

It should not be said that, even though the word of the Buddha in its three collections (Tipiṭaka)—which is like the firm embankment of a great lake—exists, it can be said that there are no sons of good family who fulfill the practice, who are like the water in that great lake;

for while they exist, it cannot be said that there are no noble persons (ariyapuggala), such as stream-enterers and the rest, who are like the lotuses and other flowers in that great lake. Thus, it is absolutely certain.
The authority lies in the scripture alone.
Regarding the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*): the great earth is two hundred and forty thousand *nahutas* thick. Regarding the water element (*āpodhātu*):
it is the water that rises from the earth up to the Subhakiṇha Brahma-world, sufficient to destroy an eon. Regarding the fire element (*tejodhātu*):...
The fire that destroys an eon rises from the earth up to the Ābhassara Brahmā-world.
The wind that destroys an eon is the wind that rises from the earth up to the Vehapphala Brahmā-world.
For not even a single phenomenon among these is able to cause the Teacher’s dispensation to disappear; therefore he spoke thus. "They arise right here."
Just as rust is a stain that consumes iron, so too do they arise within this very teaching of mine. "Foolish men" (moghapurisā) means empty men.
"Sinks at the very outset" (ādikeneva opilavati): here, "at the very outset" (ādikena) means by way of grasping or seizing; "sinks" (opilavati) means it submerges. This is what is meant:
just as a water-borne boat sinks when it takes on cargo, so too [does one sink] regarding the scriptures and so forth.
The true Dhamma does not disappear because of Pūraṇa. For when the study (pariyatti) declines, the practice (paṭipatti) declines;
when the practice declines, the realization (adhigama) declines. When the study is fulfilled, those individuals who uphold the study fulfill the practice;
those who fulfill the practice fulfill the realization. Thus, like the new moon, [the Dhamma shines] through the study and the rest.
This shows that as my [followers] increase, my teaching indeed increases.
Now, demonstrating those factors by which the true Dhamma both disappears and persists, he said, "There are five," and so forth.
In this context, *okkamanīyā* means "to be descended to" or "to be gone down to. Regarding the Teacher...
Regarding the terms "without respect" (*agārava*) and so forth: "without respect" means devoid of reverence. "Without deference" (*appatissa*) means lacking veneration, behaving without humility.

In this context, one who, while ascending the courtyard of a shrine (*cetiyangaṇa*), holds an umbrella, wears sandals, or walks about looking around and talking—this is what is called lack of respect for the Teacher.
When the time for hearing the Dhamma has been announced, he sits surrounded by young novices,
or performs other tasks such as building work; or, while seated at the head of the assembly for hearing the Dhamma, he falls asleep, or sits distractedly engaging in other conversation—
this is what is called disrespect for the Dhamma.
When one goes to attend upon an elder, yet sits down without having paid homage, crosses one's legs, folds up one's robe,
or engages in other restless movements of hands and feet, or speaks in the presence of elders without being requested to do so—
this is what is called disrespect toward the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, one who does not fulfill the three trainings is said to have disrespect for training.
One who does not attain the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), or who makes no effort toward their attainment, is said to have disrespect for concentration (*samādhi*).
The positive side should be understood by reversing what has been stated. This is the thirteenth [chapter].
The commentary on the Kassapa-saṃyutta is finished.
6. The Saṃyutta on Gain and Honor.
1. The First Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Dāruṇa Sutta 157.
In the first discourse of the Saṃyutta on Gain and Honor (*lābhasakkāra*), "dāruṇa" means stubborn. Regarding "gain, honor, and renown" (*lābhasakkārasiloka*):

here, "gain" (*lābha*) refers to the acquisition of the four requisites. "Honor" (*sakkāra*) refers to the acquisition of those very same requisites when they have been well-prepared and well-arranged. "Renown" (*siloka*)...
The sound of praise. "Pungent" means sharp. "Harsh" means rough. "Obstructive" means creating an obstacle. First. 2. Commentary on the Bāḷisa Sutta (158).
In the second [sutta], "a fisherman" is one who goes about carrying a hook, a killer of fish. "Baited" means smeared with bait.
"An eye for bait" (*āmisacakkhu*) means one who has an eye—that is, vision—regarding bait; thus, it is an "eye for bait. "A swallowed hook" (*gilabaḷisa*) means a hook that has been swallowed.
"Has fallen into misfortune" (*anayaṃ āpanno*) means he has encountered suffering. "Has met with disaster" (*byasanaṃ āpanno*) means he has met with ruin.
"To be done with as one wishes" (*yathākāmakaraṇīyo*) means that just as the fisherman desires him, so must he be treated according to his will and pleasure; this is the meaning.
"Subject to being done with at will by the Evil One" means that he may be treated according to the desire of the Māra of defilements;
that is, he may be made to fall into hell, or the animal realm, or the sphere of hungry ghosts. This is the second [sutta].
3–4. Commentary on the *Kumma-sutta* and others.
159–160. "The great family of turtles" (*mahākummakula*) means a large family of bony tortoises.
"He went" means he went with the perception: "Surely there must be something here to eat; it is out of stinginess that he is preventing me.
"A *papatā*" refers to a type of fishhook shaped like a *kaṇṇika* barb, which is caught by inserting a stick into an iron hook-case fastened with a long rope.

*Ayakaṇṭaka*: when one falls into it with speed, as soon as one sticks to the rim, the staff comes out and the rope, being tied together, simply slides away. "That tortoise" refers to that pierced tortoise. "Where that tortoise was":
having heard the sound of water, thinking there would be a place of danger, he turned back toward where that well-wishing tortoise was. "Now you are not ours": now you...
"He has fallen into the hands of his enemies; he is no longer ours"—this is the meaning.
While they were thus conversing, the hunter, standing on the boat, pulled in the rope, seized the tortoise, and did with it as he pleased.
The rest here, as well as in the immediately following sutta, is self-evident. [The Third and Fourth Suttas.]
5. Commentary on the *Mīḷhakasutta* 161.

In the fifth [verse], "dung-beetles" (*mīḷhaka*) refers to creatures that feed on excrement. "Feeding on dung" (*gūthādī*) means those whose food is dung. "Filled with dung" (*gūthapūra*) means being filled inside with dung.
"Full of dung" (*puṇṇā gūthassa*) is an explanatory clarification of the preceding term. "One would despise them" (*atimaññeyya*) occurs in the final line.
Having placed her first foot on the ground and then stepped onto the excrement with the other, she would stand there saying, "I am standing upon excrement," and thus despise it.
Furthermore, his alms-food is full; that is, another bowlful of excellent alms-food would be available for him. This is the fifth. 6. Commentary on the *Asanisutta* (The Thunderbolt Sutta)
162. "Monks, what person, monks, should a dry thunderbolt-wheel come upon, falling from above and crushing him?
One who has not attained the mind's goal—that is, one who has not realized Arhatship.
Thus the Blessed One spoke this not out of a desire for beings to suffer, but rather to demonstrate the danger. For the thunderbolt-wheel [falls] upon the head.
It destroys that single fallen selfhood; with a mind consumed by gain, honor, and fame, one experiences endless suffering in the hells and other realms.
This is the sixth. 7. Commentary on the *Diddha-sutta*.

163. In the seventh [verse], "by one who has applied magic" means by one who has employed magical power (*iddhi*). "By a poisoned one" means by one smeared with poison. "By a dart" means by a spear. This is the seventh [chapter]. 8.
Commentary on the *Siṅgāla-sutta* (The Discourse to the Jackal).
164. In the eighth [verse], "the jackal" refers to an old jackal. For just as even a body that is golden-colored is indeed called a putrid body, so too is this [old jackal].
Even urine that has been discharged at that very moment is called "putrid urine" (*pūtimutta*); likewise, even a jackal born on that same day is called an "old jackal.
By the disease named *ukkaṇṭaka*: by a malady of this name. It is said that it arises during the cold season.
When it occurs, the hairs fall from the entire body; the whole body becomes hairless.
It throbs all over; the wounds burst open as if struck by the wind.

Just as a man bitten by a mad dog wanders about without stability, so when this [fever] has arisen, one must wander about; it is not discerned that there will be safety in such-and-such a place. This is the eighth.
9. Commentary on the Verambha Sutta (165).
Regarding the ninth [sutta]: "Verambha winds" refers to great winds of that name. But in what kind of place do those winds blow?
It is where, for one standing there, the four continents appear no larger than the petals of a blue lotus. "Whatever bird goes... [and so forth].
When the rain has newly fallen, the wind-bird goes there crying out; it is with reference to this that it was said. Regarding the phrases "with an unguarded body" and so forth:
one who plays with the hands and feet, or bends the backbone, is said to have an unguarded body;
one who speaks various kinds of indecent talk is said to have an unguarded speech; and one who entertains thoughts such as sensual thoughts is said to have an unguarded mind.
"He does not guard the mind" means that mindfulness is not established; that is, he has not established mindfulness directed to the body.
This is the ninth [sutta]. 10. Commentary on the Sagāthaka Sutta (166).

In the tenth [sutta], "by lack of honor and by both": this refers to lack of honor and to both [lack of honor and lack of praise]. "Concentration" refers to the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship.
For by that he is not shaken. "Dwelling in the immeasurable" means dwelling by means of the fruit-concentration (*phala-samādhi*), which is immeasurable.

"Constantly active" means one who acts continuously. "One who has subtle vision and insight" means an insight-possessor (*vipassaka*) who has arrived having established insight for the sake of the attainment of the fruit, which is the subtle vision of the path to Arahatship.
"Delighting in the destruction of clinging" refers to that which is designated as the destruction of clinging (*upādānakkhaya*).
"Delighting in Nibbāna"—they call him a "true person" (sappurisa), meaning they speak of him as a true person. The tenth [sutta].
The first chapter.
2. The second chapter.
1–2. Commentary on the *Suvaṇṇapāti-sutta* and others, 167–168.
In the first [sutta] of the second chapter, the phrase "speaking a deliberate lie" (*sampajānamusā bhāsanto*) refers to one who speaks a lie with full awareness even for a trivial reason.
Even if it were as large as Mount Sineru, [the offense applies to] a monk who has made a formal arrangement, thinking, "I shall fulfill my virtue."

He is unable to move even a heap of conditions. But when he abandons virtue and becomes dependent on honor, then he speaks falsehood even for the sake of a handful of gruel, or performs some other improper act. The second [simile] is likewise obvious. This concludes the first and second [sections].
3–10. Commentary on the *Suvaṇṇanikkha-sutta* and others.
169. Regarding the third and subsequent cases: "of a gold coin" means of a single coin made of refined gold (*kañcana*). "Of a bronze coin" means of a coin made of reddish-gold (*siṅgī-suvaṇṇa*).
"On the earth" means on the great earth within the limits of a world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).

"For the sake of some small material gain" means for the sake of any material thing whatsoever, even down to a handful of broken rice. "For the sake of life" means when one has been seized by bandits in the wilderness and [threatened] with regard to one's life.
The reason for that [offense] also applies when she is being deprived [of her robes]. "Janapadakalyāṇī" means the most excellent woman in the country. The third [section] and so forth.
The second chapter.
3. The third chapter.
1–2. Commentary on the *Mātugāma-sutta* and others. 170–171.
Regarding the first sutta of the third chapter, "Not for him, monks, is a woman":
this means that when he is sitting alone in seclusion, even if he has need of her, a woman is unable to overpower his mind, provided that he possesses gain, honor, and fame.
The meaning is that it is able to consume the mind. The second [sutta] is likewise obvious. This concludes the first and second [suttas]. 3–6.
Commentary on the *Ekaputtaka-sutta* and others (172–175).

In the third, "those with faith" refers to stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*). The rest here is likewise obvious. The same applies to the fourth, fifth, and sixth. This concludes the third and following [suttas].
7. Commentary on the Third Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins (Tatiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā) 176.
Regarding the seventh [verse], in the phrases beginning with "arise" (*samudayanti*), the following are included among the gains and honors (*lābhasakkāra*):

the personal existence together with past karma (*pubbakamma*), noble birth (*kolaputtiya*), beauty of complexion (*vaṇṇapokkharatā*), excellence of speech (*kalyāṇavākkaraṇatā*), the manifestation of ascetic virtues (*dhutaguṇa*), the wearing of robes (*cīvaradhāraṇa*), and the perfection of a retinue (*parivārasampatti*). Thus it is said.

What is called "origination" is not understood by way of the truth of origination; cessation and the path should be understood by way of the truth of cessation and the truth of the path respectively. Seventh.
8. Commentary on the Chavi Sutta.
177. In the eighth [verse], because gain, honor, and fame cause one to be reborn in the hells and other realms, they destroy this entire personal existence;
even here [in the present life], they bring about death or at least suffering equal to death. Therefore, it is said: "It cuts the skin," and so forth. This is the eighth. 9.
Commentary on the Rope Sutta (Rajjusutta).

178. Regarding "the ninth, the hair-rope" (*vāḷarajjū*): a rope made of thread and so forth is soft, whereas a hair-rope is rough and coarse; therefore, this [hair-rope] alone is taken here. This is the ninth. 10.
Commentary on the Bhikkhu Sutta (The Discourse on the Monk) 179.

Regarding "dwelling in happiness in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*): these are the dwellings in the happiness of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). "Of these, I am one" means of those...

"I would be such a one. For one whose taints are destroyed—being accomplished in merit and receiving offerings such as rice-gruel and solid food—does not find the opportunity to sit down after giving thanks to those who come one after another, teaching the Dhamma, answering questions, and entering into the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
It was said with reference to this. The tenth [chapter].
The Third Chapter. 4.
The Fourth Chapter: 1–4.
Commentary on the Bhindisutta and following.

180–183. The first [sutta] of the fourth section is self-evident. Regarding the second and following: "Root of the wholesome" (*kusalamūla*) refers to the threefold wholesome phenomena beginning with non-greed (*alobha*).
"Bright phenomenon" (*sukko dhammo*) is a synonymous teaching for that same thing. Herein, the summary of the meaning is as follows:
because of the non-interruption of that blameless phenomenon known as the root of the wholesome and so forth, Devadatta might have been reborn in heaven or attained the paths and fruits.
...he would attain [it], and it would have reached its total eradication; it is utterly cut off and destroyed. [The terms] "first" and so forth [are explained]. 5.
Commentary on the *Acirapakkanta-sutta* (Sutta 184).
In the fifth [verse], "for ruin" (*parābhavāya*) means for lack of growth, for destruction. "A mule" (*assatarī*) refers to one born from the womb of a mare by a donkey.
Once born, she conceives a fetus for her own destruction. They mate her with a horse;
having conceived, when the time comes for delivery, she is unable to give birth.
She stands striking the ground with her feet, whereupon they bind her four legs to four stakes, slit open her belly, and pull out the offspring; she dies right there.
Thus it was said. The fifth [sutta]. 6.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Five Hundred Chariots (Pañcarathasatasutta). 185.
In the sixth [sutta], "the offering of food" (*bhattābhihāra*) means food that is to be brought forward. To show its measure:
And it is said, "five hundred *thālipāka* offerings. In that context, one *thālipāka* provides a meal for ten men.
"He might break his nose with bile" means he might put ox-bile or fish-bile into his nostrils. This is the sixth [section].
7–13. Commentary on the *Mātusutta* and following.

186–187. “On account of even one’s mother” (mātupi hetu) in the seventh [case] means that one should not speak a deliberate lie even for the sake of one’s mother who has fallen into the hands of bandits, when she is being questioned by those bandits in the wilderness with the words: “If you speak falsely, we will release your mother;
if you do not speak, we will not release her. This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. These are the seventh and following.
The commentary on the Connected Discourses on Gain and Honor is finished.
7. The Connected Discourses with Rāhula.
1. The First Chapter.
1–8. Commentary on the *Cakkhusutta* and others. 188–195.
In the first discourse of the *Rāhula-saṃyutta*, "one" (*eko*) refers to one who dwells alone among the four postures.
"Withdrawn" (*vūpakaṭṭho*) means secluded and free from noise. "Diligent" (*appamatto*) means not neglecting mindfulness. "Ardent" (*ātāpī*) means endowed with energy. "Resolute" (*pahitatto*).
"May I dwell" means that I should dwell with my self directed toward the attainment of distinction (*visesa*). "Impermanent" means impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having been.

Alternatively, it is impermanent for these reasons as well: because it possesses arising and passing away, because it is temporary, and because it is the limit of change, which is the negation of permanence.
"Suffering" means suffering by way of four reasons: in the sense of being the meaning of suffering (*dukkhamana*), and in the sense of being the basis of suffering (*dukkhavatthu*).
"In the sense of constant oppression, it is the opposite of pleasure. "It is fit" means it is appropriate. "This is mine" is the grasping of craving (*taṇhāgāha*).
"I am this" is the grasping of conceit (*mānagāha*). "This is my self" is the grasping of views (*diṭ�thigāha*).

Here, the grasping of craving should be understood by way of the eight hundred modes of the wandering of craving; the grasping of conceit by way of the ninefold conceit; and the grasping of views by way of the sixty-two views. Becoming disenchanted...

In the phrase "he becomes dispassionate" (*virajjati*), the four paths are spoken of by way of dispassion (*virāga*); in the phrase "he is liberated through dispassion" (*virāgā vimuccati*), the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) are spoken of by way of liberation (*vimutti*).

And here, only the [sensory] sensitivities (*pasāda*) are taken at the five doors; by the term "mind" (*mano*), the consciousness that ranges over the three planes (*tebhūmaka*) during the process of reflection (*sammasana-cāra*) is meant.
In the second [section], at the five doors, there is only the object. In the third, at the five doors, there is only the consciousness based on the sensitive matter;
by means of mind-consciousness, the consciousness belonging to the three planes that functions in reflection is included. In this way, the method should be applied everywhere.
In the sixth, there are the phenomena of the three planes. But in the eighth, "craving" refers only to that which has reached the stage of impulsion (javana) at each respective door.
It is obtained. Regarding the first and subsequent [sections]:
9. Commentary on the Sutta on Elements (Dhātusuttavaṇṇanā) 196.
In the ninth [sutta], "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is explained by way of the consciousness element as "name," and by way of the remaining elements as "form. Ninth.
10. Commentary on the Khandhasutta 197.

In the tenth [sutta], the aggregate of form belongs to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*); the remaining four aggregates, according to the comprehensive classification, belong to all four planes. However, in this context, they should be understood as belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*).
The tenth [sutta]. The first chapter.
2. Second Chapter: 1–10.
Commentary on the Discourses on the Eye, etc. (198–199).
In the second [chapter], the ten [discourses] have their meaning already explained. [These are] the first and so forth.
11. Commentary on the *Anusaya-sutta* (200).
In this eleventh [sutta], "in this conscious body" refers to one's own conscious body;
"and externally" refers to another's body, whether conscious or unconscious. Alternatively, by the former [phrase], it indicates the consciousness itself of both oneself and others.
[The former] shows [internal form], while the latter shows external form not bound to the sense-faculties.
"I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit" refers to the view of "I-making," the craving of "mine-making," and the underlying tendencies of conceit. "They do not exist":
he asks how these defilements do not exist for one who knows these bases. "One sees with right wisdom" means by means of the path-wisdom together with insight (*vipassanā*).
He sees clearly. The eleventh [sutta].
12. Commentary on the *Apagata-sutta* 201.
Regarding the twelfth [sutta], the phrase "free from the conceit of 'I' and 'mine'" refers to being free from the conceit of "I," the conceit of "mine," and pride (*māna*).
And it is "removed. "Having completely transcended all divisions" means having thoroughly transcended the various categories of conceit.
"Peaceful and well-liberated" means peaceful through the subsiding of the defilements, and well-liberated from those very defilements. The rest is self-evident. The twelfth [sutta].
The second chapter.

In both cases, the stage of one beyond training (*asekkhabhūmi*) is described. However, here the first was taught for one who requested it, while the second was taught for one who did not request it. Furthermore, throughout the entire *Rāhula-saṃyutta*, only those qualities that ripen liberation (*vimuttiparipācanīya-dhammā*) were taught for the Elder.
The commentary on the *Rāhula-saṃyutta* is finished.
8. The *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta*.
1. First Chapter. 1. Commentary on the Aṭṭhi Sutta. 202.
In the *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta*, this venerable one called Lakkhaṇa refers to the Elder Lakkhaṇa, who was among a thousand matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭila*).

It should be understood that one who was ordained by the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) formula and attained *arahantship* at the conclusion of the discourse on the burning (*ādittapariyāya*) is a certain Great Disciple (*mahāsāvaka*).

However, because he was endowed with a physical form (*attabhāva*) that possessed the marks, was complete in every aspect, and was equal to a Brahmā, he became known as "Lakkhaṇa. As for Mahāmoggallāna, from the day of his going forth...
On the seventh day, the second chief disciple attained Arahatship.
"He manifested a smile" means he displayed a gentle smile; it is said that he revealed or showed it.
But what did the Elder see that caused him to manifest a smile? It was a skeleton in the world of hungry ghosts (petaloka), as described further on in the text.
Having seen a being reborn—specifically with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*), and not with the physical eye (*pasāda-cakkhu*).

For these types of personal existences (*attabhāva*) do not come within the range of the physical eye. But having seen such a personal existence, why did he manifest a smile when compassion was the appropriate response?
It was because he recollected both his own excellence and the excellence of the Buddha’s knowledge (*buddha-ñāṇa*). For that...
Seeing this, the Elder reflected upon his own success, thinking: "I have been liberated from such forms of personal existence as must be experienced by a person who has not yet seen the Truths;
what a gain for me! What a great blessing for me! He then recalled:
"Oh, the perfection of wisdom of the Blessed Buddha, who said: 'Monks, that which is the ripening of kamma is inconceivable and should not be speculated upon.'"
"He taught after having made it manifest to himself; indeed, the Buddhas teach having made [the truth] manifest to themselves, for the Dhamma-element of the Buddhas is well-penetrated.
Having thus recollected the perfection of the Buddha’s knowledge, he manifested a smile.
Now, why did the Elder Lakkhaṇa not see it? Was it because he lacked the divine eye? It was not that he lacked it; Mahāmoggallāna...
But as he was reflecting, he saw [it], whereas the other did not see it because he was not reflecting.
Since those whose taints are destroyed do not smile without a cause, the Elder Lakkhaṇa asked him: "Friend Moggallāna, what is the reason, what is the cause for manifesting this smile?
The Elder, however, [explained] by which means this rebirth was personally [attained by him].

Those who have not seen [the truth] are difficult to convince; therefore, desiring to provide an explanation with the Blessed One as witness, he said, "It is not the right time, friends," and so forth.
Then, having been questioned in the presence of the Blessed One, he explained it according to the method beginning with, "In this case, friends, I saw... and so on.
In that context, "a skeleton" (*aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikā*) refers to a collection of bones, white, devoid of flesh and blood. Vultures and crows...
Regarding the term "kulalāpi" (also hawks): these should be understood as *yakkha*-vultures, *yakkha*-crows, and *yakkha*-hawks.
However, this form does not even come within the range of sight of ordinary vultures and the like. "Anupatitvā anupatitvā" means having pursued them again and again.
"Vitudenti" means having pierced them repeatedly with sharp iron beaks that are like the edge of a sword.
They move and go here and there. Regarding the phrase "she indeed makes a cry of distress," *sudaṃ* is a particle;
the meaning is that that skeleton-frame indeed makes a cry of distress, a cry of anguish.

It is said that for the sake of experiencing the result of unwholesome karma, such personal existences (*attabhāva*) as large as a league (*yojana*) arise, and they are prominent with sensitivity (*pasāda*), resembling ripe boils.
"Therefore, that skeleton, afflicted by powerful pains, made such a sound.

Having spoken thus, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, out of compassion for sentient beings and demonstrating the spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*) that had arisen—thinking, "Beings who travel in the cycle of existence are not released from such bodily forms"—said to me: "For me..."
"Friends, this thought occurred to me: 'How wonderful! and so forth," he said. Then the Blessed One, manifesting the elder’s power, said:

"Monks, disciples indeed dwell as those who have become vision," and so forth. In that context, "those who have become vision" means those for whom vision has become [their own], has arisen, and has appeared;
they are those who have become vision, those whose vision has become real, those whose vision has arisen—those who dwell having produced vision.
This is the meaning. The same method applies to the second phrase as well. Regarding the expression *yatra hi nāma*: here, *yatra* is a word signifying a reason.
The application of the meaning (*atthayojanā*) is as follows: because even a disciple might indeed know such a thing, or see it, or bear witness to it, therefore we said:
"Bhikkhus, disciples indeed dwell as become vision; they indeed dwell as become knowledge."

“...monks, my disciples dwell. “Monks, that being was seen by me even before [my enlightenment]”—by this he means that while at the seat of awakening, through the penetration of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), I directly perceived him among the immeasurable world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) and the immeasurable classes of beings (*sattanikāya*) across their various states of existence, destinies, wombs, and abodes.
Thus he says: “That being was seen by me even before.”
A cow-slaughterer is one who makes his living by killing cows, cutting off their meat while they are still alive, and selling it.

"By the remaining result of that very karma" means by the remainder of that karma accumulated through various volitions (*cetanā*) belonging to the category of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariya-kamma*).
For in that case, when the ripening (*vipāka*) of the specific volition that produced rebirth in hell has been exhausted, there remains the residual karma.
Or, having taken either the sign of the deed (*kamma-nimitta*) or the object as its support, rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) arises again among the hungry ghosts and so forth;
therefore, that rebirth-linking—due to its similarity to the deed or its similarity to the object—is called "the remainder of the result of that very deed.
And this being has arisen in this way. Hence he said: "by the remainder of the result of that very deed."
It is said that at the time of his death from the hells, the sign he perceived was merely a heap of bones of cattle stripped of their flesh.
As if making even that concealed deed manifest to the wise, he was reborn as an Aṭṭhisaṅkhalika-peta (a skeleton-ghost). This is the first.
2. Commentary on the Pesi-sutta (The Flesh-fragment Sutta)
203. In the story of the Meat Slab: A beef-killer, having cut beef into slabs and dried them, made his living for many years by selling dried meat (*vallūra*).
Consequently, at the time of his death and descent into hell, a meat slab alone appeared as the sign before him.
He was reborn as a meat-slab *peta*. This is the second [story].
3. Commentary on the Piṇḍa Sutta 204.
Regarding the case of the lump of flesh: "Fowler" refers to one who made his living by catching birds and selling them after plucking their feathers and skin, leaving them as mere lumps of flesh.
Consequently, at the time of his death and falling from hell, he appeared as a lump of flesh.
There was a sign. He was reborn as a flesh-eating peta. This is the third [case].
4. Commentary on the Nicchavi Sutta (The Skinless One):
In the story of the skinless one, that sheep-butcher, having slaughtered sheep again and again, had them flayed.
For Kappitajīvika, as before, a constant sheep carcass without skin served as his sign. He was reborn as a skinless peta. This is the fourth [story].
5. Commentary on the *Asiloma-sutta* (The Sūtra of the Sword-Haired One):
Regarding the account of the sword-haired one, that pig-breeder, for a long time, slaughtered pigs that had been fattened on fodder with a sword.
Having killed [him], he sustained his livelihood for a long time; the very fact that his sword was raised was the cause.
Therefore, he was reborn as a "sword-hair peta. This is the fifth.
6. Commentary on the Sattisutta (Spear Sutta).

207. In the story of the hunter with the spear: that hunter took a deer and a spear, went into the forest, and whenever a deer came near that one, he pierced and killed it with the spear. The very act of piercing with the spear became his *nimitta*.
Therefore, he was reborn as a "spear-hair ghost" (*sattiloma-peta*). This is the sixth [story].
7. Commentary on the Usuloma Sutta 208.
Regarding the case of Usuloma: "The executioner" refers to the man who, after having tormented a criminal against the king with various tortures, finally kills him by piercing him with a spear.
It is said that he [acted] only after knowing, "He will die when pierced in such-and-such a place."

He pierced [them]. Having thus made his living, when he was reborn in hell, the very state of being pierced by arrows at the time of his reappearance here—due to what remained after he had been roasted there—became the sign.
Therefore, he was born as a "hair-arrow peta. This is the seventh.
8. Commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta.
209. In the account of Sūciloma, "sūta" means a horse-trainer; they also call him Godamaka. His very act of piercing with the needle of his goad became the *nimitta* (the causal sign).
Therefore, he was reborn as the hungry ghost Sūciloma. This is the eighth [story]. 210.
In the second account of Sūciloma, "sūcaka" means a slanderer. It is said that he [used to] cause people to [slander] one another...
In the royal court, he repeatedly incited division by whispering, "He has this name; he did this," and thus brought about ruin and calamity for them.

Therefore, having made his own karma the cause, he was born as a Needle-Haired Ghost (Sūciloma-peta) to experience the suffering of being pierced by needles, just as he had caused men to be divided by his whisperings. This is the ninth [story].
10. Commentary on the Kumbhaṇḍa Sutta 211.
Regarding the story of the one who carried eggs: the term *gāmakūṭaka* refers to a minister of justice.
Because of his professional nature, he had eggs as large as jars (*kumbha*), the size of great water-pots. For he would take bribes in secret, hidden places, and by means of fraudulent judgments...
Because he made manifest a fault that was hidden, he made his own master one who was no longer his master; therefore, his private organ was born manifest.
Because, while inflicting punishment, he imposed upon others a burden they could not bear, therefore his private organ was born as a burden too heavy to bear.
Because, in whatever position one stands, one ought to be impartial... [in that position]...
Having stood [there], he became unsteady; therefore, his posture while sitting in the inner chamber was indeed unsteady. The tenth.
The first section.
2. The second section.
1. Commentary on the *Sasīsakasutta* 212.

In the case of the adulterer, that being—who, while touching the protected and guarded person belonging to another, delighted his mind with the filth of pleasure and sensual pleasure—by virtue of the similarity of his karma, touches the contact of excrement.
He was reborn there to experience suffering. First. 2.
Commentary on the Gūthakhāda Sutta (The Dung-Eater): 213.
The story of the wicked brahmin is well known. Second.
3. Commentary on the Nicchavīthī Sutta 214.

Regarding the case of Nicchavīthī: since a woman is not the master over her own touch, and she, having stolen that touch which belonged to her husband, produced delight in others, therefore, by way of the commonality of kamma—
Having been accustomed to pleasant contact, she was reborn as a woman who was unwilling to experience painful contact. This is the third [sutta].
4. Commentary on the Maṅguli-itthi-sutta (The Ugly Woman):
Regarding the case of the ugly woman (*maṅguli*), "ugly" (*maṅguli*) means deformed, unsightly, and repulsive. It is said that she performed the work of a female servant for a *yakkha*.

Performing such rites, she deceived the great multitude by taking their scents, flowers, and other offerings while saying, "When this and that bali-offering is performed, such-and-such prosperity will come to you. Thus, she caused the multitude to adopt wrong views and false views.
Therefore, because of that similarity of action—specifically, the theft of scents, flowers, and so forth—she became foul-smelling and ugly to behold.
Because she was seized [by that state], she was reborn as one who is difficult to see, deformed, and hideous. This is the fourth [case].
5. Commentary on the *Okilinī-sutta* (216):
Regarding the story of *Okilinī*, "the one who is oozing," it is said that she was reborn as one who is "oozing" because she had lain upon a funeral pyre of burning coals.

Tossing about and rolling around, she is cooked; therefore, her body is both blistered and cooked by the hot fire, smeared and drenched, with drops trickling from her body, and strewn and surrounded by glowing embers.
For beneath her, on both sides, and even above her in the air, there are glowing embers the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers.
They fall down. Therefore it is said: "boiling, bespattered, and sprinkled. It is said that out of jealousy, she poured a brazier of glowing coals over her co-wife;
for a certain dancer of that king’s had placed a brazier of glowing coals nearby while wiping water from her limbs and fanning away the sweat with her hand.
The king, too, would converse with her and display an air of great satisfaction.
[The Buddha] showed [this]. The chief queen, unable to endure it and overcome by jealousy, took that charcoal pan while the king had not yet long departed and poured the coals over her.
Having committed that deed, she was reborn in the world of petas to experience a corresponding result. This is the fifth [story].
6. Commentary on the Asīsakasutta (Sutta 217).

Regarding the case of the murderer of a thief: by order of the king, he had the heads of thieves cut off for a long time; thus, when being reborn in the world of ghosts, he was reborn as a headless trunk.
This is the sixth [sutta]. 7–11. Commentaries on the Pāpabhikkhusutta and following.
218–222. Regarding the story of the bhikkhu: a "bad bhikkhu" (*pāpabhikkhu*) is a base bhikkhu.
It is said that after consuming the four requisites given to the world out of faith, he wandered about unrestrained in the doors of body and speech, with a broken livelihood, sporting in mental play.
Then, having been boiled in hell for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, as he was being reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*petaloka*), he appeared exactly like a bhikkhu.
He was reborn with a physical form. This same analysis applies to the cases concerning bhikkhunīs, sikkhamānās, sāmaṇeras, and sāmaṇerīs. [The sections] beginning with the seventh are concluded.
The commentary on the Saṃyutta on Characteristics (Lakkhaṇasaṃyutta) is finished.
9. The Saṃyutta on Similes (Opammasaṃyutta).
1. Commentary on the Kūṭasutta 223.
In the first sutta of the Saṃyutta on Similes: "They go to the peak" means *kūṭaṅgamā*. "They converge at the peak" means *kūṭasamosaraṇā*.
"By the uprooting of the peak" means by the complete eradication of the peak. "By the uprooting of ignorance" means by means of the path of Arahantship, [the uprooting] of ignorance.
By eradication. "Heedful" means remaining established in the non-forgetfulness of mindfulness. First. 2.
Commentary on the Nakhasikha Sutta. 224.
In the second [sutta], "reborn among humans" refers to those who, having passed away from the human world, are born among humans. These...

The intended meaning is that they are thus few. "Except for humans" means that those who, having passed away from the human world, are reborn in the four states of misery—excluding the human world itself—are more numerous than the dust on the great earth.
And in this sutta, even the devas are included within the category of humans. Therefore, just as those being born among humans are few, [so too are those reborn elsewhere].
It should be understood that it is the same among the devas as well. Second.
3. Commentary on the Kula Sutta (Discourse on Families) 225.
In the third [verse], "easily corrupted" means easily harassed. "By thieves with jars" refers to those who, having entered another's house...
Desiring to steal another's goods after looking with the light of a lamp, they enter having placed a lamp inside a jar;
these are called "jar-thieves" (*kumbhatthenaka*), and by those jar-thieves [the house] is easily plundered. It is "easily plundered by non-humans" (*amanussa*):

even dust-demons (*paṃsupisācaka*) who lack the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*) destroy it, let alone exalted non-humans. "Cultivated" (*bhāvita*) means increased. "Made much of" (*bahulīkata*) means...
"Repeatedly performed": done again and again. "Made into a vehicle": made like a harnessed carriage. "Made into a foundation": made like a foundation in the sense of being a support.
"Established": resolved upon. "Cultivated": gathered on all sides, well-increased. "Well undertaken":
properly undertaken by the mind. Third.
4. Commentary on the Okkhāsutta 226.
In the fourth [verse], "a hundred *okkhā-santīs*" refers to a hundred large-mouthed mortars (*ukkhalī*).

"One should give a gift" means one should give a gift of a hundred large mortars filled with choice food. There is also a reading, "a hundred *ukkās*"; for that, it means a hundred staff-lamps (*daṇḍadīpikā*).
The meaning is as follows: "But if one were to fill with the seven jewels an area a hundred times larger than the space illuminated by a single lamp and give it as a gift"—this is the meaning.
"The measure of a cow's lowing" (*gadduhanamattaṃ*) means the measure of a cow's lowing;
the meaning is the distance covered by a cow's single pull while being milked. Or, it refers to the measure of a handful of perfume, that is, a ball of perfume held between two fingers.
The meaning is: "having taken it up, merely sniffing it once.

For even for such a short time as this—whether by the limited area of a womb, a courtyard, or a monastery, or by the limit of a world-system, or throughout immeasurable world-systems toward all beings—one who is able to develop a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) that radiates welfare, this [merit] is greater than giving alms three times a day for a single day.
It is of even greater fruit. Fourth. 5.
Commentary on the Satti-sutta (The Spear). 227.
Regarding the fifth [verse], "I shall enter a cave," and so forth: having struck the tip [of the spear] and drawing it back like a roll of cotton wool, [he drew it back] like a roll of resin.
Making [the two edges] meet together as if they were one and causing them to adhere is called *paṭileṇeti*.
Striking in the middle and bending it, or striking along the edge and causing the two edges to adhere together as one, is called *paṭikoṭṭeti*.
Operating like the spinning of cotton, or like spreading out a rolled-up mat for a long time and then rolling it up again, is called *paṭivaṭṭeti*. This is the fifth.
6. Commentary on the *Dhanuggahasutta* (The Archers Sutta) 228.
In the sixth [verse], "archers of firm strength" (*daḷhadhammā dhanuggahā*) refers to archers with strong bows. A "strong bow" is said to have a capacity of two thousand [pounds];
a capacity of two thousand means that when it is strung, the weight of iron tips and so forth attached to the bowstring rests upon the staff.
Having taken it up, it is released from the ground as soon as it has been raised to the height of a *kaṇḍa*.
"Well-trained" means those who have mastered their craft in the teacher’s household for ten or twelve years. "Skilled in hand" means that one who merely learns the craft is not yet skilled in hand;
these, however, are skilled in hand because they have attained mastery (*vasībhāva*). "Experienced" means those who have demonstrated their craft in royal courts and similar settings.
The speed of that man was such as no other man had ever possessed before;
indeed, it was the time of the Bodhisatta’s flight on the swan. At that time, the Bodhisatta brought four arrows.
Then his younger brothers announced, "Brother, we shall race with the sun. The Bodhisatta said, "The sun..."
"He is swift of speed; you will not be able to race with him.
Having said this a second and a third time, they one day said, "Let us go," and having climbed Mount Yugandhara, they sat down.
The Bodhisatta asked, "Where are my brothers? When it was told to him, "They have gone to race with the sun," he said, "They will perish."
Out of compassion for those ascetics, he himself went and sat down in their presence.
Then, as the sun was rising, both brothers flew up into the sky along with the sun; the Bodhisatta also flew up along with them.
While they were still in flight, before one of them had even reached his destination, fire broke out within the wings at the time of their midday meal.

He called out to his brother and said, "I am unable. The Bodhisatta comforted him, saying, "Do not fear," and having enveloped him within the hollow of his wings to dispel his distress, sent him off, saying, "Go!
The second bird flew with such speed that he reached the other side before the midday meal; when fire arose between his wings, he spoke in the same manner. To him as well—
Having done exactly that, he sent him off, saying, "Go. But he himself, having run as fast as possible until midday, thought, "These are fools;
I too must not be a fool," and turning back, went toward Bārāṇasī with the thought, "I shall see the King of Bārāṇasī, whose companion has never been seen before.
As he was wandering at the edge of that city, he reached the twelve-league city with his bowl.

It was like a bowl covered over. Then, as he circled and circled about, gaps appeared here and there, and he himself appeared like many thousands of swans. Withdrawing his speed, he headed toward the royal palace.
The king, looking out and thinking, "My dear companion, the swift swan, has indeed arrived," opened the window.
Having prepared a jeweled throne, he stood there gazing at it. The Bodhisatta sat down upon the jeweled throne.
Then the king, having anointed his wings with oil boiled a thousand times, gave him honeyed parched grain and sweet drink.
After the Bodhisatta had finished enjoying these, the king asked him, "Friend, where have you been? He [the Bodhisatta] related that occurrence.
Having announced this, he explained: "Then, O Great King, I ran as fast as I could until midday, but then I turned back, thinking, 'There is no point in running anymore.
Then the king said: "Master, I wish to see the speed of your race against the sun.
[The other replied: "It is difficult, O Great King; it is not possible for you to see it. [The king said: "In that case, Master, even a mere likeness of it—"
"Let him see," [the king said]. "Yes, Great King, assemble the archers," [the swan replied]. The king assembled them.
Then the swan, having taken four men, had an archway constructed in the middle of the city, had a bell fastened to his own neck, and sitting atop the archway, said:
"Four men, leaning against the archway, facing the four directions, each one..."
Having said, "Let them shoot arrows," he himself leapt up along with the very first arrow;
without even grasping that arrow, he caught the one shot toward the south at a distance of one *ratana* from the bow.
The second he caught at a distance of two *ratanas*, the third at three *ratanas*, and the fourth he caught before it had even reached the ground. Then, those four...
They saw them while he was still sitting at the gateway, having already caught the arrows. He said to the king, "Behold, Great King, how swift our speed is!
Thus it should be understood that those arrows were brought back by the Bodhisatta himself during his time as a swift swan.
"Running ahead" means they run at the front. However, they do not always remain in front; sometimes they are in front, [and sometimes behind].
Sometimes they are behind. For in the celestial mansions situated in the sky there are gardens and lotus ponds;
there they bathe, and while playing in the water they are behind, yet having gone with speed, they run ahead once more.
"Life-formations" (*āyusaṅkhārā*) is said with reference to the material life-faculty (*rūpajīvitindriya*), for that indeed proceeds more swiftly than those [other formations].
It decays. However, the disintegration of formless phenomena cannot be demonstrated.
This is the sixth [section]. 7. Commentary on the Āṇisutta 229.
Regarding the seventh [verse], "of the Dasārahas": this refers to kṣatriyas of that name. It is said that they used to take a tenth part from every hundred.
Therefore, they became known as "the Ten-Rays. Anaka is the name of a kind of drum. It is said that in the Himalayas there was a great Kuḷīra lake.
A large crab lived there and would devour every elephant that entered the water.
Then the elephants, being distressed, honored a certain female elephant, thinking, "By means of her son, our safety will be secured. She too was of great power...
She gave birth to a son. They honored him as well. When he had reached maturity, he asked his mother, "Why do these people honor me?
She explained the situation to him. He said, "What can a crab possibly produce for me? Come, let us go!
Accompanied by a great retinue of elephants, he went there and was the very first to descend into the water. The crab, having arrived at the mere sound of the water, [emerged].
He seized it. The crab’s claw was enormous; unable to move it here or there, he thrust his trunk into its mouth and cried out.
The elephants fled in all directions, thinking, "The one by whose power we had supposed we would be safe has been captured first."
Then his mother, standing nearby, spoke these kind words to the crab: "We are land-nāgas, while you are called water-nāgas; a nāga should not be harmed by another nāga. She then recited this verse:
"Of all the crabs in the ocean, in the Ganges, and in the Yamunā, you are the best of those born in water;
release the offspring of her who weeps!"
The sound of women stands shaking men; therefore, he made his grip slack.
The young elephant, springing forward with speed, lifted both its feet and trampled him on the back. With that single trampling, his back broke like a clay vessel.
Then, piercing him with its tusks, it lifted him up, cast him onto dry land, and let out a cry of triumph.
Then the elephant came from here and there and trampled him. One of its tusks broke off and fell;
Sakka, the king of the gods, took it and departed.
But the other tusk, having dried up in the wind and sun, became the color of ripe lac juice; when it rained, it was carried away by the flood of water.
While being carried away, it came and became entangled in the net that the ten brothers, the kings, had spread out as they were playing in the Ganges upstream.
When the play was over and the net was being pulled up, they saw it and asked, "What is this?
"It is a crab, Sire," [they replied]. "This cannot be brought for the purpose of ornament; having it tied around, [strike] the drum..."
“Shall we play it? Having thus bound it tightly, they struck it. The sound spread throughout the city for twelve yojanas.
Then they said, “It is not possible to play this day after day;

let it be a drum of auspiciousness for festive occasions,” and so they made it a *maṅgala-bherī* (auspicious drum). When that was played, the great multitude, having bathed and adorned themselves, mounted elephant-vehicles and the like.
Having mounted it, they would assemble quickly. Thus, because he brought people together as if calling out to a great multitude, his name became "Ānaka.
They set another pin, meaning they joined another pin made of gold, silver, or other materials.
Only the assembly of pins remained; that is, only the collection of pins made of gold and other materials was left remaining. Then, measuring twelve yojanas in size...
The sound was heard with difficulty even within the inner hall.
"Profound" means profound by way of the text (*pāḷi*), like the Salla Sutta. "Profound in meaning" means profound by way of the meaning (*attha*), like the Mahāvedalla Sutta.
"Supramundane" means illuminating supramundane meanings. "Connected with emptiness" means...

They reveal only the phenomena of the emptiness of the seven [bases], being similar to the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* in their concise form. "To be learned and mastered" refers to both what is to be learned (*uggahetabba*) and what is to be mastered (*pariyāpuṇitabba*).
"Composed by poets" means made by poets (*kavīhi kata*). The other term is a synonym for that same thing.
"Variegated syllables" means diverse syllables (*vicitra-akkharā*). The other term is a synonym for that same thing. "External" means those existing outside of the Teaching (*sāsana*).
"Spoken by disciples" means spoken by this or that disciple of theirs.

"They will wish to listen" means that because of their appreciation for the letters and the excellence of the hearing, novices, young bhikkhus, women, great householders, and others, being delighted, will assemble thinking, "This one is a preacher of the Dhamma," and become desirous of hearing it. "Therefore" means because it was spoken by the Tathāgata.
The discourses, not being grasped, disappear; therefore [this is said]. Seventh.
8. Commentary on the Kaliṅgara-sutta (230).
"Kaliṅgara-pillows" refers to a pillow made of a block of wood, serving both as a head-pillow and a foot-pillow.

"Having done so. "Diligent" means diligent in the acquisition of their craft. "Ardent" means endowed with the ardor of exertion and energy. "In the practice" refers to the application to the crafts and the attendance upon teachers.
It is said that at that time they would rise early in the morning and go to the school of crafts;
having mastered the craft there and applied themselves through recitation and other means, they would wash their faces for the sake of drinking rice-gruel.
They depart. Having drunk their gruel, they return again to the schoolhouse, learn their craft, and perform their recitations;

then, having eaten their morning meal, thinking, "Let there not be a long sleep through negligence," they place pieces of acacia wood upon their heads and feet, lie down for a short while, and then return once more to the schoolhouse.
Having mastered their craft, they practiced recitation. Reciting in the evening, they would go home and, after eating their evening meal, practice recitation during the first watch of the night;
then, at the time for sleep, they would place a wooden block as a pillow and lie down.
In this way, they became marksmen capable of hitting a target by sound alone and even by hair. It was with reference to this that it was said.
They enter the opening. "Object" means a condition. "In the midst of striving" means while exerting energy on the ground of striving.
It is said that during the first enlightenment, the monks would attend to their meditation subject only after having finished their meal duties.
While they were attending to it, the sun would set. Having bathed, they would again descend to the walking path for the first watch of the night.
They walked back and forth. Then, thinking, "Let us not sleep for long," they would lie down to dispel the fatigue of their bodies, placing a piece of wood beneath them as a pillow;
in the latter watch of the night, they would rise again and descend to the walking path.
It was with reference to them that this was said. This island, during the time of three kings, was a place where a single sound resounded and a single ground of exertion prevailed.
When the gong was struck at Nānāmukha, it reached Pilicchikoḷiya; when the gong was struck at Kalyāṇiya, it reached Nāgadīpa.
"This monk is an ordinary person (puthujjana), this one is an ordinary person," he would say, pointing with his finger to show them.
One day, they all became arahants. Therefore, because Māra [could not find anyone] among the Kaliṅga pillars...
It does not find an object; therefore [it is so]. The eighth. 9.
Commentary on the Nāga Sutta (231).
In the ninth, "ativelam" means a time that has exceeded its limit, a time that has passed its proper measure. "How much more, then, for me? [is the meaning].
But for what reason would I not approach him? "Bhisamuḷāla" refers to both lotus stalks (*bhisam*) and lotus roots (*muḷālam*).
"Having pulled them out" means having extracted them. "Young elephants" (*bhiṅkacchāpā*): these are young elephant calves.

It is said that they frequently make the sound "bhiṅkāra," and therefore they are called "young elephants. "Making a gesture of faith" means making the kind of gesture that those who are faithful ought to perform.
They provide the four requisites. "They preach the Dhamma" means that having mastered one or two Jātaka stories or Suttantas, they teach the Dhamma with a clear, unbroken voice.
"They manifest confidence" means that laypeople, being inspired by that teaching, provide the requisites.
"Neither for the sake of praise nor for the sake of power" means neither for the sake of praising their virtues, nor for the sake of the power of knowledge.
However, when the praise of his virtues declines, his physical complexion and physical strength also decline;
therefore, it serves neither for the beauty nor for the strength of the body.
Ninth. 10. Commentary on the Cat Sutta.
232. Regarding "The tenth: the junction, the dung-pit, and the refuse-heap": here, "junction" (*sandhi*) refers to the gap between broken houses;
"dung-pit" (*samala*) refers to the path by which excrement exits from the village; "refuse-heap" (*saṃkaṭīra*) refers to a place for rubbish. "A soft mouse" (*mudumūsi*) means a soft mouse.
"An emergence is discerned" (*vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati*) means the teaching is discerned. The tenth [chapter].
11. Commentary on the *Siṅgālasutta* 233.

In the eleventh [verse], "wherever he wishes," it is shown that this old jackal, by assuming various postures in whatever place he desires and by being exposed to cool breezes, occasionally experiences mental satisfaction.
"One who professes to be a follower of the Sakyan" (*sakyaputtiyapaṭiñño*)...
This was said with reference to Devadatta; for he will not obtain even this much satisfaction of mind in future existences.
The eleventh [sutta]. 12. Commentary on the Second Jackal Sutta.
234. In the twelfth [chapter], *kataññutā* means the recognition of what has been done; *kataveditā* means the recognition of the excellence of what has been done.
Herein, this is the story of the gratitude of the old jackal: it is said that seven brothers were plowing a field.
Their youngest brother stood at the edge of the field guarding the oxen. Then, a python seized an old jackal; he [the jackal]—
Seeing this, he struck him with a staff and caused him to release [the jackal]. Having released the jackal, the python seized him instead.
The jackal thought: "He has given me my life; I too shall give it to him.
He bit the axe placed upon the pot of rice gruel with his mouth and went back to him. When the other brothers saw this, they said:
Thinking, “A jackal is carrying off my axe,” they pursued him. Knowing that he had been seen by them, he dropped the axe near him and fled.
The others returned and, seeing the youngest brother seized by the python, cut through the python with the axe, took him, and departed.
Thus, even in an old jackal, there may be some gratitude and thankfulness for what has been done.
"Claiming to be a follower of the Sakyan son"—this too was said with reference specifically to Devadatta’s conduct. The twelfth [chapter].
The commentary on the Connected Discourses on Similes is finished.
10. The Connected Discourses on the Bhikkhus.
1. Commentary on the Koliyasutta 235.
In the first sutta of the Bhikkhu Saṃyutta, "friend" (āvuso) is the address used by disciples. For when the Blessed Buddhas address their disciples, they address them as "bhikkhus";
however, the disciples, thinking "let us not be like the Buddhas," address them as "friend."
Having first spoken thus, they later say, "Bhikkhus. When addressed by the Buddhas, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus gives the reply, "Venerable sir" (bhante);
when addressed by disciples, they reply, "Friend" (āvuso). It is called this because in the second jhāna, applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) cease;
through their cessation, the sense-sphere of sound (saddāyatana) comes to a state of non-occurrence. Therefore...
That which is called the second jhāna is what is termed "the noble silence. This is the application [of the terms] here.
However, in the phrase "either talk on the Dhamma or noble silence," both attention to the meditation subject and the first jhāna and so forth are likewise reckoned as "noble silence."
“Accompanied by applied thought” means having applied thought as its object. “Perception and attention” means perception and attention. “Occur” means they proceed.
It is said that for this elder, the second jhāna was not yet fully mastered. Therefore, when he emerged from it, applied thought and sustained thought did not appear to him as peaceful.
Thus, for him, even the second jhāna and the perception and attention were conducive to decline.
He spoke thus, showing that they had been so. "Stabilize" means establish correctly. "Make one-pointed" means make it concentrated.
"Compose" means establish correctly; place [the mind] properly. "The state of great direct knowledge" refers to the sixfold direct knowledge (*chaḷabhiññatā*).

It is said that by this means, the Teacher, having increased the elder’s concentration pertaining to decline over seven days, brought the elder to the attainment of the sixfold direct knowledge. First.
2. Commentary on the Upatissa Sutta 236.

In the second [verse], the phrase "Is there indeed anything in the world... is spoken with reference to either a being (*satta*) or a conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*), even though it is extremely sublime.
As for the phrase "Even toward the Teacher," this is because the Elder Ānanda possessed an extraordinary degree of devotion toward the Teacher.
Because of his zeal and affection, he asks in order to know whether, through the transformation [of his state], even sorrow and the like might not arise for this elder teacher:

"Could it be that for this elder teacher, even through transformation, sorrow and so forth would not arise? He says "for a long time" with reference to the time elapsed from the day the *Vedanāpariggaha Sutta* was taught to the wanderer Dīghanakha at the entrance of the Sūkarakata Cave. For in that [sutta]...
On that day, these defilements conforming to the cycle of existence were eradicated by the Elder. This is the second [sutta].
3. Commentary on the Ghaṭa Sutta (The Jar Sutta) 237.
Regarding the third [sutta], "in a single dwelling" means in one cell. At that time, it is said, many visiting monks had gathered together.
When the dwellings were no longer sufficient for the entire group of cells or the entire monastery, one cell was occupied by two elders.
During the day they sat in separate places, but at night they spread out a cloth screen between them.
Each of them sat only in his own allotted place. Therefore it was said:
“Dwelling alone”: the phrase “by means of the gross” is said with reference to the grossness of the object.
For he dwelt by means of the divine eye and the divine ear element; and their objects—namely, the sense-sphere of visible form and the sense-sphere of sound—are gross.
Thus, because visible form was seen by the divine eye and sound was heard by the divine ear element, that dwelling is called “gross.”
He was born. "The divine eye was purified" means it became pure for the purpose of seeing the Blessed One’s form.

"And the divine ear-element" also became pure for the purpose of hearing the Blessed One’s voice. For the Blessed One as well, both of these were purified for the purpose of seeing the Elder’s form and hearing his voice.
At that time, it is said, the Elder thought: "How indeed is the Teacher now?"

"dwells. Having increased his light, he saw with his divine eye the Teacher seated in the Perfumed Chamber within the Jeta Grove monastery, and he heard the sound [of the Teacher's voice] with his divine ear-element. The Teacher did exactly the same.
Thus they both saw one another and heard one another's voices.
“Of aroused energy” means one whose energy is fulfilled, whose energy is exerted.

“Merely for the sake of placing it near” means that a pebble the size of a mustard seed placed near the Himalayas, which are three thousand leagues in extent, is for the mere purpose of comparison, such as:
“Is the Himalayas great, or is this pebble great?”—thus, it is merely for the sake of placing it near.
"It would be" is what is meant. The same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. "Eons" means the duration of a lifespan.
"Of a salt-cask" indicates a salt-vessel placed upon the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), standing with its rim touching the Brahma-world.
However, when these elders brought forth this simile, they did so by way of both similarity and existing qualities. How so?
For this so-called psychic power (*iddhi*) is like the Himalayas in its sense of being loftily risen and vast;

wisdom (*paññā*), however, is like the taste of salt that has permeated all its constituents, in its sense of having entered and remained within the phenomena of the four planes. Thus, first of all, they brought it forward by way of similarity.
But the characteristic of concentration (*samādhi*) was manifest and evident to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Even though...
The Elder Sāriputta did not lack supernormal power (*iddhi*); however, the Blessed One placed him specifically in this foremost position, saying:
"Bhikkhus, among my disciples who are possessed of supernormal power, Mahāmoggallāna is the foremost.
Yet, for the Elder Sāriputta, the characteristic of insight (*vipassanālakkhaṇa*) was clear and manifest. Even though it was likewise so for the Elder Mahāmoggallāna...

Wisdom exists [in both], yet the Blessed One placed this very one (Sāriputta) in the foremost position, saying: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples, the bhikkhus of great wisdom, this is the foremost, namely Sāriputta.
Therefore, they recorded them according to their existing qualities so that these two would not encroach upon each other's domain;
for in the characteristic of concentration, Mahāmoggallāna [was foremost].
[The Elder] Sāriputta [reached] the perfection of the characteristics of insight; among these two, the Fully Enlightened One is supreme.
The third [section]. 4. Commentary on the Ninth Discourse (Navasutta). 238.
In the fourth [discourse], "free from concern" (*appossukka*) means without anxiety. "Dwells" (*saṅkasāyati*) means he abides. "Service" (*veyyāvacca*) refers to [service regarding] robes...
The duties to be performed. "Dependent on higher consciousness" means dependent on *abhicitta*, which is supreme consciousness.

"One who obtains at will" means one who is capable of entering attainment at whatever moment is desired. "One who obtains without difficulty" means one who is capable of entering attainment by easily suppressing the obstacles to jhāna. "One who obtains without trouble" means according to the prescribed limit...
"An obtainer of abundant gain" means one who is capable of emerging [from concentration]; the meaning is that his jhāna is well-mastered. "Exerting sluggishly" means having applied slack energy.
This is the fourth [sutta].
5. Commentary on the Sujāta Sutta.
239. "Handsome" (*abhirūpa*) means one whose form surpasses others. "Beautiful to behold" (*dassanīya*) means worthy of being seen.
"Gracious" (*pāsādika*) means capable of gladdening the mind upon being seen. "By reason of the excellence of his complexion" (*vaṇṇapokkharatāya*) means by reason of the beauty of his skin-color.
This is the fifth [section]. 6. Commentary on the *Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya Sutta*.

240. In the sixth [offense], "ugly" means having an unsightly bodily complexion. "Dwarfish" means short in stature. "Of contemptible appearance" means one whose birth is held in contempt by reason of his physical proportions.
It is said that the group of six monks (chabbaggiyā bhikkhū) would repeatedly touch him here and there, saying, "Friend Bhaddiya!
Friend Bhaddiya! and play with him in various ways, pulling him back and forth.
Therefore it is said, “disregarded form. But why did he become such as this? It is said that in the past he was a certain great king;

his elderly men and elderly women became repulsive to him. If he saw an elderly man, he would have his topknot tied up and his loincloth fastened for him, and then make him play as he pleased. As for the elderly women, too—
Having seen them, he would cause whatever they desired to be ruined and made them play according to his own whims.
Great terror arose in the presence of their sons, daughters, and others. His evil deeds caused a single uproar from the earth up to the six celestial worlds.
Then Sakka thought: “This blind fool is harassing the great multitude; I shall effect his restraint.”
Thus, assuming the appearance of an elderly man, he placed a jar of buttermilk in a carriage and entered the city driving it.
The king, having mounted his elephant and come out from the city, saw him and said, “This old man is coming toward us in a buttermilk-cart;
stop him! Stop him! As the people rushed hither and thither, [they tried to restrain him].
They did not see him. For Sakka had resolved: "Let only the king see me; let no others.

Then, even as those men were crying out, "Where is the King? Where is the King?", the king, together with the elephant, entered beneath the vehicle like a calf entering under its mother cow. Sakka then broke the oil-vat.
From the head down, the king’s body became drenched with sweat. Having rubbed his body dry and bathed in a lotus pond in the pleasure garden, he entered the city with his body adorned.
Seeing him again, he said, "This is that same old man we saw before! Stop him! Stop him!
The people cried out, "Where is he, Your Majesty? Where is he, Your Majesty? and [they pursued him] from there...
They ran off quickly. He reached that very same initial state of transformation once again.
At that moment, Sakka caused the oxen and the carriage to vanish and, standing in the air, said:
"O blind fool, you perceive me with the thought, 'This is a sesame oil merchant,' yet I am Sakka, the King of the Devas. I have come to restrain this evil deed of yours; do not—”
Having rebuked him, saying, "Do not do such a thing again," he departed. Because of this deed, he became ugly.
However, during the time of the Sammasambuddha Vipassi, having been a bird called Cittapattakokila dwelling in the Khema Deer Park, one day he went to the Himalayas;
while returning with a sweet mango fruit held in his beak, he [encountered] the Saṅgha of monks...
Seeing the Teacher, he thought: "On other days I see the Tathāgata empty-handed;
but today I have this mango fruit, and I shall give it to the One of Ten Powers. Having descended, he moved through the air.
The Teacher, knowing his thought, looked toward his attendant. The attendant brought forth his bowl and, having paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, [presented it].
He placed it in the Teacher’s hand. The cuckoo set the mango fruit into the bowl of the One of Ten Powers.
The Teacher sat right there and consumed it. With a mind full of serene confidence, the cuckoo repeatedly reflected upon the virtues of the One of Ten Powers;
having paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, he went to his own nest and spent seven days in a state of joy and happiness. By this—
By his karma, his voice became sweet.
However, during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, when the construction of the cetiya was undertaken, they asked, "What size shall we make it?
"Seven yojanas in size. "This is too large; let us make it six yojanas in size. "This too is too large; let us make it five yojanas."
"Four yojanas, three yojanas, two yojanas. At that time, acting as the chief architect, he said, "Yes, sir;
it is right to prepare for future comfort," and taking a measuring line, he stood at a distance of one *gāvuta* while surveying the perimeter, saying, "Let each opening be one *gāvuta*;
the Cetiya shall be one yojana in circumference and one yojana in height."
He said: "They remained by his word. The cetiya was completed in seven years, seven months, and seven days.
Thus, he set a limit for the Buddha who is immeasurable. Because of that deed, he was born as an okoṭimaka.

"Elephants and *pasada* deer" means both elephants and *pasada* deer. "There is no equality in the body" means there is no such thing as a measurement in the body; the meaning is that bodily size is not a determining factor. This is the sixth [chapter].
7. Visākhasutta Commentary 241.
In the seventh [verse], "with speech that is refined" means with sweet speech similar to that of the city-dwellers, the people of the city, which is not deficient in syllables or words.
"Confident" means unambiguous, unhindered, and not impaired by bile or phlegm.
Meaning: "Anelagalāya" means not like slow-witted people who speak words while saliva is dripping from their mouths;
rather, it means with faultless, clear speech. "Pariyāpannāya" means included within the Four Noble Truths, proceeding without abandoning the four truths.
"Anissitāya" means not spoken by making it dependent upon the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"For the Dhamma is the banner of the seers": the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is called the banner of the seers. This is the seventh [sutta].
8. Commentary on the Nanda Sutta (242).
Regarding the eighth [sutta], "hammered and re-hammered" means by striking on one side with the hand or with a mallet.
“Struck” means having been struck after being turned over. “Having anointed” means having filled it with ointment.
“A clear bowl” means a clay bowl of a translucent color. But why did the Elder do this? It was for the purpose of discerning the Teacher’s intention. For he thought:
“If the Teacher says, ‘Truly, this younger brother of mine looks beautiful,’ [then I shall know his mind].”
“For as long as life lasts, I will conduct myself in this manner.
