If he points out a fault herein, I shall abandon this practice, take a rag from the refuse heap, make a robe from it, wear it, and live in a remote lodging.
“Assasī” means you will be.
"Alms known by others" (aññātuñcha) means: when one seeks pungent condiments and fragrant food in the houses of distinguished people of high status, that alms is called "alms known by others.
However, the mixed food obtained by standing at the door while going from house to house is called "alms unknown by others" (aññātuñcha);
this is what is intended here. "Without regard for sensual pleasures" (kāmesu anapekkhinam) refers to both material objects of desire (vatthukāma) and the defilements of desire (kilesakāma).
"Without expectation. The entire passage beginning with "a forest-dweller" is spoken by way of formal undertaking (*samādāna*).
As for the sutta "without expectation regarding sense-pleasures," this was spoken later on by [the Elder] after he had returned from being shown celestial nymphs in the world of the gods.
From the day this was spoken, the Elder, striving and exerting himself, established himself in Arahantship within just a few days in the world including the devas.
He has become one most worthy of offerings. This is the eighth [sutta].
9. Commentary on the Tissa Sutta (243).
Regarding the ninth [verse], "dejected" (*dummano*) means one who has arisen mental distress (*domanassa*). But why did he become so pained and dejected?

For he was one who had gone forth from the khattiya class; therefore, having caused him to go forth, they had him put on a double-layered lower garment, draped him in a fine robe, anointed his eyes, and smeared his head with red arsenic oil.
When the monks had gone to their night-quarters and day-quarters, not knowing that "a monk must sit in a secluded place," he went to the dining hall and [sat upon] a large seat.
Having climbed up, he sat down. Wandering monks who were guests and wearers of rag-robes arrived;
thinking, "In this state, with our bodies covered in dust, it is not possible to see the One of Ten Powers. We shall first put away our belongings," they went to the dining hall.
As those great elders were approaching, he remained sitting perfectly still. Other monks [said], "The practice of honoring the feet..."
“Let us fan you with a palm-leaf fan,” they said, asking him. But while still seated, he asked, “How many years have you been ordained?
When they replied, “We are novices; but how many years have you been ordained? he said, “I was ordained this very day.
Then the monks said to him, “Friend, you have only just had your head shaved; even now there is the smell of lice at the base of your hair.”
“You are indeed blowing hot air! While so many of your seniors are asking for the proper conduct (*vatta*), you sit there silent and motionless;
you have not even a modicum of respect. In whose teaching have you gone forth? Thus they surrounded him, striking him with the arrows of their words:
“Have you gone forth because you are burdened by debt, or because you are driven by fear, or because you are unable to make a living?”
They said: He looked at one elder; when that elder asked, "Why do you look at me, old man? he looked at another.
When that one also spoke in the same way, the thought arose in him, "These are surrounding me and piercing me with the arrows of their words," and pride as a kshatriya arose within him.
Tears the color of jewels welled up in his eyes. Then he said to them: "Whose..."
“You have come into my presence,” they said. They replied, “What, do you think we have come into your presence because we have lost our lay appearance?
We have come into the presence of the Teacher, the Supreme Person in the world with its devas.
He said, “You have come into the presence of my brother; if that is so, you may now go back by the very path by which you came.”
Having become angry with the thought, "I shall do it," he departed; while on the way, he reflected, "If I go in this very manner, the Teacher will not have these [beings] brought out.
Suffering and dejected, he went along shedding tears.
It was for this reason that he was born in such a state.
"By the goad of speech" means by the sting of words. "They made it a continuous din" (*sañjambharimakaṃsu*) means they made it a continuous, pervasive clamor;
what is meant is that they pierced him from above. "He speaks as he pleases to others" means he simply says whatever he wishes to others.
"And not patient with speech" means he is unable to endure the words of others. Now, first of all, you [should consider] this anger...
"He was pierced by the splashing water of these words spoken. "But in the past, had he been banished from the kingdom?
When this was said, the monks asked the Blessed One, "At what time, Blessed One?
The Teacher said: "In the past, in Bārāṇasī, King Bārāṇasī reigned. Now there were two men: one of noble birth and one a Mātaṅga."
Two seers went to Bārāṇasī. Of them, Jātimā arrived first and sat down in a potter’s workshop.
The ascetic Mātaṅga arrived later and asked for a place there.
The potter said, "There is a renunciant who entered here earlier; ask him. He took his own requisites and stood at the door of the workshop.
Having stood there, he said, "Teacher, please give us a place to stay for one night as well. "Enter, sir," [the teacher replied].
Having entered and sat down, [the teacher] asked, "Sir, what is your clan? "I am of the Caṇḍāla clan," he replied.
"It is not possible to sit in the same place with you; go to one side," [the teacher said]. He then spread out a layer of grass right there.
He lay down; the noble one lay down leaning against the door. As the other was going out to relieve himself, he stepped upon him on the chest.
When asked, "Who is this?", he replied, "I am your teacher. [The other said,] "Hey, you outcaste! Did you not see another path?
Why have you come and stepped upon me? [The first replied,] "Teacher, I stepped on you without seeing you; forgive me."
When the Great Being had gone outside, he thought, "Even when he returns, he will come from this very direction," and so he turned over and lay down.
The Great Being also thought, "The teacher has lain down with his head toward this side;
I shall go by way of his feet," and as he was entering, he stepped on him right on the chest again. When asked, "Who is this? he replied, "I am the teacher."
He said, "First you did this unknowingly; now you have done it while trying to entice me.
May your head split into seven pieces as the sun rises! The Great Being said nothing, but before dawn he seized the sun and did not allow it to rise.
Men, elephants, horses, and other creatures all woke up.
The people went to the royal palace and said, "Your Majesty, there is no one in the entire city who has not awakened, nor does the dawn appear;
what indeed is this? [The king replied,] "In that case, search the city.
While searching, they saw two ascetics in a potter's workshop and, thinking, "This must be their doing," they went and informed the king.
They reported this. When the king said, "Go and question them," they came and questioned Jātimanta:
"Was the darkness created by you? "It was not created by me; rather, it was that wretched, fraudulent ascetic of boundless deceit—question him.
They went and questioned the Great Man: "Venerable sir, was the darkness created by you? "Yes, it was he."
“The teacher cursed me; therefore, I did it. They went and reported this to the king.
The king also came and asked the Great Man, “Venerable sir, was this done by you? “Yes, Great King,” he replied. “Why, venerable sir? “I was cursed by him;
if he asks my forgiveness, I shall release the sun. The king said, “Ask his forgiveness.”
"Venerable sir, it is so," he said. The other replied, "How could one of noble birth like me ask forgiveness from such a low-caste outcaste?
I will not forgive him. Then the people said to him, "Will you not ask for forgiveness according to your own wish?
Having said this, they seized him by his hands and feet, made him prostrate at the other's feet, and said, "Ask for forgiveness! He lay there silently. Again—
They said to him, “Ask for forgiveness. Then he said, “Forgive me, Teacher. The Great Being replied, “I shall first grant you my forgiveness and release the sun;
however, when the sun has risen, your head will split into seven pieces.
Having said this, [he] placed a lump of clay the size of his head upon [the man’s] head and [submerged it] in the river up to the neck.
"Place it in the water," he said. The people did accordingly. At that moment, the king’s army from the entire kingdom assembled.
The Great Being released the sun. A ray of the sun came and struck the lump of clay; it split into seven pieces.
Immediately, the man submerged and escaped by way of a certain ford. Having brought forward this story, the Teacher said:
“Now, indeed, you receive reproach in the presence of the monks; formerly too, on account of this very anger, you were banished from the kingdom.
Having thus established the connection, he then spoke to him, giving advice, beginning with the words, “This was not fitting for you, Tissa. The ninth [sutta].
10. Commentary on the Sutta Named after the Elder (Theranāmaka).
244. "One who speaks in praise" means one who speaks of the benefits (*ānisamsa*). "That which is past is abandoned":
by abandoning desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) for the five aggregates (*khandha-pañcaka*) of the past, that is said to be abandoned. "The future":
the five aggregates of the future as well are relinquished through the relinquishing of desire and lust for them. "Overcoming all": all aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
And having overcome the three realms of existence (*bhava*), he stands firm. "The All-Knowing One" (*sabbavidū*) means he stands having made all that has been described thus known and manifest.
"In all phenomena" (*sabbesu dhammesu*) means among those very phenomena, he is unstained by the coatings of craving and views.
"The Abandoner of All" (*sabbañjaha*) means he stands having abandoned all that very [clinging] through the relinquishing of desire and lust for it. In the destruction of craving...
"Liberated" means liberated by the liberation that has Nibbāna—defined as the destruction of craving—as its object. The tenth [sutta].
11. Commentary on the Mahākappina Sutta: 245.
In the eleventh [sutta], "Mahākappina" refers to one who bears that name, who has attained the power of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), and who is among the eighty great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*).
He was a great elder (*mahāthero*). It is said that during his time as a householder, he ruled a kingdom of three hundred *yojanas* from the city of Kukkuṭavatī.
Because he was destined for his final existence (*pacchimabhaviko*), he wandered about with his ears pricked, intent on hearing such a teaching.

Then one day, surrounded by a thousand ministers, he went out for a pleasure excursion to the park. At that time, merchants traveling on foot from the Middle Country arrived at that city and [displayed] their wares.
Having settled their affairs, they went to the gate of the royal palace with gifts in their hands, intending to see the king.
Hearing that the king had gone to the pleasure garden, they went to the garden and stood at the gate, announcing themselves to the doorkeeper.
When it was reported to the king, he summoned them; and when they had presented their gifts and stood bowing, the king asked, "Sirs, from where have you come?"

He asked, "From where have you come, O gods? "From Sāvatthī, Your Majesty. "Is your kingdom well-supplied with food, and is the king righteous? "Yes, Your Majesty. "But is there any message for you from your country?
"There is, Your Majesty, but it cannot be spoken with mouths that are defiled by leftovers. The king had water poured from a golden pitcher; they rinsed their mouths.
Facing the One Possessing the Ten Powers, they raised their joined palms in reverence and said, "Your Majesty, in our land, the Jewel of the Buddha has appeared.
At the mere sound of the word "Buddha" from the king's mouth, a rapture arose that pervaded his entire body.
Then he asked, "Sons, do you say 'Buddha'? They replied, "We say 'Buddha,' Your Majesty. Having thus caused him to say it three times, [he continued:]

“The word ‘Buddha’ is immeasurable; it is not possible to set a limit to it. Having gained faith in this very [word], he gave one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and asked again, “What other teaching [is there]? “Your Majesty, that which is called the Jewel of the Dhamma has appeared.
Having heard that as well, he likewise made a formal promise three times and gave another hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. Again, “What other...”
"What is the news? he asked. "The Jewel of the Saṅgha has appeared, O King," they replied.
Having heard that as well, he likewise made a formal promise three times, gave another hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and having written a letter confirming the gift, he sent it with the message:
"Sirs, go into the presence of the Queen. When they had departed, he asked his ministers: "Sirs, a Buddha has appeared in the world..."
“What will you do? “Your Majesty, what do you intend to do? “I shall go forth. “We too shall go forth.
Without taking leave of their homes or families, they all departed by means of the very same horses upon which they had ridden when they first went.
The merchants went to Queen Anojā and presented the letter. She read it and said, “The King has sent many [gifts] for you...”
“Kahāpaṇas have been given; what have you done, my dear sons? he asked. “A pleasant message has been brought for the Queen, Father.
“We too can be made to hear it, my dear sons,” she said. “It is possible, Queen, but it is not possible to speak with mouths that are soiled by food,” they replied.
She had water provided from a golden pitcher. They rinsed their mouths and reported [the news] to the King exactly as they had been instructed.
She too, hearing this, was filled with joy; following that same method, she made her promise three times for each verse.
Calculating by the number of promises, she gave nine hundred thousand. Thus, the merchants received a total of twelve hundred thousand.
Then he asked them, "Where is the king, dear friends? "The queen has departed, saying, 'I shall go forth into homelessness,'" they replied.

“Very well then, dear ones, you may go,” he said, and having dismissed them, he summoned the wives of those ministers who had gone with the king and asked, “Ladies, do you know where your husbands have gone? “We know, noble lady;
they went for a pleasure excursion in the park together with the king. “Yes, they went; but having gone there, [they heard] ‘The Buddha…’”
Having heard, "The Dhamma has arisen; the Saṅgha has arisen," they went [to him], thinking, "We shall go forth in the presence of the One Possessing Ten Powers.
[He asked: "What will you do? [They replied: "But what do you intend to do, Noble Lady? [She said: "I shall go forth;
I will not place on the tip of my tongue that which has been vomited by them. [They said: "If that is so, we too shall go forth. And so all of them [did].
Having had them yoked to the chariot, they set out.
The king also reached the bank of the Gaṅgā together with a thousand ministers. At that time, the Gaṅgā was full.
Then, seeing it, [he thought], "This Gaṅgā is full and teeming with fierce fish; the slaves or men who came with us..."
"Or there are none who would make a boat or a raft for us; however, the virtues of this Teacher extend from below the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence.
If this Teacher is indeed a Perfectly Enlightened One, may the hooves of these horses not sink into the water!
Thus they made the horses leap across the surface of the water. Not even a single horse...
They were not even moistened by the mere dust raised by their hooves; as if traveling along a royal highway, they reached the opposite shore and encountered another great river ahead.
There was no other act of truth (*saccakiriya*) there;
by that very same act of truth, they crossed over that river which was half a *yojana* in width. Then, having reached the third great river named Candabhāgā—
They too passed over [the danger] by means of that very same act of truth (*saccakiriya*).
On that same day, at the time of dawn, the Teacher, having emerged from the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) and surveying the world, saw:
"Today Mahākappina, having renounced a kingdom three hundred *yojanas* in extent, accompanied by a retinue of a thousand ministers, will go forth into homelessness in my presence."
Having seen that they were approaching, [the Blessed One thought], "It is fitting for me to go out to meet them.
Early in the morning, after attending to his bodily needs, he entered Sāvatthī for alms accompanied by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
After his meal, having returned from the alms round, he took his own bowl and robe, rose into the air, and went to the river Candabhāgā at the very ford where they were crossing.
In the place directly opposite stood a great banyan tree; sitting there cross-legged and establishing mindfulness directed toward the front, he emitted six-colored rays of a Buddha.
As they crossed by that ford, they gazed upon the six-colored rays of the Buddha streaming hither and thither, beholding the splendor of the Ten-Powered One, who was like the full moon.
Upon seeing his face, they reached the conclusion by the mere sight of him, thinking, "This is surely the Teacher for whose sake we went forth.
Starting from the place where they had seen him, they approached bowing low and paid homage to the Teacher.
The king took hold of the Teacher’s ankles, and having paid homage, sat down to one side together with his thousand ministers.
The Teacher preached the Dhamma to them. At the conclusion of the teaching, they all became established in Arahatship and requested ordination from the Teacher.

The Teacher, thinking, "Because these men previously gave gifts of robes, they have come here taking their own robes with them," extended his golden-colored hand and said, "Come, monks; the Dhamma is well-expounded. Live the holy life."
“The holy life is for the complete ending of suffering,” he said. That itself became their going-forth and full ordination;
like elder monks of sixty years’ standing, they surrounded the Teacher.
Queen Anojā also, accompanied by a retinue of a thousand chariots, reached the bank of the Ganges and boarded the boat brought for the King’s sake.
Not seeing the raft, he reflected through his own discernment: "The King must have gone after performing an act of truth;
moreover, that Teacher was not born solely for their sake. If that Teacher is a Perfectly Enlightened One, may our chariots not sink into the water!
He then caused the chariots to drive onto the surface of the water. Not even as much as the circumference of the chariot wheels...
They were not afraid. As they were being ferried across by that same truth-utterance during the second and third crossings, they saw the Teacher at the foot of the banyan tree.

The Teacher thought, "If these women were to see their own husbands, lustful desire might arise and create an obstacle to the paths and fruits; he will not be able to do so. Thus, so that they would not see one another...
They did not see him; thus she acted. All of them, having stepped out from the bathing place and paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, sat down.
The Teacher preached the Dhamma to them, and at the conclusion of the teaching, they all became established in the fruit of stream-entry and saw one another.
The Teacher thought, "Let Uppalavaṇṇā come. The Elder Nun came and [saw] all of them.
Having ordained her, he took her and went to the dwelling place of the bhikkhunīs. The Teacher, taking a thousand bhikkhus, went through the air to Jetavana.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "Mahākappina—so named, having attained the power of direct knowledge (abhiññā), a great elder among the eighty great disciples."
"In this generation" means "among people. "Those who follow their lineage" means those who refer to and claim the lineage, saying, "We are Vāseṭṭhas, we are Gotamas";
for them, the Kṣatriya is the best—this is the meaning.

"Endowed with true knowledge and conduct" means possessed of the eight branches of true knowledge (*vijjā*) and of conduct (*caraṇa*) consisting of fifteen factors. "He shines" means he radiates light.
"A meditating brahmin shines": the brahmin whose taints are exhausted shines and radiates while meditating with the two kinds of jhāna.
At that moment, the Elder Kāludāyī was sitting not far away, meditating with the two kinds of jhāna.
"The Buddha shines": the Omniscient Buddha radiates. This, it is said, is a verse of universal auspiciousness. It was [spoken] by King Bhātikarāja.
Having performed a single act of worship, he said to his teacher, "Recite a verse of victory and auspiciousness that is not surpassed by the Three Jewels.
Having reflected upon the entire word of the Buddha contained in the Tipiṭaka, the teacher spoke this verse;
having said, "The sun shines by day," he extended his joined palms toward the setting sun. Then, [he said], "The moon shines by night," as the sun was rising.
He extended his joined palms in homage to the moon. He extended his joined palms in homage to the king, saying, "The armored Kshatriya shines.

He extended his joined palms in homage to the Saṅgha of monks, saying, "The meditating Brahmin shines. But having said, "The Buddha shines with majesty," he extended his joined palms in homage to the Great Cetiya.
Then the king, saying, "Do not let your hand descend," [caught it] while it was still raised.
He placed a thousand [coins] in his hand. The eleventh.
12. Commentary on the Sahāyaka Sutta: 246.
Regarding the phrase "those who have long been associated," it means those who have remained together for a long time, having lived in harmony and shared common views.
It is said that those five hundred were wandering together as one.

"Their True Dhamma is the same" means that now this Dhamma of the Dispensation of these [monks] accords and coincides. Regarding "the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha," the meaning is that their Dhamma of the Dispensation shines forth within the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha.
"Well-trained by Kappina" means by his own preceptor, who was one proclaimed by the Noble Ones.
They are well-trained in the Dhamma. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus ends the twelfth [chapter]. The commentary on the *Bhikkhu-saṃyutta* is finished.
Thus concludes the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta-nikāya*.
The commentary on the Nidāna-vagga is finished.
